title: I have been very pleased with this keyboard
text:
I have been very pleased with this keyboard. Not only is the keyboard washable, but the keyboard tends to stay clean on its own. Unlike most keyboards, where things can easily fall between the keys and get stuck inside of the keyboard, these keys are wide at the top, covering a narrow base and preventing junk from getting inside the keyboard. This means that not only is the keyboard washable, but because of a high-quality design you won't have to do that much washing.

I like that the keyboard is low-profile, it's easy to slide under things and doesn't take up much space.

Overall the performance of the keyboard is about what you would expect. It has fairly good typing quality, but if you're like me and like tactile feedback for your typing, you're going to think that the keyboard is a bit mushy. The lightness of the keyboard also means that it might have a tendency to shift underneath your fingers if you're a strong typer like me.

text:

Battery life is pretty amazing. I've had the mouse for about a year and a half and have only replaced the battery once. And it still looks brand new, so quite durable.

This mouse connects to the PC through Logitech's "unifying receiver." All my Logitech wireless stuff works through the one receiver so no matter how many you have, you'll only give up one USB port.

I should note that I much prefer a trackball mouse to a traditional one. This mouse, of course, would take some getting used to if you've never used one before, but it's absolutely worth the effort. After I got used to the trackball, I absolutely do not like a traditional mouse.

title: Terrific Keyboard, With one Small Quibble.
text:
I acquired this unit to use with my Raspberry Pi 3 computer. I've had the unit less than a day but I've been pleased so far. I was initially confused that the bluetooth on the R-Pi failed to recognize that the keyboard even existed. For some reason, there is no direct driver for this available - Logitech's work-around for this is a small USB dongle (Logitech Unifying Receiver) that acts as a receiver. I expected to have to order one but checking the box a second time, found that they had actually included one with the kb - whew, evening saved. Once the dongle was plugged in the computer recognized it and responded immediately. While this does enable me to go cordless, which is nice, it does come at the cost of occupying one of the precious USB sockets on the R-Pi. I am hopeful that developers will resolve this issue with a proper driver.

Ergonomically I found the trackpad to take a wee bit of getting used to. My thumb keeps expecting the mouse keys to be at the edge of the keyboard, in stead, they are about an inch higher. I don't think this is a problem with the design or keyboard, just a question of what one is used to. I'm sure that with a bit of use the position will become a matter of habit.

I love that this unit is rechargeable! It's a great shape and size for my needs and my large-ish hands do not have trouble finding the keys, even though I'm accustomed to a somewhat larger layout.

While I got this KB for my R-Pi, I can see us using this with our home entertainment system as well, the hunt and grope using the tv remote is tedious in the extreme. My only concern is if there will be any cross-talk between the one in the study using the Pi, and the one in the living room connecting to the Samsung TV & BDP.

If it were possible to give this 4.5 stars I would probably dock that half point because of the bluetooth issue, but other than that, I'm very happy to have this cordless keyboard.

I bought this trackball after suffering nerve damage to the fingers of my right hand. My main complaint is that the unit is constantly sliding away while in use. The slick heel-rest (where the Logitech logo is stenciled) translates the downward pressure of my hand into a forward thrust that overcomes the friction of the rubber feet. Also, the trackball is easily jostled when taking fingers away, negating one of the benefits of the other trackballs I've used in the past. (This may be a result of my condition, and not an inherent defect of this design or unit.)

Although though this trackball has no scroll wheel, SetPoint allows you to assign "Middle Mouse Button" to the auxiliary (smaller) left button. When pressed, it activates a 2-D scroll function, similar to what a scroll wheel would do. On the whole, this trackball is competent, but it does not work so well for my particular situation.

text:
This is probably my 5th logitech remote over the years. They've come a long way, and this one is sooo close to being almost perfect. Keeping it brief, here's my likes/hates;

LIKE
- Lightweight, fits in your hand nicely
- The software to setup the remote works on your cell or tablet. Nice! Used to be you had to take the remotes to your computer, plug in via usb, visit a site or app, make changes, update the remote, then return to living room. Those days are gone and you can do all setup from your living room.
- Software is pretty good, was fairly straightforward to configure my tv, tivo, home theater receiver, and amazon fire tv. Plenty of features and settings.
- Battery life should be good since there's no screen.

DISLIKES
- The buttons, especially # buttons, are a little small. Why not a little bigger? Really, they seemed sized right, for a child(!).
- The buttons can be hard to discern from touch. Maybe because their low profile, and small?
- The RF aspect means if there's direct sunlight the remote doesn't always work. Oh well, at least all other times you *don't* have to point the remote at the tv/stereo all the time.

title: Very good remote, controls all my devices - Samsung TV
text:
Very good remote, controls all my devices - Samsung TV, Benq projector, Marantz AV amp, Sky HD, and PS3 (with an infra-red dongle - if you don't have one of these, this model can't control it, and same for PS4, apparently as it requires Bluetooth), even a couple of obscure old gadgets are still supported. Even if the device is not in the database, you can still learn commands from the original remote as a last resort.

I like the harmony remotes because of the Activity concept. One button can, for example, turn on the TV, receiver and Blu-Ray player and set all the inputs to the correct setting ready to watch, while turning off unused devices. The more gadgets you have, the more benefit you get from a device like this.

This was an upgrade/replacement for an old model Harmony 525, and while I like this well enough, it is more complicated in use than the old model.

General build quality is very good, much better than the older model, it feels sold and weighty in the hand. The rounded back makes it easy and comfortable to hold, but it wobbles around on the coffe table. The remote slides easily into the charging dock, and as the 525 used to chew through batteries, this is much better. However, the battery in the remote is not easily replaceable, so I hope it has reasonable longevity.

The feel of the backlit hard buttons is very good, with a nice positive click, much better than the old "dead flesh" rubber buttons on the 525.

The D-pad and navigation buttons are well placed and easy to use, but the main play/pause/FF/RW controls are a bit awkwardly placed, but still useable.

The touch screen display provide customisable soft buttons and obviously conveys much more information than the tiny monochrome LCD on the old model, but as it is a capacitive type, like a smartphone, it is very sensitive and easy to hit the wrong soft-key. The remote beeps and vibrates when a touch screen button is used, but it's not as positive as a real button and you have to look at the remote - you can't navigate by feel.

Fortunately the touch screen is used mostly for secondary functions, and the hard keys cover the typical primary controls. Number keys are only touch-screen buttons and therefore more difficult to use than real buttons, but favourite Sky channels can be shown as a colourful page of icons, which is easier than remembering the channel number. However, to be honest, if you are like me you use the Sky Guide page anyway, which only needs the direction pad to navigate. To be fair after a few weeks, I really have put away all the original remotes as I don't need them, so this device does the job.

The programming software is pretty easy to use, a bit quirky in some ways, but since I was used to the old version, I found it easy enough, and the new version is an improvement. Also, unlike the old 525 model, a certain amount of customisation can be done directly on the remote without using a PC at all. You can do a basic set up in a few minutes, but you will probably need a couple of hours to set it up perfectly of you have several devices to control.

text: These are a great value for a robust-sounding set of speakers that is perfect for gaming and some types of music. The bass response is really good with a lot of body; it's not just a thumpthumpthump. The mid-range and treble are well balanced with the bass, though it is slanted toward heavy bass music, video game sounds (explosions are one example) and TV and movies. If you are listening to music with more melodic nuance, classical instruments, spare indie singer-songwriter with ukelele, etc. they may not provide what you are looking for. For the price, they are impressive. The fit and finish is very good, with nice tactile details and the cords seem nice quality for the price. There are lots of input options. The headphone jack, while not visible from the front, is very easily accessible; that is a nicely thought out touch. All in all, if you are looking for rich bass response and will use these for gaming, watching movies or TV or listening to certain kinds of music, these will really shine. title: Excellent for the price. Thankfully more compact than my older Z2300.  No remote.  See edit.
text:
Latest edit after some frustrating months of use.

I ordered this as a TV speaker. That was in the description.
With no remote, and no way to raise or lower the sound without getting up, the item is useless to me. I like to watch TV in bed.
Who wants to keep getting up. As a computer speaker, it takes up a lot of space.very dissapointed.
I will donate it a church, where they will appreciate a loud speaker for youth groups.

Edit after 5 days use.

There is no remote. The volume is controlled by a dial. When using this connected to your TV, it's a major disadvantage getting up every time you need to change the volume. I have to downgrade from 5 stars to 4, because of this. They need to add to either a remote, or an app letting your phone control the volume. Not a problem when using this as a computer speaker, since the control is by your hand, not across the room. This is promoted as a TV speaker, not just a computer speaker, so it's a major fault.

Original review below.

I have been using the Logitech Z2300 that I purchased years ago. Connected to my computer and much appreciated when I listen to my apple subscription music. A real monster for a computer speaker. Thankfully, the Z 625 is decidedly smaller and fits on the bottom shelf of my 42 inch wood TV table with room to spare. There is also room left for my Amazon Echo and Braven wireless bluetooth speakers. The smaller size results in a much cleaner, more attractive package.

The dialog is much clearer than I expected. I have a ZVOX 450 on my main TV, so I do appreciate clear dialog.
I was disappointed that there is no bluetooth. The computer and Man Cave TV are on opposite sides of the same room, and having the Z2300 for music, and the Z625 for the TV is a bit too much. However, the problem was easily solved. On the Z625, I'm using the optical cable for the TV sound, and am using the enclosed jack to connect the speaker to my extra Iphone. As I type, I'm listening to Herman's Hermits through my Iphone to Z625 jack connection. The music is very soothing and suits my needs perfectly. No adjustments are needed when switching from the music through my smartphone via jack, or the TV sound through the optical cable. Automatic switching,

My TV test via optical was the opening of Game of Thrones. The subwoofer bass sounded great and added greatly to the enjoyment of watching the series. The galloping horses sounded thunderous.

Other considerations. I gave away my monstrous Polk system when we moved to our condo. Soundbars provide the cleanest look but really don't have any bass. My wife is picky. The soundbar is on the main TV for a cleaner appearance, while the Man Cave is a perfect home for this unit.

There was absolutely no documentation/instructions in the box, other than safety information. However hookup instructions were printed on the cardboard box. Don't destroy them opening it. Hooking up via optical was very intuitive and took minutes. I'd still like some instructions. For example, the power button is a push button. Does it shut off after inactivity? I'm doing it manually. Going by the Z2300, it probably won't make any difference. These are built to last.

title: A nice surprise
text:
Surprisingly robust sound in a desktop package. Please refer to photos.

I'm a long-time Logitech fan, so my expectations were fairly high. The speakers were nicely packaged and easy to set up. Wordless instructions for neophytes were printed on the flaps of the box, impossible to miss as you opened it.

The bass unit is surprisingly thin given its sound. Small footprint. The left and right speakers are heavier than they look. The control puck has a Bluetooth connection button you press for three seconds to scout around for a Bluetooth source. It's also got an on/off switch and the entire face of it is a volume control. There's a bass control on the back of the bass which I left at about halfway.

The Bluetooth connection is functional, but pales in comparison to the wired connection. The novelty isn't really worth it. My understanding is that Bluetooth was not intended to carry sound. For whatever reason, the wired connection is much better.

Plenty of wire to separate channels. The sound is very good for a desktop setup, and by that I mean when I listened to songs I am familiar with, each instrument was nuanced and shaded, for lack of a better word, distinct and separate. I've never heard better sound from a system this size, really impressive. Nothing muddy or blurry about it.

Bluetooth aside, this sounds so much better than previous desktop speaker solutions I've tried it's hard to compare them. This has genuinely good sound. It's not going to fill a room, but it's an outstanding personal sound solution. I'm not a fan of headphones or earbuds, so this is ideal.

This would make an excellent gift.

title: similar to the Logitech Harmony Elite except without the Harmony Hub
text:
Logitech makes the best universal remote controls and they keep introducing new models that are better and better. If you have half a dozen (or more) remote controls on your living room table and are always losing some of them or forgetting which does what, then a universal remote is for you.

The Harmony 950 appears to be mostly the same as the Harmony Elite, except without the Harmony Hub device. The Harmony Hub can be purchased separately later, though the Elite package is cheaper if you're getting it anyway. The Harmony Hub greatly expands the range and capabilities of your Harmony remote, so you should think twice before skipping it.

Logitech also sells much cheaper Harmony remotes without the touch screen. The main benefit of the touch screen is to program shortcuts to your favorite TV channels and to control more devices than the non-touch remote controls can access. If you always use your DVR or cable box's on-screen channel menu and only have a few devices, then maybe a much cheaper Harmony without the touch screen is a better value for you.

The Harmony is pretty easy to program by connecting to your PC and connecting to the Logitech website. If you have an older Harmony remote, you may be able to transfer all your device settings to this one. The buttons on the Harmony are easy to see, well spaced and give you good feedback when pressed.

Battery life is OK for a touchscreen device, but like your smartphone you will need to recharge this at least every couple of days. Most people will leave the Harmony in the recharging station most of the time, so make sure you have an electrical outlet close to where you will be using the Harmony.

If you're in the market for a universal remote, Logitech Harmony should be first on your list. The only decision you have to make is which model to buy. If you're trying to control a handful of devices (TV, cable box, DVR, stereo system, game system, DVD player), then you really have to ask yourself if the touchscreen feature is worth the big price premium. If you have a "smart home" with remote controlled lights, outlets, thermostat, etc or if your devices are spread around a large room so the IR remote has trouble connecting with them, then the Harmony Hub is a good idea.

title: a good camera, worth the money.
text:
this camera's picture quality (see first photo) is definitely superior to that of the iSight camera built into my mid-2011 MacBook Air (see second photo), as well as to that of most, if not all, other webcams i've seen images from - though the Logitech's colors are a bit washed out due to its light sensitivity.

the mounting system is pretty ingenious - or so it seems to me, who's been out of the standalone webcam loop for probably 10 years now - allowing you to mount it on top of a flatscreen monitor of just about any thickness, lay it on a flat surface such as the top of a CRT (if anybody still uses those) or an LCD's sunshade - the camera has a rubberized bottom surface and a little bit of weight to it so it won't slide around easily - or to mount it on a mini tripod (not included).

it has dual (i.e., stereo) mics which sound decent, though you won't get great sound from them unless you're in a very acoustically dead room, since their integration with the body of the camera means you're going to be at least a foot away from them most of the time, so they're going to pick up any reverberation present and many background noises. i choose to stick with my Blue Yeti for sound input as i can put it closer to where i'm sitting...plus it's just a better-sounding mic to begin with, as well it should be.

the camera can be pivoted up and down about 45 degrees, and while it can't be pivoted side-to-side when mounted atop a flatscreen monitor, that's mitigated somewhat by the fact that it's a widescreen camera, so it captures a wider area side-to-side without being pivoted. if lateral pivoting is really important to you, you can mount the camera either on a flat surface or a mini tripod as mentioned before.

on the Mac, it's 100% plug-and-play; plug it into an available USB port and you're in business. FaceTime, Photo Booth, Messages, Skype...it just works, and well. Windows users just go to the URL given on the instruction sheet, download and install the software, and i imagine from there on out their experience will be similar.

the unit itself is very nice-looking and, again, produces a picture most other webcams can't match. i think Logitech's set a new standard here, and it won't be long before all new webcams on the market produce an image at least this good. at the $71.00 and change i paid, i consider this camera well worth the money. i'm sure i'll be using it for years to come.

title: Expensive, if it works
text:
I am comparing this to a Logitech C910 HD 1080p webcam which I've been using almost daily since 2012.

I don't stream games but I stream my live DJ broadcasts. I use 4 webcams and a green screen. I use xSplit exclusively.

This C922x Pro Stream is for gamers so they can stream on Twitch or YouTube. The camera is supposed to automatically load a background removing program so you don't have to use a green screen. This special software, Personify ChromaCam, is free when have the C922. Installing is another matter entirely. Myself, like others, have older, but capable systems that cannot install this software. I checked on Personify's website and the PC requirements are: Processor: Intel 4th generation or higher Core CPU, or the AMD equivalent (Quad core AMD Phenom), OS: Windows 7, 8, 10, and Memory: 4GB+ RAM. My system, even though its 3 years old, meets all these specs but when installing I get a 'unable to install due to ABX or ADX" something.

The camera's clarity is not any better than my 4 year old C910. In fact, my C910 has Carl Zeiss, the new cam doesn't not. The colors appear washed out with too much brightness. I expected better, but the C922 regressed a bit in the lens department.

Now here's a kicker for you...you cannot, and I mean, cannot, view the camera while changing it's settings. Yes, you heard me right. Open the camera settings and you get a windowed box for changing the settings, but the webcam does not come on or is it viewable. So, am I supposed to change the settings, open the cam, close the cam, change the settings, open the cam...etc..etc?

The mount is sturdy and multi-positional. I like the added tripod adapter. At this price point there should be a privacy shield.

I had an issue getting the camera to initially turn on. The outer ring would flash but no camera picture. Then I realized that some webcams don't like being plugged into a USB hub. After adding an extension cord and plugging in directly to my PC the cam worked.

The big question...is this camera worth the $50 more than the entry level C920 series camera? For the money you get a ChromaCam program which may or may not work and you get 6 months free xSplit service. Hmmmmm...OBS, which is quite capable, is a free service.

Logitech has so many choices lately, each with increased pricing. Let's face it, it's all about the price. Do you really need your ugly mug put up in a live game? Probably not since it's going to use PC resources that would be better used for gaming. For the $50 extra you could get a couple decent games, or a new mouse, or a mouse pad, or a boat load of peanuts.

The choice is yours.

title: I really wanted to love this mouse
text:
This is a hard review for me to write.

I really wanted to love this mouse. The Industrial Design is stunning, its geometric grip surfaces are both functional, and add greatly to the aesthetics. The thumb scroll wheel is amazing for photo editing, and the forefinger scroll wheel is perfectly weighted, and when freewheeling, its a dream. The whole mouse feels substantial, and strong in hand, all the while remaining relatively light weight. You get none of the creaks or flex that permeate the cheap mouse market.

I wanted to love this mouse. I owned the revolution before it, and I thought it would be the answer to all of the revolution's downfalls.

I find this mouse to be very uncomfortable in my hand, even more so than the MX Revolution.
The software is a substantial downgrade to almost every mouse software out there.
The side buttons, while suitable for photo editing, simply are not designed with gaming in mind. I have to pull my entire thumb off of the mouse in order to differentiate the two buttons.

Keep in mind, this review, like all others is incredibly subjective. I have no doubt that this is a high quality mouse, it simply does not work for me.

With much regret, I will be returning this mouse.

The button that changes the speed of the mouse scroll is very high and right in the way of your finger when you reach for the scroll wheel, and the first of the two side-buttons is placed too far forward, and angled too sharply upward, for the awkward angle that the weird shape puts your thumb into.

For the price, this should be a pretty sweet mouse, and it's not. It's kind of clunky and awkward and doesn't feel good to use. I'm going to try to hang with it for a week and if it still feels this bad, I'm going to return it. If my opinion changes after some use, I'll change my review. I think maybe Logitech should find a design that works and just use it, not try to make every single mouse look different from every other mouse. All human hands are basically the same in terms of function - and yet for some reason Logitech seems to think they can use an infinite number of grip-designs and still have an equally comfortable end-result.

title: Incredible device, especially for the price.
text:
So far we have been very pleased with the Logitech Group. It's a huge step up from the way we were doing conference calls before, which is a pretty much weekly occurrence. The audio quality is great, especially with the remote mics for our bigger groups. Video quality is good too. Pretty standard for a higher-end webcam. The zoom is pretty impressive. Set up was super simple and it works well with RingCentral meetings (which is essentially Zoom meetings underneath).

The build quality is great. I was very pleasantly surprised with how sturdy everything feels. The remote mics are nice and heavy. I was expecting light plasticy things that I was going to have to tape down, but they are very well built and hold themselves down.

My one wish is that the cables were a little longer, but I know we're an odd case with a bigger conference room. Likewise, the lens could be just a touch wider, but I really can't complain.

Overall, we're very happy with it, especially for the price. You can't go wrong with this as long as it fits your use case!

title: Good and cheap, but cord is flimsy
text:
The good:

They're exactly what you paid for. Cheap and small speakers that do the job. I don't really need to tell you that these won't deliver any kind of multi-dimensional soundscape for music buffs or anything like that. But they're exactly the ticket if you just want to listen to your daily podcast, or if you're not picky about sound and you just need something cheap that works.

The bad:

The cord. These speakers were made with laptops in mind, not desktops. Your desktop HAS to be on the right side of your monitor, not the left, in order for the cord to reach. Even then... it's plenty long for laptops, but just barely workable for a desktop set-up. My speakers sit way further behind the monitor than I would like, just because that's as far as the cord will reach.

The extra bad:

The cord turns out to be pretty flimsy, and if I nudge it even a little the speakers will emit a horrific buzz/screech that makes me jump out of my pants. I have to wiggle the cord around until it finds juuust the right position for the sound to stop. It's fine 90% of the time, but it's annoying to have to do this every time I accidentally nudge it when plugging in a USB drive or something.

TL;DR
-good and cheap
-cord good for laptops, too short for desktops
-cord flimsy and may cause sound problems

title: I like the keyboard well enough
text:
I like the keyboard well enough. It is not silent, as others have mentioned, but I don't notice the clacking unless the room is silent.

I've dropped one star for the way the spacebar interacts with my onscreen keyboard (SwiftKey). The spacebar selects the suggested word regardless of whether it is the correct/intended word or not. I have always used SwiftKey with that feature turned off (SwiftKey does not always guess the word correctly, so the feature is a nuisance), and the onscreen keyboard's spacebar behaves as expected. However the Logitech keyboard ignores the setting and instead selects the suggested word. This means the user has to find a way to trick it into using the intended word (intentionally typo, then correct it manually). I honestly do not know if the fault is with SwiftKey or the Logitech keyboard.

Otherwise, I really like having the option to use a real keyboard with my phone and tablet.

Ken

title: This is the worst Harmony I've ever used
text:
This is the worst Harmony I've ever used. It's an ergonomic disaster with little that is done right. It is however still a Harmony, so it somehow salvages 3 stars for what they all do right.

It seemed nice in the box, and it was a breeze transferring everything from my Harmony 700 to this via the My Harmony program. The weight and balance are good and the charging cradle works well. Everything else ranges from bad to worse.

Maybe one day the screen/pad will do what I need it to do, but for now it's rubbish and it's in the location where the most used buttons should be. As a result those buttons are below (4 way controller, volume, channel, etc... or above (play, pause, etc...). Ugh! Worse yet the screen/pad isn't just dead space (honestly it would be better if it were), rather it's live. That can be ok when it's acting like a touch pad with various taps and swipes to do things (it never works that well, but I see what they're trying to do), but it's a disaster when it's live with functions that are so seldom used there's no dedicated button. So channel favorites, random superfluous functions, etc get accidentally pressed. Even then they hardly work in the case of the favorites with my Motorola cable box running Uverse (95% of the time 2 or 3 of the 4 digits are recognized). When you avoid that pad the other buttons are cramped and arranged poorly even within their poor locations. The 4 way pad is small, as are the play and pause buttons and the skip and fast forward buttons are shared. Of all the sacrifices made for the screen/pad, those red, green, yellow, and blue buttons you never use are still there--UGH!!!!!

Move the screen up, move the key buttons where the fingers land, kill the color keyed buttons that don't ever do s***, and try again. Oh and the battery life sucks too. Please make a new flagship controller ala the Harmony One (original) 880, etc... Hell the 700s I have are better than this!

The Harmony software and ecosystem is still strong, and as noted before, there's a lot this gets right, but so does every other Harmony and they lack this ergonomic disaster.

title: heavy mouse not great hadn position but it does have a charging station
text:
Mouse comparison.
3 relatively new mice are compared to 3 older mice:
New
Mofii G52
Foxcesd gaming mouse C20
Qisan E100
Older
Evoluent Vertical Mouse VM4RW
Logitech MX1000 Laser Cordless
Microsoft Natural Wireless laser mouse 6000

My dream mouse would have a nice shape that allows the hand to relax (like the Microsoft6000), move easily across the mouse pad with gentle pushing (like the Qisan), be whisper quiet during clicking (like the Mofii) and have an easy to reach button that can be set to be a double click (like the index button on the Foxcesd). Also it would have a charging system (like the Logitech) instead of batteries – but this probably not compatible with the idea of it being light enough to float with gentle pushing. I have not found a single mouse that has even most of these qualities.

Microsoft – 4 stars (probably ~ $50 when I bought years ago – today a new one is $450)
The closest and my preferred mouse of this bunch is the Microsoft. The shape of the mouse is perfect for those that will have your hand on it more than 8 hours a day – like me. It has plenty of buttons – I tend to not use all the extra buttons – the two near the thumb are pretty far away on this mouse and therefore not convenient. The scroll wheel has down and side clicks (so settable to double click). The clicking is not the loudest (which is the Qisan), but it is the 2nd loudest. I have owned this mouse for many years – I’d guess about at least five years. The reason I stopped using it is that the scroll wheel button has started to disintegrate – sticky and unpleasant to touch. The thumb pad is also sticky and no longer pleasant to touch. I’ve tried various ways to clean it – nothing seems to help. This sent me on my search for a new affordable mouse similar in shape to the Microsoft.

Logitech – 2 stars (probably about $40 when I bought it years ago)
This particular Logitech mouse is probably as old as the Microsoft one. When I bought it, I liked the idea that I didn’t have to run through batteries – and could sit it on the charging station each night. The hand position is ok, but not nearly as good as the Microsoft or Qisan. It has 7 buttons. They are all conveniently located. I don’t like the shape of the mouse and compared to newer ones, it feels heavy to push around. Somewhat quiet clicks – but not nearly as quiet as the Mofii.

Evoluent - not for me but could be 5 stars for someone else (costs > $100 today)
I’ve owned this also for several years, but not as long as the Logitech nor Microsoft. The idea of the vertical mouse is supposed to be a better position for your hand. I could never get used to it. I found that when I wanted to relax my hand and was not actively clicking or pushing the mouse around it would not be comfortable to have my hand just sitting vertically positioned (weight of hand is on pinky and part of hand extending from pinky). Your hand essentially falls off the mouse if you are not actively holding it there. I just didn’t like this. It has 2 thumb buttons and a scroll wheel button and another button for setting scroll wheel speed. All buttons are easy to reach. Clicking is relatively quiet. This like all of these mice other than the Logitech uses batteries – not charging station.

Qisan – 3.5 stars ($19.98)
I bought this recently because I didn’t want to pay $450 for a new Microsoft mouse and this Qisan is the closest in shape to the Microsoft. I like the shape of the mouse - it is comfortable (Microsoft still better, but this was only $19.98). The movement of this mouse is particularly nice. It feels like it floats across the mousepad – probably because it is the lightest of all the mice. It has 2 thumb buttons, a scroll wheel button and a button behind the scroll wheel (plus of course normal left and right click). The forward thumb button is definitely too far for my thumb, but this doesn’t bother me, as I don’t typically use thumb buttons anyway. This WOULD be my new mouse if it weren’t for the loudest mouse click I’ve ever heard. When you work around other people in a (at least sometimes) quiet environment, this is really annoying. There is a youtube video showing how to make a mouse quieter – I plan to do this for the Qisan – then it may be my new permanent mouse.

Foxcesd – 2 stars (19.99)
I bought this recently (after the Qisan) because the reviews said it was quiet. It is quieter than the Qisan – but it doesn’t come close to the nearly silent Mofii. On the Foxcesd, hand position is not bad for a ‘flat’ mouse rather than the rotated hand positions (which are better) of the Microsoft and Qisan. It is cool looking with a skull on the back of the mouse and green symbols and writing – if you are into that – I don’t particularly care about that aspect. The buttons are the most conveniently located of all the mice. In addition to standard left, right and scroll wheel, there are 2 thumb buttons – both easy to reach, an index finger button, that I like a lot and a button behind the scroll wheel button. I was relatively happy with this mouse – had it for less than 3 months when it died. It died slowly – over ~ 3 days – it would work for ~ an hour and then stop working – I’d turn it off for a while – then I could turn it back on and get another hour out of it. I finally realized it was drawing way too much power out of the batteries – as the new batteries had leaked battery acid all over the case. There are 6 different settings on the bottom of the mouse – including on/off, 250 vs 500 and 2 other settings that I didn’t look up – so maybe I accidently got it into some weird setting or maybe the batteries were bad – not sure – but after only 3 months, it is trash. I would not take a risk and buy it again, especially since the reason I bought it was for the quiet click, but the Mofii is much quieter.

Mofii – 3 stars ($9.90 – BEST price!)
I bought this after the Foxcesd died. It is called “Whisper-quiet” and it is even better than that. I cannot hear the click at all. The clicking has a very nice soft feel. The scroll wheel button is not great however – you have to push it very hard to get it to click. The shape of the mouse is a standard flat shape – so if you are prone to carpal tunnel syndrome, this is NOT the mouse for you. In addition to the typical left, right and scroll buttons, it also has 2 thumb buttons, located in a convenient position and easy to push. It has a DPI button behind the scroll wheel which is supposed to allow you to change mouse sensitivity. I have not gotten this to work – but you can change mouse sensitivity the normal way through the control panel. This mouse is definitely heavier and doesn’t glide as easily as either the Qisan or the Foxcesd. So the main reason to buy this mouse would be the silent clicking.

Conclusion – because I don’t want to pay for any more mice right now, I will probably rotate between the Qisan – when hand/wrist are tired and the Mofii when I want the silent click.

title: Defective from the factory
text:
Logitech used to be the by far best peripheral equipment for computers. I loved their stuff! When you bought a Logitech keyboard or mouse you knew it would perform flawlessly and last for a long time. Sadly this is no longer true. Logitech's quality has deteriorated hugely in the past couple of years.
I bought two of these high priced mice because they are perfect size for a traveler like me and both mice after about six months or so developed button issues and scroll wheel issues. Buttons would no longer function and the scroll wheel became unbalanced so that on hyper scroll it would at the end of the scroll try to roll so the unbalanced part of the wheel would be on the bottom scrolling your page up and down in front of you. After a loooong warranty process that took me two weeks of daily emails with Logitech "customer service" (not really a service but more a pain in the neck) back and forth, they finally sent me a brand new MX mouse as a replacement. Guess what. The new mouse was defective right from the factory out of the brand new box with the same scroll wheel issue. I give up. Actually my cheap M505 mouse performs decently so far but this high priced mouse is of inferior quality. Be warned! I'd stay clear of this mouse! So sad to see Logitech go this way.

title: Terrific App, Dashboard Mounting System Could Be Better
text:
I really like the "ZeroTouch" voice-command app that comes with this ZEROTOUCH DASHBOARD CELL PHONE HOLDER (With Voice-Command App for Android Phones). It was easy to set up on my Galaxy S7 Edge, and it seems to work very well "on the road".

I haven't tested it a whole lot (because of physical installation issues, more on that later), but it seems to have an excellent, up-to-date GPS Navigator, and a terrific Text Message Handler. To send or reply to a text, you wave a hand to wake the app, tell it to "Send a message to (name a contact)", dictate the message, listen to the readback, and answer "yes" to the query "Should I send it". If you have the Samsung "S Voice", it's quite similar, except that "ZeroTouch" notifies you of incoming text messages, and lets you reply to them strictly with voice commands.

The "ZeroTouch" app only works when your cellphone is docked with the cellphone car mount base. Docking and mounting are where I ran into problems. First, there aren't many places in a Honda Civic that are suitable for a suction-cup-base cellphone holder--at least not if you worry about the suction cup losing its grip and dumping your expensive smartphone on the car floor.

Second, the cellphone docks with the car mount base via a thin, adhesive-backed magnetic plate that you're supposed to attach directly to your cellphone or cellphone case. (Tip: If you're having trouble pairing during setup, place the thin metal plate that attaches to your phone directly atop the round part of the base until the magnet grips.) Attaching the plate was an issue, because I didn't want to apply it directly to my new phone (and maybe mar the finish). Applying the plate to my cellphone case worked for a short time, but the adhesive wasn't strong enough to hold the cellphone case through repeated dockings and undockings. Now the adhesive is worn out and won't adhere to anything.

However, there is a workaround. If only the magnetic plate is docked on the base, the "Zero Touch" app will work whenever your cellphone is NEAR the base--within Bluetooth range, I guess. So my hands-free calling/messaging arrangement uses the Honda Civic's two cupholders. The base with the docking strip goes in one cupholder, and the cellphone with the "Zero Touch" app goes in the other.

With this setup, I can use all of the "Zero Touch" features. Of course, if I want to use the handy "parking location finder" feature, I need to undock the magnetic strip from the base when I leave the car, just as I would if the strip were still attached to my cellphone.

The magnetic plate did NOT interfere with my S7 Edge's wireless charging feature, when I had the plate attached to the lower quarter of the cellphone case. (The "ZeroTouch" app setup has a diagram showing you where to attach the plate, if you use wireless charging.)

Because I love the easy-to-use "ZeroTouch" app, but am dissatisfied with the holder mounting arrangement (suction cup and adhesive may not adequately secure the cellphone), I rate this product at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Contender for best mouse I've owned
text:
Contender for best mouse I've owned, going up against the Logitech g900. They are very different mice, for different people though.

PROS:
-excellent feel. the ergonomics are on point, and it's honestly a pleasure to hold. slides nicely on any surface, weight is perfect, and fatigue is zero.
-separate buttons. so tired of the trend of mice that have one piece of plastic on top, rather than individual cut out buttons. (e.g. razer deathadder) it looks nice, but feels like crap.
-the auto switch scroll mechanism. I miss it on all other mice now. my G900 has a mechanical button to switch modes, and while that is nice, it's not as incredibly satisfying and intuitive as the MX master
-beautiful. my office mates are jealous
-LONG battery life. I forget it needs to be charged after 3 weeks to a month, which is about when it starts blinking at me. (I use it 4-8 hours a day at work), and when it does charge, the charge port is in a perfect place to not impede your work.
-excellent bluetooth. I leave it on my desk at night, and when sit down with my laptop it wakes right up and immediately works. I've had some input lag issues with it, but those are few and far between, and can be fixed by flipping the switch.

Neutral:
-the side scroll wheel. It's a nice feature, but doesn't respond all that well in GIMP or chrome. it's always either too sensitive or not enough. that said, it's the best side wheel i've ever used. they must be hard to do right or something.

CONS:
-mine came with a bump in the scroll wheel, due to bad molding. normally this wouldn't be a complaint, but for a $100 mouse (at time of purchase) it better be absolutely perfect.
-back and forward buttons are tiny. you get used to them for sure, but a more conventional layout would be a lot better, and more efficient.
-the gesture control button. might as well have just omitted it. It has its uses, but it's so awkward to press (the actual button is on the seam of the plastic and the metal) that it is 99% of the time easier to just do the thing the gesture was replacing. now, if the button had been under where your thumb rests naturally, this might have been in the pros category.
-the omission of side clicks on the scroll wheel. I can see why they wouldn't on a non-gaming mouse, but I would like them just to assign controls to.

title: Heavy, noisy wheel, awful button placement, an ergonomic disaster
text:
As a long-term logitech fan I've been increasingly disappointed with Logitech mice and this one continues the trend. This mouse is just plain awful.

With all the positive reviews, I'm not sure what to think. One thing for sure: never trust reviews, try for yourself!

This mouse is unreasonably heavy. Much heavier than any wireless mouse I have and it only uses one AA battery! M510 with two AA batteries weighs 132g. This one with one AA battery weighs 165g!

The scroll wheel is noisy, you can hear me scrolling from a different room. It also makes a weird "banging" sound, that resonates through the body of the mouse, you can feel the mouse vibrate, when the wheel comes to halt, it's very distracting. And it takes considerable effort to click the wheel.

There is no mechanical click when you press the wheel sideways, zero feedback, and again you have to press very hard. Practically unusable.

The Back and Forward buttons are way too small, are placed way too high so they're hard to find by feel. You have to move your thumb high up, back and around the bulge. Very uncomfortable and you end up clicking the weirdly placed resolution toggle button.

The thumb button is useless as well, requires a lot of force and moving your thumb too far back to press.

I wear size Large gloves so I don't have small hands.

This mouse is simply terrible. I just don't know what they were thinking. I'm puzzled that so many people like it. It's an ergonomic disaster. I'm sending it back.

title: Lightweight keyboard (works with Windows, Android, ChromeOS)
text:
This is a lightweight keyboard that works well for its intended purpose, but can also serve as a backup or portable keyboard for Windows (10 and 8.1), Android (tried it with Nexus and Galaxy) and ChromeOS devices.

The touchpad is a nice touch when using a PC as a TV, and so are the three volume buttons. What could have made it great was if the play/pause buttons were given a high profile position as well. The letters (A to Z) are of decent size and easy to type, important when you are trying to search for specific shows to watch. The underside of the keyboard is also nice, you can hold it while sitting on a couch using the index finger rests on the underside, and using your right thumb for the volume and trackpad area.

That yellow thing on the top left side you see in the pictures is the mouse press button.

On ChromeOS, this was true plug and play. No drivers to install, just plug in the USB nano receiver and turn on the keyboard and it worked just like that. On Android, you need to have a device that supports USB On The Go (and you need to have your own microUSB to USB cable).

This can work in parallel with an existing keyboard, whether it's a desktop or a laptop computer.

It is powered by two AA batteries. They come pre-installed, you just have to pull out the protective flag. The box says they can last up to 18 months (if normal use as specified). The included batteries were GP brand. The power button for the keyboard is on the back (on the side facing away from you), to the right of the battery compartment. There are no lights on the keyboard. No power light, no caps lock light or any other lights.

When opening the box, you will find the tiny universal receiver wedged right upfront. It has a little flap announcing its presence, but if you are ravenously opening the package, you may not notice it.

If the play/pause button was featured prominently either on the right or left hand side, I would have given it a 5-star. Other than that, this is a good keyboard that you can use for other purposes, it doesn't have to be a dedicated couch keyboard.

title: Fantastic for the price
text: Very simple to setup and use. I edit video on my laptop, so when doing the final sound mix I listen to it both on the laptop's tinny speakers and a set of "good speakers." I use these as the "good speakers." I used to plug my laptop into a thrift store amplifier, but that setup was too unwieldy and unreliable so I decided to get some speakers specifically designed for computers. The speakers and subwoofer are a good size, and the dongle with the power button, volume control, and headphone jack is very convenient. There's enough cord to run the different speakers anywhere on my desk. The volume control on the dongle doesn't control headphone volume, it's just a passthrough so you'll have to re-adjust the volume from the computer as if you'd plugged the headphones in directly. That simplifies things though, and I know that the headphone sound isn't being modulated in a weird way. The subwoofer is non-adjustable, but it's calibrated well so nothing comes out with too much bass. An extremely good value for the price, and I'm sure I'll be using it for many years to come.

title: High Pitched Buzzing Sound Ruins Otherwise Great Sounding Speakers
text:
I bought the Logitech Z623 speakers a few months ago for my husband but due to unexpected work scheduling issues he was not actually able to test them out until recently, and unfortunately after Amazon's 30 day return policy. Like many, many other reviewers this product has the very high pitched buzzing sound from the right speaker (some from the left, but not nearly as pronounced, and the sub-woofer is completely fine).

We tried every bit of troubleshooting we could but the sound persists, and it is so bad it quickly leads to a headache, and actually makes me nauseous if I am in the room too long. The only time you can't hear it is if the sound/music you're playing is loud enough to drown it out, or if you turn off the speakers all together, which right now is their most common state.

I have contacted Logitech support but so far no response (they seem to frequent these reviews often so maybe that will help). My husband typically defaults to buying Logitech computer components, so hopefully this will eventually work out. I will update this review as I work through Logitech customer support.

title: This Is The Way It Should Have Stayed
text:
This mouse is great. I prefer it to the newer Logitech mice; those unifying receivers always seem to go faulty on me. Maybe I'm unlucky, maybe they're flawed. I also strongly dislike how they're making the mouse wheels now: "smooth-scrolling for web", or something like that.

Also, the separate pieces of plastic for the left and right buttons (which they aren't making anymore) give a more satisfying feedback to the fingers upon clicking. I imagine the difference is probably like the difference in feel with mechanical keyboards. I don't have one of those yet, but I will.

So, this model is great because:
- the receiver works,
- it scrolls without "web-scrolling" nonsense, and
- the buttons are more fun to click.

title: Cat tested, mother approved
text:
My ONLY downside to this mouse is it's a bit heavy for my hand. I prefer a mouse that is a bit lighter, especially since I have a bit of carpal tunnel flaring up in my wrists.

Otherwise, we all know that Logitech makes some really stand-up products. I've used this mouse on every conceivable surface in my house. On my bed sheets, on my dresser, on my desk, on my pants leg, on my couch cushion, on the back of my cat (he wasn't a fan of that, by the way)... and no matter where I put it, the mouse functioned perfectly. Okay, I may have had to blow out a bit of cat hair on that last one, but that's a user error all the way. The grip is comfortable, the buttons are in just the right place and function perfectly, and overall I'm happy with the product. I have a feeling it will last me years and years.

title: I'm falling in love with my music all over again
text:
I love the sound on these speakers. Again, as noted in other reviews where I'm talking about technology, I don't know jack about all the in-depth specifications.

So from a Layman's terms--I can't exactly blast metal because the base starts to get a little crackly, but I can certainly ratchet it up there. Enough that my neighbors begin to eye-roll. For my less head-bangy music, these speakers go above and beyond what I had before (an old Phillips POS that I got at a thrift store, so that's not saying much), and I'm super happy with them. Streaming videos with these speakers work perfectly unless it's one of those base-heavy car chase or club scenes, when again the base gets cranky.

I honestly didn't think they would sound this good for the price, but the last time I bought brand-new speakers was back in 2007. Five out of five stars from this Luddite​.

title: Best mouse for precision photo work
text:
I hate trackpads and since I do a lot of editing in photoshop, I've found that this type of trackball mouse is the absolute best for precision and ease. The best thing about the ball style mice is that you never run out of room on your desk and never have to pick up the mouse to reposition it lower on the mouse pad. It also feels more comfortable than thumb-controlled trackball mice. If I'm doing a lot of scrolling, I can "walk" my first and middle fingers on the wheel to continuously scroll.

This particular mouse come with four programmable buttons. Really it's just two if you keep the standard right and left click. I programmed one of the smaller buttons on top to use a shortcut for my RSS reader. It lets me click to the next article without having to use my keyboard. I programmed the other small button to activate the scroll wheel, so I can turn that on and use the trackball to quickly scroll up and down on any website.

I've bought three of these mice over the years. All three of them work, but I've literally "dropped the ball" several times on my tile floor and it creates little dents that catch on scroll cradle. Since the balls cost almost as much as the mouse itself, I just end up replacing the whole unit. I've learned to be a lot more careful with this third one. You also need to remove the trackball every once and while to clean it since it does gather dirt and grime and can make the trackball feel like has more friction. That's easy though. You can either clean it off with your finger, or for a more thorough cleaning, just remove the ball, wet a paper towel and wipe the whole thing down.

I have lot's of options for small, portable multi-device keyboards, but why are so few acceptable as a replacement for real desktop keyboards, that can be used by those of us who actually need a good keyboard? title: Not good for linux user
text:
This review is from the point of view of Linux user. I have not used this keyboard from Windows all that much, just paired it with the receiver. I got this keyboard for work to use in Ubuntu Linux with LXDE desktop.

I start with the good parts. This keyboard is comfortable to type on especially if you do not have to venture outside of letter area. The curve is nice and the palm rest is very nice. Palm rest has a feel of artificial leather and is placed well and very comfortable. I have not had any key misses related to the hardware. The curve takes a bit of getting used to but nothing too bad. Keyboard was detected in Linux without any problems and regular keys work just fine. Additional keys all show up in xev except for the ZOOM keys and the key under them. All the special keys therefor can be mapped to some action in Linux.

Now for the bad parts. For this keyboard Logitech broke the rules on placing function keys and also rearranging Delete key cluster in weird way. This was terrible choice! Ins key is very useful in Linux since paste sequence in X is Shift+Ins. I also use other keys from this cluster for movement in editor and rearranged keys make it so much harder. Also if you are Windows gamer I want to bring your attention to Function keys. They are grouped in 3s instead of usual 4s. Insert key is moved out to the very top row and the Delete cluster is arranged in a very bad way. This for me completely breaks my typing pattern especially when I need to cut and paste between different windows.

title: Perfect. Frustrating. Works Great.
text:
Everything wrong with this item is my own fault. I'm frustrated with it and can't give it more than 3 stars but it's all my fault.

Originally I purchased this for a little extra sound with my television. Just something to add a little thump and a boom, you know? Good stuff, inexpensive, easy to put on and forget about forever.

Except my television does not have the necessary hook ups for this. Just that little plug to plug it into? If that exists somewhere on my television then it has made itself invisible to my eyes and there's just nowhere to plug this in.

NO BIG DEAL! Cool, actually! Instead, I'll use this on my computer and have some nice sounds instead of just listening through my monitor. Cool enough; not what I wanted but maybe I'll like that even more.

I have plugged this into my computer in every configuration that a human being could do so. I literally used to do this as my job. My wife used to do this as her job. We cannot get it to work. Even a little. I took longer on this project than I think I took the first time I ever put a computer together beginning to end. I am not doing anything wrong. I have talked with other people. Nothing works. Not even a little bit.

So, I'm frustrated.

But.

I am moving this into my workshop and just using it to hook up to my iPad as a really nice sound system. It works fine this way and sounds very nice in the workshop. It's not at all what I wanted it for and just seeing it frustrates me because I have no idea what I could have done wrong with it so badly in the beginning.

As a sound docking station? Something to play with in the shop? It's perfect. The sound quality is absolutely great for this little set up. The "boom" goes "boom," the speakers spread out the sound nicely and I'm actually happy with it. If you know more than what I'm doing with your computer toys and you want an inexpensive, worthwhile sound system then you can't go wrong with Logitech.

I'm just going to pretend from now on that that's exactly why I bought it and maybe I'll stop being frustrated at myself.

title: Wonderfully useful mouse.
text:
I've been searching for my 'holy grail' mouse for a while, and I think this may be it. I was coming from an Apple Magic Mouse, which I really did like, but any sort of configuration of additional features relies on either a: touch zones that aren't physically (or even visually) discernible, or b: irritating, finger-contorting gestures. As it was slowly starting to give up the ghost, I thought I'd look around at some other options (particularly since the new Magic Mice use proprietary Li-ion batteries instead of standard cells - a point which I admittedly gave in on anyway since the MX Master is the same). I can't stand slowly click-click-clicking a scroll wheel to get from here to there on a page - some sort of inertial scrolling was a must-have (in fact, I tried a Razer Orochi which was a nice little mouse, but confirmed that I cannot deal with such an antiquated-feeling scroll wheel anymore). The Magic Mouse (and the pleasant Microsoft Explore Touch mouse that I use at work) do inertial scrolling via touch, the Logitech does it with its crazy clutch wheel. Mine hasn't failed yet, if/when it does, I don't think I'll mind having it in free-spin mode all the time; I have my sensitivity set very high and tend to enter free spin more often than not anyway. The inertial scroll on this thing will go for a long, long time. I've spun it just for kicks on some of these annoying infinite page websites, and watched page after page load after having quickly scrolled to the bottom.

Bluetooth was also a must-have, and as of yet I have no connectivity issues between the MX Master and my Mac Pro 6,1. Horizontal scrolling was also important to me, and the thumbwheel on the MX Master, while not as magical as the vertical scroll wheel, works very well. It's also positioned conveniently such that scrolling horizontally off the page to trigger back/forward in Chrome feels very comfortable and natural.

Aside from left, middle, right click, there are four additional buttons. All of this (as well as sensitivity, scroll wheel mode, etc.) is handled by Logitech software that seems occasionally unstable but not terrible. Hopefully they get it to a better place as time goes on, but I won't hold my breath. The button under where the thumb rests is very convenient and natural. The button behind the scroll wheel is ok. The two buttons behind the thumb wheel are... really not great. Not immediately obvious which of the two you're about to trigger, not immediately obvious what angle triggers them best, takes a bit of dexterity to hit either one of them. So that's how I've prioritized them - most-used under the thumb, then behind the vertical wheel, then the two behind the horizontal wheel.

It's a pretty large mouse, and the color scheme doesn't match anything else that I have (a white edition would be nice, or some special edition pastels!) but these are rather petty concerns. Optical tracking has been great for me so far (though I don't find this to be a problem with any modern mouse) and the resolution/allowable tracking speed in software is fine (better than my Magic Mouse was), though faster would be nicer (the Razer I briefly had definitely handled that well!). All in all, using this mouse just makes me happy, and I'm not even much of a mouse user. I get most things done from a mechanical keyboard, which in some strange way this mouse just seems to compliment well.

title: Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum
text:
I’m not a hardcore gamer anymore, so for the past few years, I’ve been using a Logitech M570 Wireless Trackball (thumb trackball). I like trackballs for everyday use, and it’s adequate for casual World of Warcraft playing. Most of the time I just futz around leveling alts or doing 5 mans with friends.

But lately I’ve been wanting a mouse I can customize, with more options to adjust my playstyle. It’s cold in my house in the winter, so I wanted to set up mouseover macros and use more mouse buttons, because my hands are cold sitting on the keyboard. So the G502 Proteus Spectrum seemed like a good mouse to review.

I just had one problem: my computer can’t customize the mouse. Why? I have a Mac Book Air.

Now, I know the G502 says on the box that it supports Windows. There’s no mention of Mac support. But I’ve never had a problem with my Mac recognizing Logitech mice, so I figured I’d be safe. What I didn’t know is that Logitech gaming mice have separate software from the Logitech Control Center for regular Logitech mice.

After some Googling, I found the Logitech Gaming Software, which supports Mac OS X 10.8.x and up. I installed it on a Mavericks machine and a Yosemite machine. Neither computer’s Logitech Gaming Software was able to find the mouse. The G502 Proteus CORE is supported, but not the G502 Proteus SPECTRUM.

So right now, I’m unable to customize any of the extra buttons or RGB lighting or any of the other special features. It’s a really fancy basic mouse. I will continue to check for Proteus Spectrum support in the Mac Logitech Gaming Center, and update this review when I can customize things. I’m going into so much detail on the Mac side of things because I know I’m not the only Mac person who tried to use this mouse. I think there’s a workaround with Bootcamp or using a Windows computer, but I’m unable to try that.

I did use the mouse for a few weeks, to test the comfort. I’m really picky on how mice feel in my hand. I’m female and have smaller hands. I like how this mouse didn’t feel too short, and it wasn’t too heavy or wide for me to use comfortably for hours at a time. I also liked the included weights, so you can adjust the weight of the mouse. I haven’t had a mouse with an adjustable weight before, and I liked that extra level of customization.

title: Outstanding!
text:
Ordered this keyboard because I was getting tired of pecking at the keyboard on my Samsung 9.7 Tab A. Was not sure what to expect quality wise, but was impressed when the item arrived. The keyboard is not large, but comfortable and there is ample finger room to type, not peck. The instructions were scant, a half page fold out with two thirds dedicated to none english buyers. There really are no precise written instructions, rather relying in large part on pictures that were less than informative. The whole "pairing" of the tablet to the keyboard is quite simple -
1. Turn the bluetooth option on your tablet on;
2. Insert your tablet into the keyboard case;
3. Tip the keyboard into position on the black rail to hold it in the upright position;
4. The keyboard will immediately begin to search for your device and when it locates it the keyboard device will show the pairing on the screen;
5. Tap on that pairing showing on the screen and you will be prompted to enter a code and hit the return key. YOU MUST TYPE THE CODE SHOWN ON THE TABLET KEYBOARD, THERE IS NO LINE TO TYPE ON, NO VISUAL ACKNOWLEDGMENT THAT THE CODE IS BEING ENTERED, EVEN THOUGH YOU WILL NOT SEE YOUR TYPING, JUST TYPE IN THE CODE AND HIT RETURN;
6. The keyboard device will link and activate and you are ready to go.

Just that simple and easy. I will say that one device had to be returned because it simply would not maintain the pairing, but the second one works just fine. If you want something closer to a two handed typing keyboard for your Tab A I highly recommed this unit for its ease of use and quality. These keyboards are tablet specific so be sure you order the correct keyboard for your particulat tablet.

title: Programming devices is the best part of this remote.  Day to day operation...not so much.
text:
Solid remote with major flaws. Yes, the battery does last a long time...no issue there. But there is no battery life indicator on the screen and you don't get any warning when running low. So unless you plug it in regularly (which defeats the purpose of long battery life) you go from working perfectly to dead with no warning. While plugged in a battery graphic with a bolt tells you it's charging, but doesn't tell you the % charged or when it is done. When you unplug it the battery graphic doesn't go away, and it doesn't return to normal operation. You can push all the buttons you want, the battery graphic stays on the screen and it doesn't work. The only way to get it working is to take out the batteries and put them back in. And after you do that, you have to go through the tutorial before you can start using it again (thankfully, it does retain the device programming). What a hassle.

And when is Harmony going to get rid of the remote assistant? Like previous models, it constantly asks you if you want to hide the assistant, and it won't operate until you answer. Does the assistant even do anything the help button doesn't? If Harmony is so in love with this outdated 1990s feature, just put an assistant button on the remote and keep the damn thing hidden unless WE decide to turn it on. And the ability to skip the tutorial would be nice too. Nobody wants to be constantly answering to their remote.

Harmony is very good at making initial programming of the remote easy, but seem to give up on the interface after that. Once I'm done programming it, I don't want to mess with it any more, and I CERTAINLY don't want it to interrupt operation. Do what I ask you to do, otherwise sit there and look pretty.

title: More like "Penultimate" -- But Still Pretty Cool
text:
Okay. At first I was not impressed with the Harmony Ultimate. After getting the system up and going, however, I love it.

Desired goal: control two entertainment systems in two rooms with four remotes -- two in each room.

3/29/16 update: I thought having a single remote talking to a single hub was a drawback. But the app on my iPhone is so effective, it's really a second remote for no extra cost. I don't even touch the actual remote that came with the system. That's for the wife, who has taken to the system easily and understands how to work it. I now love my system. Five stars.

3/17/16 Logitech Ultimate Remote w/Hub
Cons:
1. Only one remote can be paired with each hub. Want the wife to have her own remote on one side of the room and you to have another, both controlling the same equipment? Forget it. You can't.
2. Two hubs cannot talk to each other. So you buy two remotes and two hubs, thinking they will talk to each other over WiFi? Forget it. They can't.
3. Pricey at list. Acceptable when on sale ($120 off is nice)

Pros:
1. Excellent phone app. You do all programming from the phone after you create a Logitech cloud account. This gives you control of your system if your phone can reach the internet.
2. Excellent desktop app. Logitech has given up trying to use browsers; you use genuine local apps on your phone and laptop.
3. Easy to set up: Enter MFG and Model number for each device. Done. Full remote buttons download for each device.
4. Touch screen on both the remote and the app has "gestures" with one- or two-finger swiping to control devices. This is nice and unexpected.
5. Colorful
6. Recharges in the cradle -- no more AAA batteries!
7. Wakes up when you pick it up
8. Backlit buttons
9. Haptic feedback when a virtual button is pressed
10. Phone app is great for setup and works as a second remote.

Setting up the first remote was wonderful and very exciting. I couldn't wait to expand the system with my second hub and its remote to create a really capable, flexible system. When the second hub failed to talk to the first hub and I discovered that I had purchased two systems that cannot talk to each other, my elation went to mild disappointment.

Sequence to set up:

1. Create an account with Logitech Harmony at myharmony.com
2. Download the Harmony phone app and download the desktop exe to your laptop.
3. Log in to the account
4. Name and connect the first hub with you WiFi router password
5. Add devices to the room's hub by entering the Manufacturer and the Model number for each device
a. These devices can be far more than AV devices, including lights, blinds, thermostats and other things to a limit of 15.
b. Each device can be renamed for accurate familiarity
6. Create "Activities" for the devices you want to control:
I.e., "Blu-ray Living Rm"
a. it will ask first, "what devices are involved in this activity?"
b. checkbox "AV receiver Living Rm," "TV Living Rm," and "Blu-ray Living Rm"
c. the app asks, "Which input for the TV?" and "Which input for the AV Receiver?" and "Which device controls the volume?"
d. click "run test" to see if everything shuts off and turns back on correctly
e. if it's good, click "yes." Good to go to create next activity.

After you get one room's devices entered and working, if you have a second hub and remote, program it separately in the next room. You can rename the hubs using the desktop exe, but not from the phone app. This is very helpful if you are using the phone as a second remote. You'll have to switch hubs on the phone if you go from one room to another.

You can reorder the activities on both the phone and the remote for most logical order for that room
You can edit buttons and gestures and more.
You can add delay time if a unit needs more time to warm up before it can receive a command
You can change the timeout for the remote to go into standby
You can use your phone as a fully functional remote, but you do have to select which hub you want to talk to.
The Hub connects wirelessly to your WiFi router. It also acts as a giant IR blaster to send commands to the devices. It also has two 2.5mm mono sub-mini plug sockets and two "mini blaster" IR emitters that plug into these sockets so you can send IR to other places.

If you have a device in another room that needs to be controlled, you can extend one of the mini-blasters using an inexpensive 2.5mm extension cord like the 5-meter [[ASIN:B003OSR5TE kenable 2.5mm Stereo Jack Plug to 2.5mm Jack Socket Extension Cable 5m (~16.5 feet)]] or a wireless remote IR extension system like the [[ASIN:B0087S9CJ2 Monoprice 109194 Wireless Dual Band IR Remote Control Extender Upto 328-Feet]].

This wired or wireless extension to another room would be moot if the hubs talked to each other.

What Logitech needs to make happen is to allow multiple remotes to talk to multiple hubs and for the hubs to talk to each other. They've been promising this added capability since at least 2013 on their forums, but so far, it's one remote to one hub and workarounds.

Logitech should not market this as "Ultimate." It's very capable, but also not quite as flexible as required.

title: great 1990's throwback keyboard for system builders
text:
It's 2016, you say. And here you are, on Amazon, looking at keyboards. Why in the world would I buy a PS/2 keyboard? PS/2 was introduced nearly 30 years ago (1987!), and the currently reality is that not a single laptop in the market supports this input, and even desktops are starting to phase them out. Well, as sexy and shiny USB is, the geek in all of us seem to still prefer PS/2 when it comes to debugging system builds.

Frantically hitting DEL, F8, F9, or whatever cryptic combination of keys to get into the BIOS is a well known thing. Turns out, when motherboards are on the fritz, the USB controllers sometimes stop responding, leaving PS/2 as the only way to get access to the BIOS. That alone makes this keyboard worth it's weight in gold, because as far as I can tell, it's the ONLY new PS/2 keyboard available on the market. I went to Fry's, and the kid working there replies, "wrong century dude." Thanks man, cause I didn't feel old enough already.

The keyboard is light, but well built, and feels very solid. The key actuations are a bit mushy, and feel very 90's. Which is not surprising, since this keyboard feels like it rolled right off a 1990's assembly line - all it's missing is the beige plastics to give it that authentic feel. The NUM lock and SCROLL lock LEDs are nice and bright, which means you can't miss them. Most importantly, the DEL, ENTER, and arrow keys work great - a must have for mucking with the BIOS.

TL;DR, a really great throwback keyboard for a ridiculously great price. More importantly, every system builder should have one of these in their closet, for the typical once a year usage. I'm sure if you trolled one of those surplus warehouses you could find a used PS/2 keyboards caked in who knows what, but why bother when you can get one brand new?

title: Perfect.
text:
I am surprised at how much I like this remote. I've had several Harmony remotes in the past, the most recent being the Harmony 550, which I bought in 2007. That remote was good and still working, but showing it's age with some of the paint on the numbers worn off and an occasional button sticking. It also doesn't have the colored buttons witch a few of my devices use.

I saw the Harmony Smart Control on sale pretty cheap around xmas and I decided to give it a shot. I thought it would maybe be a little nicer than what I had. I didn't realize what a great remote it is until I got it in my hand.

For starters, the pictures make the remote look boring and ordinary, and really don't convey how crazy thin and light it is. It's practically as thin as a smart phone but much, much lighter and with a nice curve to it and a pleasant grippy texture on the underside and bottom. The remote just feels fantastic in the hand. The lightness is due to it taking a CR2032 button battery instead of AAA batteries. If you aren't familiar, it's a common and inexpensive battery. They also last a long time in storage, so you can buy a few cheap online and just keep them until you need them. Good chance your car's remote takes these batteries too. I haven't had it long enough for it to die, but in my experience button batteries tend to last a very long time. I've read in other's reviews that it lasts over a year, but I can't confirm that.

My biggest worry was that there aren't a ton of buttons on the remote to customize. I had previously liked to re-assign buttons on my older harmony remotes for functions that I liked to use. Fortunately, pretty much every button has the option to assign a long-press function. So, for instance, I use my DVR's skip forward and back function frequently, but rarely use fast-forward and rewind. So I reassigned the buttons so a single press of the FF button skips forward and a long-press does FF, same for rewind. I also assigned additional activities for via long-press options so my DVR, Blu Ray, and Amazon Fire are single press, but my Chromecast and music functions, which I use less frequently are long-press. With the re-mapping functionality, the customization options are tremendous.

Next is the smartphone app. I used it on Android and it works very well. It gives you access to some of the strange buttons on your original remotes that you may infrequently need. And it's nice to be able to control the TV from anywhere in your house. Sometimes I'm in another room and shut the TV off from there.

I was initially attracted to some of Logitech's higher end remotes with the fancy color touch screens, but put off by the fact that there were very few physical buttons, which in my opinion are easier to use. It is nice to be able to use a touch screen for some of the odder functions that you can't really have a dedicated button for but in the end I think it's a waste of space on the remote and a waste of time to have to charge it. Since most of us have smartphones now anyway, having an app with all the extra functionality really is the idea solution.

Now on to the specifics of how it works. The remote does not have infrared (IR) capability. Meaning nothing shoots out the front. Doesn't need to be pointing at anything, could be under a blanket or whatever and it will still work. It does this by having a hub plugged in in your entertainment center. That shoots IR commands out of it to control your devices. It bounces all around the room, so doesn't need a direct line of site to control things, but depending on your setup, might take some playing around to find out where to locate it so everything works. I have a glass enclosed cabinet with 4 cubbies for equipment and the TV mounted above it. I put the hub on the right side, behind the glass and the included IR blaster (a little cord with a tiny plastic piece on the end) in the other cubby. It controls everything. The only way I'd imagine you have a problem is if you had a totally enclosed system with too many spaces for both the hub and the blaster to reach. It will go through glass, but not wood and such. Also, you can buy another blaster to plug in if you needed it. The hub controls devices with bluetooth remotes, like the Amazon Fire TV directly, with no line of site needed.

Set up for the remote can be done via the smartphone app, or by an app on your PC or Mac. I'd recommend doing on your computer as this interface was a lot easier for me. It is not quick. Maybe if you had a really simple setup, it wouldn't be bad, but expect it to take 1-2 hours. You enter all your equipment info, pick out what activities you want, customize them, customize buttons, and make sure everything works the way you want it to. In my setup I had to play with delays for the A/V receiver and TV so that it waited a little extra time between turning it on and sending the command to change it to the appropriate input. These devices frequently need a few seconds after powering on to be ready to receive a new command.

So to sum up, what I thought would be a slight upgrade and functional enough for what I needed ended up being the nicest remote I've ever had and pretty much perfect for my use.
