title: Superb business-class video communication tool
text:
The C925e is a business communications video tool. You can use it for video conferencing with all the major video conferencing platforms. And you can use it for static recording of presentations, lectures and the like, particularly when mounted on a pan head with automatic tracking.

The video is full 1080p and can be truly described as gorgeous – if you don’t mind having every pore, mole, wrinkle and other artifact of life presented in crisp detail to your viewer(s). Audio quality, with twin omnidirectional microphones is good. Almost too good. My work area is in a pretty live room which is not good for audio. It is also not conditioned, so ambient noises such as the air conditioner and, right now, thunder are picked up. A testament to Logitech quality, but sometimes good is too good.

Autofocus works pretty well. I got within a couple of inches of the tip of my nose before things went fuzzy. This kind of camera is not intended to be used with fast moving objects and the autofocus is more than adequate.t

Two of the very best features are that video is processed in-camera: using the C925e does not put a big burden on your computer: video is H.264 encoded in the camera which means much smoother video streaming. The other biggie is that no additional video driver software is required. For some , that may be a disadvantage. You don’t get to superimpose cartoon clown noses and funny hats. (I haven’t tried it with the driver software for my other Logitech webcams, but I do intend to try it later with ManyCam virtual camera software.)

There is a physical privacy shutter and a ¼-20 tripod mount screw. The typical adjustable bracket works easily and well. Adjustments for zoom, focus, pan, tilt and such are available in Skype and presumably in other video conferencing programs as well.

Setup is no more difficult than plugging the USB cable into an available port. That’s it. No software to load.

The 78 degree field of you is adequate to capture two or three people sitting pretty closely. I am not sure how that flies in today’s legal environment. If you have a group and want to video conference on the real cheap, get an auto pan head or a tabletop tripod and just shift the camera for each speaker. Logitech, however, offers a variety of group video conferencing systems that you might want to look into.

Overall, this is indeed a business class video conferencing tool. The 1080p video is gorgeous and the audio is good as well.

Jerry

title: Excellent low-priced video and audio conferencing system.
text:
Not very long ago, teleconferencing systems – as they were called then – cost many thousands of dollars. Now for about a thousand dollars, you can get an audio and video conferencing system produced by Logitech that will work in medium to large conference rooms with up to 14 people. (20 people with expansion microphones.)

Group works with most popular video conferencing applications. My tests were conducted with Skype Desktop.

Setup was exceedingly simple. My initial setup which included unpacking the components, unwrapping components and uncoiling cables took less than 20 minutes. I estimate subsequent setups will take less than 10 minutes, much less. The system is delivered in a very sturdy and well-organized box, which can be reused for system storage. I would suggest that Logitech consider revised packaging with a built-in carrying handle, which would be a convenience for those carrying the system place to place. Suitable handles are also available from a variety of sellers.

There are four primary components: 1) a camera, 2) a cable hub, 3) a remote, and 4) speakerphone with power adapter. A multi-role bracket for use with the camera is also included. Both the camera and speakerphone have Kensington security slots.

Custom color-coded cables are used to connect the camera and speakerphone to the hub. A USB cable is provided to connect the speakerphone to a Windows or Mac computer.

To use, start up your conferencing app on the computer and choose Logitech Group as your video and audio devices. That’s it. There are a few plug-ins available to increase the control flexibility of certain applications such as Skype.

The speakerphone contains all the controls for video and audio. (Smartphones with Bluetooth capability can be paired using NFC.) The remote control mirrors most of the controls which include pan/tilt/zoom, presets (5), selection buttons for expansion microphones if you use them and a toggle to take control of a compatible unit at a remote location.

All the instructions for using Group are contained on one side of a laminated card inside the box. It is really simple. A more thorough set-up guide can be downloaded from Logitech.

The camera can be described in one word: superb. It’s 10x 90-degree field of view Zeiss-certified zoom lens is very sharp and clear. The pan range is 260 degrees and the tilt 130 degrees.

There are four microphones built-into the speakerphone and they are marvelous. Audio tests with a person speaking at distances up to 15 feet from the speakerphone resulted in absolutely clear audio on Skype. (Much is dependent on your bandwidth conditions, Skype responsiveness and all the other usual factors.)

The unit can also be used purely as a speakerphone, but I haven’t tried that capability yet.

It is fantastic how rapidly video conferencing has evolved. Not so many years ago, esoteric systems were needed, along with many thousands of dollars to buy and support them. Now Logitech is offering three video conferencing systems for groups of various.

Group is high-end of their current offerings and I think it is superb. Very easy to set up; very easy to use and simply superb audio and video quality.

Jerry

title: Logitech Type-S Thin and Light Protective Keyboard Case for Samsung Galaxy Tab S 10.5 (920-006401)
text:
FEATURES:
* Built-in Bluetooth keyboard: Well-spaced keys, Android shortcuts and auto wake/sleep for great typing anytime, anywhere
* Thin and light design: Precision engineering and state-of-the-art materials make this keyboard case amazingly thin
* Dual-view stand: Holds your tablet upright for typing and chatting or flat for browsing and reading
* Essential Protection System (E.P.S.): Covers both the front and back of tablet; protects against accidental bumps, scratches and spills
* Tablet Compatibility: For Samsung Galaxy Tab S 10.5

As advertised, it doubles as a case and a Bluetooth keyboard. I own another Android Logitech keyboard that's standalone (not part of a case), and the Type S keyboard is quite a bit smaller, and the keys are a bit shallower, but it's still big enough for decent touch typing.

All of the major Android functions are represented: Home, Back, and Search all have dedicated keys, and other functions such as volume, multimedia, menu, cut and paste, and application shortcuts are accessed via the FN button.

The keyboard has a power switch on the side, and pairs with the tablet by doing a scan from Bluetooth settings. During normal operation, no LEDs are active (including caps lock) draining the battery. Next to the power switch are the USB charging port and a connect button (which you don't need to use the first time you power it up, since it starts out in discoverable mode).

The "manual" consists of a few small and not-very-clear diagrams showing how to attach the case. The fit to the tablet is secure. Getting the tablet back out of the case isn't especially easy. Build quality is very good.

The case lets you prop up the tablet at an angle for typing, or lie it flat on top of the keyboard. In the upright position, the bottom of the tablet locks magnetically to the keyboard section. The tablet is reasonable sturdy in this position, but there's a fair amount of give when you're using the touch screen. In the flat position, there's no lock, so the tablet can slide around on top of the keyboard

I received this product in exchange for my honest review.

You can't get great bass out of a speaker of this size but it has more bass than any small, $20 speaker out there.

The downside, I use the speaker to listen to talk radio in the morning while getting ready for work and it's not that good when listening to the spoken word. It's tuned to give music a deeper sound and it works but it muffles speaking voices. My Phillips "grenade' speaker does not have the mellow sound of the X100 but the stronger highs and mids mean it works better for radio or when streaming video onto an iPad.

text:
The webcam works well. It's capable of HD video calls and recording which is nice. However no one uses the HD video chatting service that this webcam comes with and many people do not have an internet connection or computer which works well enough to view HD video without a lot of lag. As such it's a great webcam, but it is somewhat impractical for video chatting purposes.

On the other hand it works great for recording HD video so it would be great for someone blogging on YouTube or for recording your face along with your video game stream (which can later be uploaded to YouTube along with the video game recording).

It is basically plug and play, but does come with some additional software which may enhance your overall experience with the device. Personally I find the software dated, but there are some cool features. Such as setting up the camera to follow you while you move about the room and auto-zoom in on you.

A conclusion: People just looking for a webcam to video chat with, would probably be better off going with a cheaper webcam (if money is an issue). This however would be great for streamers/YouTube bloggers. However, I'm going to go ahead and guess that there is something better out there by now.

title: Recommend despite quality concerns.
text:
In this review, I will compare the G930 to a cheaper gaming headset: the SADES SA-708 (currently ~$17 on Amazon).

Pros:
Sound is noticeably better during gaming and just listening to music/youtube videos. I've read articles saying you can't tell the difference between 7.1 and plain old stereo, but I disagree. Besides that, the isolation, software equalizer, and general dynamism of the drivers adds up to a great sound experience -- one that is noticeably better than the SADES headset.
Wireless connectivity is nice -- and worth the expense I'd argue. The charge life is great, and you can still use the G930's while charging.
They're slightly more comfortable than the SADES headset. The earphone section seems deeper, and the liner material seems more breathable and rigid. My SADES would get hot and felt like they were squishing my ears, but that's much less so with the G930s.

Cons:
Disclaimer -- I bought my pair refurbished for $65. I still expect them to work fine after they've been refurbished though. The issue I had with mine was that the charging cable/wireless adapter combo that came with my headset would not charge my headset. I had to use my wife's camera microUSB connector.
In order to get the Logitech Gaming Software (the program specific to this headset) to recognize the headset, I had to go into the Control Panel and update the headset drivers manually.
Finally -- a pet peeve -- it takes a few second to turn the headset on or off. May not be a big deal to some but it annoys me.

Conclusion: I thought a Logitech headset, at this price point, wouldn't have these sorts of inconveniences and quality issues. If you get lucky and get a pair that work fine, these are a good set of cans for the price. What you're really paying for here is wireless connectivity, comfort, and relatively above average sound quality.

The left and right buttons have a positive click, and are no longer heavy and hard to press.

The T400 is now my mouse of choice.

title: Fairly heavy with loud clicky keys
text:
This keyboard did not quite cut it for me.

First the good points: The keyboard has a wide slot that can hold my iPad horizontally or vertically. And my iPad fits in there even with its shell case on. The keyboard works with up to three devices at a time and they pair with the keyboard easily. (I occasionally use it with my phone too.) It has a nice clean white design that complements the white border of my iPad well. It is a sturdy base for lap or desk use, and the iPad's weight in the cradle doesn't cause it to tip over.

But this keyboard has several drawbacks. Most importantly, I don't like the feel of the keys at all. They aren't anything like a laptop keyboard. It's hard to describe but they are rounded off with have a plasticy feel, somewhere between a desktop keyboard and toy keyboard. The also produce a good deal of click noise when pressed, again unlike a laptop keyboard which is usually pretty quiet when typing. The base has some heft to it... It's about 1 lb 12 ozs with the 2 AAA batteries installed. Lastly, although not a major issue, the keyboard's plastic casing creaks when you move it because the it flexes slightly. I don't think the keyboard is going to fall apart or anything, but I would think coming from Logitech this type of build quality issue wouldn't have occurred.

Had I been able to test this keyboard out in-store before purchasing it, I probably would not have bought it. But I recently purchased a Zagg Limitless keyboard instead and it is better is several ways: It's thinner, has rechargeable batteries built-n and is 10 ounces lighter. Plus the keys are much quieter and type better, similar to to a laptop keyboard. I'll be selling the K480 now that I've found the Zagg. title: After 6 years, I switched to this for my HTPC
text:
I had been using IO Gear keyboards (model GKM561R) for 6 years, but switched to this one because the roller ball on the IO Gear gets flaky and you have to remove a bunch of screws to clean it. So this time, I trying a touchpad!

PROS:
1. Extra mouse button on the left is great for "two handed" operation.
2. No drivers or reboot needed, it "just worked" (using Windows 10).
3. I can use 2-finger drag as a scroll wheel.
4. Much lighter than my old keyboard, so I'm less likely to drop it.
5. Great "out of the box" experience - just pulled a plastic strip out and it was ready to go - didn't even have to load batteries!

Cons:
1. No "Media Stop" key - although I can probably live without it.
2. Function keys are merged with media keys. Previously, I used Alt+F4 to exit Kodi, now I need to hold down Fn or use the menu.
3. Some things feel more natural on the roller ball than the touch pad. 3d camera positioning in the Trainz simulator game for example.
(But those "Cons" are minor and could really be considered "things to adapt to" - I look forward to the maintenance-free touchpad....)

title: Deal of the Day indeed.
text:
Well what can I say that hasn't already been written about this product. It truly is a great bang for the buck, and definitely one of the better items I've purchased via Amazon's Gold Box Deal of the Day.

For the most part, I love my apple keyboards. They feel sturdy and I love how the keys "click". As far as I'm concerned, they're my standard for a quality keyboard.

This, absolutely DOES NOT, feel like a quality keyboard. It feels flimsy and cheap with its plastic parts. I'm afraid if I drop this on my porcelain floor, it'll shatter. Why did I give it 4 stars then? Well, for what I paid (less than $20) it's a pretty damn good deal. Although it feels like should only cost $10, once I started typing away on it, I actually started to like the way it felt on my fingers. I'd almost admit (unwillingly) that I like the keyboard feel more than my apple keyboards. Almost. AND, it has a trackpad built into it? For under $20? Winning! Love the tiny footprint of it as well; it fits really nicely on my desktop and very easily into my slim drawer underneath. And let's not forget these two other extremely important features: 1) logitech's unifying USB dongle lets me use both the keyboard and logitech mouse on the new pc, and 2) I can also use this on my mac, whereas the apple keyboard isn't as easily connected with my PC. ... so it's very possible that I may even replace the apple keyboard with this one in my studio room.

Please keep in mind that this is a simple keyboard. If you're into gaming or something, this may not be for you. Also, like I said, I don't think it's very durable. Who knows how long it'll last, but it's essentially staying in a carpeted room, so it should be fine. If you plan on taking this with you while you're working "on the road" or traveling a lot, just be wary of the fact that IF you drop it once or twice, it'll probably break and stop working to whatever degree.

BUT for the price, and for the "Deal of the Day" ... it is a DEAL!

title: Best mouse ever made. Period.
text:
Love this mouse so much bought a 2nd one. This probably has been a marvel of a mouse in terms of productivity at the office. I literally fly in all my applications and everything I do on the computer. You will notice once you are used to it, you will be faster than most people in navigation. I have large hands so the shape is a perfect fit for a large hand due to the curve. If you look at your hand it has a natural curve to it and the mouse creates that natural resting curve for your hand. I then discovered that this mouse actually puts minimal movement on your muscles in the hand. By far this is the least challenging mouse on the wrist, fingers and hand. Your hand does not move and the only thing that moves is just your thumb! Yes, your thumb controls all movements and this is where it’s awesome. People who never used this freak out because they want to move the mouse but there is no mouse movement. For gaming, this is not for FPS games. Those will require more precise wrist controlled movements, however most non FPS games will work just killer. The battery on this never dies either. 18 months, are you kidding me?
Pros:
Minimal muscles used ( thumb for movement only )
Precise mouse navigation
No need to move mouse around
Contours the hand completely in resting position
Very fast navigation due to no wrist movements
No fatigue
18 Month battery life

Cons:
Not compatible with new Macbook 12” due to receiver being USB and Macbook having no USB ports
Should be designed closely to compliment Apple products with apple like finish
Should be Bluetooth model (no receiver needed)

title: Very nice features; better than nest
text:
I already own a Nestcam, but I wanted to try an alternate brand that didn't have a subscription fee. I bought this Logitech Circle (Logi circle) camera today and am very pleased by some of its unique features.
1. the power base has a strong magnetic, so I was able to easily mount the camera on some ULine shelving
2. the camera can be rotated up or down and has a 130 degree field of view, so it is much easier to position than Nest
3. has a nice long lightweight 10 ft USB power cable
4. there is a power save mode so that the camera doesn't stream until you view it in your app
5, but in power save it is still detecting movement, so you will get a notification on your iphone to look at the video
6. viewing the whole day's video in 30 seconds is a real kick

What I don't like about the product:
1. It runs pretty hot. So I am afraid it is not going to last very long.
2. You have to charge it up when you first open it
3. I set it up and then moved it to another room, the app suddenly gave me a big red sign that "Your Circle service is under maintenance. Try again later". It took an hour to come out of maintenance mode.
4. I believe you can only view the stream on the app and not from your computer

So far I'm very pleased, but I will update this in a few months.

title: A somewhat pricey mount, with some great hands-free functionality via a well-designed app.
text:
The Logi ZeroTouch has a lot of promise as a premium car dashboard hardware and software solution for cars that don't have built-in Bluetooth.

It's about the nicest way I've seen to attach your phone to your dash, working with a magnetic strip that you put on the back of your phone and that clicks into place on the Zerotouch in a very snug and secure way. It's a Strong magnetic bond that makes me feel very confident that it's not going to slide off, but not so strong that it's a struggle to remove. Installation is very easy, just clean your dashboard, and apply the Zerotouch, pressing a tab down to apply suction. In other words, it is not at all permanent, and doesn't use any adhesive, so you can remove it quickly and easily without issue.

Besides the hardware, there is of course the software - the Zerotouch app, that is also easy to set up with lots of instructional images and animation that step you through both the hardware installation and some of the software features. The software acts as kind of a middle-man between your phone's OS/apps. You interact only with Zerotouch until it activates an app for use, at least in the case of maps and Spotify/Music. For those, it brings up the given app so that you can control them yourself, or see the navigation turn by turn. This makes sense, but it also breaks a bit of the interface because then you are just tempted to interact directly with the apps in question, rather than doing things in a more hands-free way. You can always go back to the Zerotouch app, but you will need to put your hand over the top of the phone. While this isn't difficult, and far safer interacting with buttons on a touch screen, it isn't exactly "hands free." I guess it's the next best thing, but it would be nice to be able to go back to the Zerotouch app with a voice command, although that might not be technically feasible.

This phone will work fine whether your car has Bluetooth or not, but of course having Bluetooth built in will definitely help with hearing phone conversations and music. If your car's sound system doesn't come with Bluetooth and getting a replacement unit with bluetooth is not an option, I highly recommend getting a portable Bluetooth speaker, which is not quite as powerful or convenient as one that's built in, but certainly a lot less expensive! Maybe Logitech should even consider offering a deluxe version of this product that includes such a speaker?

The other downside is that it takes regular alkaline batteries, so you'll have to replace them every once in a while. I generally would prefer something that's rechargeable either via the car charging port, or even just using a standard USB charger via a wall charger or PC.

While this is definitely a quality product, the price seems a little high for a car mount. If you're not concerned with that, then go for it, but I'm not sure that I would normally pay that for a car mount. Maybe if this came with a decent Bluetooth speaker and a rechargable battery, but given a limited budget, I'd rather stick to a relatively cheap mount and purchase one of the myriad hands-free apps from the Playstore that do more or less the same thing - some of which allow you to do even more than Zerotouch, although maybe not with quite the degree of hands-free operation that Zerotuch can provide. If cost is not an issue and you don't need a gazillion features, and hands-free operation is important for you, than Zerotouch would definitely be a fine choice.

text:
This Logitech M330 Silent Plus Wireless Large Mouse is a decent product with a great storage area for the wireless USB fob-a-ma-jig, that "plugs" in right next to the battery when not in use. I've lost these little USB connectors on my other wireless mice/ mouse-I/ meece in the past during a move or while storing, so I really appreciate this feature. I think it's great that Logitech has considered making this more quiet click in their mouse. It's not silent; the package even says it's a 90% reduction in sound. So, you can hear a little muted click, but it's about as loud as when i've use other (non-silent) mouses in bed and kept my hand under the covers to keep my husband from getting irritated. Personally, i don't notice the clicking much (i mean, the keyboards are louder in general anyways, and i can tune out the clicks), BUT, i have to say, this quiet mouse has been a real plus for my husband's ears, as he's actually told me not to use the computer in bed cuz he can't stand the mouse click sound. He didn't even notice this one at all.

This is a great product, that let's me surf the web in bed and not be harassed. I deducted a star tho, because i find the wheel a bit "sticky." It has a micro-calibrated click feeling (not sound, but the feel), that i actually find a bit irritating to use. I didn't know it until I tried this one, but I prefer smoother action wheels. Also, I have smaller hands, and I found this mouse to be just about the right size- My husband thought this mouse felt more Medium-sized...so, I'm not sure I would advertise this as a "Large" mouse necessarily. Still, all these are fairly subjective issues. The function of the mouse is high level, and it scans and reads all the surfaces I've used it on (bed sheet, plain table top, granite counter, etc...) with no problems at all, and it feels very responsive to my movements.

title: Amazing audio output from such a small system.
text:
For the price these are selling for now its a no brainer not to buy a set!

I recently bought the Logitech Z523 which sell for double the price, The Z523 are a very nice step up from the Z323 BUT for the price the Z323 produce very good sound, they can get loud if you crank up the volume to. The clarity and bass is close to the Z523 but the overall ability of the Z323 is a bit less, however again for the price you absolutely can't go wrong.

I'm using the Z323 for a retro gaming setup and find that it has no problems handling old school systems like the SNES, Genesis/Sega CD and NES. My old games sound so loud and clear now, it really is amazing, the rear of the Z323 has left and right RCA jacks to use with my old systems which is great, I use a switch box and have them all hooked up to the Z323. The Sub also has a Bass control knob at the back as well which is a nice feature, some subs at the price don't give you the option to adjust the bass level.

I compared the Z523 and Z323 side by side and found that the Z523 will outperform the Z323 in almost every regard, however the Z523 is only a better system, a step up so its actually a close match.

Overall if your looking for a better sound system then an entry 2.1 setup buy these, they are worth the price and don't take up allot of space. But if your looking for a good step up buy the Z523.

title: Absolutely amazing sound for the price and size.
text:
Absolutely amazing sound for the price and size! I was looking for a compact 2.1 speaker system with a small sub, the Z523 fit the bill. I was fully expecting to be only mildly impressed with these speakers, but I'm absolutely shocked by the clarity and overall sound that these speakers produce.

I was also debating whether to buy these or the Z333, but after looking at the Z333 it became apparent that the Z333 weren't made with the same materials, they are cheap looking in comparison to the Z523.

As for the sound quality, these speakers are a bit heavy on bass which is similar to my older Logitech Z2300 system. (The Z523 can't touch the Z2300 in terms of sound and loudness, so don't try to compare the two). However the highs and mids aren't drowned out so it all goes together just fine. For being 40 watts these speakers sound as if they are much more then that. The Z523 utilizes passive drivers for the satellites and the sub. Passive drivers allow the speakers to produce richer and deeper sound from a smaller size, that explains why these speakers sound so good. Using quality drivers and audio circuitry also helps things out.

From a styling perspective its a love it or hate it kind of look. The satellites have a simple "flowing" design to them that does go with allot of different PC and Monitor designs which is a good thing. Having the volume and bass dials on the right speaker is really nice, I prefer this over the usual of putting the bass dial on the sub itself.

Overall I'm very happy with these speakers, they are well worth the asking price and really do provide and great listening experience for their size and price. Logitech really did a great job with these speakers and I'd buy another set like this if I needed to.

title: Huh, I didn't know you could buy these
text:
So I guess this is a review of the Unifying system overall?

I have a couple of Unifying devices for my Raspberry Pi -- a K400r keyboard and an m315 mouse -- and, well, it works fine, even if I have yet to try the third-party software you need to configure it on Linux. There's no tricky driver stuff to deal with or anything like that, so that's good; it just looks like a basic USB HID device.

I'm still not a fan, particularly, for two main reasons. The first is that reverse-engineered or not, it's still a proprietary protocol, and there's no way to build devices using it; this is not necessarily an issue, as most DIYers would probably use Bluetooth LE for that sort of application, but it's still sort of annoying. The other is this: on the Raspberry Pi B+ and 2 (which have four ports each), you're going to have to take a port up for the keyboard and mouse anyway, and it doesn't really matter if it's wired, Bluetooth, Unifying, or some other kind of proprietary wireless protocol. And most current computer models have built-in Bluetooth. However, this is a real problem for computers with only one or two USB ports like older iMacs, the BeagleBones, or the original Raspberry Pi (or the A+ or Pi Zero for that matter); if you need wireless networking for one of those boards, you're very likely out of luck for using a Unifying device. Bluetooth/Wifi combo devices tend to be hard to find and technically outdated, and Bluetooth input devices tend to be rather overpriced, but if you only have one USB port to deal with, this is a tremendously hard sell nevertheless. A third concern: it is yet another 2.4GHz-band protocol. If your house or workspace is already suffering from spectrum congestion in that band, this isn't going to make it any easier.

I don't know that Unifying needs to exist. It's there, it works fine, it's even been hacked on the host end, but it means giving up a bit of flexibility that you probably wouldn't have to if you were using Bluetooth devices. It's also a closed system that only Logitech has access to; it's their prerogative, of course, and Bluetooth is better for most purposes you might consider using this for anyway, but it still seems kind of pointless to me to continue to develop and offer a proprietary wireless connection when Bluetooth is readily available on nearly everything for the last almost ten years.

title: Old-school keyboard for new-school tech
text:
The frustrating thing about Bluetooth keyboards is that even though the technology has been around for over a decade now, manufacturers still charge premium prices for the things. At least with the Logitech k480, it's obvious where the money is going.

This isn't a keyboard case. It's a no-compromises compact desktop keyboard for your tablet, phone, and/or computer (and you can control up to three devices with it, contributing to the obsolescence of the KVM switch). The keys are not quite full-travel, but they're definitely a step above your typical membrane keyboard. I'm particularly a fan of the dual-platform modifier keys, something even Logitech usually doesn't do; Microsoft is probably mildly annoyed that the "Windows" key says Start instead, but with the exception of some Surface users, this isn't really aimed at their market to begin with. There's no integrated numerical keypad, but that to me seems like it'd be little more than a source of frustration from wonky OEM or AOSP keyboard drivers anyway.

Construction is very solid. It's not too terribly heavy, but the groove for your tablet or phone is fairly deep and lined in nonskid rubber; you won't have to worry too much about shaky tables dislodging things. (Although I'm not sure I'd rely on it for something as big as an iPad Pro; might be better to improvise a separate stand for that.) There's an actual knob to switch between devices, which is a little anachronistic but fits right into the aesthetic, and two different pairing buttons depending on whether you're hooking it to Android/Windows/Linux or OS X/iOS. It certainly works great with iOS; I've also tried it with the Raspberry Pi, and it worked fine, but Raspbian's Bluetooth HID support remains an incomprehensible dungeon crawl through a seemingly straightforward UI that never seems to work right, so I'm sticking with my k400 Unifying keyboard with built-in trackpad instead (for which I only need the mouse for RISC OS anyway). And overall it beats the pants off its anemic, mushy little sibling the k380, which appears to have been designed by a completely different group with only a visual to go on.

This is obviously not for everyone. A frequent flyer might find it to take up just a bit too much space in a flight bag. If you have RSI issues you may need a 90s-style wrist rest to use it properly. And although it works fine with a desktop system, if you're a designer using it with a Mac Pro or HP Z workstation, it'll probably make you feel more than a little OCD about it. (Maybe you could use the slot as a pen or stylus holder.) The neon key lime trim on the grey version is garish, to say the least. (Hey, some people really care about visuals.) But if you like old-school keyboards, this might just be the best choice for your tablet.

title: Not the best option
text:
This keyboard suffers from these THREE major flaws, each of which resulted in the removal of 1 star:

1. TOO HEAVY: One of the most beautiful aspects of the iPad Mini 4 is how sleek and lightweight it is in your hands. This case adds so much weight, you're essentially in laptop territory. At that point, with the cost of the Mini and the cost of this keyboard, just buy yourself a Macbook Air.

2. SEMICOLON AND COMMA KEYS ARE TOO SMALL: Whomever decided to slim down the semicolon and comma keys made a poor decision. I absolutely cannot type even the simplest email without accidentally hitting the return key because my finger travels too far given my muscle memory that the return key is two keys from the L key. This is terrible as I can't imagine willingly weighing your iPad Mini down with this case unless you have some serious work to do.

3. NOT DESIGNED FOR QUICK ON/OFF: If you're like me and you don't always need a massive, keyboard-enabled case on your iPad Mini, you'll want something you can take on and off with ease. This isn't it.

All in all I feel like this case is trying too hard to be all things and ends up doing nothing well.

MY RECOMMENDATION: My current solution for an as-needed keyboard for my iPad Mini is the [[ASIN:B008OEHPKM Microsoft Wedge Mobile Keyboard]]. It's fantastic! The cover folds to create a stand for your iPad Mini and you can adjust it for any viewing angle or distance from the keyboard. The keyboard and keys are the appropriate size. Your Mini can rock any case you want it to. And when you don't need a keyboard, you can enjoy the beautiful, light-weight keyboard in all of its glory...as Apple intended you to.

title: My Husband was a Bit Skeptical of This Mouse Because of the Cost but It is Really Growing On Him!
text:
I'd like to preface this review by stating that, even though I am not the primary user of this mouse, my incredibly patient husband took a lot of time answering my many questions about this mouse, demonstrated what it does, and read through my review before I submitted it so all of the information in here is accurate.

My husband is an IT guy and computer gamer so he always purchases a programmable gaming mouse whenever he needs a new one. Prior to this mouse, he had the [[ASIN:B002J9GDXI Logitech G500 Programmable Gaming Mouse]] which he really liked so when that one started wearing out after three years, he started searching for a good replacement. There was another mouse that he wanted instead of this one but it was older so he decided to purchase this one, since it is basically the newer version of the G500 and he really liked the number of programmable buttons (this was a requirement of his and the main reason he purchased this mouse).

We have now had this mouse for almost two months and my husband is very happy with it. Initially, he was hesitant on purchasing this mouse because of the cost. He typically prefers to spend about $50 for a mouse and this one was $30 more when we bought it so this mouse was a bit more expensive than his usual purchase but it is really growing on him after using it for a couple months. When I first laid my eyes on the mouse, it looked like it's something from the future with how technical it looks!

***The following information is taken directly from the packaging.***
What's In the Box:
Mouse
Tuning weights and case
User Documentation

What You Need:
USB Port
Internet connection for optional software download
Windows 10, Windows 8.1, Windows 8, or Windows 7

Now, back to my review. Upon opening the box, my husband immediately set to work setting up his mouse for his gaming specifications. There are 11 programmable buttons which you can calibrate depending on how much you use them and you can always change them. You are also able to set up the buttons that will apply for all different games you play or you can set up each game differently with the mouse. For instance, my husband has the left button as his running mode since he uses that so much but he could set up the right button for running in a different game if he wanted. The cord is made of a braided material rather than plastic and is a good length. My husband also doesn't currently use a mouse pad so he was able to program the mouse to be more sensitive to a desk and it moves smoothly on his desk. This mouse has a great, ergonomic feel and is very comfortable to use. My husband has big hands and this mouse is a good size for him. So far it's even withstood our twin toddlers pressing the buttons and playing around with it, which is always a good thing! The symbol on the top of the mouse changes colors which I personally think is pretty cool.

Overall, my husband is very happy with this mouse even though he was skeptical at first because of the higher cost. It isn't his favorite mouse only because he liked his older ones better but since those are very hard to find, this one was the option that best suits his needs. He uses it while gaming, working remotely on his work computer, and everything in between and hasn't had any complaints about it. If anything happens that alters his opinion or we think of any more information to add, I will update this review but he said this product currently deserves a five-star rating because it does what he wants and he gets a lot of daily use out of it. He highly recommends it!

title: Skype for Business (previous Lync client) works fine. I can hear the conversations and people can ...
text:
I spend about 90% of my day on conference calls. I had a Jabra wired headset and I needed to be a little more mobile around the house. These looked similar to the Jabra wireless at half the cost. I've used these for 2 days in a row so far. It paired with my Windows 10 Surface Pro, Skype for Business (previous Lync client) works fine. I can hear the conversations and people can hear me. I haven't tested this in a loud environment so I can't say how well the mic noise cancels. My only con so far is they do hurt my ears after long use. I have to adjust them around to keep my ears from hurting. I'm actually looking for any cushion adapters for comfort. I think it has a tight fit on my head so that's why my ears hurt after a few hours.

Update: I'm going to need to knock this back a star because I just found out the Micro USB cable seem to be proprietary. I recently changed jobs and mixed up my USB cables and accidentally took the cable that came with the headset home. No big deal it's micro USB any cable should work. So I used the cable that came with another headset and plugged it into the base. It did not recognize the headset on the new laptop. I thought well maybe it's a bad usb cable. So my new coworker let me borrow his. I plugged it in. Yet again the headset base failed to connect the headset to the PC. Fastforward 1 day I locate the original cable bring it in Voila it works. I don't know why it works as it looks like any cable should work but it doesn't. That's why I knocked it down a star and won't be buying another version like this. I'm still using it but I don't like that I would have to buy a proprietary cable if I ever lost mine or the original one was damaged.

title: Got This For Streaming
text:
This webcam is better than I expected it to be. I was initially drawn to the price, and the fact that it can just rest over a monitor.

PROS:

- This cam takes a really nice picture and records or streams crisp, and without blur or distortion. It worked better than my laptops built in cam.

- I can place it on my secondary laptop, or in a different area of my desk, to get multiple angles while recording or streaming.

- Nice and portable-sized. Not big and bulky, heavy, or with the need to sit on the desk.

- Sleek appearance. The webcam has a nice, rounded appearance that gives it a higher end feel.

- I like that it accommodates a wide screen view and can capture in HD without problems.

- I use this on my laptop and it rests on top. I'm able to slide it around until I get the preferred angle.

CONS:

- The only real con is that it doesn't clamp down too well. If I accidentally tug on the cord, the webcam easily falls off. I sometimes will let it set on the top of my laptop screen by the hinge (the part that bends) to make it a little harder to knock off. If it could have just a little more stability, it would be awesome.

Overall however, I'm very happy with the purchase and really like this little cam.

title: Logitech TYPE+ was WAY better, which was for the Air 2
text:
Logitech TYPE+ was WAY better, which was for the Air 2. The only reason why I bought this is because Apple moved the location of the magnets on the IPad Pro vs the iPad Air 2, so it does not stand up firmly. But this new CREATE keyboard is a step backwards.

CONS:

1) They removed the Fn button and put a stupid "on screen keyboard" button in its place at the bottom left of the keyboard. Why? I see absolutely no purpose of a button on a physical keyboard that turns on the on screen keyboard. So I'm typing on the phyicaly keyboard, then suddenly I want to start pushing buttons on the screen? I don't see the point in that. Now, we can't use Fn + C for copy and Fn + V for paste, we have to use the awkward Cmd + C and Cmd + v - they buttons are way too close together to use normally!

2) Lack of internal battery. I don't think it's that cool that the new keyboard drains my iPad battery. Why would I want that. I think I only charged the TYPE+ keyboard once time in a year, it lasts so long that it's inconsequential to charge it. Plus, it allows my iPad to use its battery for the iPad, not the keyboard.

3) The magnetic strip is not strong enough. The left side doesn't even seem to have a magnetic connection, the iPad is held in place primarily by the center and right, meaning the left side always seems to come up first.

4) Major fail: The upper portion of the case does not even hold the iPad without slipping out. Constantly when I open the case, the iPad came out of the top, which does not even grip it at all. This could be a major disaster if the iPad fell onto the floor. WHAT THE HECK? It should be firmly in place, yet easily removable when I WANT to, not at random.

5) BIGGEST FAIL: How the heck are you supposed to open the case? There no tab, grip, or slot to put your finger in to open the case. You have to use 2 hands and you have to carefully pry it open. I mean seriously, they didn't even consider how a user is supposed to open the dang case. That is just place stupid. STUPID. The most used function of the case is opening and closing it, next would be the keyboard itself. For this reason alone, the case is a deal breaker. Why should I struggle to open the case every time???

6) They changed the iOS buttons at the top row from the TYPE+. They removed the "app switcher" button which I thought was really useful. Now I have to press the "square" button twice, which simulates double tapping the home button. They should have left the app switcher (two squares) button and removed the Globe "internet" button.

7) The Globe "internet" button literally does nothing on the home screen. When I am typing on text input, it brings up a silly emoji menu 😄😀😁😬😅🙂😆😂😅🙂 yay I can make smileys - not. I would rather have the app switcher and make this emoji button accessible via a combination shortcut.

8) Why does their brand on the keyboard say LOGI now when they are Logitech? That just makes no sense. LOGI???

PROS:

1) The keyboard is very nice to type on, but still it is no better than the TYPE+, as I mentioned it's a step down due to the loss of the Fn key. I'm typing this review on the keyboard with great accuracy.

2) The backlit keyboard is a nice step up, the TYPE+ did not have that which it definitely needed.

LOGI/Logitech, please restore the form factor of the TYPE+ keyboard for the iPad Pro / iPad Pro 2 (when it launches). It is much superior to the CREATE keyboard in virtually every way. Just add the backlit keyboard back to the TYPE+ and make the magnets compatible with the new iPads, and stop there. PLEASE. Thank you.

title: this is a really nice set of tools
text:
If you're looking for something you can use to talk to friends or family over a webcam, this is probably going to be way more than you need. If you're looking to have group meetings with moderately sized groups (say 8 or so), this is a really nice set of tools. The most expensive/sophisticated piece of the set is the camera, that you can control by remote control. That's actually kind of handy, because if you have a group sitting far enough back so that everyone is visible, it'll be awkward for someone to jump up and make camera adjustments. It looks a lot smoother and more professional to be able to make it adjust from where you're seated.

The rest is basically a central station to control the whole thing, and a microphone (so that it can pick up audio close to where the people are sitting, while having the camera farther in back so they're better in view). If you need to do meetings with really big groups, you'll want the version of the set with an extra microphone so that it can do a good job of picking up audio over a larger area. Don't expect to be able to plug in any microphone that you'd like (unfortunately).

My early experience is that it's a really good set, which is consistent with what I've gotten from Logitech webcams and similar products I've bought for myself in the past. It's not very fussy to set up, and they've made a deliberate effort to be sure that it works properly with some business-level video conferencing services to make things easy on you. I think the people who'll get the most value out of it are small to medium businesses and teams. It's expensive, but it doesn't take very many good videoconferencing sessions replacing airline tickets to break even considering how expensive flying is (and that's before you add in the cost of things like hotels, taxis, eating out, and time away from home).

I wouldn't recommend it for home use unless you're looking to do something like hold special family gatherings where you use video conferencing to let someone else kind of feel like they're with the family when they need to be far away. For normal use, a much cheaper webcam (or even the camera and microphone built into most phones and tablets) makes a lot more sense and takes up less space.

So it's a good set, just make sure that it lines up well with what you're hoping to do because even a good product like this is a waste of money if it's not a good fit for your needs.

title: Heir to the Laptop mouse kingdom.
text:
I got this mouse as a trusty replacement for my good old Logitech M305 that lived for may years but recently passed away. I loved the size and feel of the Logitech M305 so I got this one as it is the same size. I also liked the unique color of the mouse. This mouse has the same basic features of the Logitech M305; it is the same size, uses one battery, has 4 way scrolling, has a on/off switch on the bottom, and has the battery indicator light on the top.

The M305 had a neat little switch on the bottom that opened the battery compartment which was on the top. In the M325, the switch has been removed, and the battery is located on the bottom of the mouse, under a sliding compartment. This mouse also is a bit lighter than the M305. I find the tracking a little less precise, and also the clicking action of the mouse buttons is less satisfying to me. The middle click is also different. The scroll wheel was redesigned so that it feels more like a free wheel scroll--I can barely feel the notches as I use the wheel. Some people may like this, but I miss the way the old Logitech mouse felt when I was using the wheel. I prefer the defined notches in the old wheel.

The one neat thing this mouse has that the M305 does not is that this mouse can be used with the Logitech Unifying Receiver. That means if you have a unifying receiver, you don't need the one that comes with this mouse. You can connect the mouse to any device using your existing dongle.

The color of this mouse is not represented accurately by the picture. The mouse is the sea green/mint color, but on the two mouse buttons it fades to white. It is still very unusual but I would have liked it without the white on the mouse buttons. I prefer the M305 to this, but adding the unifying receiver support makes up for a lot of the mouse's shortcomings. I hope it lasts as long as my M305 lasted me.

title: Responsive And Quiet Wireless Mouse With Perfect Connectivity- Not Quite Long Enough For My Hand (Women's Size L Glove)
text:
The Logitech M330 Silent Mouse is a very good, right handed wireless mouse. The wireless connectivity is excellent. The dongle stores inside the battery compartment, and once plugged into my computer USB port the connection was immediate and has remained constant. The AA battery is included and should last about 24 months (realistic based on other Logitech mice I own). This mouse is indeed virtually silent, so it's a great choice to pair with my living room computer and also my laptop. I can still hear it ever so slightly and can feel the wheel and my clicks, so the near silence doesn't throw me off in any way.

This Logitech mouse has an excellent sensor as it's highly responsive and also works great on all surfaces I tested- including a mouse pad, metal, wood, glass and even my pant leg. This mouse initially seemed inconsistent in terms of movement- I was getting different results despite consistent movements with my hand. But that turned out to be a Windows issue resolved by turning off Windows acceleration (go to settings/devices/mouse/additional mouse options/pointer options/enhanced pointer precision and then uncheck the box and click apply).

The sizing of this mouse is okay, but it's not ideal for me. The description says it's a large mouse. The width feels fine and the rubbery thumb rest is comfortable, but the mouse is just too short for me. I wear a woman's size large glove and my fingers are long, and this mouse just has a short, chubby feel to me. The surface area on top is only about 3-1/2" long and from there it abruptly drops down from its highest point (about 1-1/4" high) and has a total length of only about 4-1/4". The proportion feels off and would fit me better if the surface extended about another 1". My Logitech mouse at work is truly a large mouse that fits me great (it's about the same height and width but longer) and noticeably reduces fatigue. title: USB port failure
text:
I'm a Logitech fanboy I guess. They have been the one brand of keyboard and mouse that I was always happy with whether it was a cheap $20 combo or a $300 plus steering wheel. Even had their programmable remotes. I bought this to replace an old K400 that is at least 6 years old. I'm using it to type this, the only thing wrong with it is some of the letters are worn off.

I get home tonight go to get on my computer and the keyboard kept losing connection. Then I noticed the power indicator blinking red so the battery was dead. I had noticed the charge port/USB connector was getting loser and loser over the last two months. I plugged it in and the thing didn't feel like it was hooked and no indication it was connected. So I went and got a better cable from my bedroom I used to charge my phone. Same thing and then I noticed the USB connector was pushing inside. Took the keyboard apart, which was not easy and cracked the outer housing on one end. There was nothing that could be done to reconnect the charging plug.

text: I searched and read reviews for 2 days before I decided to take my chance and purchase a Logitech ClearChat H390. I am often one who believes if you pay more you get better quality.  However, not so in this case!  I had compared the prices of a few other brands and it was in the back of my mind that I should spend more since I plan to use this for online class and seminar participation.  For the price, this headset had superb performance - crisp clear microphone (everyone in the seminar could hear me clearly) and I could hear the content from other presenters also very clearly.  I saw the comments about discomfort but I did not experience that during participation in about 3 two hour seminars so far.  My head is a size 7 1/2 and there was probably up to another 1/2 inch to expand the size.  So possibly if your head is larger than that or your ears are wider than that span, it might be different.  This has a USB plug in only and it was plug and play for me, I am using a 2014 Intel i7-3632 QM CPU processor.  There was no installation, but it did delay for two seconds before my computer picked it up.  For the microphone function, it does have the capability to talk hands free, the silver button in the center activates it with one click and then you will see a blinking light.  ONE OTHER HUGE NOTE:  I see that the reviews go all the way back to 2008.  This in itself should be a positive indicator.  Most companies will take their product off the line if it is not having success.  I thought this product was brand new, so I am surpised that it's been around for 8 years.

title: Just received this today and I am returning it - Doesn't function like other Harmony remotes I've owned
text:
This remote has such limited functionality you might be better with several separate remotes. It does not function like other Harmony remotes I've owned, not even a model I have which was their bottom of the line 12 years ago.

I should have read the one star reviews before purchasing it. While you can program it to control up to 8 devices you can not program it for more than one activity. The activity most people will program is watching TV and it will do that OK as long as you don't need complicated options. So if you've programmed the one activity to watch TV then you can't program it to watch a DVD (and/or Blu-Ray/and or Roku, etc). Oh it will control the DVD, but there is no easy way to switch the TV to the input you need for your DVD or turn the DVD on automatically when you hit the DVD button. Same with other devices. So you end up having to go through a very confusing sequence of steps or, easier yet, keep multiple remotes on hand.

The other Harmony remotes I've had did multiple 'ACTIVITIES', in addition to watching TV. So if you wanted to watch, for example, the DVD all you had to do was hit the Watch DVD button and it would turn on the DVD, and switch the TV (or receiver) to the DVD input settings automatically and turn off any devices that were on for the last activity that are no longer needed. You could also program any button within that activity to issue any command for any other device (such as changing the input on the TV when the DVD is selected). Not so with this model.

I'd recommend either getting a Harmony that can do many different ACTIVITIES or just sticking with your mess of old seperate remotes.

I'm tutoring a fifth grader in reading. One of his vocabulary words this week was "opera". To illustrate, I pulled up one of the Pappageno/Pappagena duets from The Magic Flute available on YouTube, and plugged my iPad into these speakers. We watched and listened, and...Oh wow, oh wow, oh wow! The sound was ah-mah-zing, and the kid was absolutely rapt for the seven+ minutes of the video. It was one of the best sessions we've ever had, and when I asked if he'd like to see and hear more opera in future sessions, he said, "yes, please."

This kid always responds to questions with a shrug and an "I don't care."

title: 6+ Years of Good and Bad
text:
I recently had to buy this keyboard as a replacement for my old K750 (exact same model), when I tried to connect my old keyboard to a new Macbook Pro and found out that they old keyboard would no longer send out the connection signal. (It still worked perfectly with my old laptop, but it just wouldn't connect to the new one). In any case, I've been using a K750 for years and, for the most part, it's been a pretty good keyboard. I type a LOT and use several applications that require the use of a number pad, so these keyboards have been absolute workhorses for me.

The Good:
Its wireless and very light! I love that I can just pick it up and move it out of the way whenever I need to have something else (like a graphics tablet) right in front of me. They never seem to die (except for that connection signal). Solar = wireless with no batteries! As long as you don't have a problem with connecting to a new computer, they really do last forever. No lag - I honestly cannot tell a difference between typing on this and on a wired keyboard. The action is very quiet. For whatever reason, clicky-sounding keyboards drive me nuts, so I really like that it doesn't bug me while I work.

The Bad:
Solar can be a real pain in the butt. Don't get me wrong - most of the time its great and everything just works. They keyboard stores a fair amount of power to ensure than it'll still work for quite a while, even when you're in very dim light. However, all too often I find myself working for long periods of time in a room that is just a little too dim to make the keyboard happy (especially when working at night). Eventually, I run out of stored power and I've actually had to prop my iPhone up on a book and use its flashlight to give myself enough light to keep typing. It just feels silly to have to do that. Also, the action is not great on this keyboard. Each key sits in its own little indentation and sometimes they catch against the sides of those indentations when pressed. The keyboard as a whole feels somewhat cheaply made, especially the little plastic kickstands on the back. Those little kickstands are so flimsy that I'm amazed that I've never broken one. Finally, if you like gaming even a little bit, this keyboard will drive you a little crazy because it isn't great with the complex simultaneous button presses that you inadvertently find yourself making as you guide a character around the screen. Because of this, sometimes your character won't turn left or right when you want them to and it can really become frustrating.

In conclusion, its a totally decent keyboard, but I honestly regret buying a second one. If I had to do it all over again, I would just get the official Apple keyboard (the one with the number pad). Although its wired (and usb ports are at a premium on a MBP), they quality of the Apple keyboard is dramatically better that the K750. Seriously, it like the difference between an Audi and a Ford. Anyways - hope this helps someone someday!

title: Not perfect, but pretty close
text:
I own three of these all bought over a couple months in 2013. After 3 years, none have ever failed and I've never replaced a battery. One is used for my office PC and the other two are at home; one on a Chromebox and the other gets extremely rare use on a HTPC. I've also used them with an Xbox One, PS3 and a Ubuntu PC. I began buying these after the transmitter in my previous wireless keyboard/mouse combo died on my office PC.

This isn't a perfect keyboard, but it's for what I wanted (no cords, no batteries) it's does the job fairly well.

What works:
1) It's a keyboard with a fairly conventional layout. It performs it's core function well. It's amazing how hard it seems to be to get the basics right when you look at some of the other keyboards out there.
2) It's solar powered. It's really battery powered with the solar cells to keep it charged, but I've never needed to swap the battery. Normal office lighting is more that enough to power it.
3) My office PC is a laptop with a docking station. The Unifying receiver is small enough to just leave plugged to one of the laptop ports when I take it with me. I forget about it. The same can't be said of several of the competing designs.
4) The keyboard is thin and light enough I can fit it in my backpack alongside the laptop sleeve.
5) It has a few media playback function keys. They work fine, I just don't use them much.
6) There is an on/off switch if you need to store/ship it where it won't get light to charge
7) It's so thin I find there's no need for a wrist support. It's almost flush to the desktop.

Now on to the complaints:
1) You really need the PC app to pair the keyboard with the Logitech Unifying USB receiver. I've never had any luck getting the keyboard to pair with a receiver otherwise. This is a nuisance since a good number of the devices I've used with the keyboard aren't PCs and I can see a day coming where I don't have a Windows or Mac PC in the home.
2) It's a bit flimsy feeling. I've occasionally had the rear support legs can pop off, but I've never had one break. After 3 years the rubber feet on my office keyboard began to slide off letting it slide around on my desk too much. I swapped it with my least used one from home.
3) For daily use the keyboard can take some getting used to. My coworkers find it awkward to use the keyboard because of the thin design, but I acclimated in just a couple days.
4) I have a Chromebox I use mainly for Internet surfing which doesn't take much keyboard use. When I use do pick up the keyboard seems to always take several keystrokes to wake up the connection and start working, but then it's fine.

text:
Logitech gear can be hit or miss, most of what I've seen of it is cheap junk that works, but won't last long. This remote does not give me that impression--it feels fairly solid. Beyond that though, it falls a bit short. Here are my con's

1. What I don't like about modern day devices is that you have to create accounts on the manufacturer's web site to manage the devices. For the Harmony, the up-side to that is a quick and fairly painless setup. So at best this issue is a mixed bag.
2. The amount of batteries required to operate the Harmony is ridiculously small considering it has an LCD screen with back-light. An e-Ink screen would be better for its small power requirements, but without that, You'd think that more batteries would be better.

title: A very capable rumble and wireless gamepad
text:
I have been using a controller from my PS4, which has mostly worked fine. Two major problems I had was that it seems a lot of game designers for PC, use the Xbox button layout and color, so I would have to keep looking to see what I should be pushing. Second, being there is no wireless receiver, I have to keep the joystick plugged in, which limits your distance from the computer and since the connection is loose can come unplugged from the joystick.
So I looked for a comparable game pad that wasn't too expensive. There are quite a few and you can go cheaper but I have used many Logitech products in my life and enjoy their quality and the reviews were mostly positive.

The gamepad has a good weight to it and certain aspects have a good feel. The grip coating underneath feels smooth yet gripping. The thumbsticks look very similar to a PS4 thumbstick though the movement seems a little more loose that a PS4 controller.
The buttons on the right are modeled after an Xbox controller scheme so button mappings shown in games match up exactly in those games.
The gamepad looks like you took prominent features from both PS4 and Xbox controllers and put them together.
The gamepad also has a rumble feature you can turn off or on, this is nice if you want it and that you can turn it off to save on battery usage is also nice.
The gamepad uses 2 AA batteries, which is nice in some ways. Easily replaceable but a continuing cost, at least you do not have to remember to put it on a charger or cord. Logitech also was generous enough to include Duracell batteries instead of a cheaper generic brand.
For connectivity, the gamepad comes with a standard small Logitech usb transponder just like their mice and keyboards do. I did wind up going to their page and downloading drivers to get the gamepad working on all games, some just didn't want to recognize it.

The negatives I would say about the stick are few but may be big depending on how you feel about them. First, the handles seem a little on the short side. To me its like a lot of compact pistols where your pinky hangs off the end, same here. It just does not feel like you have a good firm grip, you don't feel like you are going to drop it, you just don't quite feel comfortable. Maybe it's just me. If you are close to a computer store that has products on display and this one is, I would suggest picking it up and holding it to see what you think.
Second, The thumbsticks have a thinner clackety kind of sound too them, which I don't notice as much with the PS4 controllers. Upon hearing me use the F710 for the first time, my wife asked if something was wrong with it. Though a little noisy and a little on the looser side, it doesnt seem to affect any game play. I notice the noise more since she pointed it out.

Overall I like the F710, I think for the most part you will be happy with it. There are many many products out there, especially in a cheaper bracket but you will get what you pay for. I highly suggest reading reviews on them and if you can put your hands on them, do so before buying.

title: Yes, I really submitted this review with my big toe
text:
Trackballs, far superior to the mouse, but relegated to red-headed stepchild status in the world of human interface devices. For those of you here because the great Cordless Optical Trackman has been discontinued, like all other successful trackballs, you will be disappointed.
--This is a light weight, cheap feeling tack ball. It serves its purpose with some level of competence, but is no competitor to the Trackman and other quality trackballs.
--The buttons and wheel have the feel of cheap mouses that are pre-packaged with towers, and are immediately shoved in the darkest corner of a desk drawer.
--The ball is very light, and although smooth, it's a thumb-ball. This is a major point of contention for me, so I feel that it bears special attention in the hopes that somebody who has leverage at Logitech or some shake-it-up device manufacturer will realize, for once and for all, that

***The Thumb is Great for Grasping Bananas, but NOT for Fine Motor Control or Precise Movements***

Millions of years of evolution and specialization, bucked for the thumball. Yes, you will adapt to using your thumb, but you could just as easily use more dexterous appendages such as your elbow or your big toe.

In an effort to find nice things to say about this trackball so that Logitech will continue to at least make it, the colors are very trendy, the batteries last a long time, the Bluetooth dongle is discreet (although it would be absolutely fantastic if some MBA could earn his keep and get the engineers to put a blue LED in it), and there is a very nice finger rest to the left of the left click button. Of the non-mouse options out there, this thumbball is the best of the options out there, which is kinda like saying that "Milwaukee's Best".

title: Overall good full coverage protection and stand feature for an iPad Mini 2
text:
On a recent family road trip I ended up dropping the family's ipad 2 (in the standard apple case) out of the car, shattering the screen. Instead of paying $100+ replacing the screen on this old iPad, we bought a new iPad mini 2. Since our young kids use it regularly and not wanting to break the new one, I looked for a case that offered full protection.

Overall this case offers great protection on all the edges, full back coverage, as well as a cushioned front cover to help protect the screen when closed. The edges of this case are fairly thick compared to other case options, but I am sure this will help if dropped. Once opened, the front cover creates a base with multiple ridges in it where the edge of the ipad can be set into to hold it up. If you just want to watch a video in this fashion it works great, but if you touch the ipad too much or too aggressively it can easily fall out of its ridge. Also when you want to just hold the ipad the front cover can be kind of awkward to fold behind the ipad.

My only real concern for the case is the limited front protection. When closed I think it does pretty well, but in a drop scenario I worry the front cover will come loose and allow the screen to be unprotected. Also the rear case only raps around the ipad to be just about level with the screen, thus the screen would hit the ground at the same time as the case if dropped face first with the front open. Also, due to the thickness of the side of the case, the volume and sleep/wake buttons can be a little harder to operate.

I first found this case at a local store but ended up getting an exceptionally better price on Amazon!

title: Fits my Work Needs
text:
I am currently using this on a work laptop for my many online meetings, primarily though WebEx but also Skype for Business and GoToMeeting. My co-workers tell me my voice is clear, I can hear theirs very well, and the mute and volume buttons on the line are very useful. I find the on the ear design a little tight for me, and I would really say it's comfortable nor really uncomfortable. The padding really is okay for an on the ear style. It is definitely a set I take over pretty quickly. In comparison I use a Bose set for my phone, and a wireless set for my desktop for gaming. This was really just something I wanted to attach to the work machine all the time and readily available to just hook up. For the price, it's actually pretty good for what I use it for... I just wouldn't ever choose something like this to wear for hours. However if a family member wanted something for under twenty and to put on for no more than an hour... this is a good start until they decide to upgrade. This is also good for anyone concerned about the cost of replacing it.

As for ease of use with the software, Windows 7 picked it right up with no problems. I haven't attached it to my Windows 10 machine. The only program that seems to have trouble with it sometimes is Skype for Business. This is mostly when you attach it after someone rings you. I am told by some other co-workers this something they too experience with other sets and brands so it's not a downside.

title: Excellent mouse. Battery life is AMAZING! I haven't charged it yet!
text:
The only other wireless mouse I've ever owned was the Razer Mamba and then the Mamba 2012. To call them wireless is kind of a joke. They would last maybe a day or 2. It was really a wired mouse that can go wireless for a little while. I thought all wireless mice were like this until I purchased this mouse. It's been 3 weeks and I still haven't had to charge it yet! It's amazing! When I checked the status on the mouse, it still has one light on, meaning it can still go for another few days!

My favorite feature so far is being able to switch computers with the push of a button. I have a desktop and a laptop. Whenever I need to switch between them, all I have to do is press the button from 1 to 2 and it seamlessly changes to the next computer or back. There's no time to repair, or find the new computer. It's amazing!

Tracking: Excellent. It works on pretty much all surfaces that I've tested. My previous mice worked on most surfaces but on black or very dark surfaces (like my black computer desk) they flake out or go erratic. This mouse works on everything I've tested. It's truly all-terrain!

Battery: My chief concern, is excellent! Like I said, it's been weeks and it still has juice. The mouse has the option to be charged while in use, so when it's low I can just plug it in and continue working while it juices up.

Wireless: EXCELLENT! I LOVE the fact that you can connect to different computers with the push of a button. The mouse came with a unified Logitech dongle which I plugged into my desktop. It connected to that flawlessly. The mouse is also compatible with BLUETOOTH 4.0 and I use that to connect to my laptop. No more keeping a wired mouse around for my laptop. Once set up, I just push the button on the bottom of the mouse from "1" to "2" and it's connected to my laptop. It's effortless. There's a "3" for a third device should I choose to use it. The only issue is that it does NOT connect to BLUETOOTH 2.0 dongles. I tried on another older laptop and the BLUETOOTH cant discover the mouse. The ONLY issue I've noticed is that the wireless signal does get conflicted with other wireless devices. When my Xbox 360 is turned on and the controller is in the same room the mouse SPAZES OUT! IT becomes unusable. With my PS3 the movements sometimes gets jerky once in a while but is still usable. Be careful if you have one of these devices in the same room.

Ergnomics/feel: This is the only part that I feel the mouse could use some improvement. While most of the buttons are great, the two thumb buttons for forward and BACKWARD for internet pages are not very well designed. The back button is large and easy to feel-push. The FORWARD button (the smaller one) is near impossible to find on your thumb. It's tiny and far recessed and I often have to poke around to find it by feel. It needs to be much larger. Furthermore the extra button hidden at the thumb-rest is also near impossible to find. The placement is awkward and only works at a very specific point on the rest. I would honestly prefer a real button than a hidden button underneath the plastic. Furthermore the action of busing the button downward with your thumb is also awkward and uncomfortable.

Finally, the scroll mouse is great. It took some time to get used to the "free scroll" spin but I use it all the time now.

Overall it's an excellent mouse. I highly recommend it even with a few awkward button issues.

I spent hours trying to fix this and finally gave up.

2. The headset is way too tight, and there is no way to adjust it. My head is of average size, so if yours is just a little bigger, you aren't going to like this at all.

3. You can probably charge it off an AC adapter, but it comes with a real kludge of a charging stand that only plugs into a USB port. Forget about trying to use the headphones while they are charging - you can't despite the advertising hype.

4. There are probably a lot more broken features, but since none of the features work thanks to the broken software, I have no idea what those might be.

On the up side, you can make it work if you just plug the receiver into a USB port and turn it on. It actually sounds fairly good. I am keeping mine as a spare to be used only when my other good ones die.

Programs straight from an iPad very simply. Name a few actions and what devices you want to use, I think this was even suggested. It cycles through and corrects itself if things don't turn on the way it's supposed to.

My system is a DIRECTV dvr, LG UHDTV, Bose surround sound, Xbox one s, and LIFX bulbs. I also have an ecobee3, not sure what this needs integration for though, but it does work.

My entertainment stand is open but the hubs IR works every time without using the secondary blaster. Even on the Xbox that says it would likely be needed.

The remote itself feels really nice and feels nice and sturdy. The only button I miss is the "skip ahead" button. Not really much to mention, it's RF and not IR so you don't need to aim it. A little worried about the little "watch" battery having a long life, I will update if that's the case.

Photo isn't great, but the Hub is top left by the purple vase thing. Works from there, even to the Xbox down on the bottom..

I wanted physical Red, Yellow, Blue, Green buttons to coordinate with our DirecTV service.
I already had an IR repeater system in-place, so I didn't need any thing else.

Regular AA batteries, no need to a charger stand. I got tired of having to return the Harmony One to its stand. Rechargeable batteries work great for this remote.

I will absolutely get a second one of these for my basement entertainment system, and replace anyone's Harmony remote with this one, as long as it meets the needs for the number of devices they need to control.
