I've been using this trackball for nearly 5 years now with no issues at all. I'm on my computer off and on throughout the day so I don't ever turn the trackball off. I use it several hours a day and batteries typically last me 6-8 months. I use several other wireless devices in close proximity (including a Logitech wireless keyboard on this computer) and have no problems with the signal or interference or anything.

I do have to pop the ball out every couple of days and clean the rollers inside. I have no idea how they get so gunky! The scroll wheel started acting up recently so I wound up taking the whole thing apart and found a bunch of lint and dust tying that up. But like I said, that's after nearly five years of HEAVY use.

When this trackball finally dies, I will definitely replace it with another Logitech product.

text:
The dream of a cordless, battery-less keyboard at a non-Apple price lured me in to buy this keyboard, but I have been constantly frustrated by lag of typing and lack of charge.

Don't buy this keyboard if you have a dark room. Even if you have a lot of windows, you might prefer to use a computer in a dark room, especially if you are watching Netflix or something, and in this case you probably won't like this keyboard. Indoor lighting has not been enough to keep a charge, and as a result I have been regularly interrupted by keystrike lag and charging delays, which has caused me to botch sections of video games, to execute typos in emails, and to have to point a light source directly at the keyboard while I go take a dump to stall for time.

Fair judgment on me: don't buy a solar-charging keyboard if you live in relative darkness. Nevertheless I was too optimistic that *any* light source would work, and even during the best light days I still have lag issues.

I'll go back to the battery powered ones.

title: People love this keyboard because it uses solar power - they ...
text:
I give it a 3.5 overall, but not leaning toward a 4.

People love this keyboard because it uses solar power - they don't have to buy batteries or plug it in. This is true, but what most people don't realize is that this still requires a battery to store that power inside of the keyboard, and just like every other rechargeable battery, it does have a life span of usability. Logitech installs a flat lithium rechargeable battery inside, but they didn't give us the ability to replace the battery when it starts to fail. So, you are left with one of two options... 1) find hacking instructions online that tell you how to do it. The problem is that the battery compartment is built so that it is very difficult to remove the battery, and from reports by people who have hacked their keyboard, they find their keyboard often failing after spending the $10 for a new battery. 2) Toss the old keyboard and buy another. This is not environmentally conscience on Logitech's part. It is greedy.

If you are in this to save money, I would estimate you would use about 16 AA batteries in a 3 year span with typical use of a Mac wireless keyboard. That would cost you about $15 if you bought them in 4 packs. You can most certainly use rechargeable AA's as well in the Mac wireless keyboard. If you are in it to be environmentally conscience, well, you have to dispose of this at some point because either the battery or solar panels will eventually wear out. Mine has lasted about 3 years (coincidentally, the warranty is 3 years).

The only other real issue I have experienced is that sometimes there is a lag in what I am typing and what appears on the screen. When this happens, I also notice a tendency for the keyboard to double up on characters. For example: If I type "Amazon", it may show on my screen as, "AAmazzon". This has happened on 3 different iMacs I have owned, so I'm certain this is an issue with the keyboard communicating with the dongle properly. This happens rarely, but does happen.

Also, the feet seem flimsy. I haven't had issues with feet breaking, but I can see that being an issue with someone who has children that can be a bit more rough with it.

I'm not suggesting not to buy this keyboard. I'm just point out the facts that many people don't consider when they buy this. Most write a review after first use up to a month of ownership.

Overall, it worked well for me over 3 years. Will I buy another? Well, I'm considering that right now. So far, I haven't found a better keyboard out there that offers the 10 key and solar charging. If my wireless mac keyboard had a 10 key, it would be the keyboard I use... but not even the new keyboard that charges via lightning cable offers that.

Just keep all this in mind with this.

title: It's lasting fine / how to clean after a spill
text:
My review below about cleaning up after a spill is rather old now and the keyboard still has all important functions- it cleaned up great. However, one of the legs on the underside finally broke when the keyboard was dropped from a height of a few feet- frankly it is a marvel they are so sturdy, though I wish they were designed to be more robust. Fortunately, I was able to buy a replacement on another site for $7. Rather steep for a one-inch piece of plastic, but without it, I'd either be replacing the whole keyboard or just constantly irritated. Old review below.
----
I've used this keyboard for several months. I've forgotten my initial irritations with the layout and feel, whihc differes a bit from real apple keyboards- I think anyone can adjust to it. Most importantly, the keyboard just flat-out works. No power or connection issues at all.

Here's one other fact that matters a lot. I spilled a glass of wine on the right half of the keyboard. Wine flowed into 8 keys. After draining and drying, the keyboard still worked, but the keys were stiff and lacked the same feel of the others. The good news is that the keys can be popped off for cleaning. But you may want to do it carefully and in a specific manner.

First, the big keys are pretty easy to deal with and can be pulled up and viewed up close to determine how to pry them away from the surface. I've done that with the space bar and a few others. Each of the small keys is held in place at the position closer to the operator by a slide-in hinge arrangement. This is not the area to pull against. On the side furthest from the operator, the key is attached by a snap-and-hold arrangement. This is the side to lift, almost as if you are opening a lid that faces away from you, in order to free the key. Once that side is free, the key can be removed from the hinged side area easily. With the key open, the plastic cap and the interior space on the keypad can be cleaned- again, I've seen no adverse reaction to applying small amounts of water- and the key just push-snapped back into place. Obviously, there is no guarantee that you can do this over and over without long-term damage to the attachment points, but this keyboard has survived the process once and dried up to demonstrate complete functionality. [That was 18 months ago, at least.]

title: Room for improvement but it's the best option out there for complex home theater systems.
text:
Remote has long life battery. Hub includes one IR transmitter with a really long wire. Hub can support another IR blaster.

This is absolutely a 5 star product that can really replace all your remotes. But there are some caveats:

1. It's not a universal remote. Someone can't walk into your house and just pick it up and start watching TV. But if you launch an activity (from your smartphone or tablet most likely), then the remote will be usable by anyone.
2. The pre-set buttons on the remote (3 buttons, which can do 6 activities): It is hard to remember what each of the 6 activities are, so I end up not using them and use my iphone to launch activities. I wish there was an easy way to identify what the 6 activities are. I ended up taping a small piece of paper to the bottom with the 6 activities listed.
3. The activities can be edited to add programming steps, but there are still some limitations. You can't add a step to turn off a device, for instance. So you can't have an activity that turns on your amp, changes the input, turns on the tv, but then turn off your amp (which would pass sound through to the tv). Minor complaint but sometimes I just want to hear the news on the TV speakers, not my thumping home theater speaker system.
4. Why is it limited to 8 devices. Sounds greedy, but there are other things that would be nice to control. Electric movie screen, electric room shades, Nest thermostat, etc. So it can control all those things, but I used all 8 slots (PS3, PS4, Amp, TV, Projector, Roku, Apple TV and Xfinity Set-top box). I would have added the window shades and projector screen if I could have.

Still a great thing, and I really truly put all the other remotes away and I use this to watch all those things. The other remotes are still needed for special tasks specific to each thing (going into setup screens, for instance, to make changes to the Amp setup, Projector setup etc). But for the normal stuff like watching a movie on the projector, I use the Harmony.

title: Limited, But It Works
text: I now have in place four -- yes really -- FOUR Logitech Harmony remotes up and running in my house. I have two "Elites," one "Hub," and the Harmony 350. The sophistication and versatility of each seems proportional to the price -- there are very few desired functions that I could not find a way to implement with the Elite or the Hub. The 350 is MUCH more limited. Maddeningly, although it is capable of controlling up to eight devices, it controls only ONE activity automatically. That means, for example, if you have cable TV you can program the remote to turn on the TV and the cable box and set the appropriate input with one push of one button., after which, the remote is automatically set to control all necessary functions (Volume, channel changing, DVR, etc.) However, if you, say, wish to watch a DVD, you're going to have to turn on each device separately and then set the appropriate input. This stuff isn't intuitive for the non-techie -- my wife keeps notes next to the TV -- so I'd never use or recommend this entry level unit for general use. I note that for a few bucks more, the Harmony 650 would seem to address most of my caveats, but I have not had an opportunity to test it.

title: Perfect keyboard as long as you give it enough light
text:
The touch on this keyboard is perfect. It is unusually light but you can feel the key depress. It has a standard layout. It is not miniaturized -- the keys are a good size and well spaced. There is a number keypad (I use it a lot). The arrow keys are in the usual formation as are the other directional keys such as page up and page down. They didn't squish them into two columns to save a half inch of space. So far it checks off all the things I look for in a keyboard and a little more.

What makes this a great keyboard rather than a merely good one is the fact that it is 1/3" high. I'm a touch typist and I usually type without pulling my keyboard shelf all the way out. Unfortunately, the shelf is too close to the desktop. There's only 3" clearance. With thicker keyboard my knuckles kept hitting the shelf. That doesn't happen here. I can even flip up the little feet and type easily.

My only problem was that it wasn't getting any light. I rarely remembered to put it where my desk lamp could charge it. It worked great for about 5 months before dying. For a while I put it in the window every night when I went to bed and it got enough sun to run it a day or two. A month ago I bought this LED strip light https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01HXB38MU/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1
It comes with double-sided mounting board and I stuck it on the underside of my desktop. I plug it into an adaptor on my surge protector. I have it on for about 14 hours a day and, because it's LED, it never gets hot. And my keyboard is fully charged at all times.

Mount placed on driver's side center vent right under the stereo.

I have been a mechanical engineer for 35 years. With extremely limited insight on how this attached to the mount (I first saw it on the Logitech site and it links to Amazon), I wondered how this would mount to the base. It arrived yesterday and boy was I in for a surprise. Oh, here's this thin little glue tape strip on a metal strip to use if you wirelessly charge your phone. You also have to put it at the very bottom of the back. Now as a mechanical engineer, immediately saw a real possible issue with this. The definition of one of the simplest mechanical machines is a lever. "In order to reduce the force needed, the distance over which the force is applied must be increased." So now you have the phone attached by a magnetic force at it's lowest point in the back, thereby making the rest of the phone able to jar and break the force of the magnet. Nothing like commuting 20 miles and wondering more about your phone separating from it's mount than the volumes of traffic and constant traffic lights. It separated from the mount 3 times on the way in, and once on the way home. Luckily it fell into the console and not on the passenger side floor. I had had enough on the 4th fall, the one on the way home. How many times did it move and I stopped it from separating? I lost count. It would be easier to have had a suction cup windshield mount like my Garmin GPS.

Some other issues-
1) Seems to conflict with the vehicle bluetooth, something that this should not circumvent as the vehicle bluetooth is easily louder through the car speakers and better at easily better picking up vocals as opposed to a phone hanging by a magnet and far enough away from your ears and mouth with road noise to affect both.
2) when installing, I did the wave to wake it, etc, but on the road, when trying to initiate a text, forget it. Maybe my Waze being constantly on had some conflict, but still...
3) There were only two choices for music. No way to add other services, nor instructions to play other services already installed on my phone.
4) I received a text which it read, but being that it was going through the phone and not the vehicle bluetooth, the sound was bad, as words were not distinguishable. It asked if I wanted to reply. How could I go wrong at least saying hello? It did not capture the dictation, issue the text.
5) It blocks off a vent completely (air conditioning on an 80 degree day anyone?)
6) As I went to grab is as the top bobbled around with each startup at a light, rounding a turn, numerous times it hit the knob and turned off the radio

Who road tested this? F- grade. $60 dollars? $60 gets me more than a nicely made magnetic pad (The quality of the non-marring finish and it's grip of the vent are exceptional), an app (what do apps usually run on Google Player? A few dollars?), and a slick packaging box. It gets me stability and an app that ties in to the vehicle and seamlessly works. This is not that product.

title: Absolutely love this thin, light, pleasant to type on keyboard
text:
This little guy is the best. When my favorite ipad small and light keyboard (Logitech Ultrathin Keyboard case) was discontinued, I looked exhaustively for another solution that had multiple viewing angles and was thin and lightweight. The best substitute I found was this keyboard combined with the Logitech AnyAngle adjustable cover/ipad stand. This keyboard is soft to the touch, easy to type on, has a really pleasing 'click' when you hit each key - like you're really typing on a chiclet key, and oh my goodness is it thin and light. It fits anywhere. It also opens up a lot of options - like if you're working somewhere without room to prop up your ipad and lay out your keyboard, split them up and put them in different areas! Stand the ipad up and hold the keyboard in your lap - endless options. The only time this isn't the best solution is if you're on a subway or bus or similar, where you're trying to work on your lap and sudden stops can send things flying. In that case an all in one integrated case like Canvas is the easiest and safest option to work with, but in just about every other situation, I prefer to keep an AnyAngle on my ipad and throw this keyboard loose into by bag.

The soft velvety but rubbery fabric-esque 'skin' that covers the whole keyboard is very nice to work on, seems like it would totally protect the keyboard against spills, and the blue is bright and pleasing (slighty less teal/green than it looks in the picture). The 'skin' does stretch out a little over time, but not in a way that makes this unusable. I have used mine daily and thrown it in a packed bag daily for 6 months and the only reason I might by another would be slight aesthetic reasons. And really only slight - it has hardly stretched at all. If I had paid $200 for it, maybe I would be frustrated, but honestly at the price I love this so much that I honestly would buy a few as spares.

One tip - always turn the power switch off on the top right corner of your keyboard once you are done, before throwing it and your ipad, and all your other stuff back in your bag. I learned the hard way when I kept getting locked out of my ipad because everything in my bag was pressing on the keyboard and my ipad thought someone was repeatedly entering the wrong password. That was ridiculously annoying. But once I got in the habit, I always turn it off now before packing up, and flip the power switch on so it connects (5 seconds or less really) when I pull it out again. Really great product - actually going to check out what kind of deals there are on Amazon on other colours!

title: Great in combination with the Logitech Keys to Go portable stand-alone keyboard
text:
This is a great product. I like to have the angle of my ipad just right, and that is constantly changing based on where you are working and what you are doing. This adjusts to whatever angle you bend it to, and it stays there securely until you readjust or close it.

When you first get it, look at a picture online of it in the open position - you actually have to flip the cover all the way over onto the back of your ipad, and then fold the coloured flap down so it faces away from your ipad (colour side out). I used it wrong the first few times - it wasn't intuitive at all how to position it at first, but now I could do it in my sleep (and I probably have!).

I used to swear by the Logitech Ultrathin Keyboard Case for ipads, but my latest one was defective, and the product was discontinued so I couldn't get it replaced. None of the all in one Logitech cases offered the key benefits of that one - very thin, lightweight, and 2 viewing angles. Logitech gave me a replacement Canvas all in one case, but after a bunch of research I realized that the AnyAngle combined with a Logitech Keys to Go was the closest I was going to get to the Ultrathin Keyboard. I would recommend that for times when you have your ipad out on your lap typing on the go, like on a subway or bus - sometime when sudden movements could case multiple pieces to go flying. But all the rest of the time, the AnyAngle and the impossibly tiny and thin portable Keys to Go keyboard let me work with my iPad anywhere. I would still like this to be a little thinner and a little lighter - but it's the best option currently on the market for the flexible and portable type solution I was looking for.

title: Well-built mouse but uncomfortable and much narrower than expected
text:
The mouse was much smaller than I expected. After seeing the images here, reading descriptions and even watching videos about the mouse I was extremely surprised at how actually narrow it is. I don't know, maybe my claw grip is too tight or my position at my desk is not very good but using this mouse gave my hand more cramps than using my Anker Precision Gaming Mouse which had also begun to give me hand cramps and straining my wrist.

The mouse is also just not very comfortable. The texture sides for the thumb and index/ring fingers are a bit too rough and the curved plastic line down the center of the palm area can get a bit irritating to depending on your position. Also, the positioning of the buttons is rather uncomfortable; my thumb kept rubbing against the side "sniper" button and, as others noted, your finger has a tendency to slip on the scroll wheel. However, the fact that there is a thumb rest is definitely a positive and something I discovered I can't live without in a mouse.

The RGB lighting is VERY lackluster, with only the Logitech G staying lit up (which gets covered by your hand anyway). Also, there's sadly no gold plating on the USB plug which I found odd since this is marketed as a heavy-duty gaming mouse. Also, I read and heard a lot of people say this mouse was too heavy for them. I didn't notice this at all. I was expecting like a big, monster of a mouse but this was smaller than the Anker Precision and lighter too.

Overall, this is a decent gaming mouse and is definitely a much more well-built product than the Razer Deathadder and probably on par with my Anker Precision. The main mouse buttons are definitely nicer and sturdier than the Deathadder's so it's most likely going to last much longer. Still, from an $80 gaming mouse I still rather expected more and I learned I'm just going to have to go out to a Best Buy and try mice out before I buy them.

title: Fantastic case for the iPad Pro—longtime user of Logitech keyboards for iPad
text:
I also own the Logitech Type+ keyboard for the iPad Air, which I've used for several years without issue, so when I heard Logitech was making the keyboard for the new Pro, I was up for trying it.

I'm a writer and a child of technology generation, so having a keyboard with my iPad Pro 9.7" is a must. This is the only option, to be honest. Even putting aside the unique connectivity you get with the Logitech keyboard (or the Apple keyboard), this keyboard has the best action and responsiveness of any of the iPad keyboards. While I've owned and used the Zagg Rugged and the keyboard Folio, they are very glitchy and uncomfortable to type on.

Logitech gets it right in every way with this keyboard. The keys are backlit, have a firm responsiveness that mimics a laptop keyboard, and the layout is just right for almost anyone's hands. The keys are where they belong.

The overall protection for the iPad is solid. There are openings on both ends for speakers, which leaves a portion of the aluminum body exposed. But otherwise, it's a solid, firm case that fits the iPad snugly.

The color selection is paltry, and I'd recommend the black material case over the rubberized plastic version, both because it will hold up well and because the black will be easy from which to remove stains.

I had the Mars Red case on my iPad Air, and it's held up great, but the stains are significant. Great color, but on this side of things, I would have chosen a darker shade.

There's no learning curve to this keyboard, so you won't have to worry about getting used to the key spacing.

The only downsides:
The keyboard key on the lower left for those of us who use Mac. If you use your delete key as your backspace and delete key on a Mac keyboard, the keyboard key will drive you batty.

There is only one angle for the screen, which is frustrating for some. But given the build of the keyboard and folio, there's no other way to do it.

The keyboard is not detachable, which would be a huge boon. *However,* Zagg has detachable keyboards, and they are bulky and awkward to work with. So overall, I'd rather deal with removing the case.

Keyboards are going to be heavy. There's no way to make a quality keyboard without that, so the complaint is irrelevant. This is a much lighter keyboard than Zagg's, for example, and it works phenomenally well long-term.

I use my iPad both as a travel laptop and as a graphic arts screen. It's easy to use when you fold the keyboard under the iPad--I just travelled across the country and back, and was able to draw and type and read without any issue with the case.

This is a great case--the best keyboard case out there for iPads. I highly recommend it.

title: Think twice on this one if you have a Mac
text:
I wanted a bluetooth mouse to use with my MacBook Pro. After looking at all the alternatives I decided to go with the MX master, even though there were sporadic reports of the mouse having issues. When I first got the mouse there was a little adjustment period since the pointer was not quite as "smooth" as my previous mouse. But, I loved the form factor and the bluetooth so I kept using it and eventually got used to it. I would have rated this mouse in the 4-5 star range at that point if that were all the issues. But they weren't

Besides the mouse I also use a pair of bluetooth headphones. And I had used the two in concert for last few months without any issues. Unfortunately a few weeks ago my headphones started stuttering continually, making them completely unusable. I tried re-pairing the headphones to no avail. Next, I got a different pair of bluetooth headphones. Same thing.

At my office we do make bluetooth devices so I thought it might be interference from one of our prototype devices so I asked around. Nope, nothing new or being worked on. So, after months of working just fine I ended up with a pair of bluetooth headphones that no longer worked. It happens. However, when the second (completely different brand) of cans had the exact same issue I started looking for other sources of interference. And it did not take long, when I turned off my mouse both pairs worked just fine. Nice

Once I had discovered this, closer scrutiny also revealed that the mouse was continually trying to pair even though it was connected and in use. I am guessing that is why the battery went from needing a charge every couple of weeks to every couple of days. A quick google search indicated that I was not the only one with these types of issues.

So, after just 7-8 months I ended up having to replace my mouse again. This time I bought an Apple Magic Mouse 2, and it was not until I started using that mouse that I realized just how jerky and difficult the MX master was to use. I had initially avoided the Magic Mouse based on reviews and I now know I made a mistake. The Apple mouse works great and if nothing else is a lot more refined and behaved. Will it last longer than 7-8 months? Not sure but to date the only mouse I have ever had that did not was the MX master.

If you are a mac user and in the market for a mouse, do yourself a favor and at least try the Magic Mouse 2. You will notice a huge difference. At the very least think twice about the Mx Master with a Mac. Logitech has a track record of issues with Apple bluetooth and as a user it really matters very little who's "fault" it is. In the end if they don't work well together it is not worth it.

title: Why mess with tradition?
text: Let me start by saying that I have tried many keyboards over my 35 years with computers.  This is my favorite to date.  I was looking for an illuminated keyboard for working late at night.  I also wanted keys that had a soft touch and quiet operation (no klickety klack).The built in palm wrest is a nice bonus.  The only reason I am knocking 1 star off is that they doubled the size of the delete key and moved its partner, the insert key, up into the function keys which in turn shifted the print key over and hid the scroll key as a secondary function key on the pause/break key.  WHY?  This keyboard totally screws up the traditional layout of these keys.  Do people really need a large delete key 4 times the size of the insert key?  I use the print key quite a bit for screen capturing and the scroll key for my KVM.  This continually throws me off from every other keyboard I have owned and my keyboard that I use at work.  Many of their other keyboards preserve the traditional layout so I'm not sure why they would mess with this.

title: The included FPS profile enhances footsteps further more so now it's so easy to know the position of your enemy to make ...
text:
This headset definitely brings your FPS gaming experience to the next level! The 7.1 works well in CS:GO and when I used a regular stereo headphone, enemy positioning has been okay. I was able to distinguish if the footsteps are coming from left or right.

With the G933, I now am able to pinpoint the footsteps whether they are coming from the front or back as well as left or right. The included FPS profile enhances footsteps furthermore so now it's so easy to know the position of your enemy to make a kill.

There are also a handful of headphone connectors included so you can use this with almost any device possible. The lighting is pretty cool but burns battery pretty quickly, and you charge it with a USB cable, there is no cool cradle included.

Update: few month since I've owned this headset. Now I play a lot of Overwatch, and this headset works well with the game as well, can hear footsteps and pinpoint the location of the enemy.

Battery life is very good as well, can last 10+ hrs of gaming before needs a charge. (I turn all LED effects off)

The microphone works ok, not the best I've used. But it's easily retracted for storage when not in use.

Overall highly recommended headset for FPS gaming.

text:
This keyboard is very cool. I have been using a Microsoft wireless keyboard that's been driving me nuts with it's lag, battery appetite, and general bugginess, so I'm happy to be going back to a wired keyboard. Opening the box showed me this isn't any old keyboard. The cord is long, and has a cloth exterior. The keyboard itself is 2-3 times heavier than any keyboard I've owned in recent years. The font is a bit different too, and I really like it. The plastic seems to be a high quality, some of the seams are a bit sharp though. My box didn't have any instructions or software, so I'm not sure that they are included.

Windows instantly recognized the keyboard, and I had no problem using it immediately. The default behavior for the keyboard is cycle through a bunch of colors. That was cool for a minute, and then it got really distracting. So I googled and found the software to install. The software is pretty intuitive to use, and I was able to lock in a color I liked in a minute or so. I also found out what the two mystery buttons are on the top, one is a toggle to lock certain keys during game play, the other turns off the keyboard lighting. The media control buttons worked fine with no setup. Looking around the Logitech software, there are games with pre-defined setups that can be applied to the keyboard, very cool. This keyboard is sort of retro, in that it makes alot of noise, so if you're looking for silent gaming, this isn't your keyboard.

title: Logitech Z623 Speaker System.....Mind blown!
text:
Well....mind blown.

After my Bose Companion 3 Series II set went bad (distortion then lost a channel) I thought I would have to spend a large sum of money to get similar sound for my computer. The Bose system was some of the best computer audio I have heard but that model is no longer available, and similar Bose systems are nearly $300. I paid $250 for my Bose system several years ago.

For 128 dollars I didn't expect much from this Logitech Z623 system. A guy posted a video here on Amazon and I thought the sound was pretty good so I took a chance, knowing that Amazon is really good about returned merchandise and I could send it back.

I WON'T be sending it back! The sound easily meets or exceeds my old Bose system and the fit, finish and workmanship is superb. The bass is clean, deep, realistic and TIGHT and most important NO BOOMING which is almost a given with cheap speaker systems (don't turn the bass up to max though). The highs are crisp and tight both on commercial recordings and my own creations (I do home recording for fun).

I love the controls being mounted on the right speaker too. Many sub-woofer systems have the bass control mounted on the back of the woofer....a complete PITA.

One caveat; You won't have to worry about disturbing the neighbors with this system (you might have a problem with folks in another room however..LOL!!!). Turning the bass and/or the volume up too high will easily overdrive this system into distortion. So, my thoughts on the 200 watt output? That's designed to impress the innocent. An RMS specification would be more honest and would not be 200 watts. I would have thought Logitech would know that by now. For sitting near the computer or being in the same room you'll be rewarded with clean rich sound with realistic bass.

At $128, this system is a bargain in my opinion.

title: Good But Not Great (UPDATE)
text:
I purchased this mouse from a big box store a couple of months ago. It’s connected to a MacBook Pro Retina (early 2013) notebook which is clamshelled and attached to 2 large displays. I’ve had no problem with this mouse integrating with my Mac hardware or software, with the possible exception of the arrow buttons not working as well as I would like for web browsing. I use the mouse several hours daily for many business apps, including web, graphics, MS Office, coding, etc. I am not a gamer, but other than that, I am certainly a power user when it comes to a computer mouse.

My hands are on the large side, and I’ve been told they are strong, which I state to describe that my mouse needs to be durable. This mouse has held up well in that respect so far. This mouse replaced an old Microsoft ergonomic mouse (yes, I used a MS mouse on my Mac, Apple mice not my thing), which had a high profile and was somewhat round in shape that I used for several years but is no longer made. I am pleased with the ergonomics of this Logitech mouse.

The wireless connectivity and responsiveness of the mouse have are very good, though I use the mouse in close proximity to the USB receiver. I’m surprised that there is no way to insert the small receiver in the mouse for travel purposes. For me this is not an inconvenience, but it might be for someone who needs to pack the mouse for travel. I leave the receiver in the USB port all the time since it does not protrude much or interfere with inserting the notebook in a protective sleeve, so I’m ok with that. But it’s not a plus.

The programmable buttons overall are good. Their functions can be customized in many ways and the programming interface is easy to use and understand. The clickable thumb button has come in very handy. I use it to activate Mission Control since I often have many windows open at the same time. However, zoom button and two arrow buttons are essentially useless to me. The zoom button is so tiny and awkwardly placed that I find it more trouble than it is worth to assign a function. The arrow buttons are not as dependable as I would expect for web browsing, so I do not use those either. The left and right click buttons are responsive and comfortable to click. The scroll wheel is dependable, though I’m not much of a middle-clicker and the scroll wheel click on this mouse is not so great that it’s prompted me to use it.

Now to the battery life. This mouse is touted to last up to 30 days between charges. That’s completely false, assuming you actually use the mouse. My experience has been 2-3 days at most, and that is a huge disappointment. As of this writing, I had been using the manufacturer-provided GP ReCyko rechargeable battery that came with the mouse. Today, I swapped that for a Sanyo Enloop to see if that rechargeable battery lasts longer. If it does, I will update this review. However, I have read other reviews that state that the Sanyo Enloop was not an improvement in battery life on this mouse.

One last thing that I am very disappointed with is the how the charging cord connects to the mouse. The port on the mouse is very small, and it is quite cumbersome to plug the charging cord into the mouse, it usually takes 2-3 tries. That makes the short battery life even more of a problematic issue. When the mouse is plugged into the power cord, it the mouse works fine while charging, but since this is promoted to be a wireless mouse, that shouldn’t need to come into play as often as it does.

UPDATE: I've been using the Sanyo Enloop rechargeable batteries for 3 weeks and the battery life is about twice as long. With the Sanyo rechargeable battery the mouse will hold a charge for 5 to 7 days depending on use. Although this is less than advertised, it is reasonable IMHO. My conclusion is that the GP ReCyko battery that was included with the mouse is inferior, which is often the case with manufacturer-provided batteries that are included with electronic devices. I cannot say definitively whether or not the Sanyo Enloop is the best rechargeable battery to use in this mouse. Perhaps a different brand would do even better. But I certainly recommend using a name-brand battery in this mouse. My rechargeable batteries are Enloop and Amazon brand. The Enloop typically outperforms the Amazon rechargeables (which are satisfactory for their lesser price) in other devices -- and since this mouse is a heavy-use item, I wanted to use the best rechargeable battery I had on hand. At least now I can use this mouse for a decent stretch of time without needing to recharge it while I'm using it. If you are going to use a premium battery with the mouse, you can consider this an update to 4 stars.

text:

My cohost heard the drastic change in my audio and decided to get her own soon after.

So, it's easy to set up. Good ol' plug-n-play technology. Works great for recording into Audacity or whatever your software of choice is. The design's cute, the sound is great, and I love the handy tripod - perfect for balancing on a desk. For a hobbyist, this is just all around fantastic.

My one complaint is so minor as to not lose any stars - the red light on the front of the mic to indicate it's on is a bit bright, and since I tend to get all up in my mic's business while recording it can be a lil annoying. I wish the light were on the side or back instead of right there on the top. I'm planning on getting some electrical tape to deal with this issue, though, so whatever. Just something to take note of.

Also note this iCE one doesn't have the little switch thing advertised on the regular Snowball. I decided to cheap out and get this version, which I'm happy with, but that one looks like it lends a little more flexibility. Which you choose depends on your budget and whim.

Just a great mic. I'm really happy with this purchase, and it's made my show sound loads better.

Biggest issue for me is that to use all of the function keys require the download of an app that hasn't been updated to OSX Sierra and the Logitech site does not say so. Using the app caused my system to crash and I had to revert to an old version of my system (using Time Machine) to get my computer functioning again. Logitech folks weren't all that helpful only saying to wait until the app is updated.

It is a bit of a pain to have no quick way to check the battery status of the keyboard as I can using the bluetooth icon at the top of my screen.

I also notice that at times the bluetooth connection is lost for 2 or 3 seconds but then reconnects. Otherwise it has a very good feel when typing and I love that it is rechargeable.

Update as of 9 July 2017. Now I do have experience switching back and forth between my Mac Mini 2011 running Sierra and my iPad Pro. The switch can take as long as 5-7 seconds but sometimes it is with 2-3 seconds. Acceptable but not as advertised. Plus the connection is sometimes dropped, not often, but often enough to notice. On Friday I went to the Logitech site to get help and could not login, even though I'm registered. I gave up trying to ask for help on my connection issue but noticed that the app for the 811 was updated so I downloaded it hoping it might help my connection issues. Within an hour it again crashed my Mac (PC style) and I had to restore it from a Time Machine back up. It's a good product with lousy support and an amazingly careless software release process. DO NOT DOWNLOAD THEIR APP to make the keyboard controls visible on your desktop. I'm also dropping my rating from a three to a two in the hopes their product support people take notice.

title: Doesn't work & worst customer service ever
text:
I purchased this as a more ergonomic alternative to a mouse for my husband, who does most of his work on the computer and has chronic repetitive strain issues. He was unable to get it to work while I was deployed overseas, so it went back in the box and waited for me to come home. I was also unable to get it to work, and in troubleshooting I noticed that the green LED that is supposed to come on briefly when you flip the power switch was never lighting up, indicating a defective unit.

I went to the Logitech website, registered the product, and filed a claim to try to get it replaced. I was unable to respond to their initial e-mail for a few days because of the Christmas holidays, and they decided to just close the ticket as "resolved", plus I noticed that the e-mail they sent me addressed me as "Jose", so apparently a copy/paste job. I was miffed, frankly, but I did at least get an apologetic response and was finally able to get some movement on the claim to get the unit replaced under the warranty.

I provided all of the information requested, along with photos of the unit with the claim number, as requested. It has now been two weeks and I have re-sent the e-mail, and nothing. Complete radio silence. I am very, very displeased.

title: Great headset if on sale. Be aware of possible wireless issue (fix included in this review!)
text:
The G930 is a great headset if you can get it at a good price (I got it during an xmas sale for $70). I would rate these higher, but they have a strange, but totally fixable, issue with disconnecting while wireless. I will include the fix at the end of my review.

Feel 4/5: The padding on the earpads and headband is very nice. It feels like having pillows pressed up around your ears. It's a small gripe, but I wish they didn't have the "pressed around your ears" feel. I feel that the tightness will go away with use though.
Sound 4/5: Great quality and the 7.1 surround sound is noticeable. The earpads make it a little difficult to hear yourself or other things. For some, this is great. Personally, I like to know if someone is talking to me from across the room, even if I have my headset on :)
Mic 5/5: Sounds great and doesn't pick up much background noise. I use a loud clicky mechanical keyboard (cherry mx blues) and the mic only picks up my typing slightly.
Extra Features 5/5: All the extra features are great and totally usable by any type of user. My favorite is probably the mic-mute-when-raised. Very easy to just put the mic out of the way when not in use.

All-in-all, really recommend this headset if it's on sale (I got mine for $70). Really wouldn't get it for any more than $100 though.

And now, the wireless disconnecting fix. This was copied from reddit user /u/TheIsaia:
Go to this Folder: C:\Program Files\Logitech Gaming Software\Resources\G930\Manifest
Copy the Device_Manifest to your desktop or any other location exept the logitech folder. (this will serve as a backup if you mess anything up)
Open the Device_Manifest.xml with notepad, Find Battery turnoffinterval, you can easily find this by pressing Ctrl + F, then searching for "turn" Change the number that should be 980 or similar, change it to 0. This should fix the problem.
Also, if you struggle to acces the file, try to make a copy of it, put it in another folder, do the Changes to the file there, then put it back and replace the Old one. Hope this helps!

This review is written after owning this keyboard/mouse for a little over a year. I used it daily for that period of time in a home office environment. Primarily I use the computer for graphic design, so I am a HEAVY mouse user. Here we go:
The mouse, from the very beginning, had too much time delay in the response. I continued to use the wireless board until just a week ago. I removed the keyboard after a little over a year for two reasons, first, the keyboard keys became VERY sticky. I had to pay attention when I was typing as several of the most commonly used keys would stick (with an associated 'squeak' noise) and not complete the contact with the internal circuit board. Second - and this is more of a 'personal' issue, the keyboard does not have a "Caps Lock" light on it. Believe it or not, the lack of an illuminating light for caps really was a problem for me. I had to start typing to see if the All Caps key was on or off. Bothersome. Went back to a wired keyboard (which has the 'Caps Lock' and 'Num Lock' indicator lights on it). Anyway, thought you should be aware of my experience over time with this keyboard and mouse in my particular business application.

title: Logitech can do no wrong... except with the G933.
text:
I've owned multiple 930 models, and they've all worked flawlessly. The new 933 model leaves much to be desired.

- The headset squeaks constantly around the pivot point between the earmuff and the wishbone that connects to the headband, and is amplified inside the earmuff when you move your head.

- The light patterns will reset every time the machine it's connected to is rebooted.

- The unit constantly needs to be re-synced to the bluetooth dongle. This can be reproduced multiple ways. Walking out of range of the dongle and then having the unit go into power save mode, restarting the computer, or switching audio output devices will cause this issue. This requires you keep a pin to reset the dongle on hand at all times, and then you need to hold the mute button for 15 seconds(sometimes multiple times) to get it to re-sync.

These issues all exist as of firmware 8.82.151 (this issue has persisted across multiple firmware updates), tested on three different Windows 7(SP1 & SP3) machines.

Still a fan of Logitech as a whole. Having owned almost every high-end model of mouse/keyboard/headset they produce, this is the first lemon, but it is a big lemon. Do not buy.

title: Camera works fine, but it has one big issue when running ...
text:
Camera works fine, but it has one big issue when running on linux: its onboard video compression uses UVC 1.5, which isn't currently supported by the linux kernel (despite its release 3 years ago). This means the CPU will have to handle to compression itself, which can be cpu-intensive, or simply impossible on slow machines (like a raspberry pi).

Also, YUV at 30FPS only go up to 848x480. 720p is limited at 10FPS, and 1080p at 5FPS. To keep 30FPS with those resolutions you'll need to go mjpeg (one independent jpeg image per frame), which can become quite big. And no 60FPS option.

These limitations are common for most webcams, so they don't affect the final note too much. It's still a great webcam, and will work nicely with skype or hangout.

All the expected touch gestures for mouse are available, and you can customize how things behave with its software. Mouse click button on top left of keyboard is a nice feature as well. Top row of function buttons can be toggled to normal F buttons, or these pretty cool shortcuts they built in, like media control, launching browser, many others. Light weight design, feels comfortable holding it or laying it my lap. I will say it is entirely light plastic, could definitely easily twist and snap the whole thing into oblivion if I were a child or oblivious to it laying in a chair prior to sitting in it. Luckily neither have proven true.

I've had my pc connected to a large tv for both game and media use, sitting far away obviously a first world problem we all need to solve, and this will do it perfectly. Humorously enough, I've had my wired logitech keyboard and mouse randomly freeze recently and was able to use this to bail me out of the situation (in game / restarting manually to fix the issue). So for me this works in the best of times and the worst of times.

title: So much for the claim of Android Support
text:
Live and Learn. After being worn out by the byzantine process of trying (and failing) to get ANY kind of a straight answer from the script readers at Logitech Product "support" I decided to simply buy one and see if it actually worked with Android devices better than the original K400 (which works just fine with Kit Kat and Cyanogen 12.1 devices). Alas, the K400 Plus does NOT, so it gets a big "minus" in my book. On a totally unmodified cell phone and tablet, both running Android 5.1, the keyboard was nowhere to be found. Those devices, by the way, have no problem seeing all kinds of other USB devices such as a USB storage device, etc., plugged into them. SO, if you happen to have an Android device the K400 Plus WILL work with, great, but you should confirm that first by seeing if any other Logitech Unifying Receiver device works with it. If the answer is no, this keyboard will probably not work with it, either. PITY, Logitech used to have really excellent product support but they've apparently joined the ranks of the: "we've got your cash, so please just go away now" vendors of mediocre products that all too often do not work. The claim of Android support for the K400 Plus is as much hype, based on coincidence, as it is verifiable technology (in my opinion as a frustrated purchaser).

To whoever ultimately gets mine as a "like-new" used return, it was only out of the box for the four minutes it took to confirm it just doesn't work.

title: excellent wireless trackball!
text:
Update 2017-10-14

I've been using this trackball for over a year. And I still really like it. It's had the same battery in it since I first started using it and the software reports that 58 days are left. And that is with nearly daily use with 8 or more hours of use on most days.

The other thing to note is that it is occasionally necessary to remove the ball to clean the around where the ball rests inside the socket. There are 3 small "nubs" in the socket that are easily cleaned with a dry cotton swab and a puff of air. I do not consider the need to clean it as any fault of the trackball, it's just normal maintenance.

You can tell when cleaning is required if the movement of your mouse pointer becomes a little erratic or appears to "stick". To remove the ball simply push the ball out from the underside with your finger. In addition to cleaning the "nubs" I recommend wiping the ball down with a dry tissue.

---------------------------------

I love this trackball! It is the second one I've bought. Please note the first one was bought at retail. And the price here at the time of purchase was measurably less than retail.

What I really like about this trackball is -

1) Very comfortable to use. However I find occasionally myself pressing the wrong mouse button. I believe it only a matter of getting used to it.

2) The Logitech Setpoint software isn't necessary for normal use (as a plain old point & click device). But it is worthwhile to install it. It provides a way to assign actions to the two buttons closest to the trackball. I've found those buttons very useful because you can assign different functions based upon the program that your running. For example, in my browser I've assigned the buttons to scroll to the top and bottom of the page, but in my tabbed editor I've assigned them to move forwards and backwards through the document tabs.

3) The Setpoint software shows the remaining batter life, not sure how accurate it is but it is nice to know when the battery needs replacing before it becomes an issue.

I would purchase this trackball again, and I would recommend it to friends and colleagues.

title: Good product but not large
text:
SIZE NOT LARGE: As of this writing, the Amazon product description includes the word "large" in the product title. There's nothing large about this mouse. I have long fingers, so I generally like a larger mouse. My previous mouse is the Logitech 510, which measures 2.56 in. wide x 4.72 in. long x 1.61 in. high, with dimensions noted with the perspective of how you hold it in your hand. The M330 model is 2.67 in. long x 4.15 in. wide x 1.51 in. high. So, it's a little wider but quite a bit shorter and a little lower than the large mouse I've gotten used to.

No big deal if you have an average grip, but ignore the product title word "large" if a large mouse is important to you.

Interestingly, the Logitech website doesn't use the word "large" at all to describe this mouse. It is a little larger than the compact, "mobile" M220 quiet mouse, but it's not large per se.

QUIET OPERATION: If you try this out in a really quiet room, you'll be amazed at how quiet this mouse truly is. The left and right mouse clicks are very, very quiet. It almost seems to me that the tactile click you feel in your finger is "louder" or easier to perceive than the sound of the click. The roller wheel also has a click function when you press down on it, and that's quiet, too. And the roller wheel itself, while providing a tactile bumping feel while you rotate it, makes only the slightest sound. So, no, it's not completely "silent," as the product name claims, but it is very, very quiet overall. If that's what you're looking for most of all, this mouse is a good solution.

SETUP: Very, very easy! Logitech's little "Nano" receiver takes up a USB port, but it completely cuts out the need for pairing or managing multiple connections the way you have it using their "unifying" receiver. title: Earpads are comfortable and feel nice for a few weeks but after ...
text:
I've owned 3-5 of these headsets in the last 10 years. The macro key functionality is something not replicated on other headsets and sadly this is the only reason I've yet to go with another headset.

The Pro/Con tradeoff:

Comfortable/Even side to side weight distribution.
Can with some ease falls off the back of my head if I lean back.

Battery life in the beginning, hard to put a time frame, but I'd say 1-2 months in, the battery is as stated 10 hours.
However I do overuse my headset, 10-15 hours per day. After a few months the battery life does drop off and 6 months later I can expect 4 hours of battery life. 1 year later I would be lucky to get 2 hours. Although logitech does sell replacement batteries for ~$10.

Earpads are comfortable and feel nice for a few weeks but after a few weeks until the sweat kicks in and after a few months of heavy use you will begin to see the pealing start. After the earpads start pealing the is no going back. You will end up with black specks in your hair and all over the floor until you managed to peal all of the glued fake leather off.

Microphone quality is adequate, it is a gaming headset, what do you expect?

The stereo and 7.1 directional audio is great, obviously though this depends on the source of the sound.

Audio quality if genuinely nice. The logitech gaming software lets you modify the bass and treble or if you want to get more detailed you can change individual frequencies from 32 to 16K.

The software often has trouble remembering the macro keys set and will OFTEN revert to the default. The ONLY reason I use this headset is for the blasted keys and so often I will have to unplug the headset. power it off, and/or hit the hard reset button with a paperclip, just to get the keys working again.

The signal strength is stronger than some cheap wireless headsets but is still limited. You may be able to get 1 to 2 rooms away but you likely will not be going up or down any stairs with the G930, although I've had friends refute me on this one.

Lastly and if you know anyone who one of these you will likely have hear this. The connection for unexplained reason just disconnects once in a while. You know your friend has this if you randomly hear a springy noise after not hearing them for a few seconds. Not usually a huge issue but in some situations and depending on what you do with the headset it could be a game changer.

Modding:
One star of the review is only because I can fix the problems present in the headset with a little tinkering.

The sweat-inducing tearing fake leather ear cups can be replaced with a more tollerable poorous g230/g430 replacement earpads for ~$10.

While lesser talked about, the battery is actually pretty easy to override with something more powerful with the appropriate tools. The right ear houses the battery, I took a spare battery (since I kept some of my old headsets) and cut the connector off of it (although not required). I picked up a cheap $2 3 AA battery holder and Velcro'd it to the side of the headset. With a little soldering (though you could electrical tape if done correctly) to connect the old connect to the new battery pack I can now get 20+ hours on 3 rechargeable AA batteries.

The wires in the left side of the headset started breaking after overuse (not misuse/abuse) and I had to eventually reroute the cables to the outside of the headset and solder them back together. I'm not the best so it ended up more temporary than permanent.

The one big pro:
Logitech's warranty program is phenomenal. I am stubborn and impatient so I do not usually wait for them to replace something for me but instead I usually just try to fix it myself. However I told them over the phone my headset, with no receipt, was not connecting to the computer and in the same phone call I had a box on my way to my house to send the old one back.
Somewhat related as well, my G700 mouse macro button broke and I told them one of the buttons broke and in one single call I had a new G700s on the way, however since the G700 was no longer sold they told me to keep my mostly functional mouse without needing to send it back.
So yeah, if you don't want to mess with your stuff like me, call logitech, they are pretty awesome.

The result of each of my headsets:
Headset 1: Probably physically broke it
Headset 2: Right ear lost sound and left ear was choppy with sound
Headset 3: Unable to connect to computer - Logitech replaced this pretty much no questions asked
Headset 3.5: Right ear losing audio
Headset 4: Stopped powering on - This is when I really started modding the headsets and started resoldering the broken cables and stuff.

I am currently cycling between 3.5 and 4 at the moment trying to fix them while wait for someone to release a decent wireless headset.

title: Potentially great mouse with a deal breaking design flaw
text:
This mouse, like most Logitech mice EXCEPT the MX Anywhere, has a really stupid design flaw which makes it completely unusable for me and I suspect many others as well. That is that they have doubled the function of the top scroll wheel to act as a middle mouse button. There is a perfectly good button below this which is WASTED by using it to change the "mode" of the scroll wheel from free spinning to racheted. THIS button should be the middle mouse button, NOT the scroll wheel. The MX Anywhere gets this right, all other Logitech mice get it hysterically wrong.

So why is this such an issue? Well, one of the most common uses of a middle mouse button is to open browser links in a new tab instead of the current window. When you press the scroll wheel to click things, the wheel shifts slightly as well meaning that the screen scrolls a little just as you're clicking the link. Result? You either miss the link or worse still, click a nearby link you didn't want to click. You have to really concentrate in order to click the scroll wheel without scrolling it. This is horribly frustrating and shows that whomever made this rotten design choice has never really used the mouse in a wide variety of everyday situations. There is no need for this. In the MX Anywhere, the ONLY Logitech mouse which gets it right, you change scroll wheel modes by clicking the scroll wheel. The button below the scroll wheel acts as the middle mouse button and is programmable. Therefore you can click the middle button without accidentally scrolling the wheel. I'm really amazed that more people don't point this out in the review - perhaps most people aren't "power" users who utilize things like middle mouse buttons. If however the middle mouse button is important to you, then AVOID THIS MOUSE. Otherwise you'll be accidentally scrolling screens when you click it.

I'm always amazed by the extent to which so-called "professional" designers get something so horribly wrong. Logitech are an infuriating company - they used to make the best mice around but over the past few years have really started to deteriorate by making some horrible, ill thought out design decisions, as well as cheapening the building quality so that most of their mice suffer from the dreaded "phantom double click" problem whereby after a few months of use your mouse buttons will start sending out an unwanted extra click every time you press it. I have been through about 5 Logitech mice with the same problem and the forums are overrun with people complaining about it and yet Logitech continually ignore the problem. I really wish some other company would step up and start making a perfectly designed mouse to take over the role that Logitech once had.

title: A budget premium mouse, in a very light package - but do not underestimate.
text:
A lot of mixed reviews here about this mouse, but I took a chance seeing as how the difference in comments varied on the mice users are accustomed to. First, let me say my primary mouse is a Logitech G9x. And my secondary is an Anker (Generic) Wireless mouse.

If you don't know this, Logitech is by far the best, or one of the best, in regards to mice & peripherals. I have stuck by them for years, and love their warranty support (at least while it is still under warranty). I am an avid PC gamer, and work with a multitude of mice in my work field. And here is what I think of this M560.

Pros:
*It's light.
*7 Customizable buttons
*Pairs along with other peripherals on a single receiver
*Comfortable
*Good range
*Fantastic Battery Life

Cons:
*May feel too light to some
*It's Mid-sized (some may say full size if their hand is smaller, but this is shorter than a 530)
*Customizing buttons is a bit of a pain, there is no guide on which buttons are which. And by default, back/forward are not programmed on the side buttons.
*Signal can be interfered if there is alot of metal around (I have a metal desk in my office, metal drawers, and metal cabinet - and I experienced lagging until I ran a hub and placed the receiver on top of my desk)
*Scroll wheel is very "fluid". This makes scrolling very smooth, but also very sensitive. Can be quite tedious sometimes.

Now here is the thing, IF you are a gamer or avid user coming from high quality mice - this WILL feel cheap. The plastic is very light compared to other materials found in different models of logitech mice. But, it also has a very smooth matte finish, which i actually enjoy. If you come from using common/generic mice - this will feel better than what you are used to. So given the nature of the user, I feel that this mouse is not given enough credit. Accuracy is like any other Logitech mouse, same for battery usage, and button customization.

BUT, it is light, and when I compare this to my G9x (with customizable weights) it feels like i'm holding paper. If I compare it to my Anker mouse, it feels like a budget premium mouse. Hopefully this helps someone if they just can't decide to go for it or not :).

title: Currently the best bet for HTPC owners.
text:
This is pretty much the ultimate htpc remote/keyboard on the market currently. And I've tried most of them. Some folks might not prefer something with this type of size and would like something more like one of those in hand two sided remotes with a very small keyboard and possibly air remote functionality. But I haven't found a single one of those with good range, good durability, or implementation that I would rate more than 3 stars.

The exception to that would be the now defunct Lenovo N5902 with backlighting. The problem with that remote is the very poor durability and failure rate combined with bad range or simply buggy connectivity issues. The buttons malfunction erratically. And don't even think of dropping it. This is why it is no longer manufactured. It's too bad they never made a solid model based on that design as it would have been the ultimate small sized htpc keyboard remote.

The other next bast option is the Logitech K400 keyboard. It is the predecessor to this keyboard and is probably the most popular htpc keyboard on the market. The biggest flaw with that one is the lack of backlight. Some don't care about that but it renders the item quite useless as a family htpc remote if anybody else needs to use it and isn't familiar with a keyboard layout without looking at it. And lets face it, that is the vast majority of people. And most people don't use an htpc in a well lit room for the most part. Another major flaw is the placement and small size of the right shift key. If you are use to typing on a standard keyboard, you WILL be hitting the up key instead of the right shift key. It is a major annoyance.

PROS and CONS of the K830
PROS:
- Very good range. Zero connectivity issues. No erratic behavior do to connectivity or range.
- Smaller than than the K400.
- Bigger trackpad and better button placement, including the volume buttons, than on the K400.
- Standard key layout including the right shift button. The direction keys are much more distinct for more intuitive media control.
- More solid feel than the K400. Better ergonomic feel in your hand. It feels like it was built to be held like a remote rather than placed on a desk for typing.
- Upper left mouse click button in combination with trackpad on right side lets you hold the keyboard in two hands and use it like a mouse remote rather than a keyboard.
- The back light is phenomenal.
- The rechargeable battery lasts a surprisingly long time considering the backlight. It last and lasts.

CONS:
- It's a lot more pricey than the K400 or most other options. If you don't care about the major gripes I have with the K400, at 1/5th the cost it would be a no brainer to go with the K400.
- The new software is called Logitech Options and is much less robust and buggier than the Logitech Setpoint software. The pointer options don't consistently work and need to be used in conjunction with OS system options. As of one week of ownership I am unable to get the mouse pointer track speed to save after reboot. Others have this problem and I'm still troubleshooting it.

title: * * They Made One Mistake On MARC The Monkey  * *
text:
I Love my little MARC. I have other mice, but He’s A Cutie!! Yes, I still call him Marc (the Monkey), because that is the name the manufacturer gave him & is on his card. My sister will say, “What’s that noise?” “I just dropped Marc on the floor” Poor Marc get knocked off the desk a lot. Logitech Mice Work Great, I’ve always had lots of luck with them & they’ve always been Plug & Play. Everything always recognizes them easily that I’ve used them on.

I’ve always loved the brand. Marc is no exception. Works Great. Has a place inside to store his USB Receiver for travel & I’ve never had a problem, except ONE!! The one thing that is Logitech’s Dirty Little Secret On This Mouse Is: THEY RECESSED THE ON/OFF SWITCH, which makes it difficult to switch it on & off. If you have long fingernails, no problem. My Dirty Little Secret Is, that I’m a Nail Biter. So, I have a Hard Time Switching this Mouse On & Off. If you don’t get the switch Completely over to the Left, it Remains On & Drains Battery Power. That has happened to us more times than I can count. No problem, since I use rechargeables, but might be a hassle for some people. The Red can look like it’s Showing, but the switch Isn’t Completely To The Left, so it’s Still Drawing Power. Again, with my Stubby fingers & that Switch being Recessed, I can’t FEEL that it is Off. So, each time I turn it off, I end up having to Double Check. There was just No Need to make a recessed Switch, as I haven’t had it on any other of their wireless mice. I bought this Logitech Wireless Mouse at Best Buy, as it was a Best Buy Exclusive at the time & I liked the design.

All in all, I like this mouse, but just wish Logitech would do something about the Recessed On/Off Switch. I Do Not Like That & it's a Bad Design. If it weren't for that, I'd give it Five Stars.

title: Well thought out and crafted remote control.
text: This is a well thought out and crafted remote control. Positive features are that it works seamlessly to control multiple devices once you set it up. It is also rechargeable so you do not have to buy any batteries. You can recharge it on the provided charging dock/cradle or with the supplied USB cable. The device does go into sleep mode about 10 seconds after you put it down but it wakes up when you pick it up again. It also has a nice, albeit somewhat small, color touchscreen. A feature that may be a bit of a drag for some is that this is not one of those remotes that you just point at the device you want to use it on and the remote recognizes the device, after programming in the make and model of the device. Instead, you have to first plug in this remote to your computer, with the provided USB cable, then download an app from Logitech and set up an account. At that point you will have to input the make and model number of each device that you want the remote to operate. Setting up all this programming can be a bit time consuming depending on how easy it is for you to find the model number of your devices and how many devices you want the remote to operate. After that, it's all pretty much a breeze, except if you need any help there is no manual that comes with the remote to provide any operating instructions, other than to plug into the device to your computer, etc., as described.  So, internet access is critical to the whole operation. Finally, I must say that this remote has a sleek and well-crafted design to it, with just the right amount of heft, balance, and snazziness.

title: Ow ow ow
text:
TL;DR:
* painfully tight
* range is worse than bluetooth
* returning it

This headset is TIGHT. It's sturdy and well-built, and the headband allows left-to-right adjustment with marked increments -- excellent for making sure you balance the size on both sides. Unfortunately, the headset grips my head like a vise. I occasionally have issues with TMJ, and I could tell immediately that this headset will aggravate it badly. I started to get a headache within 5 minutes. Even after taking off the cushy but dense ear pads, it STILL gripped too hard.

I might have tried to make it work if that were the only problem, but it's not. The range is abysmal -- worse than my bluetooth headset (P311). It doesn't degrade gracefully either. Once you're out of range, sound cuts out entirely rather than sounding choppy but audible like my P311.

On the plus side, this thing is extremely solidly built. I am fairly sure that I could _not_ loosen its death grip by attempting to bend the headband out. It's just too sturdy. If it doesn't hurt you, the grip will be excellent and the earpads will block out a great deal of noise. The sound is good (didn't test this much). I love that the on/off button is a switch -- no holding down a button and waiting. I also love that the mute button and the little mute light on the microphone boom. It's almost out of view, though, so I'd have to look hard over to see it, but that's not a big deal because I don't often need to check my mute status.

It works beautifully in Linux (Ubuntu 15.10). Right out of the box, pulseaudio picks it up and can route audio to it. The volume wheel adjusts the system volume with the OSD. I didn't test the G buttons before repackaging it, but I suspect one can simply remap them using one's window manager, or failing that, using a tool like pystromo.

Bottom line: I'd love this thing if it didn't want to squeeze my brain out and if it would let me walk across the house and help my kids while I'm in a meeting. It fails both of those, so I'm afraid I have to return it.

title: Great cost-to-sound ratio
text:
I actually have these hooked to my TV.

Now I know you're thinking, "Why on earth would you want to do that?"

Because I live in an apartment, that's why. And they are quite loud even at half volume. I once got a knock on the door from my neighbor asking me to turn it down when I had these speakers up only halfway! I was only trying to hear the TV over my loud furnace.

The bass is surprisingly strong too. Definitely a nice upgrade over my TV's crappy built-in speakers.

Are these 30-watt powered PC speakers going to compete with a real 1000-watt home theater system? Of course not. But for the price they might just be good enough. They're more than capable of filling up a room with sound, although I certainly wouldn't recommend them for a big party with dancing.

I believe every stereo system, no matter how small, can benefit from a subwoofer. And this one does a pretty good job for what it is.

If you want your PC or TV to sound good without spending too much or annoying your neighbors too much, these are a fine choice.

title: Weak GPS and voice recognition, in conjunction with BLU Android phones
text:
I’m new to high use of voice-activated commands and smartphone GPS technologies. Does Logitech Zerotouch save me time or hassles? About me—careful driver who refrains from many text or phone calls while driving and owns an older GPS that suction mounts on top of dashboard.

Zerotouch can be compared to a simplified, voice-activated, menu system supported by a smartphone mount for access to a set of drivers’ Android apps in telephone, text, audio play, and GPS capabilities. My SUV is without Bluetooth, so Zerotouch’s audio control of my smartphone’s tiny speaker is unuseful and not reviewed here. Then, how effective is Zerotouch’s voice control of smartphone’s Call, Text, and GPS capabilities?

Zerotouch and my BLU Android smartphone will be referred to as Zerotouch-BLU. Zerotouch-BLU grabbed the air vents well. Before buying, it is important to note where your car’s air vents are. Might your smartphone block a desirable air vent? What will be the ergonomics of viewing?

Viewing Zerotouch-BLU’s GPS in my SUV requires glancing downward; whereas my old TomTom GPS sits in my driving’s line-of-sight. TomTom GPS’s viewing-presentation included a useful driving-on-the-road view perspective. BLU-Android, at its best, offered a non-intuitive, above-the-street viewing perspective.

Also, my older eyes are unable to refocus fast enough to glance-read Zerotouch-BLU’s in its mounted position, while I'm driving. Overall, the outdated, dash-mount TomTom GPS is a FAR superior GPS and safer to drive with.

Zerotouch-BLU numerous other GPS problems included: 1. Inconsistent voice recognition. When voice was recognized, it was great time savings. When not, spent 5 to 10 times more time than would have using touch input to fix the error. 2. Very poorly designed GPS road-driving perspective viewing. 3. Lack of optional touch input, when voice recognition fails. Overall conclusion of Zerotech-BLU GPS a 1 star.

As for Zerotech’s TEXT features, Zerotouch-BLU’s voice recognition is adequate for only a minimal amount of conversion text. Beyond 4 words, and confused text occurs. 2 star. This could be a useful feature. For example, quick replies. Or 5 minutes before car arrival, voice text out "There in 5".

So far, Zerotech has recognized my contact manager’s stored names, resulting in more convenient dialing. I’ll give Zerotech a 5 star in voice telephony.

A 2 star overall—useful device for faster voice telephony, very simple texts, and occasional GPS use. BLU Android, T-Mobile, and Zerotech is a bad combination. Ideas behind Zerotech are outstanding, so maybe it’ll work better with your phone.

7/18/16 Logitech's tech support is pro-active, and requests that I contact them to fine tune my Android. Up 1 stars, until further review.

It may work for others, but we'd really like something a bit wider angle, especially if the camera used software to un-fishbowl the image a bit.

The white cover over the lens is a nice touch, now you'll know for sure when you've disabled your video feed and can tell from across the room. This gives a little extra confidence to anyone using the conference room when not on a conference call that they're not being 'watched'.

title: Love/Hate
text:
This remote has wonderful features for the price, but it has two glaring faults that potential buyers should know about:

1) Based on my experience and others I have read about, it has some weak components inside, which makes updating (or syncing) unreliable. Neither of my two remotes would update using the new MyHarmony website. I was able to use the old Harmony Remote PC program (7.7.0) but one of them needs fresh alkaline (not lithium) batteries every time in order to make the connection.

2) My 2015 Sony smart tv (not the latest) was poorly represented in the database. When the remote first loaded it was missing all the replay button functions as well as the video display aspect ratio. Those are essential buttons on the Sony remote. title: Noisy and intermittent scrolling
text:
The scroll wheel's "click-to-click" scrolling setting is noisy. After a week of usage the scroll wheel also developed an intermittent "clunking" sound in addition to the noisy operation. The noise and clunking might presage an up-coming failure. At times, during mousing around, the cursor movement paused for no apparent reason, and likewise, during a scroll, the scroll would pause. Other Logitech scroll wheels are nearly silent, why not the one on this mouse?

The page-forward and page-pack buttons are too close together, and are inconveniently located--they probably should have been placed side-by-side instead of end-to-end or at least have been separated to a greater degree--like on the Logitech M510 mouse. The current locations of those paging buttons require a forward-back movement of the thumb instead of a more ergonomic side-to-side movement or a distal-proximal thumb-rocking movement as can be performed on the M510. The forward-back motion requires an essentially partial-hand-movement motion instead of just a thumb movement.

Mouse with Logitech keyboard thoughts:

Nice to have one keyboard and mouse for up to 3 devices, but the device switching could have been improved. There should be an "on-off" "pairing" switch on the Logitech keyboard that would allow pairing of the K780 keyboard with the M720 mouse. That way, setting the keyboard switch to "pair" would automatically pair the keyboard **and** the mouse to whatever device is selected **either** by the mouse device button **or** by the keyboard device button without having to press both the mouse button and the keyboard button to select a device. The pairing should be optional (using an "on-off" switch as stated above) because someone will inevitably not want pairing at times.

The range seemed good with the supplied USB stick; I didn't try Bluetooth.
