text: After using an entry level Turtlebeach brand wired headset for two years I figured I would splurge and get myself a nice wireless headset that has some more features and comfort to it. Needless to say this was not what I was looking for. The drivers for this product are endlessly finnicky, having issues that have been reported for several years and yet never fixed. (Sound in one ear only, mumble voice not working in the other ear, etc.) I should have done more research before I purchased this headset but was in need of a new one as my old one fell apart. In terms of comfort, this headset is excellently designed. The padded ear cups are some of the most comfortable that I have used, and the headband is adjustable to just the right size. The volume scroll is nice, being able to adjust sound volume at any given time no matter what I am doing. However that is about all that I have to say that is positive about this headset. The surround sound is horrible, way more echo than anything I have ever experienced and almost garbled at times. Some of the sounds play at way too low a level to even hear and that bothers me as well. Overall, after having to fight with the drivers for many hours to get the sound to play properly at all, and having it still cut out and require me to go through the same hour long process on almost a daily basis, this headset isn't worth it. Do some research, find an alternative, preferably wired. It's worth the mess of having a cord to have something reliable and useful.That way you don't cut out every time someone three apartments over turns on the 1100 watt microwave.

It's nice to be able to move spells and abilities to one-key commands; I actually end up playing Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup with one hand on the G13 and one on the keypad, and it works great. I'll admit that sometimes I wish there were more than 22 G-keys; even with the ability to program the side buttons and stick, there are occasions I'd want to map even more. For a lot of games, three sets of 22 keys will be more than enough!

One thing I've just started doing is using it with Tales of Maj'Eyal - and by using the G13, I can map keys so that my DCSS and ToME profiles are similar without changing the in-game mapping. The custom backlighting helps me remember which profile is up ... and also warns me on the occasions when the G13 doesn't pick up a change in focus (usually when closing an app brings a game to the foreground).

On rare occasions, the G13's joystick will be picked up as controller 1 rather than my F710 - I think it may have had to do with the order in which I activated them. If that was the case, then I unplugged the G13, connected the F710, then connected the G13, and all was well. (It hasn't happened in quite some time.)

Even using a percentage of the G13's abilities (I don't bother switching the display to other information) makes it worth the money I spent - if you find yourself running out of keys or needing a more compact layout for gaming, you should give it a try yourself.

title: It's Okay. Can't Complain for the Price.
text:
Took a chance on this versus the Microsoft All In One Keyboard which is also getting equally good reviews. I was going for the Microsoft, but because I already have a Logitech Unifying receiver plugged in the same computer, I decided to use this as well.

Impressions:

- The keyboard is too compact for my liking. It's not a full size keyboard, but it has full size QWERTY keys. The rest of the keys are compact so it's a bit getting used to especially if your fingers have muscle memory on where the other keys are at this point.

- The keys have a full stroke up and down so there is more effort in typing which does get tiring and produces more noise when hitting the keys. I wonder why they went this route versus a shorter stroke and less noise.

- To make full use of the functionality of the keyboard, please ensure to download the Logitech software for the K400 Plus. This will give you complete custom over the function keys to have assignable actions based on your liking (i.e. my Music key launches Spotify instead of the Microsoft App). This also enables multi finger gestures on the trackpad, increase trackpad scrolling, as well as enable smooth scrolling that people are complaining about. Also being an Apple user, I inverted the trackpad to have scrolling follow my finger direction rather than the traditional way.

- Two AA batteries is all that's needed to power this keyboard which is included to get you started. It also says it can last up to 18 months. We shall see. Otherwise, I'm glad this is the route they went versus a rechargeable battery that you have to plug once in a while and you can't replace down the road.

- Switchable function keys or custom keys from the start. People have been complaining about the Microsoft keyboard that the function keys are not readily accessible. Over here with Logitech K400 Plus, you have a choice. Of course you'll need to download the software to make the changes.

- An ON and OFF button to help save battery life further.

Needed improvements:

- I wish the trackpad was built bigger. There's a lot of space on the keyboard to occupy and Logitech wasn't logical.

- Trackpad is too sensitive in touching that I sometimes inadvertently move a file.

- Illuminated keys if you want this to be truly a keyboard for the Living Room like most are buying this for.

- A full size keyboard so it can truly rest on your lap with no issues.

- Less noisy keys and shorter key stroke for less fatigue when typing.

- Bluetooth capability.

title: Awesome travel mouse
text:
I didn't actually purchase this mouse it was a gift from a friend that bought it for himself and ended up not liking it. When I travel I tend to take a lot of stuff with me and I absolutely hate using trackpads so I always have to have a wireless mouse with me. I used to take this mouse with me [[ASIN:B016QO85WS Logitech Wireless Marathon Mouse M705 (810-002525)]], which is an amazing mouse, but is a little big for travel. This one, size wise, is absolutely perfect!

I've seen people saying left/right click is harder than it should be. That's because the buttons aren't actually on the top of the mouse they are on the bottom so you do have to be very deliberate when clicking. I've found if you click toward the corner it helps out a bit, it takes me a bit to get re-accustomed to it but I usually do within a few minutes. Scroll is nice but the middle 'button' is a bit far back for my tastes, it feels like you have to reach way back on the mouse to reach it. Using it on 2 different devices 'at the same time' is as easy as flipping a switch, the hardest part is remembering what you have on 1 and what's on 2.

This mouse has found a permanent pocket in my backpack, I will not leave home without it. I definitely wouldn't use it as my permanent mouse but for something while I am travelling for up to a week at a time? Yes most definitely. For someone with average to smaller hands it should work just fine as a backup.

title: Great cam for 720p capture!
text:
We got two of these for our streams.

They are great webcams. The only thing I don't like about them is that they don't screw down or anything, so you have to hold the base when you turn the cam, but we rarely ever move it anyway. It has a little orange light on the front to show you that it's on. It doesn't come with software (that I recall, it may have had a CD in it) but you can download the software from Logitech's website for free anyway.

The software is great! It lets you either set autofocus and follow my face or manually control the camera.

One thing that I would like to note is that you cannot control the camera while you have autofocus or follow my face turned on. You have to uncheck these before you can move the camera with the software. It took me a while to figure that out.

The focus is great. The light capture is great. It picks up my face well in dim light and is actually a bit surprising at how well it performs in low light. It is sharp and the HD is crisp.

I would absolutely highly recommend this webcam for anyone looking for a solid, but affordable cam. It's great for streaming to twitch. It hasn't missed a beat in several months now.

title: We Love This Little Keyboard

Highly recommended!

title: Great reviews gave me high hopes, but disappointed
text:
Not a fan of this mouse. I bought it with high hopes since it works natively with the Mac as well as being very pleased with other Logitech products I have bought in the past (the K811 bluetooth keyboard being the most recent before this mouse), and after comparing it to Apple's Magic Mouse, the reviews seemed to be tilted much in favor of this one.

The size is tricky for me. It's small which is convenient for carrying in a laptop bag I suppose, but I find it's a little uncomfortable for holding and my hand will tend to get tired after using it for a while (like 30 minutes or more) due to the muscles in my hand staying tensed the whole time I have my hand on it to keep my hand and fingers in the necessary position for using it.

I also struggle with basic movements when moving the cursor around the screen. Apples latest OS, El Capitan, has a feature which will briefly enlarge your cursor on the screen if you jiggle the mouse. I find this happening constantly because of the jagged movements that result to the cursor when I'm moving the mouse. It's more of a minor annoyance than anything, but it suggests the cursor movement coming from the mouse is not smooth.

What annoys me the most about it though is it will sometimes just quit working for no apparent reason and I have to turn it off and back on to force it to re-pair with my computer. Sometimes it will not pair and moving it around won't get it to pair, so my cursor is setting there dead on the screen. Other times the scrolling functionality will quit even though I can still click and move the cursor. Again, in either case, I am forced to reboot the mouse and cause it to re-pair over Bluetooth with my laptop to get it going again. As I'm writing this review, for instance, I've lost the ability to scroll through the text box and go back and re-read the text of my review, having to use the up and down arrow keys on the keyboard instead. Frustrating!

I wish I'd just gone with a much simpler Bluetooth mouse that has just clicking and a scroll wheel. I have never used the more advanced touch gestures on this mouse anyway, and with these other problems, I find myself wishing I'd just bought something simpler that would have less room for error.

title: Ultrathin and Ultra Awkward
text: The Logitech Ultrathin Touch Mouse T630 really is ultrathin and very compact, but that's also part of its downfall. It's so thin and oddly shaped that it forces the user to hold his or her hand in a very awkward, uncomfortable position. In addition, the clicking mechanism is activated by pressing and tilting the entire body of the mouse down onto either the left or right side of the base plate. The consequences of this configuration include cramped fingers, imprecise pointing, repeated failed clicks, and unwanted actions and movements. On the plus side, the appearance and fit and finish of the hardware are excellent, and the Bluetooth connectivity works flawlessly.

text:
I've been using this mouse for a year with my 13" MacbookPro and I like it a lot. It is thin, lightweight, and the battery seems to last for a long time.

With Logitech Tech. Support's help, I just resolved my one annoyance with the mouse. The mouse would not pair automatically when the laptop boots up. I could always select it in the bluetooth application under OSX, but I wanted it to connect automatically when the computer starts. There is a selector switch on the bottom of the mouse to select Bluetooth Channel "A" or "B". When the switch is set to "A", the computer will connect to the mouse at start-up. With the switch to "B", the mouse won't connect automatically.

The mouse looks sleek and cool sitting next to the laptop, which is a big reason why I bought it. Some may prefer a mouse with more volume or mass in the hand. For travel, and especially when making presentations to customers, I like it a lot.

title: Solid Small Room Conferencing
text:
Most of my experience with Logitech cameras have been in the portable webcams that are self protecting fold up like the C525 720p which is always in my briefcase along with my Microsoft Surface and its terrible integrated camera. I work for a company with a presence in every country in the world except Turkmenistan... (Don't ask me why.. I don't know). Travelling is a budget impacting necessity, so for daily constructive collaboration, we rely upon both Cisco Telepresence and even more so now, Skype for Business. Telepresence is an outstanding but fairly expensive way to hold video conferenced sessions, so we're testing small room Skype for Business certified video conferencing solutions that are evolving in the market that can work with our existing infrastructure without the running cost of Cisco TP. While Polycom is definitely competing well in this niche, it looks like Logitech is putting a strong foot forward in inexpensive solutions that leverage its skill in cameras and microphones.

The build quality is solid - metal - reliable. This is something that can be installed into a small conference room with some cable management and last the expected abuse of and active small conference room. The buttons, speaker, and microphones all perform very well. Sound fills the room and there isn't any falloff from participants at the edge of a typical 10x8 small conference room.

Mounting the center of the display monitor at eyelevel and the camera beside seems to provide the best simulation of direct viewing in a skype session. Lighting is very important and always has to be controlled in a videoconferencing room. This unit doesn't perform well with rooms that have direct sunlight or blinds cannot be pulled down, but that's true of all video cameras. So expect this and use a room with controlled lighting. Dimmers will give the best level adjustment. Logitech also has an adjustment application to help with the autobrightness levels, but letting the camera makes its own decisions seems to work best.

The single downfall to this solution is the lack of automatic camera tracking... The camera is capable of preset views using the remote, or active control, but since there is no directional microphone on the camera, there is no tracking or automatic framing of the person speaking. We really get used to that technology in poly-com or Cisco solutions... that are more expensive.

The second thing to know is that this is still a computer driven device like most Skype for business videoconferencing devices.. it requires a PC logged into the Skype sessions using this as the external camera and microphone. It's what the market has now, but next gen devices for S4B will be standalone client capable.

Rating: Solid performer, inexpensive, good for small rooms and small team meetings. Technically performs flawlessly.

title: Expensive, Short Battery Life, Ridiculous Charger Port location
text: Wanted to like this mouse--touch sensitive top, compact design. It paired effortlessly, and maintained it's connection as long as I was in range...and once I brought my MacBook Pro within range, it unerringly and quickly re-established the connection. However, it's downfall: to charge the mouse, you have to plug in a USB cable...to the mini-USB port on the *bottom* of the mouse. Meaning, you can't charge the mouse and continue to use it. That wouldn't be a concern if the battery lasted longer--it only lasted me, on average, a week. And while that may seem like a long time, it was annoying to wake up one day, attempt to use the mouse, only to realize it was dead, and have to plug it in, falling back to the laptop's touchpad...waiting half the day for it to fully charge back up. I've since stopped using this device and instead purchased a Uhuru Rechargeable Bluetooth mouse...which was about 1/3 of the price of this mouse, and can be charged while still using it (the cable plugs in at the top edge of the mouse). The Uhuru mouse isn't perfect, but for $17 is well worth it.

title: Good, but major connection issues
text:
Ultra compact mouse that is responsive, yet with issues. In the search of a portable mouse that has a scroll and back feature w/o a wheel as I continue to wear those out from use. It connected easily and maintained all default mouse settings, which I hate how some require resetting tracking speed when a new mouse is paired. It tracks well and slides easily. I then attempted forward/backward option the mouse says it has, only to discover it doesn't work. I installed the recommended Chrome add-on before beginning anything and then tried out the touch features. Scroll worked as did changing the open screens. What didn't work was the back/forward on the internet. I checked for, and installed, the driver and it began working. There was no info I saw stating the drivers were required for full functionality, but if something doesn't work that's the first place I head to. It is an ULTRA compact mouse, which is good and bad. The size is great for transporting, but size and shape made it difficult to hold and use some touch features with the size of my hands. If you have very petite hands, it would be perfect. If the connection issues were not present I'd give it a four-star rating, but having to wait for it to re-establish connect when it's less than 18" from the computer is a major problem.

Pros
-easy to pair
-scroll, forward, backward buttons
-maintained default mouse settings
-smooth tracking
-compact
Cons
-disconnects from bluetooth every five to ten minutes
-drivers required for full functionality, yet doesn't say this
-poor ergonomics

title: Well Built Keyboard Case but Not as Innovative As iPad Version
text:
So I finally decided to get a keyboard case for my Tab S and got a Logitech since I like Logitech gear.

I haven't used Bluetooth keyboards with Android tablets much before but so far the key options seem fine to me.
I can understand a few compromises to fit into the equivalent of a 10" laptop keyboard space.

The case is built nicely and the keys feel decent enough (I'm a mechanical keyboard fan, no portable keys ever feel good).
The fit is tight - which is good for being secure. However it is a bit hard to get my tablet back out. Thankfully that is rare.

The tablet and keyboard dock into place securely with magnets - which is a very nice touch.
However the case is light enough that it moves with touch presses.

Battery life is working as advertised so far and it wakes after touching a key (and remembers what you typed too) so no need to hit the power switch much.

The main reason for docking stars is that I'm comparing it to the version I got for my parent's iPad Air 1.
First, no color options. Black is too neutral and bland.
Second, no magnetic wake. The iPad version uses the built-in magnets (very clever) to dock - which I can understand because iPad has those.
But the magnetic docking action also wakes the keyboard.
As the iPad Air 1 and the Tab S 10.5 are around the same time frame, why couldn't Logitech use the same ideas.

title: collecting dust
text:
I struggled to find use for this unit. the W,A,S,D keys are located at the very top row which seems to suggest this pad was made for FPS shooting games. And even still if this unit is for FPS then why in the world would you indent some keys, suggest them as W,A,S,D and then place them all the way on the top of this pad?. I feel like someone in the dev team just tunnel visioned into their own paradigm and despite the obvious argument of "hey!! there's a row of numbers directly over the WASD keys on every keyboard ever made"... I didn't have this unit long enough to really speak to the extra functions related to the led panel because I gave it to a friend that does Photoshop retouching for a living. I haven't heard a single bit of feed back from him and I have do not doubt that it is collecting dust in his drawer now. this unit might be too versatile for its own good. Almost feel like this unit should have been released in tiers. A version of this unit that maybe didn't have the LED or the side joystick and cost somewhere closer to 30USD. Honestly though we bring these bad purchases on our selfs because although there aren't a million keypads out there; there are certainly much better units than this and the more you research the closer you get to making that 360 degree journey right back to a keyboard.

The pros:
1 . Well built unit with good keys that feel something like the cherry mx brown keys.
2. Macro recording, every single key on this unit is configurable.
3. wrist rest if this unit didn't come with one built in I would most certainly have to get one so thanks for that!
4. Price: the price is both a Pro and a Con because at 59.99 (after all these year??) it is still cheaper than the razer keypads

Cons:
1. Price: no one actually needs this thing and was released in 2008 and its 2016; this unit still sells for 79.99 on the Logitech website/ 59.99 on amazon. Why? I like to use my cat tree analogy.. no one actually needs a cat tree and that is why you'll be paying upwards of 300 dollars for some 2x4s with cheap rug stapled to them.
2. keys positioning. notice how keys sort of fan out to mimic your hands, well they do such definite job of it that your hand actually covers everything and leaves you guessing what key you have your palm over most of the time.

thats it.. sadly for this unit most my issues with it are actually related to the overall concept of a gamekeypad and its actual usefulness. I've tried to make this my weapon of choice in games like guildwars 2, final fantasy 14, tera, fallout 4, blade&soul, black desert online and quake 3 arena. I just end up having to put it to the side as it is more of a hindrance. Just my honest opinion and my experience using this unit; it's lead me to understand that what I really need is just a nice mechanical keyboard.

It's really that small. However, if you use a desktop computer or a laptop all day with an external mouse, spring for the Apple Magic Mouse 2 (or even get [[ASIN:B016E4RVWA Apple Magic Bluetooth Mouse (Certified Refurbished)]] to save money) and you will be much happier.

title: Great Mouse, Minor Flaw
text: This is a great little mouse. I use it with my Surface Pro 3 tablet. I love the touch pad capabilities built right into the top of the mouse, and with the Logitech SetPoint software, you can customize what different finger swipes will do. The only issue I have with the mouse is the left and right click buttons. This mouse doesn't have two separate buttons on top of the mouse like any other traditional mouse. If you look under the bottom of the mouse where the buttons would normally be on the opposite side, you'll notice kind of a flattened V shape that stretches across the mouse. Under this extrusion is where the two click buttons are located. Because this is one long piece of plastic instead of two separate pieces, you have to very particular in where you "click" to produce either a left or right click. There are times I intended to right-click but I pressed too close to the center of the mouse and ended up left clicking instead. About 90% of the time, clicking to the far right edge of the mouse is enough to produce the right-click you want, but anything closer to the center of the mouse is going to be a gamble whether you get a right-click or a left click. Aside from this, I really like the mouse. It's very compact and easy to store in a bag without giving large protrusions from the side of your bag like other traditional wireless mice would do. The battery life is also really long. I've accidentally left it on overnight and would still be able to get another couple of days of use out of it before recharging it with your typical micro-usb charger cable.

title: Glaring design fault render this mouse far from perfect
text:
I love Logitech devices. Quality has always been superb although prices have generally reflected that. I bought this during an Amazon lightening deal so price was right.

Why the 3 stars then? Thing about Logitech is that when they do fault, it's generally in design and that's not always easily remedied. This mouse is a perfect example. It's sized right, great Bluetooth response and dual profiles so you can connect to 2 devices. The one thing that Logitech didn't think through was how it cannot detect two simultaneous mouse click (left and right simultaneous). The mouse really only has one button, but the driver determines which mouse button you're clicking based on your finger's position on the touch sensitive surface. But the driver does not allow for simultaneous click, so if you happen to be playing some games that needs both mouse clicks (Overwatch or other fps) you cannot.

Ok don't crucify me for playing Overwatch with this mouse.

Anyway, it is a glaring omission in Logitech's part, and I probably wouldn't have gotten this mouse had I known this. Threads going back as far as when the mouse was introduced a few years ago had been begging for this feature, which until today, end of August 2016, still has not happened. Bummer

title: Premium slim design, average mouse.
text:
The aesthetics and slim design is why I got this mouse in the first place. Surely, the build quality is on point and the surface feels good to the touch. It can easily slip into a laptop sleeve and looks and feels premium–a perfect match for my Blade Stealth in terms of design.

However, the design left me with high expectations, and a mouse this thin comes with a few compromises.

Because of how small the mouse is, I'm always gripping onto the metal rail, which can get uncomfortable over extended periods of time. This also means that I'm often inadvertently touching the surface in my grip, making some gestures not register.

The touch surface is smooth, and even though it's gesture-aware, you can't tap to click. There are only so many gestures, that only sometimes register. You can't hold a click and scroll at the same time. I'm using Windows 10 and the right/left edge swipes don't work for me and I haven't found them in the settings. Would've loved to see more gestures such as 3-finger swipe or tap.

The buttons themselves need a bit of force to click and are loud, which compromises the overall sleek and low-key profile. My Razer gaming mouse sounds quieter. This makes the lack of tapping even more of an issue.

In the end, I got this mouse for casual on-the-go use, and I believe this is what it's meant for. This is by no means a productivity mouse. If you treat it as such, a Bluetooth mouse this thin & light that you can easily slip into a laptop sleeve–or even your pocket–is killer.

title: All the snazzy features work as advertised.
text:
I bought this mouse because I needed one that could be easily paired to multiple devices, and because it’s so cute.

I was mildly surprised by just how small it is. Even for a mouse that’s designed explicitly for portability, this mouse is excessively small. You end up holding it more by its sides than you do most mice. It takes a little getting used to.

The touch surface works beautifully. Scrolling, etc is smooth and consistent. I accidentally clicked when I meant to swipe a few times during the first couple of days, but I’ve cultivated a gentler touch since then. It would be nice if the surface were a little larger, so you’d have room to really glide around. All the documentation you see online lists touch gestures for Windows 8, and they’re a little different for Windows 10, which has no charms bar. They’re configurable, but the defaults all made the most sense to me.

The thing where you have to flip it onto its back to charge it is straight-up dumb. I’m sure it’s like that for some practical reason owing to how everything is arranged on the inside, but come on. I’ll bet they would have had room to put the USB port in a more sensible place if they had made the whole thing a little bigger.

Despite a few minor annoyances, I’m quite pleased with the mouse. I plan to stick with it for the foreseeable future, unless they make a new, larger version.

title: Great mouse for work and play. Plus one of the best looking mice on the market I think.
text:
First off, didn't purchase this from Amazon but well worth reviewing here.

I have an M705 that has served me well and still does as my laptop go bag mouse. This is a great successor. I can use it for gaming and working.

First off, the overall size and shape is great. Everything is just about in the right place. The forward/back/side scroll you may think are initially a little off but they're not. They're there to keep you from hitting them by accident. The charging port is in a good place to make it useable instead of being on the bottom. Yes, that was a dig at the engineers at Apple.

You can pair it to three devices using one of two communication methods. My home laptop is Bluetooth. My travel is unified and that leaves the third slot open. Speaking of slots, there is no slot for the receiver. This is really the only WTF aspect I've encountered so far. I already have about five receivers all over so no need for a compartment but others may want one.

The right/left click are where they need to be. The side buttons and even that little left bottom click button you never use is just right. I have mine set to minimize all windows. The battery indicator is in the smart place. The scroll wheels are brilliant. The side is just right and perfect if you're working in something that you need to go left and right. I keep trying to click it for some reason, so in the second one, maybe they'll add that. The Main Scroll wheel is just brilliant and frankly, sexy. The old M705 has hyperscroll. This turns it on and off with the button and automatically. You'll want to find your sweet spot for that otherwise you'll be turning it on and off without thinking. I ended up turning it off by default and I just turn it on manually.

The bottom controls are smartly laid out. Three devices adjusted by button. Just make sure it's on and you are on the right device.

I've been eyeing this mouse a long while but could never justify getting it. I regret that. It's pricey but I don't regret it. It's smooth and works well. The software is simple and on point. You can use this for work and gaming without issue. The battery life I presume is gonna be good. It's gonna sit on my home/work desk so if I need to charge it, no big deal. Bluetooth seems to us a little more battery but that's no huge shocker.

If you're a techie and want to invest in mouse good for work and play, this is well worth considering and putting at the top of your list.

title: Solid and secure mount with magnetic attachment; holds phone securely; your mileage may vary with the software/app
text:
What you get:
The physical dash mount; two magnetic pads (different shapes/sizes); instructions

Setup is super easy, you just remove the plastic covers from the suction pads and affix to your dashboard and push down the plunger. It holds tight and I've noticed that even in very hot weather it remains sticky and doesn't move around unlike other mounts I've tried. You'll have two choices for magnets which can either be affixed directly to the back of your phone, or in my case I put it between the phone and the phone case. The magnets are very thin and do not impact the case fit at all (if you use a case).

In the car you just hold the phone up to the mount and the magnets will attach. It's a nice tight hold, but easy to remove the phone when you need to. I haven't detected any shifting around or sliding that wasn't easily corrected - and you can adjust where you put the magnet to make it more convenient for your particular needs.

One of the bigger complaints I've seen about the product is that you can't use the app / software without having purchased the mount. That's because the software will automatically activate when it comes into proximity with the mount - essentially automatically turning your phone into a hands free device. If you're not a big user of hands free / voice activated phone control then this isn't the mount for you, because that's really how it's meant to be used.

When you install the software and pair it, you'll be able to do all sorts of things including having it read your messages to you, respond to messages, start maps and music apps (and I do like that you can make your default maps app waze instead of google maps or otherwise), and the voice is pleasant and easy to hear. However, if you're a regular listener to the radio or music from your car's native setup, then you're going to find some issue. Almost every morning for the first week I tested this I would be listening to the radio and a text message would come it. So she's talking to me on the phone asking if I want her to read the message, and the radio is talking to me as well. So I would turn the radio off, respond whether I wanted her to read or not, and then when done turn the radio back on. That's not convenient really. You could use your phone as a bluetooth transmitter for music into your car (if your car can do it) and then all the audio is integrated - but I mostly listen to the radio on my commute and so having her announce messages just isn't that effective.

Using voice control to start the maps function - also less useful because I do that while sitting in the driveway before I even move the car. It's one click on my home screen and waze starts up and takes me to work. So another area where the voice control is less useful.

So for this review I'm going to give is a solid 4 stars for the mount itself - which holds tight to the dashboard and has the magnetic attachment (two of them) which you can use on two phones and which fits snug underneath a case.

For the software / app aspect, it's less useful for me and so I don't use it. But that means you're paying a lot for a magnetic mount and not taking advantage of the real purpose of it which is the hands-free functionality.

Your mileage will vary!

title: Jack of all trades, master of none
text:
Logitech makes several wireless keyboards but basically there are two different types. One is for desktop computers: it connects via a USB dongle and has a complete set of large, full-travel keys in a fairly standard layout and also has a number pad, function keys, and at least a few specialized keys for media software, etc. The other type is for tablets and smartphones or for travel: it connects via Bluetooth; it is small, thin, and light; it omits the number pad and special keys, uses chiclet-style keys, and reduces the function keys to small buttons across the top (though some of Logitech's desktop keyboards do that as well). I have used both types for years; my desktop keyboard is a Logitech K350, my tablet/travel keyboard a Logitech K810.

The K780 attempts to combine both types. Its purpose, according to promotional material included with my Vine review sample, is to "type on everything: use one keyboard on any computer, tablet, and smartphone." It is thin and uses chiclet keys but has a number pad. The buttons across the top can act either as regular function keys or as media/specialized keys; some keys can be toggled for either Windows or OSX (for example, "alt" or "cmd"; the Windows key is labelled "start" rather than use a Windows logo). The keyboard connects either with Bluetooth or to Logitech's "Unifying" USB dongle (which comes with the unit, packed in the battery compartment). And the K780 adds a new feature of its own: a metal backplate with a large lip above the function keys that forms a slot in which tablets or smartphones can sit, tilted back at an angle that is not adjustable but is reasonably appropriate for viewing while typing.

I have tested the K780 with both an iPad Pro, using Bluetooth, and my Windows 10 computer, using my K350's USB dongle. Both connected easily and quickly. My Windows machine has Bluetooth but I was unable to pair it to the K780; based on my experience this is more likely Windows' fault than the keyboard's. Even though it uses both Bluetooth and USB this keyboard is, like Logitech's Bluetooth keyboards, limited to three connections programmed into it at a time, switchable using function keys.

Whether you think the K780 combines the best of both keyboard types or the worst depends on what you will use it for and what you are accustomed to. Though smaller than desktop keyboards it is not very portable; the metal plate makes it quite heavy, much more so than even the full-size K350. As with most small keyboards there is no height/tilt adjustment. But a bigger issue concerns the keys. They're laptop/ultrabook/portable-keyboard keys on what is supposed to pass as a desktop keyboard. As chiclet keys go they're not bad, though they seem to have less travel and to be less responsive than those on the K810. They've typed this review without any particular problems other than having to remember their layout (the K780 puts the "delete" key above "backspace" rather than beside it, like K810-type keyboards but unlike full-sized keyboards). But many people who still use full-sized keyboards do so because they do a lot of heavy keyboard work or else are just heavy-fingered; for those people chiclets become uncomfortable after awhile. That's a price you pay for small size and easy portability but when you don't get those, why pay a price?

For those who don't mind chiclets this could be a fine keyboard; like the K810, its build quality is great and it looks gorgeous. For me the keys are a deal-breaker. If its weight were anywhere near that of the K810 I would consider using it as my new travel keyboard; having a number pad is convenient for me. But the compromises it makes in order to "type on everything" mean that it isn't the best choice -- nor, in my case, an acceptable alternative -- for any one thing.

title: A good, simple HD camera for Skype
text:
I started out skeptical of this camera. Logitech puts its name on a lot of products; some are great values, others are just cheap. And when I received this one through the Vine program there came with it a Logitech form letter addressed to Vine reviewers, thanking us and complimenting us on our fine reviews and pointing out the camera's features and giving us a number to call if we had any questions. We all know that manufacturers try to influence and shape reviews from the tech magazines and web sites but I hadn't realized that Amazon allowed that to extend to Vine reviewers.

Yet this turns out to be a nice little camera -- simple, basic, and easy to use. The HD picture is of very decent quality. Auto-focus works well. The camera's mount fit easily and securely on top of my monitor and can also act as a simple stand for the camera or can be fitted to a tripod. Installation consists simply of plugging in the USB cable, which also powers the camera; the drivers (at least on my Windows 10 machine) install automatically.. There is a manual shutter than can slide over the lens for security (the green light that appears when the camera is on might presumably be hacked somehow).

This camera is intended for use with Skype or similar software. Skype recognizes the camera and allows control over it. The picture-quality adjustments -- brightness, contrast, sharpness, etc. (though not hue and gamma; those controls are greyed-out, as they apparently cannot be adjusted on this camera) -- let the image be tweaked a little bit, though they can't be changed much before the picture becomes odd and unnatural. The camera has no optical zoom nor physical pan/tilt controls (though it can be manually tilted on its mount) but allows those adjustments digitgally through Skype. (The Windows 10 "Skype Video" app can use the camera but allows only rudimentary control of it.)

The camera also has two microphones. They are sensitive but their sound, though clear, is hollow and boomy. I thought this might be due to my positioning but the sound wasn't a lot better when I leaned up to speak directly into them.

All in all this camera does a nice job of being what it is apparently intended to be: a quick, simple, "it just works" way of adding HD-video capability to computers. One star off for the microphones, as well as for Logitech's attempt to put its thumb on the scale.

title: Great Keyboard, Adds Weight, Difficult to Insert/Remove iPad
text:
The Logitech CREATE Backlit Keyboard Case with Smart Connector for iPad Pro was ready right on launch day of the iPad Pro. Indeed, due to the shortage of Apple's own Smart Keyboard Cover, the default choice for many that day was this very Logitech case.

The product has both strengths and weaknesses.

What it got right? The Logitech keyboard case integrates Apple's new Smart Connector. This allows both data and low power to flow from the iPad into the keyboard case. That means there is no pairing of the keyboard, it will "just work," once in the case and on the smart connector. The data of the keyboard has a hard wired connection via the smart connector. There is no battery to charge either, since again, it uses power from the iPad Pro.

Finally, the coolest feature is that the Smart Connector even powers the "backlit keys," on this Logitech case. Wow, it is impressive looking when you see those keys light up. Very cool feature.

Finally, the keyboard case also wins points for looking like a notebook keyboard. No, it doesn't have the exact quality of an Apple keyboard, but it is high quality, and there are shortcut keys that the Apple keyboard cover is missing. iOS shortcuts for screen brightness, search, volume, etc. You won't find these shortcuts on Apple's own iPad Pro keyboard cover. Therefore, the keyboard itself is more full featured.

The drawbacks? Firstly, the weight and size. With this keyboard case on, you're looking at an iPad Pro that is heavier and thicker than several Mac notebooks. Can I just put it on when I want a keyboard? Not really. The Apple keyboard cover is lighter, thinner, and much easier to remove. This Logitech product is very cumbersome to put the iPad in and out. I did it one time and I will never put my iPad in the case again. It takes too much force and the iPad goes into a hard plastic shell. I am concerned you could put light scratch marks or scuffs into the iPad by sliding it in and out of the hard plastic. All of the aftermarket cases tend to use hard plastics. Apple always uses a microfiber lined material on their cases and covers. I don't know why third parties don't consider this.

Overall, the Logitech Keyboard Case for iPad Pro gives you an absolute full featured keyboard with beautiful backlit keys. You will think you're using a notebook with the case on, albeit without a trackpad or mouse since such functionality is not supported by iOS thus no case will offer that. However, the drawback is you're not going to want to pull the Pro in and out of this case regularly, if ever, so you are going to add lots of weight and bulk. Plus, I worry that so much force must be used, you could put scuffs into the iPad.

My recommendation? I prefer Apple's offering for this particular iPad model. Some people are also getting the Apple case and cover, and then simply using an external bluetooth keyboard so they don't have to carry a keyboard when they don't need it. Visit a retailer that offers the various cases so you can check them out, before ordering.

title: This Wired Keyboard Doesn't Have the Same Security Risks as a Wireless One
text:
Since October 2011, I've been using this Logitech K120 Ergonomic Desktop USB Wired Keyboard after a few keys on the wired one that originally came bundled with my desktop computer began failing. I decided to replace that keyboard with another wired one because security can be an issue with wireless keyboards. It has been long-known by wireless keyboard users that transmitted keystrokes can be intercepted by hackers using wireless sniffing technology. Everything from credit card numbers and passwords to private business and financial data can be put at risk by the use of a wireless keyboard, unless the keyboard is encrypted. However, even encrypted keyboards from leading manufacturers are susceptible to surprisingly simple brute-force attacks.

While shopping for my new keyboard, I was primarily interested in finding just a basic keyboard that provided provided both a traditional layout and good key travel. This one fits that bill. As promised by Logitech, the K120's low-profile keys provide a fairly quiet "clickety-click" and comfortable typing experience. The keyboard is also very lightweight, yet sturdy.

As some other reviewers have commented, however, the two plastic feet (see attached photos) on the underside of the keyboard that can be adjusted to raise the keyboard's rear height are a bit flimsy and could easily be broken if you're not careful. Further, on mine at least, one of the four tiny foam pads, affixed to the bottom of each adjustable keyboard foot and and the bottom-left and bottom-right keyboard corners, has fallen off from simply moving the keyboard around on my desk.

Despite these minor shortcomings, I still recommend this keyboard because of its functionality and decent quality for the price.

title: comfortable mouse with precision and sensitivity
text:
I Love this mouse. I did a lot of research on wireless mice on various sites (CNET, PCMAG, others) before deciding on this one. This one was reviewed as one of the top on most sites. I have used wireless mice for awhile, and have no complaints with any of the ones I have used. But, I do have an arthritis condition in my hands and wrists and I have a thought that a better mouse, that is more ergonomic, might be more comfortable for long days of computer/mousing, and days of flaring. Also, this mouse was reviewed as being very sensitive and responsive.
I have fairly small hands, and some of the smaller, not ultra small travel mice, but the semi small mice, fit my hands adequately. That said, I decided I wanted a full size mouse. I wanted good performance. And the ergonomics interested me. I also like the color blue. Though that was not a deciding factor but a gilding.
So. I received this mouse and my initial reaction upon viewing it was one of hesitancy. It is kind-of big, and sort-of looks squashed, with a little more squashing to the left side where it bulges out a bit. I commenced to try it out and after a short period of time, mere moments, I found that I was adjusting to both the size and feel of it and that it is actually very comfortable to use. And now, having been using it quite a bit, I really love it. It feels very natural under my hand. It follows the natural curve of my hand, allowing my hand to for the most part rest on it easily, without any tension in my hand or wrist. The clicking is easy to do, and the scroll wheel can be set to free scroll or with a push of a button on the mouse, ratchet so you can feel little clicks as it scrolls. There are two buttons on the left of the mouse but I have not used them yet. I will. The sensitivity of the mouse is wonderful, and allows great precision and less work with the hand. Amazon sells the mouse at about half of what other sites charge, so it is a bargain, as well. The blue? Well, it IS blue, though in some light is hard to tell that it is blue. Basically the sides and bottom are black and the top inset is a matte dark blue. Hard to see that it is blue at first. But that is not the deciding factor anyway. But since I mentioned that I like blue, and I did order it in blue, I will mention that although it IS blue, it is not so easy to tell that it is. In some light, it might be two shades of black or perhaps a dark grey. No matter. It is mostly covered by my hand when in use and it functions wonderfully.

title: Picks up all breathing - and other quirks. Go with Jabra.
text:
I got this headset for remote teaching in a high school classroom. Main complaint: the microphone is WAY too sensitive.
Comfort: It's acceptable, but does start hurt my head a little after about one hour.
Ease of use: Plug-and-play works perfectly, no problems.
Microphone quality: Microphone is WAY too sensitive. I get lots of complaints of hearing my breath or other things in the room. I think it should have a foamy boom.
Sound quality: What you'd expect from a chat headset, but don't expect to be impressed using it for music, games, etc.
Cord controls: The cord has a block with buttons like volume. They work fine, but the block is a little too heavy and pulls down on the headset.

I have a similarly priced headset at work - I think it's a Jabra 550. I've had much better luck with that one. Microphone is perfect. It's more comfortable to wear. The cord's control block doesn't feel too heavy. Since I've been using both on a weekly basis. I highly recommend going with Jabra.

title: Meh, I'm very underwhelmed. I thought I was going to get a product that worked.
text:
What is UP with this thing? The first 2 weeks were awesome. I've never had a wireless keyboard before and it was kind of freeing. Every once in a while though it would seem like it didn't want to respond. No big deal. 2 weeks after that however and this thing is cutting out on my like crazy. I thought it might be the receiver but when the keyboard cuts out the mouse works fine. A couple days later and the problem is EVEN WORSE. And now the mouse is starting to cut out too! I tried some new batteries and that doesn't help. I'm not too far from the receiver (or I hope I'm not considering the keyboard and mouse are only about 20 inches from it!), so that can't be it.

Well, this sucks, I guess I'll just return it, or have amazon replace it. Oh, what's that? You say my window for a return closed 2 days ago. Well that sucks. Now I'm stuck with a janky keyboard.

Forget about the people complaining that the letters wear off. I mean, this is 2016, do we not know where the letters are by now? Are we all still hunting and pecking? Regardless, I haven't had this thing long enough to notice any wear to the stickers. Anyway, the real problem with this keyboard is that it cuts in and out constantly. Don't even think about gaming with this thing or you'll be tearing your hair out as someone in PvP ganks you while your character stands there motionless. I should have known better than to try to game with a wireless keyboard + mouse, so that's on me.

I guess a lot of other people are super happy with this keyboard. I'm happy for them, I really am. I wish mine worked flawlessly. But it doesn't. And it doesn't seem to work for an awful lot of other people.

So the question is, do you want to chance it?

If you do, good luck. I hope your experience isn't as bad as mine. Also, remember to watch the date, so if you DO want to return it, you can do so within the allotted time. Unlike me. Though to be fair, it didn't start getting super wonky until it was too late. Oh well, whatever.

title: Decent symmetrical corded trackball but no dedicated scroll wheel and ergonomics aren't perfect
text:
This is a decent corded trackball. It isn't perfect but that is mainly my fault as I should have looked at the photos more. Since it was my first trackball purchase though in my defense I was no expert. However I think most people are going to want a dedicated third mouse button with a scroll wheel as is standard. Now yes it does come with four buttons and you can program one of the buttons to act as the third mouse button and you can also use that button with a combination of the trackball to emulate a third mouse button scroll. However in my opinion it's just not the same. Perhaps I just need to get used to it though?

Another thing is that this is symmetrical. This has a benefit for left handed people in that it isn't a mouse designed primarily for the typical right handed user. However due to the symmetry I feel just isn't as ergonomic as it could be for myself as a right handed user. I find that I would have preferred the small and large button on the right to be quite a bit higher up in position where I could click them with my pinkie finger or the one right next to it. That would feel more natural to me whereas with the current positioning I have to bend my fingers down to click the two buttons on the right side..

Other than the above it is a decent trackball. For Linux users note that it works just fine and is programmable by various methods such as editing your Xorg config file.

title: Great features like remote app and integration with Amazon Echo via IFTTT, with just a few limitations.
text:
First, it is best if you setup the hub on a WIFI network with full access to any AV equipment that uses WIFI, this will simplify the setup process and may provide some extra capabilities depending on your components.

Using a mobile device to start the setup was pretty painless to a point, I plugged in the charger base and inserted the remote to start charging. I then positioned the hub and plugged it in, like many newer IoT devices the app used Bluetooth to connect to the hub, I had to press the pair button on the hub to get the connection but the app showed that. Once it connected it asked me to name it then it searched and found my non-hidden WIFI network and I provided the password for the network. This is where I had the first hiccup in the setup process, it said there was a update required on the remote and that I had to hook the remote to a computer using the USB cable and finish the process on the computer, I had just given it internet access by hooking it up to my network so why couldn't it just download the update and install on its own? I am guessing this is because I hooked the hub up to the internet but the remote is only communicating to the hub via RF and doesn't have the bandwidth to receive updates from the hub. It took me a few minutes to find the computer software which I finally found at:[...] once I had that installed I thought I was dealing with the hub at this point and the mobile app hadn't made it clear enough for me anyway at that point so I plugged the hub into the computer and once I logged into the app it told me it couldn't find the hub and that that needs to be plugged in to the wall. OK, I plug the hub back into the wall and plug the remote in, but it wouldn't see the remote. I unplugged the remote, exited the app, and got back into the app and logged on then plugged the remote in once told to do so and it found it then and I was able to start the update process. Once that completed it asked if I wanted to complete the setup process on the computer or mobile device, I chose the mobile option for mobility. I opened the mobile app again and it searched the local network and found the hub but when I clicked on the hub it wouldn't connect it just kept spinning, eventually I decided it wasn't working so I closed the app and tried again with the same results so I unplugged the hub and plugged it back in then closed the app and tried again and it worked.

Now the setup went pretty smooth from here on. It scanned my network for WIFI devices and found my Yamaha receiver but not my Sony DVD player so I turned the DVD on and re-scanned and it found both so I clicked add for those. I then added my Samsung TV, Xfinity Cable Box, and computer by manufacturer and model number, or in the case of the computer by OS. It then had me setup a Watch TV activity and I added more like Watch Netflix, Watch Amazon, Watch a movie, and Listen to music. The Watch a movie, Netflix, and Amazon activities all use the same components they just launch the corresponding app on the DVD player at the end of the launch sequence.

I haven't had time to try the computer activity yet and the Watch TV option turns everything on however it doesn't get the input set to the tuner correctly, maybe because it doesn't delay long enough after turning on, I added a delay but I can't move it above the input command and I tried to add another input command but it doesn't show up in the list of options I was able to add the source menu option with an up command and select command which works but is kind of hokey. Also I couldn't find a way to change the layout or the look of the activity or device screens in the app which I would really like to be able to do, you can change the hard buttons on the remote but nothing in the app as far as I can tell. In the past I have owned the Marantz RC5000, RC9001, and the RedEye hub. The Marantz remotes where by far the most customize-able but extremely time consuming to setup (weeks since I customized most icons and the layout of each activity differently). The RedEye wouldn't let you add custom graphics easily but would let you change the size and move buttons around and change which buttons are available on the mobile device activities screens which is all I was really expecting here, unfortunately the company ThinkFlood that made the RedEye went out of business and when their servers went down it limited my ability to add new devices so it was time to look for a new option, and so onto one of the deciding factors in going with the Logitech.

I also have an Amazon Echo which I wanted to use with this remote so I loaded the IFTTT app on my mobile and tried to setup the Harmony Recipe, but had issues connecting the Harmony channel which took a few tries and closing out of the recipe and reopening it before it showed the available activities. I then created a recipe for each of my available activities with a matching phrase, so I can say "Alex, trigger watch Netflix" and the TV, receiver, and DVD all turn on, the TV switches to HDMI1, the receiver to HDMI1, and the DVD player Netflix favorite is sent! I do wish Logitech and Amazon would integrate the Harmony Hub directly with Alexa though rather than through IFTTT as it adds some lag as it is.

So far I have spent about 3 hours getting the hub/remote setup, devices added, activities setup, and integration with Alexa working, this is by far the quickest setup of the advanced universal remotes I've owned and the easiest even with the few issues that I ran into. I just wish I could remove some of the buttons in the app screens and move things around so everything I use most is on one screen.

This weekend I'll do more testing and try to update the review then.

Update (October 10 2016):
I have found how to modify the default device delay to help with my TV not getting the correct source, I also figured out how to modify the mobile and touch screen activity buttons however I had to do it on each device (iPhone, iPad, Android Tablet, and remote). The one big downside to the Alexa integration is that it only starts activities and I have one IR light switch since they don't make advanced switches like the Lutron MIR-LFQTHW-WH Maestro switch with Z-Wave yet. So I can only turn on the light not dim it or turn just the light off since I had to change the activity to not power off the activity when the activity switches. I can turn off the light with the power off all AV command but that also powers off the rest of the components. It would be great to be able to use Alexa to push individual buttons as well.

Update (October 28 2016):
Harmony released their Alexa skill last night, currently it offers little more than the IFTTT integration offered, although I got a reply from Harmony saying they are working on device level control, so I have hopes that this skill will soon far surpass what we have had the ability to ask Alexa to do up till now.

title: Great!
text:
I've always been hesitant about switching to trackball mice. They've felt awkward in some models that I would test out in stores. But I have to say, this one is probably your best shot at making the switch, and after a few days of getting your muscle memory going you'll never want to go back to the standard mouse.

Out of the box, it's simple enough. Plug it in and go. However, because of the lack of a proper scroll wheel, even the Setpoint app you can install from the Logitech site isn't enough. I grabbed an app called Marblescroll, which lets you press and hold the default back button, turning the ball into a scroll wheel. Releasing it lets the button revert to its back function. Also, this special add-on app doesn't automatically activate after rebooting your PC, so all I did was add it to the startup routine.

Once that was all done, holy smokes the product is seriously unbeatable. Super smooth and intuitive. Love it.

title: One Star
text:
I solve how to activate tap-to-click function.

Because no tap-to-click out of the box, need to hack it with some AutoHotKey obscure workaround.

After a couple of hours trying to figure out I found it. Have to remap Setpoint special gestures with AutoHotKey soft.
You'll have to double tap to click and 4 times tap to double click. It's a pain but it's desperate measures for desperate people.

Short steps instructions:
- In Setpoint, set "double tap with one finger" to show\hide desktop.
- Also set "double tap with two fingers" to switch applications (task view)
- Trust me and run this file in your pc (...)
- Done.

Long steps instructions:
- In Setpoint, set "double tap with one finger" to show\hide desktop.
- Also set "double tap with two fingers" to switch applications (task view)
- Install AutoHotKey, during installation confirm the "add right click context menu options"
- Right click your desktop, create new script and fill as this:

#NoEnv ; Recommended for performance and compatibility with future AutoHotkey releases.
; #Warn ; Enable warnings to assist with detecting common errors.
SendMode Input ; Recommended for new scripts due to its superior speed and reliability.
SetWorkingDir %A_ScriptDir% ; Ensures a consistent starting directory.

*<#Tab::
MouseClick,right,,,1,0,D
KeyWait,LControl
MouseClick,right,,,1,0,U
Return

*#d::
MouseClick,left,,,1,0,D
KeyWait,LControl
MouseClick,left,,,1,0,U
Return

- Save file and right click it to run script, done.
- If you want a .exe file, use AutoHotKey convert in start menu.

Cheers.

title: Multi-device keyboard with built-in stand
text:
Logitech makes some great wireless keyboards that can easily switch connections with various devices. The K780 is another helpful addition to their line. It's important to know what it is not - it's not meant to be a keyboard that you can easily toss in your bag and carry around everywhere. They have other keyboards (e.g. K810) that are much better for that. The K780 is meant to stay on your desktop, so although it is small it has a decent heft to it, mainly due to the rubberized tablet/phone stand. This additional weight helps to keep the keyboard from flipping over easily if a tablet is placed in the stand.

Pairing the keyboard with different devices is relatively straightforward (although the model I received didn't include any written instructions - just diagrams). You can pair it with up to 3 devices, and switch between them with a touch of a button. The keys are the chiclet-type that all Mac users are familiar with. One difference is that the keys are rounded - I prefer the traditional squared keys but didn't have a major issue with this. The keys had a slightly less amount of travel than other Logitech keyboards I've used, but overall the typing experience was quite smooth. I'm happy to see a dedicated numeric pad.

Logitech took an interesting approach to key labeling in order to make this compatible with both Windows and Mac keyboard layouts. There are a couple of keys next to the space bar labeled Start/Option and Alt/Cmd. This seems like a reasonable compromise. Overall, I'm pleased with the keyboard but will plan on leaving it on the desk most of the time.

title: An absolute bargain with first-rate components and technology
text:
Audio-video telephony is upon us -- Skype is currently this technology's most visible manifestation. But as the other big developers, including Facebook and Twitter -- move toward the industry's Number One goal -- real-time communication -- having a webcam that doesn't make you look like something from "I Love Lucy" at the other end is becoming more and more important.

There are the cheap webcams that are built into PCs and are so bad they don't deserve mention here. At the other end of the spectrum are the pro units that cost hundreds and need a well-let studio and sound setup to do them justice. And then then there is a vast middle range of so-so cams with limited capabilities.

Over the years I've owned all of these except the top end. None of them made me happy, especially as video technology got better and data speeds got faster. After my last one bit the dust, I opted to go a bit above my price range and get the Logitec C920.

Its specs are SO impressive -- full 1080p HD resolution, UVC H.264 video compression (just like high-end camcorders), two stereo mics, low-light correction, mount for a tripod, and to top off the list, a first-class Zeiss lens.

The result is an absolutely gorgeous picture. Use the image adjustment software from Logitech's website (easy), make sure your face is well lit (not dark but with some contrasting light and shadow), and check that you're broadcasting at the maximum quality your software and data connection allow. Your expectation should be an image as good as you'll get on your HD TV. You'll never use a cheapo camera again.

The Logitec C920 camera cost a bundle when it first came out a coupe of years ago but I see a new model is taking over and Amazon is discounting the 920 heavily. My recommendation -- and I've not been given an "evaluation" unit or any of that nonsense -- is to add a few bucks to your budget and, if you carefully adjust your lighting, you'll come across like a movie star to the person on the other end of your Skype call.

title: Very pleased!  I use it for many PC repetitive tasks.
text:
Love this! First I'll address some items that I had trouble ascertaining from product description, questions and reviews:
1. May be a no-brainer to some, but I wanted to know if my laptop would take 3 input devices with no problem (mouse, keyboard and gameboard). It does! But I switched my mouse and keyboard to Unifying wireless receiver (from Logitech) to take up one less USB port. I understand wireless mouse and keyboard is not the best for hardcore gaming- I've had hardware hesitations in WoW using wireless input.
2. I really wanted this for repetitive PC tasks, with gaming far secondary. So happy it has no problem with almost anything I want in several pc programs. It's great for many things as long as you figure out the shortcut keys for your programs. It will not program any mouse cursor movement (only mouse clicks).
3. The image makes it appear that it will sit upright. I hoped it would sit upright but it doesn't. I wanted it to take up less desk space. I would be very happy if it didn't have the handrest. But I suppose it needs a handrest for hardcore gaming hours on end. Perhaps next iteration can include a removable handrest or some sort of upright stand device.

Right now I use it for several repetitive PC tasks including:
1) -entering my name - saves seconds but it's worth it
2) -entering email
3) -highlight the address bar in Chrome, copy it, then switch to another tab in Chrome and paste it.
4) -switching to a certain tab in Chrome without looking at the keyboard for the right number.
5) -selecting a full sentence in Chrome (three clicks), copying it, alt-tab to OneNote, then pasting
6) -alt-tab without me accidentally hitting the windows button. also eliminates any human delay. same for copy, paste, ctrl-t to open a new Chrome tab, ctrl-shift-t to reopen a closed tab.
7) -open a new tab, enter an address and go to it. great for often visited websites like email, news, etc. I also have a sequence of opening several tabs with all the websites I work in.
8) -click, tiny pause, click, tiny pause.... (one task I do takes hundreds of clicks - it sucks. Note: I do not set this up for hundreds of clicks itself, but rather 5 to 10. so I cut the hundreds of clicks by 5 or 10 times).
9) -middle mouse click to open a link in a new tab - this way I can use two hands for more efficiency, instead of the right hand both moving the mouse and clicking the middle mouse key.
10) -open Chrome download screen without memorizing the right Chrome keys or moving mouse and finding it in Chrome settings.
11) selecting a whole sentence and replacing it with a common phrase I use.

Even though several of these save me mere seconds, those seconds add up fast with all my repetitive tasks. Plus, since many of my tasks follow one another very soon, I can memorize the key pattern and that saves me even more time.

Many of my multi-key settings involve things that I would normally have to move the mouse to do; moving the mouse takes an amount of time that quickly adds up.

I don't understand people qualifying their review with "it takes some time to set up." Of course it takes time, but one time set up, plus testing, are exponentially outweighed by the time-saving benefits.

- I will use it for gaming in the future. It works so well with my repetitive tasks that I'm sure it will be just as awesome in WoW and StarCraft.

title: A Love/Hate Relationship (But Mostly Love)
text:
PROS
+ Key spacing is comfortable, especially for touch typing
+ It has a dedicated delete key (although it could be larger); I mention this because I’ve come across one too many keyboards which omit the delete key in lieu of the backspace key to conserve space
+ Pairing with Android and iOS was quick and easy
+ It seamlessly switches between three devices without breaking a sweat (I have it set up with an Android tablet; an Android phone; and an iPhone--haven’t needed to re-pair any of them)
+ The bottom has non-skid bumpers so it stays in place while typing on a table or other surface, even when on a slight incline
+ Keys have great tactile feedback while typing and the home keys (F & J) have raised indicators
+ It respects most common keyboard commands (ex: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Z, etc.)
+ Great battery life (I’ve yet needed to change my batteries after using it near daily for over a month--I am, however, careful to switch it off after I’ve finished using it)

NEUTRALS
* Every so often, it will miss a keystroke as though it can’t quite keep up (I’ve listed this under neutrals because it happens so infrequently as to not be problematic)
* This thing is hefty and thick (nearly 1/2" at its thickest part); some may view this as a positive (as it’s less inclined to tip while typing) and some may see this as a negative (because it can be a bear to carry around)
* Keys are not backlit (I know this wasn’t a listed feature, but I’m pointing it out because this keyboard would be a million times better if they were)
* It requires two AAA batteries rather than using a built-in rechargeable battery; some may view this as positive (as they can be purchased almost anywhere) and some may view this as a negative (because it means more potential waste and clutter)
* No illuminated indicator light when it’s on (it will light briefly when you switch it on and it pairs, but the only way to know whether you’ve left it on/off is to flip it over and check the power switch on the back)

CONS
- The keys are noisy; I don’t mind this so much, but they’ll definitely be heard if you’re typing in a quiet area
- The low battery indicator is on the bottom of the keyboard rather than in a more visible location (the logic of this baffles me)
- Area for the tablet/phone is only so deep and only so wide, which means you’d be hardpressed to use your tablet or phone with a protective case (even a thin one) unless you have an ultra-thin device
- Because the recessed area for the tablet/phone is only so wide, it means you can’t adjust the angle of the device and it’s at nearly a 90 degree angle which could be uncomfortable for some

I have a love/hate relationship with this keyboard. In so many ways, it’s absolutely fantastic, but there are others that simply irk me to no end. That said, I do find myself reaching for it quite often when I need to draft emails, letters, or other writings which require more than a device’s onscreen keyboard will comfortably allow. In fact, I typed this review with it.

If in the future, though, Logitech comes out with an updated version which allows for a deeper angle, using a device in its case, backlit keys, and quieter typing, I’ll be first in line. In the meantime, I’ll just need to make due with this one.

As I continue using it, I’ll update this review as necessary. Before then, if you have a question about the keyboard or my experience with it, please leave a comment and I’ll do my best to answer.

title: its not as comfortable as everyone says, but its ok
text:
i bought this at BH photo, the price was the same, the shipping is faster (expedited, amazon waits like a week before sending things).

anyway, i had the perfomance MX from 2009 and replaced it twice, they seem to last about 3 years or so before something breaks. i never liked it because my hand would cramp up, and i finally wore through the button.

i needed a new mouse fast and everyone loved this new mx master mouse, some claimed it helped reverse their carpal issues, others said it was like an old glove, and it really isn't. while my wrist does not hurt, i'm having a hard time figuring out where to put my hand exactly. with my hand on it, its not bad, with it on the wheel, my hand slides off. this is partly due to the sandy texture they put on it. i don't like the grip on the side. the facets make it feel like there is grit on there. the old mouse had rubber on the sides, giving it more grip, this is all plastic.

button response is good for left and right, the center is also much improved, i use it to open my mail program. the button clicker changer thing, is not a mechanical switch any more, its all electronic now. i use that button to close programs, since its out of the way (i used to use the useless zoom button on the other mouse for that).

back and forward, the back is easy to get to, i don't need the top one that much, so its hard to say if its bad or not, but i don't like the pointy feeling of the button. the side thumb wheel has its uses, it doesn't free spin, it drags like an AM/FM dial. and you can adjust how sensitive it is. it side scrolls in everything, but the media player, i have that set to forward and backward the movie. the under thumb button is a bit soft but usable.

the software... you can make custom controls in each program. however, set point does not recognize this mouse. you need logitech options, a different program, something else you have to remember to load up. and it takes like 2 min to open. no splash screen, i think it scans for all new programs, but it doesn't look like its doing anything. the software is easy enough to use, but the sensitivity controls, doesn't let you use the thumb wheels to adjust, and they don't seem to have a fine tune. more like notches, but the scale doesn't have numbers or lines, so its hard to make finer adjustments and there is no internal help telling you what they do... but the WORST part is -- it doesn't come with any software. you need to download it. now if this was my first mouse, i would have no way to download it. the old dongle didn't know what to do with the new mouse, and my keyboard uses a dongle. and it was messy to install what i needed.

the box it came in has two neodymium magnets to keep the lid shut. i think this is a nice bonus... however if you have little kids, they can swallow it, and it can really hurt them. so be sure that box is out of sight.

if your replacing your current mouse, i advise you to feel it and others in the store. i like the freewheel, and that's why i chose this style mouse.

title: So far so good, controls almost everything I need.
text:
I was a bit skeptical at first because of my setup. I have all my Audio stuff in a closed closet at the front of the room (Onkyo receiver, Samsung BD, Panasonic VCR, Sonos, Roku, XBone) and a projector at the back of the room. I knew the remote came with an external blaster, but I wasn't sure if it would be strong enough to go from the front of the room to the back of the room (~14 feet).

I'm upgrading from an old Harmony 720 using the old software (non-web based). Conversion of the software was pretty straightforward, I just imported all devices and activities through the Phone app. The phone app was also somewhat worrying because on iOS, it only has a 2.5 star rating.

So far so good though. The blaster works without fail on the projector, and the hub works great in the closet. I've had to tweak some settings for the physical remote buttons to control stuff (especially for the Sonos) but so far, I've had MUCH better luck with this than the 720. The 720, I always had to hit a button, then keep it pointed and not stand in the way. Especially for things like the projector that requires a double tap of power to turn it off. This, I can just hit the power button and walk away. Even the app is good so far, no problems on that, and I would also rate that highly in the app store.

Only problem so far is that I haven't gotten it to control the Xbox One. not sure if that's me, or Microsoft or Logitech, though. more to come. The only downside of this is how they artificially cripple it at 8 devices. Obviously, it's just software, and memory is cheap these days, so the only reason they set it to 8 devices is so you are forced to buy the model with a screen, which I don't want.

But so far, this definitely passes the Wife Acceptance Factor as well as potentially the Mother In Law Acceptance factor. Much higher than the old Harmony did.
