text:
Edit: Though my rating remains the same, the keys on the keyboard began to lack fluidity when trying to type so I've informed Logitech and a new set is on the way out, replaced under warranty. Hopefully the new keyboard lasts longer than 6 months!

------------------------------------

I bought this keyboard and mouse combo at Best Buy around a month ago because it was on sale for $30 Canadian (as of the time of this writing, around $23 US). The keyboard is the perfect size for me and has an excellent spacing and feel while typing; it even makes a sound slightly resembling that of a mechanical keyboard which I would have liked though found them very expensive and to find one this size as well as wireless is likely an impossibility in a reasonable price range. The idea was for me to be able to bring the keyboard and mouse into my living room sometimes an use the bigscreen connected to my machine by HDMI as the monitor, though I haven't this done yet so I'm not able to yet review the distance they will work other than to say the keyboard is currently only two feet from the USB plug and works fine. When I tested the mouse I found it somewhat laggy compared to my old wired optical mouse.

While the keyboard so far has been exactly what I wanted, I find the mouse absolutely useless. It seems fit for about the use of a child; I do not have huge hands so it is really bad. Because of this I'm stuck using my old wired Microsoft mouse which is the original design of the optical mouse released probably 15 years ago. It seems this problem isn't limited to Logitech products; why is it so damned hard to find a normal sized wireless mouse? I shouldn't have to spend a fortune to find one.

Because of the mouse issue this review should really be 2 ½ stars, but since I paid for this awful mouse and am stuck with it I must round down rather than up. I suppose the mouse will just have to work for the odd time I may decide to move into the other room as long as the 10 or 15 feet distance doesn't prove to be a problem.

title: So I came looking at the possibility of replacing the battery and was absolutely shocked by the price tag of one of these new!
text:
This morning I was rewiring the recharging dock because the wires were exposed and figured i'd see about the battery. After taking apart the mouse and the charging dock, this is a very serviceable mouse. The battery appears to be replaceable though it is not their new dongle so be sure not to lose yours.

I bought this mouse in 2010 because I really liked the way it sits in your hand. It's very comfortable and has many buttons that are done well. Most mice just sprinkle buttons all over but they are very distinct. With the earlier drivers, you were able to set so many cook tasks or key presses to the buttons. This was before the software we have now. I used this mouse for 4 years before finally switching to the G700. 1 G700's wireless receiver fried and they sent a second. The MX revolution has served me without question for many many years and as long as any issues are serviceable, I won't give it up.

+Many buttons. The second wheel isn't really a wheel so much as a spring loaded roller to activate 2 switches. The main scroll wheel can tilt to add 2 more buttons.
+Extremely comfortable. The G700 tries but there is something about the revolution that is amazing in the hand.
+Brilliant charge indicator
+Nice little dock
+Easy for small DIY repairs - I have had to fix some exposed wires on the dock from a bad fall (My Fault) and many users have done videos on replacing batteries and micro switches. I can see this mouse still working in 10 years.
- It's a bit heavy but I personally don't mind that at all.
-Some of the surfaces have not aged as well as I would have hoped. After 6 years (how dare you make a mouse that lasts this long Logitech), some of the coatings are wearing off.

In closing, would I pay 500 bucks for a new one? Not a damn chance... Would I consider buying one used for around 70-110? Absolutely. It's sad to say that I really feel like Logitech has let their bean counters ruin their products. I say this as someone who has many Logitech products that when made, where the best on the market and have lasted. My TV/Media pc runs through a set of Logitech Z680's that sound absolutely awesome. I love these so much, that when I burnt an internal fuse (Also my fault) on 2 different occasions, I completely disassembled the amp and replaced the fuses.

I really do hope Logitech finds their roots and starts making the amazing hardware built to last that they once did. I still have a 518 that works after many drops...Having a G700 burn out the receiver after 8 months of use is unacceptable from a company that has made so many amazing products. They honored the warranty and replaced it though.

text: I have used Logitech products for a long time--they are good quality and tend to last well.  When I wore out (literally--the printing on the buttons was mostly gone from use over 13 years) my last logitech keyboard, I ordered this one to replace it for my desktop computer.  I plugged it in, waited for the computer to recognize it and tell me that it was okay to use...and all heck broke out.  The screen started flashing, the keys on the keyboard were only partially functional (some would work, most would not), and I hastily turned the system off, removed the keyboard and its little flash drive and put the old one back on.  Then I discovered that my husband's and my Windows passwords were erased, our Facebook passwords had disappeared and the Facebook settings had been completely messed up.  I don't know if there was a virus on the little flash drive or what, but it certainly played havoc with our desktop computer (running Windows 8.1).  The keyboard went back in its box, my husband went downtown and paid for a corded Radioshack keyboard (which is working beautifully as I type this), the passwords were restored eventually, and all is now well.  I have returned the keyboard.  Good Riddance.  I am still curious, though, about what the heck it was actually happened.....

title: Broke in 10 months. Pointer no longer works even when the Gesture Button is turned off.
text:
UPDATED REVIEW:
After using the mouse for just 10 months, it broke down. Pointer no longer works.

The MX Master Wireless mouse is supposed to be the premium choice for professionals due to how it's marketed but for it's price you would have hoped for a longer lifespan. It's frustrating, perhaps to my fault, not having an extra mouse that I can easily adapt to. After using an MX Master, using the cheaper $6 optical ones feels like a terrible ordeal. That's because a working MX Master is amazing. One that breaks in 10 months with probably no hope of customer service even due to faulty hardware & not accidents? That's a baaaaad situation. Especially when you're a graphic designer trying to meet deadlines. Now if there were only other premium mice that are as beautiful & functional without bearing some gaming logo.

UPDATE #2
I think Logitech made up for the faulty mouse by sending me a completely new replacement without requiring me to send it over. That's great because it is pointless for me to send the mouse over a courier back to the US from PH. Shipping would cost me way more than a new mouse. However, within a week of corresponding to some certain Pierre from Logitech's customer service on their website, I was informed they were sending me a new one. It's on its way to my country and would be happy to confirm if it will be working... and within a few more months if the new mouse had no such defects over time.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I like its heft. It's not really heavy for me. I also have some pretty average hands and it feels nice.
The Logitech software is also very useful. I've set different settings for general desktop use, for Excel use, for Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, etc and it works so seamlessly. The gesture control is exceptional.

title: Don't buy, save your money and stress levels.
text:
This has been by far the worst headset I've ever owned. It NEVER works without issues. A $30 pair I bought over a year ago performed better. MUCH better.

When connected to the controller via the 3.5mm adapter, you CANNOT use the headset's mic. The mic will ONLY work when the headset is powered on (great info on this part later).

The way your instructed to use the headset is as follows:

1.If you want to use it with a console, the headset needs to be powered off. Once you connect the 3.5mm adapter it will push audio through, But the mic will not work.

2. To use it with your PC wirelessly, connect the dongle and power on the headset, it will connect automatically. This "normally" works. I've had so many issues getting this to work as well. Either I will be able to hear people, but not be able to talk, or I can talk but not hear them or the game. Believe me when I say I messed with every freaking setting on my PC and on this headset's trash software.

This headset can also connect to a PC with the wireless dongle provided, sweet right? No. Not really. The connection to the PC is trash and constantly drops. There's moments mid game that I have to unplug the dongle and plug it back in because it stops producing any sound. By the way, rarely will this fix the issue.

Software:
The app constantly freezes up, and loses connection to the headset. At least changing the colors works right? Kinda. There's no different shades of any color, you get different brightness levels though. Yeah... Nice... (You can select different colors, but can't make different areas different colors, everything is one color at all times)

I would also like to point out that I've installed firmware updates as Logitech suggested. I think their "fixes" only achieved one thing: letting me change when the headset goes to sleep when not in use (and by not in use, I of course mean mid game/in use)

When this headset works, it's great. I have no complaints, in this 1% range of use.

Don't buy this thing. Use your money to get a good ~$50 headset that ACTUALLY WORKS. Like the hyper X cloud.

Hey Logitech, how about a refund? I'll even send you your device back with a pretty bow. And a little birdy to boot!

text:
The sound on this pair of headset is amazing but the microphone is okay, nothing special. Although the headset sounds amazing, I am rating it 2 stars for one main reason: problems with the USB dongle.

The first pair I got came in and worked perfectly fine until a week later, the USB dongle would not work at all. No matter what I did, Windows refused to recognize the USB dongle. I even thought it might of been my usb ports, but I tried with my ASTRO A50s and my ASTROS worked perfectly fine, meaning my usb ports aren't the problem. I figured it might of just been a defective unit I got so I returned it for a replacement.

The second pair came in, and I used it for about two weeks, within two weeks, the USB dongle disconnected twice on me randomly. After that I went to research more about this headset reading other reviews and it turns out problems with the USB dongle are pretty common. I decided to return the second pair afterwards as I do not want to risk it especially when the warranty is over.

TL;DR: Great headset, wanted to love it, but experienced problems with the USB dongle.

title: Perfect iPad case
text:
Since this case can tilt to nearly every angle, it makes viewing the screen SO easy. Especially when watching videos. Just push it to where you want and it stays there.

The case lid magnetically attaches to the back with a good amount of force when you flip the lid behind. So you can pick the iPad up without the lid flopping all around.

Very nice for your lap too. Since the back of the case extends the full length of the iPad, it can straddle your legs even when they are spread apart. When your legs are farther apart, just tilt the case at a steeper angle to keep the screen facing you.

You have to use more force than you think to bend the case, but it's really not that difficult. There is also a right way and a wrong way to bend it. But if you bend the case backwards, it won't break it even though it feels like it might break.

Very sturdy.
Magnetic screen lock works great and has never failed.
Screen cover doesn't make marks on screen. I hate other cases that leave marks.
Clear back is nice if you want to see the Apple logo, or if you have an engraving, or viewing the model/serial number.
Doesn't look damaged at all after 8 or 9 months of use. No tears in fabric or pieces breaking off. Very good construction.
Provides good drop protection.

Only real downfall is that the buttons for power and volume require a lot of force to press. I usually opt for on-screen volume control. And instead of pressing the power button, I just shut the lid and the screen turns off. So I don't even have to use those buttons.

I would like the front of the case (the border that you can see when looking at the screen) to be black instead of gray so that it doesn't stand out so much, but it's really not a big deal.

title: I love this thing!
text:
My old MX-500 remote died after 10 years or so, and I was scared. The MX-500 had been discontinued, and I didn't want to spend almost $200 on the model that replaced it. I have a complex home theater system with many devices - AV receiver, 2 DVR's, DVD player as well a Blue-ray, cd carousel, Roku and an Echo Dot. Oh yeah, and 3 TV's for football Sundays. I looked around and found this harmony 650, but was skeptical that a $52 remote would suit my needs.

Boy, was I wrong. This remote is great. There was a slight learning curve with the programming software, but once i realized that using "activities" to power on, change inputs and remote functions to the specified device while still having the volume buttons utilize the AV receiver, I found it easy to program this to do exactly what I wanted. One button press to change everything to use the desired item. Even little things delight me - when i set down the remote,m the LCD screen goes to "sleep" after 10 seconds, but it has a motion sensor, so when i pick it up again it automatically comes back on.

Yeah, it doesn't work with my Roku (it has a Bluetooth remote) and it would be nice if you could have more than 8 devices, but those are really minor quibbles. Especially considering the price, i don't know how you could beat this remote.

text:
Pros:

I have an older Logitech set that is similar to this except it does not do 7.1 and the Mic only works with the old gen Xbox system. Padding around the ears and head is soft and these are headphones you can likely wear for many hours. Logitech software also include audio presets for many games and allows for adjusting audio settings such as Bass, Treble, and Equalizer settings.

Cons:
I dropped one star for a charge issue I had right out of box. I wanted to put a full charge on the set however the Logitech software after hours of being plugged in still showed 3 hrs remaining on the charge and the light never changed to orange which the manual says means its fully charged. I tried a cable from my phone since Logitech suggested this to others on their forums. The charge light started flashing and went back to red. The software still showed 3 hrs of charge time remaining. I went ahead and removed the cable again power cycled the headset and then the software then showed it was fully charged. If the unit indicator is not correct and the headset lasts for 7-10hrs I can overlook the software reporting incorrect charge info. However if the unit doesn't charge and last for the specified time in the manual then I will update this review and likely return the headphones or get a warranty replacement.

text:
I thought with this I could use two different remotes with one hub and control two different TV's in two different rooms with the shared components located where the hub is. But it can't work that way because the companion remote is essentially just a dumb slave to the Ultimate (or smartphone app) and if you set an activity on one it's also set on the other, thus raising the question as to what the purpose of this thing is. And to make matters worse it doesn't have its own IR emitter. So if you hub or Ultimate isn't aimed at your TV, forget it.
Bottom line there's no reason to ever buy this. As a "companion" to the Ultimate it is worthless because the Ultimate already does everything you need for that room. title: Very easy to add a new device
text:
Pros:
1. It works well for simple setups and getting started is a breeze.
2. Very easy to add a new device.
3. I had no problems adding my SmartThings hub and controlling different lights.

Cons:
1. The remote will get stuck sometimes and will not control the TV. I am stuck opening my phone to correct the problem.
2. There are times when the light buttons do not work properly, especially the dimmer buttons. I am not sure if its a SmartThings or Harmony issue, but its still an issue.
3. Setting up advanced controls with the desktop or phone apps can be extremely time consuming. For instance, if you want to open a specific FireTV app with a button, you need to manually select many button pushes. Each button push has multiple steps to add it to the sequence. If I only had to do this once, it would be fine. Unfortunately, there is no way to copy or reuse sequences or steps in a sequence. If you have 2 different activities for FireTV, one to watch and one to watch with the lights down, you need to manually build every sequence a second time in the second activity. Really, you should just be able to record the steps as your are doing it on the remote without having to choose each button click manually from a list. That would save a lot of time.

Overall, I like the remote and can deal with some of the nuances. If the remote wasn't so expensive, I wouldn't mind as much. Normally, you get what you pay for. In this instance, you get a little less than you pay for, but it happens to be the only game in town!

title: Easy switching between devices.  Heavy, though.
text:
The best thing about this keyboard is the ease of moving it from one device to another. I tried an iPad and an iPhone, and once paired, it was an easy matter to switch between devices. My older style Mac required the included "Unifying" tiny USB plug-in.

The second best thing is the design of the cradle that holds a mobile device at just the right angle. The keyboard has enough heft that even the weight of an iPad Pro does not tip over the keyboard. The cradle is soft rubber in the back and plastic in the front.

The design and feel of the keys is good and took very little getting used to. The non-backlit keys are concave and are arranged in a pretty much standard arrangement with some exceptions, like the delete key moved up to the function key row, and control and fn keys flipped. It has both Mac and PC keys, and once paired automatically determines which type of device it's being used with. Typing is very quiet, and the round keys, which look different from the square keys I'm used to, are fine.

There was no included instruction sheet. Setup instructions are online, including a chart of hot keys and shortcut keystrokes. The hard-to-find power switch (on the right side of the keyboard ) is never mentioned in the instructions. The keyboard supposedly has an auto-off or sleep feature, but I did not see this explained anywhere.

The major downside is the weight--almost 2 lbs. But as mentioned above, this is so that a large device won't tip over the keyboard. Still, it's a lug. I like to travel light so on the road I would take an Apple Bluetooth keyboard which weighs about half as much and is smaller. An Origami case for the Apple keyboard includes an easel which serves the same purpose as the cradle on the Logitech.

title: setup was fairly easy. Harmony had all my devices in the database ...
text:
I have mixed feelings. I originally bought the Harmony Companion with the hub and I was not aware that it was limited to only 6 devices. During setup I found my Denon receiver counted as two devices (Zone 2 is a separate device). I only had 4 left and I had a TV, Apple TV, DVD, PS3, a Hi Def player, and several Sonos players to go. 15 devices in all. I called Logitech and found I could add 8 more devices (total 15) by buying this remote. That is the only reason I bought this second remote. The installation of the second remote was not straight forward and I had to get tech support to walk me through it.

Anyway, setup was fairly easy. Harmony had all my devices in the database and even linked up with both my PS3 and the Apple TV. A nice feature is Harmony can upload the Sonos favorites list and set the favorite of your choice on the activity start. The remotes have a nice feel to them and I especially like the Companion. The Companion has the bare minimum in buttons. It has only 3 activity buttons and you can "long press" these buttons for three more. There are very few extra buttons for custom programming, a major bummer for me.

I bought this system to interface with Amazon Echo and Smartthings and it does do this but I found I rarely use this feature. As I rarely use the smartphone app. The remotes are always the first to be grabbed. I was trying to replace the wonderful URC remotes I have now. My oldest remotes required Windows XT and I can't program them anymore. The newer URC R40 remote is still the family favorite and after hiding it, my wife declared that she hated the new remotes (Harmony Companion and Harmony elite (950)) and I had to retrieve the URC. Now we have problems since the Harmony remotes keep track of what is on and off and the URC remote changes are unknown to the Harmony. My wife turned on the system with the URC and I later tried to change volume with the Harmony and it didn't work. I pushed the "Watch TV" button and it changed the channel to the Harmony initial channel I specified for startup. ARGH!. Then, I wanted to turn on our deck speakers (Zone 2) for guests and Harmony did it perfectly but it also turned off the MAIN zone where we were watching a movie. I'm still not sure if I can fix that with programming.

The 950 remote by Harmony is sometimes challenging as it has a lot fewer buttons (no numbers for example) and puts the missing buttons in the touch screen menus and controls. It also puts the frequently used buttons like GUIDE, & DVR below the arrow keys. I like the placement with the COmpanion and the URC much better.

I think overall, the Harmony remotes are OK...but the URC remotes are an almost perfect button layout and Harmony is a slight step down in comparison. Harmony remotes have no backlighting (URC does) and finding the buttons in a dark room is almost impossible.

Update: Note the Harmony software no longer works with the latest Mac operating system (macOS 10.15 Catalina) - and there doesn't seem to be a rush to make it happen.

title: Great Speakers.  Weak Mid-Tones.
text:
This is a great self-powered home theater speaker system. It delivers plenty of room-shaking power and doesn't require a separate receiver. The console allows you to adjust the volume of each set of speakers separately (sub, fronts, center, and rears).

The only downsides to this speaker system are: A) weak mid-range tones, B) consumes over 30 Watts of power, even when idle. Like most speaker systems that utilize a sub-woofer for bass, the 5 satellite speakers don't deliver any bass at all. Unfortunately, they're also very weak on mid-range tones. If you step away from the sub-woofer, the sound lacks bass and mid-tones. If you're close to the sub-woofer and the bass is over-powering. If you're using this for a home theater, this will probably not be an issue. If you're using this for gaming, it's what I would consider too much of a system for that, but that's your choice.

In my case, I'm not using it as intended. Instead, I've distributed the speakers throughout the entire first floor of my house to evenly fill my house with background music (lounge, jazz, etc.). I've placed the sub-woofer in the center of the house and put speakers in the kitchen, den, dining room, and living room. Unfortunately, with this configuration, the bass and mid-tones suffer, as the satellite speakers only deliver treble.

The only other thing I don't like about these speakers is that it continuously draws about 33 Watts of power, even when not generating any sound. I wanted this to be a speaker system I just leave on all of the time.

Overall, this is a great speaker system. I just wish the satellite speakers delivered a little more bass and mid-tones.

Enjoy!

title: Good in Many Ways, But Not Perfect
text:
The keyboard is good, but could be better. I love that it has a long battery (supposedly 3 months). I like that I can kind of convert my iPad to a make-shift laptop (good for meetings, etc.). Unfortunately, typing on the keyboard could be better. The biggest issue is the positioning of the keys. I thought the off-center positioning of the keys wouldn't bother me, but it does. I'm a touch-typist. No matter how hard I try, I always miss the "ASDF" keys and end up on "SDFG" keys instead. The keyboard has combined the left-most keys (tab and caps-lock) with their adjacent keys (Q and A), causing the keyboard to be slightly off-center. While this didn't seem like it would be a problem, it kind of is. I find it a bit irritating to type on this keyboard; while it's far better than the on-screen keyboard, it's not as good as it should be. I would have preferred slightly smaller keys (like what netbooks had).

PROS:
- It's an actual keyboard with a number row and arrow keys.
- Arrow keys make it MUCH easier to move the cursor around on the screen.
- Number row keys mean I don't have to do some special key combination to type numbers
- Fairly slim and lightweight (but should be lighter)
- Magnets come in handy to keep the cover closed and secure the iPad when in "laptop mode"
- Long battery means I don't have to worry about charging it often
- No power switch (as it comes on with the magnets) means I don't have to remember to turn it off
- Sealed keys means I don't have to worry about dirt getting under the keys
- Material feels good (kind of like neoprene) and won't slide out of your hand easily

CONS:
- It's still a bit too heavy, making the iPad a bit clunky (like a laptop)
- Off-center larger keys are difficult to get used to. I would prefer smaller, but centered keys.
- iPad holding clips are a bit flimsy. The iPad doesn't feel very secure in the two clips that hold it on. When undocking it from "laptop mode", the iPad tends to slide out of the clips (the magnets at the bottom hold the iPad more than the case clips at the top to, allowing the iPad to slide out when trying to separate it from the magnets on the keyboard).

Overall, I wanted to use this to help transition away from my paper Moleskine notebook. I use it with OneNote. Recent improvements to OneNote, plus this hybrid tablet with a keyboard approach make it a feasible, but not perfect possibility to do away with the paper notebook. However, the bulkiness make me want to leave it on my desk when I get up, instead of taking it with me everywhere I go.

title: Can't go far wrong with Logitech
text:
As usual, I have to start this review out by stating I didn't buy this on Amazon. I bought it at Walmart Just reviewing it to inform.

I will just quickly list what I think are the pros for this keyboard, as there are a lot of reviews and it does do pretty much everything you expect a basic keyboard to do.

The main pros are....

1. Has a pretty solid and sturdy feel for the price. Lots of things these days do not inspire too much confidence when you take them out of the package. The plastic on this feels heavier and thicker than I expected. I have had a couple of real cheap keyboards and they were just junk. They probably cost about the same as this one but they were nowhere near the same quality.

2. The keys actually feel good and work well for my typing (which is hybrid/barely better than hunt and peck). I have had problems with my typing style and hitting the right keys on keyboards that do not have good feedback. The cute "low profile" keys on some boards are basically just flat keys that are just barely raised from the surface. I don't like those and I find I make a lot of mistakes the way I type. This one is MUCH better and I actually make far fewer mistakes even with my craptacular typing skills.

Now for the CONS...

1. As I said, the keyboard itself seems sturdy for the price but I'm not so sure about the cable. Which is kinda dumb because with a wired keyboard, the cable is as important as any other part. The cable on this one seems really thin and looks and feels like it might not hold up too well. Maybe I'm just spoiled on the older keyboards where the cable was almost as thick as a pencil and you just didn't have to think about it. I don't know. It just doesn't seem that sturdy.

2. Also, the cable isn't very long. I don't know why they do this. You would think it would be at least 6 feet. I have my computer in a place where I need to snake the wires through holes and around things so I need some length. This can be kind of fixed with a USB extension cable but I don't have an extra one laying around (they're useful little things and like most useful little things, you tend to be using the ones you have). So I will have to buy an extension. That's five bucks right there.

3. This keyboard is USB only unless you're willing to buy a PS2 CONVERTER. A PS2 adapted WILL NOT WORK. I have 4 adapters laying around but they're useless for this. I can only get this to work with USB. This is really not Logitech's fault, I guess. It's just the changing times. People mostly probably don't bother with PS2 anymore but if you'd prefer to or if you NEED to, for some reason, it's getting harder to do it because so many new keyboards are USB only. I don't know. You'd think it would be standard for manufacturers to throw in an adapter that does work. Just in case. I guess that's just too much these days when a keyboard that doesn't break instantly is a luxury item. I remember when there used to be useful items that were just included in the box as a courtesy because they knew some customers would end up needing them.

4. I debated on whether or not to include this as a con. I guess for the price it isn't really but I used to have a keyboard with multimedia keys and they turned out to be pretty useful. I find myself missing the play/pause and stop buttons and especially the volume keys. This keyboard has none of that. It's just a plain, straightforward keyboard. What it does, it does well but if you need to use any keys for media, you'll have to tinker and program hotkeys or something.

5. Again, as with #4 this may not be much of a con because this IS really just a budget keyboard and it does work well and has a lot of good qualities for what it costs. Some of the keys are a bit noisy. They're not bad but if you tend to really hit the keys pretty good when you type, this is not a silent keyboard by any stretch. I don't mind because I'm used to inexpensive keyboards and the sound just doesn't bother me or anyone I live with. The noisiest key seems to be the spacebar. It kind of has a rattle every now and then. I don't think this is indicative of a likelihood of any kind of early failure because I have had keyboards with noisy spacebars before and the keys all still worked when I retired them for other reasons (usually a bad cable). It just sounds cheap. If that doesn't bother you, it shouldn't deter you.

CONCLUSION - Even with the cons, I was kind of surprised that you can still get such a decent keyboard for such a low price. Don't get me wrong. I wouldn't have objected to paying less for the same quality but I would not want to sacrifice the quality that is there for a cheaper price. I'm frankly tired of buying stuff that is made of plastic that is so thin it feels like it will just fall apart in your hands. This one feels nice and has some weight to it. Though I think a keyboard in the same price range would have probably been even beefier 10 years ago (and probably would have lasted 10 years).

I expect this will last a while but if it does fail early, I'm betting that thin cable will be the failure point. Unless it has some cool modern mojo I don't know about going on, it's just common sense. Thin cables are going to probably wear out faster. But.......it was 15 bucks. I can live with it if it dies in a couple of years. I just hope I'll still be able to find a comparable product if/when it does.

Overall, Logitech continues to be a reliable company that usually produces decent products at just about any price point you need them at. I generally don't think twice about buying Logitech when I need simple and functional for a low price.

title: Great replacement, challenge to get the old battery out
text:
After years of dealing with declining battery life in my Harmony One, I finally went searching for a solution. While it looks like I may have missed a recall or free battery replacement period that Logitech offered some years back, I was happy to find a cheap solution for a universal remote that works well (when it is charged up).

The battery replacement instructions on the Logitech website are complete rubbish. I found a few forums and videos that talked about the need for lifting up the battery (use a small flat head screwdriver) and forcing a pair of needle nose pliers in to grab the battery. I was a bit more forceful than I would have preferred, but once I got a hold of the battery it pulled out easily. The old battery was incredibly warped, so it was no surprise it had declined in performance.

I've only had the new battery in for 12 hours, but I was happy to see that not only did it already have a decent charge to it, I did not have to reset / reprogram the remote!

I will update this review if I see the battery start to fail, but my fingers are crossed that this one will last for many years!

title: Double-Click issue after 1 year - Good Customer Service Replacement
text:
I originally gave this 5 stars, but then after about a year of use it started having it's infamous double click issue. It seems that after much usage, this mouse starts losing functionality in the left click. It's a pain. I have tried a few different fixed found on different forums, but it seems to not help at all. So, after a year of use, the left click button double clicks about 25% of the time. I'm trying to contact Logitech for a warranty, but I'm still waiting for them to email me back. We'll see what happens.

Update: By the end of the day writing this review, the button had degraded so much that it became unusable and super frustrating. I went out and bought a temporary replacement until I could either get a warranty replacement or find a decent permanent replacement. 2/15/16

Update 2: I got the mouse rather quickly, and forgot to update this. Customer service was great, I had no problems with them and they were very willing to send the new mouse. No problems at all. Updated to 4 stars from 3. Still not 5 because the double click issue shouldn't have happened within a year in the first place.

Update 3: I have contacted Logitech's customer service, and they replied asking for shipping addresses and serial numbers. So I think it's good news. Let's see how long it takes to send the replacement. 2/18/16

Update 4: I have now used the replacement mouse MUCH more than the first one I got, and I've been very satisfied. The mouse has been functioning flawlessly since I received it. I plan on getting a second one now for home, since I use the other at work for 40 hours per week. I utilize every button on the mouse, and have really put it to the test. Great product. I think they figured out left click button problem. Let's hope it continues to last. 3/10/18
This mouse does have a 3 year warranty, so that's a big relief. And if anyone needs to contact logitech quickly, their email is customercare@logitech.com

Update 5: The mouse is end of life. It's starting to have a glitchy issue which makes the mouse not move on the screen consistently. I thought maybe this was a mouse issue with the computer, so I tried the track pad and did not experience the same issues. So it's either the mouse, or the Logitech Unifying receiver, however, I have my keyboard I'm typing on connected via the receiver so I don't think that's the issue. So Adios, mouse. It's been a great 4 years. I've already ordered my Logitech MX Master 2s, and I hope it also lasts another 4 years. 09/26/19

title: The only mouse I use. It's faster and more accurate than any other mouse I've tried. But no scrolling wheel.
text:
I'm 24 years old and I've been using this type of mouse for as long as I can remember, at least 10 years I believe.
- I've owned about 3 of these over the years. I have a habit of using them in bed with my laptop, so I drop them every once in a while. Yet over the past decade I've only needed to replace them every few years. If you treat this mouse right I'm sure you won't ever have to buy another one.
- I have never gotten cramps from using this mouse.
- You can use the mouse pretty much anywhere.
- The design allows for excellent control with the index and middle fingers.

The main issues with the mouse:
- No dedicated scroll wheel. If you're playing a game or using a program that benefits from having a scroll wheel, this may be an issue for you. In some cases there are ways to map the other 2 buttons to emulate a scroll wheel's effect, but note that there is no dedicated scroll wheel for this mouse.
- There is no sensor for side scrolling. But again, it may be possible to re-map the mouse to allow for this in specific programs.
- Because the ball spins on 3 prongs, the oils from your hands will build up around the inside. So you're going to have to clean it every once in a while if you want it to look nice. I've seen some people who never clean them and it looks really really really disgusting to see all that dirt build up.

Anyway, for the price just try it out. I don't use any other mouse than this one. I find that for ME this mouse has superior accuracy and speed than traditional mouses, and it costs less. It's also simple, yet has 2 additional buttons which can be programmed to do different things depending on the program that you are in.

I really think this is the best mouse money can buy. It's form and function all in a price for under $30.

title: I would cry if this mouse stopped being manufactured
text:
I have 5 of these mice. Am I crazy? Yes, but not because I have 5 of these mice.

I am a professional software developer; I'm on the computer all the time. Using a normal mouse hurts. Using these thumb trackballs does not, and they work really, really well. They are comfortable, on a AA battery they last for approximately 3-6 months. I don't even think about the battery. The transceiver is extremely small and unnoticeable if left plugged in. I have played thousands of hours of Steam and Origin games (Battlefield, Borderlands, Terraria, etc.) and have used only these mice to do it. I'm not too bad at FPS (I have something like a 1.5:1 kill-to-death ratio), and these mice give me no trouble. I'm not an insane gamer, so I guess I don't care about having 16 million DPI of mouse resolution. Seems like overkill to me but hey, maybe I'm a noob.

The back and forward buttons are a nice plus. The ability to power off the mouse with a physical sliding switch is not to be overstated. I like having control over the battery that way. When I pack up the mouse or leave for long periods of time (if I'm gone for days-weeks) I switch it off to conserve battery. The deep sleep mode probably lasts for months regardless, but I switch it off anyway.

Since it's a big ball, you'll have to clean the dirt from the little low friction rider balls (inside the "eye socket"; yes I know that's gross, but you'll be ok). I just use a plastic tool or twistie tie to clean the gunk out of there about once or twice a month and it keeps gliding smoothly. Since the rider balls are plastic, they won't scratch the mouse ball. I've had that problem with much older mice (Microsoft Trackball Optical) that used regular metal balls (the metal balls actually cracked eventually and started to score the mouse ball, making it unusable).

I have had two major problems with these mice, and they only occur on my first purchase (probably made 3-5 years ago).
1. The left mouse button has started to double-click unexpectedly when pressed. Sometimes the button remains pressed although the detent has released, other times it just clicks many times. Since I have played hundreds of hours of FPS games with that mouse, it's no surprise. I replaced the faulty microswitch with one from an old optical mouse and it kept it alive for a while. Since the mouse has been used for probably millions of clicks and thousands of hours, this is really not a problem.
2. With the first version of this mouse (old one as mentioned in #1), I have experienced random permanent disconnection of the mouse from the transceiver. This is very annoying and very had to recover from. Sometimes, just letting the mouse rest for an hour or two (go into sleep mode) and waking it back up will re-pair properly with the transceiver. Other times, I've had to try special button press combinations (hold middle click for 30 seconds with left-click depressed, etc.) to try to force a firmware reset. This is not documented and doesn't work consistently. Finally, other times I would just use the logitech unifying receiver software to unpair and repair the transceiver. This usually works. I have not experienced this problem on any of the newer versions of the mouse, so I think it was an early firmware bug that has been fixed.
3. The rubber feet on the bottom have a more gooey adhesive than you might expect. This leads them to eventually slide off as dirt and dust get into the grooves around the feet. Not much you can do about this. If you keep the feet when they fall off, you can remove the fabric adhesive sticker (it's basically double-sided fabric tape) and just glue the hell out of it. Just know that the screws are under there so if you want to access the circuit board to replace microswitches, it'll be difficult if you super glue it. Yes, I know I'm strange for trying to repair my mice, but I want them to last as long as possible.

5 stars! Thanks Logitech.

title: Two problems (one serious).
text:
First, this system replaces an older Logitech system that finally failed (one channel died). I liked my old system very much. This replacement, although about the same size, has one major "missing" feature: the ability to adjust the volume of the "subwoofer". I don't like audio with exaggerated bass--a problem this system suffers from--IMHO. If you like bass, then you might like this system (I like a "brighter" sound). I am able to adjust the frequency response of by messing with the equalization controls on my PC, but I preferred the older Logitech "subwoofer". Second problem (serious): the subwoofer suffers from a very audible hum. I tried positioning the subwoofer, but no matter where I place it I can hear the hum from anywhere in the room. I called Logitech and they are sending me a replacement. Hopefully the replacement will solve the humming problem, if not I'll be looking for a replacement. If I can I will update this review when I receive the replacement.

Update: I received and installed the replacement "woofer/controller" ... it is definitely better, but still hums. I added an extra star to my review. I can hear it if the room is quiet and I'm sitting by my computer. To me it sounds like an unshielded transformer or a low frequency feedback problem. BTW, I found Logitech very responsive to my problem. They sent a replacement out quickly, so kudos to the company.

I ultimately might purchase a small dedicated amplifier with two decent small shelf-speakers to replace this Logitech system as I still find it to bassy for my taste.

title: Great remote - well worth the price.
text:
Revising my initial 2 star review from earlier today - I hope no one actually paid attention to it. I had reservations buying this remote after reading the critical reviews. Especially after reading about the "reset" issues. I think I was just waiting for something to go wrong, and when it did (a month and a half after I bought this remote), I immediately thought I had a lemon, and of course, there is only a 30 day return policy!

I loved this remote right out of the box. Easy setup and it worked great controlling my TV, Onkyo receiver, cable box and dvd/cd player. However, as mentioned, after a little over a month, it stopped working correctly. Of course, I immediately thought I was experiencing the same reset issue that others have expressed concern over. The remote would only turn the TV on, wouldn't control the volume, or any other device, and would spontaneously reset after a few seconds. I tried manually resetting it, re-syncing it, jammed paper in the battery compartment, etc., all without success. Finally giving up, I was all set to return it - until I found out about the 30 day return policy. So, not wanting another useless paperweight, I broke down and called customer support, something I loathe to do as, generally, that is simply a waste of time. Well, 5 minutes later, and a new set of batteries - I know, who'd a thunk it - my remote is working great again. Just goes to show, sometimes it really is the obvious!

I'm not saying its a bad system, because its not, but I am saying that until they get the ap that controls the system debugged, its not ready for prime time.

title: Finally found what I love!
text:
Wow.....just....wow! This is exactly the kind of sound that I've been looking for!

Let me start off by stating that I'm no audiophile. I don't know much about frequency response or whatnot. All I know is that everyone has their own preferences. But this is what I like and this headset brings it! So here it is.

The sound is rich and warm with good clean base that packs a good punch without distortion. The base is soo good that it fills my ears and makes them vibrate a little making it feel immersive, for me at least. Games a music just come alive. I'm glad I went with these over the more expensive A50s or the H wireless from steels series.

They are very comfortable and do not get in the way of my glasses. I've worn them for 3 hours with my glasses and have felt no discomfort whatsoever.

They last pretty long too, 12 hours or so. I can go on long gaming session on top of a movie later and it still has power to spare. It works well with the PS4, just plug and play. You can also save your favorite or custom EQ settings to the headset, with the software included, so you can also have it on consoles.

Don't really csre about the mic quality, that's not why I got them nor for the fancy rgb lighting, although it is nice.

All in all, the best $200 I ever spent, and the best headset I've ever owned.

title: But that two year period was the best experience I've had with a keyboard up until that ...
text:
Worked for about two years before it died on me and wouldn't work anymore. But that two year period was the best experience I've had with a keyboard up until that point. This thing is just so damn functional, it's hard to give it up when it breaks. The solar recharging is a serious god-send, saving you serious coin on batteries, and works surprisingly well in low-lighting. Logitech has a downloadable app that displays exactly how many lumen are getting to the solar strip, which is activated even with LED light, so that's either super convenient, or pretty misleading. Either way, if you're the type that spends most of their computer time behind blinded windows and dimmed lights, you can just leave it in the window when you leave for work and it's done by the time you return. It works with the Logitech universal dongle, which is useful for people with multiple Logitech products either currently or previously.
All in all, was the best keyboard I'd ever had, (excluding the one I got after it, of course, the [[ASIN:B003VAGXWK Logitech Wireless Illuminated Keyboard K800, Computer Keyboard Wireless, Desktop Keyboard]], which is also a great choice for those not too picky about solar charging and want illuminated keys for their darkened hovel).

title: I recommend - great keyboard, doesn't even have to be in direct sunlight
text:
I absolutely love this keyboard. I bought it almost a year ago, in July 2015. Previous to this keyboard, I had been using an HP Wireless Elite keyboard that I was getting for $20 at a local computer store. The reason I liked that keyboard was its slim design and low profile keys, which was actually really hard to find in keyboards. But the problem with that keyboard design is it was possessed with a battery-hating poltergeist. I would use the keyboard for a short time and then it would stall when I typed, and then it would straight up ignore some keys, and then it would play havoc with my ability to type and just about drive me insane. I had to keep popping out the batteries, putting them back in, replacing batteries, using rechargeable batteries, normal batteries, Eneloop, Duracell, Energizer... didn't matter, that keyboard ate through batteries like nobody's business and kept driving me nuts with its massive lag.

So I decided to get a new keyboard but it was difficult finding a nice slim design, low profile keyboard that looked good and wasn't a bajillion dollars. I ran across this one and decided to give it a go based on the good reviews. I am very glad I did and definitely recommend this to others.

PROS:
*The solar power legit works and is SOOOOO freaking much better and less annoying than those (expletive here) battery-powered keyboards I used previously. I have had zero problems.
*I have never had any lag issues.

CONS:
None really. I guess one thing is the keys do clack which annoyed me a little bit when I first got it because my other keyboard had silent keys, but to be honest I don't even notice it anymore.

SOLAR INFO:
For anyone considering getting this who hasn't had a solar powered keyboard before, like I hadn't prior to this, maybe this helps for you to have a bit more context: I am on the computer like, always. If I'm home, I'm probably using the keyboard, for hours at a time. The room where I keep my computer has only one window but it's a large window, which faces south. So it doesn't get direct sunlight pretty much ever. And the desk rarely gets direct light except certain times of the day in certain times of the year. I open my shades when I wake up, close them when it gets dark, and most of the time the shades are angled away from the keyboard so any direct light it might have gotten is blocked. My keyboard is over 5 feet away from the window. And I live in a temperate climate that for over half the year is like WHAT IS SUN THERE IS NO SUN HAVE SOME CLOUDS :D

Despite that, I have not had any problems with this staying charged. There was only one time, I think early in the winter, where it alerted me that the charge for the keyboard was somewhere around 50%. So, for the next two days, when I left for work I set the keyboard on a table that would get some direct sunlight during the day and then I used the keyboard like normal all evening. That was all it took. I haven't had to do anything different than I normally would since. In fact, I often forget this thing needs any charging at all or that it's solar. Even now with the lux level at 18 because it's winter and it's already dark outside (ugh), my energy reserve is at 98% and going strong.

So, if you worry that you'll have to change everything around to charge this keyboard with the sunlight, let me tell you. I have had to change nothing and it's been a-okay for me. I am super happy with this purchase and if this ever dies, I will definitely repurchase. This has taken away SO much annoyance I dealt with previously, constantly, with my battery-powered keyboards.

title: Sub is decent, but look elsewhere (perhaps a bit more $)
text:
I bought these to accompany my sound bar in my desktop sound system. It's a casual setup.

PROS:

- made by Logitech, a good brand in the low-middle range of price and quality
- the desktop controller can CRANK the volume if you wanted to. I don't know if the sub could handle it for a long period of time, but it's possible.
- comes with a sub, which can also be used with other speakers so long as they have a 3.5mm aux jack
- volume controller sits nicely on desktop (with some tape on the bottom)

CONS:

- the sound quality was good for a few days, until I began hearing a vibrational noise from the left speaker. I tried getting others to hear it, but it was so faint that you had to be listening to them for a decent amount of time to really hear the problem. However, as someone who has pretty sensitive ears, nothing makes me more upset than hearing my music through bad speakers. I was very upset, as well, that this happened in a product only a few days old. And as anyone who buys and uses a lot of electronic tech knows, returning these types of products is difficult and borderline impossible, due to the fine print.
- I wish the cords were a bit longer. You can get about 6 feet between them, but it'd be nice to have a bit more.

title: Broke after 2 months and a week.
text:
I purchased this case with a new IPad Air2 and thought it was the best thing since sliced bread. I was going to write a review but then thought Id wait a few months. Well its been 2 months and a week and the case doesnt work anymore. It's not the keyboard but the plastic corners will not hold the IPad secure. The IPad will slip slightly, even when in an upright position. It's slips down to where the on/off button is being hit by the lower secure tabs. So now it basically turns my IPad off any time I try to type on the keyboard. Then when I try
to just use it as a case, the whole ipad will skip out because the secure tabs aren't holding it in place anymore. I had purchased this at Best Buy and didnt read the reviews here to see this is a common problem.

Update..After writing this review I contacted the company's customer service since the product is still under warranty..I received an email from the company requesting some additional information, which I provided....several days later I received an email stating they hope I was satisfied with their customer service...I responded stating I haven't been helped with my issues, to which I received another email requesting the same additional information I had sent previously. So far they have asked for the same info 3 times and sent 5 emails hoping I was satisfied with their service. As of this update 1/26/2017 Ive sent the company numerious emails but have not received a replacement or any real update to my warranty claim.

Update.. I never heard back from the company via email so I mailed copies of all my communications, copies of my receipt and a letter regarding my dissatisfaction with the service I was receiving from the lady who dealt with the claims via email to their home office. Within 2 days I received a response and was advised a replacement would be in the mail. I received a replacement within a week.

Update...I treated the case with the greatest of care and never removed the ipad from the case so as not to damage the clips in the corners. The corners clips broke almost immediately but the side clips still held the iPad in place. The case last until Oct at which time the side clip broke and the case was useless. I did use the case everyday.

My only complaint is that the dongle seems to be specific to this mouse. I have another, smaller logitech mouse that I use for travel, and the dongles are not interchangable. It's a pain to have to switch them out.

title: Fine wireless mouse, with highly sensitive scroll button.
text:
Fine wireless mouse, but a little hypersensitive. I bought this as a replacement for a mouse that I left somewhere. This mouse connects easily once the dongle is inserted. There was very little delay in getting it to work. The dongle is small enough that it can be left in a USB port if you have one available. If you want to take it out, there's a handy storage space inside the mouse itself (just open the battery case). It has an on-off switch on the back to save battery, which I really appreciate. I use my wireless mouse 1-2 times a week, and this will preserve battery power. It fits OK in my hand, but is a little small. I have medium-large hands for a woman, and I suspect a man with large hands would find this too small.

It tracks nicely and is easy to use. My major complaint is that the scroll button is really sensitive (other reviews have mentioned this). A medium flick will send you scrolling far down the screen. Because it's far more sensitive than my other mice (also logitech mice), it's quite disconcerting. I'm learning to work with it, but I would much prefer less sensitivity there.

text: This is by far the best Bluetooth speaker I've used. It's about the size of a DVD if that helps. And maybe an inch and a half to 2 inches thick including the cord. I've used big cylindrical shaped Bluetooth speakers before and you really can't take them with you anywhere. They are usually too big to fit into your pocket and just awkward to try to fit into a bag. You basically have to buy one for wherever you want and keep it there. This thing can go anywhere. I actually find myself taking it almost everywhere. The cord is just amazing. You can strap it pretty much anywhere. I've used it at the beach and strapped it straight to the umbrella. Gone longboarding and actually strap it to a belt loop and don't even notice it's there other than the amazing sound. It has a great sound that doesn't distort when you really crank it up. When I go riding I turn it up and my wife can hear it perfect even if she's far behind. Once i figured out the secret button combination i haven't had it die on me while i was out. When you press the + - buttons simultaneously it lets you know how much charge is left. And it lasts a really long time between charges. I already said i pretty much take it everywhere so it gets a lot of use. I've read you can pair 2 of them. Or pair 1 with a ue boom or megaboom. I didn't have either, but on the Android app I saw the instructions. I really really like this speaker and I'm considering getting another so my wife can enjoy it as much as me. I had a jbl clip+ and didn't use it as much. This sounds way better and honestly they aren't even close. It's like comparing apples to a watermelon. Sure they are water resistant Bluetooth speakers, but the clip just didn't really clip to anything. The sound wasn't as good either. I do believe the clip+ has a microphone though. Still it's not a selling point for me. I'm sure it won't be long before i grab another one of these

title: A worthy successor to the MX Revolution with a couple of small flaws.
text:
I am a long time MX Revolution fan, and held of on buying this for a while because of the initial poor reviews for OSX. My MX Revolution finally went out to pasture, so it was time to roll the dice - and I'm pleasantly surprised. This review is for MacOS Sierra 10.12.

Pros: Logitech's software appears to have matured, because last time I used LCC it was a mess. This is clean - it integrates into the OSX preferences pane and the configuration panel is easy to use. Customizing buttons is quick and easy and the available options make sense. (I like this software a LOT better than Razer's needlessly-cloud-based Synapse driver, for example.) The mouse itself has that same solid, heavy feel that the MX Revolution had, and the ability to run it corded is always a plus.

Cons: The forward/back buttons on the side could have been designed better, as it's awkward to find the two small slivers with your thumb. I'm sure it'll be better after I have time to get used to it but it's really just a lousy design choice. I also don't care for the vertical side scroll wheel - the horizontal wheel with the same ratchet feel as the primary wheel on the Rev was a lot better.

This would be 5 stars if not for the side wheel and the thumb buttons, but all in all I'm extremely happy with the Master on my Mac. I haven't tried USB Overdrive or Steermouse with it because it does everything I want it to do by default, and the driver is unobtrusive. This is an all around great mouse.

title: Great Multi-Device solution, with one missing thing...
text:
Pretty great keyboard. I have many Windows tablets, many Android tablets and 1 iPad, so I've set it up for quick use with 1 of everything.
I wanted a device I could sit on a small table (like a personal dining couch table) and put my tablet and/or phone into so I can type stuff up quickly as I'm not as fast a type on a virtual keyboard, even using Swype, etc.

It works flawlessly.

The only missing feature for me is a pointing device. This would have been an all in one solution if it just had a mouse built in, alas, it does not so I have to still tap on what and where I want to go OR have a Bluetooth mouse connected as well, which almost defeats the purpose of using this device. I envision this having either a slightly larger format and sticking a trackpad on the bottom or right side, or go IBM/Lenovo-esque and have a pointing device in the middle.

Still, as I mentioned, it's a great device. It's heavy enough to serve as a base (pretty much why it's so heavy) and the tablet slot is long enough that it will fit some tablets as well as phones at the same time. You can't pop most devices into it while they are in a case, it just doesn't seem to work out no matter how 'slim' the case is. I only have the devices I carry around all the time in cases (except my phone), though, and I don't typically use those around the house so I'm good there. Keep this in mind if your intention is to not have to peel your cover off whenever you use it. You will, and so would be better off getting either a case with keyboard built in or separate keyboard/holder solution. Otherwise, you won't regret buying this thing, I don't.

-1 star for no pointing device. I feel like it's a missing feature.
If you don't care for or want a trackpad, then this would be a 5 star review.

title: Very please with this remote
text: Bought this yesterday and spent an hour or so getting it setup with my equipment.  This is my first new universal remote since an Acoustic Research unit I've been using for 10 years finally died.  I went with this one rather than one with a fancy touch screen as I really don't need all that.  I just need three buttons:  Watch TV, Watch my BR device, Listen to music.  Perfect, this remote has that.  The iPad mobile app was very nice for setting things up... much more intuitive than tools I've used in the past.  Sure it's not allowing me to custom map buttons and program my own macros, but instead it functions more like an Apple device would: "Hey, we know what you're trying to do and here you go.  Done"  The RF/IR responsiveness is good, the buttons are reasonably tactile and decently laid out, the remotes you end up with on your phone or iPad are actually pretty nice!  My only complaints so far are minor:  1) I wish it had back-lighting on the keys, and 2) I wish it had separate buttons for the 30 second-skip features some DVRs have.  (instead it's long press vs. short press).  All the home control features are sort of useless to me, I'd toss those and add a couple programmable buttons.  The IR blaster is good, but I'm ordering a second one as my stuff is spread out between cabinets.  So, overall, very happy!

title: I had a Harmony One for years and loved it. I decided to get the 650 because ...
text:
I had a Harmony One for years and loved it. I decided to get the 650 because the One software was installed on my now defunct PC. The instructions implied that I could access my Logitech account and simply use it to configure the new remote, but for some reason it couldn't find my account. I installed the software on my Mac, put in all the information about my system, and eventually got it set up correctly. I'll have to say that I found this newer software more confusing to use--it took longer than it had with the One. One problem I had was in turning off my TV's speaker. I use an A/V system and want silence from the TV itself. In the old software I just specified Mute for the TV in its activities. The only way I could get it done with the new software was to add the Mute command at the start and end of each activity. The command is treated as a toggle.

ADDED 7/26/17
After I'd had the 650 for about a year, I noticed that it was no longer able to control some of my devices. When I would choose the activities for playing Blu-rays in my player, DVDs in my changer, or for playing Roku selections, the activity button would turn everything on but I would have no ability to do anything once there, e.g., I would press the Play button for a Blu-ray but nothing would happen, or the arrow keys would no longer move the cursor in Roku. That meant that if I wanted to, say, watch a Blu-ray I'd have to retrieve the original remote to do it. In other words, as a universal remote the 650 was worthless. Fortunately I still had my Harmony One. I downloaded the software for my Mac, successfully made one update to my configuration since I had stopped using the One, and all was well.

I had a problem with properly configuring the One for my indoor amplified antenna--I got rid of cable TV after the 2016 election--but a call to their customer support line got my problem corrected, this despite the fact that I purchased the One in 2008. (Thank you, Logitech!) Now I am happily once again using the Harmony One. If you are planning to buy a 650, please realize that the Harmony One is probably a better choice.

title: Where's your head, Logitech?
text:
Plastic is pretty good. The back is a bit of an oil magnet so you'll want to wipe it down often. The face buttons have a nice push and release response. Some might find them stiff but they have a nice, sharp break that works great. D-pad is good, not great, but just good. Ergonomics are fair, there is a lump in the back. I'm a single finger shoulder button guy, so that lump makes it very uncomfortable: my middle fingers are either pushed up against the shoulder lip (designed to go) or below the lump pointing towards my thumb muscles. I like to position them horizontal and it's just not doable here. The nestled spot is kind of tiring for me to keep it there, and the bottom is just uncomfortable. It's where the batteries go, yes, but I would have liked them to figure out a slimmer way to do it.

The two stars, however, is for the more technological side of it. These use a receiver that plugs right in to USB and is very discrete. Looks like the Unifying receiver, but it is not compatible with that and they are not the same at all. You cannot pair these controllers with the same receiver that handles other Logitech inputs. What's worse, is that they can't SHARE, either. I picked up two of these and I need two receivers plugged in. Keep in mind the Unifying receiver has been out since 2009. These controllers' connectivity mindset is at least 7 years in the past.

Now the other gotchas. There is a vibration feature, but it's not available in XInput mode, which goes back to DirectX 9. Just about every game today uses XInput, so, again, 7 years in the past and missing functionality to boot. You only get vibration in DirectInput mode which is deprecated and not going to help you for modern games. Another quirk is that in DirectInput mode, the analog L2 and R2 buttons are treated as digital ones instead. Switch over to XInput and they're analog, but they're wired to the same axis! That means they cancel each other out.

I've got to wonder what these guys at Logitech are doing? They're so behind the times I can't believe this is still on the market. Meanwhile a mouse you buy today from them might be discontinued within a year. They're completely ignoring this part of the market and I wish I knew why. With a different microcontroller inside this could be a great controller and a fantastic value for the price. Instead, well, I'll have to say pass. I'll keep looking for a non-console controller that works out of the box with all the functionality it ought to have.

title: Computer Speakers, not for a modern TV or Console
text:
Can't use them for my TV without SPDIF coaxial support. These speakers are intended for a computer with Green, Black, Orange connectors or the equivalent 5.1 surround 3.5mm headphone type connectors.

All my 5.1 media devices have Coaxial SPDIF which is Not supported by these speakers. Not without some kind of powered converter box, down to 3 headphone jacks that could be plugged into the green, orange and black 3.5mm connectors.

There is an additional Stereo RCA (Red and White) connector input, and that is supposed to be converted into 3D audio, and you can use the Green connector alone to connect to any headphone jack, including on a TV, but that's NOT a surround sound connection. Why would you want that? Better to get something that actually supports SPDIF Coaxial or optical or something like that.

They exaggerate all the connectivity. There are only two inputs, one might be full 5.1 surround if you have the computable sound card ports. Modern game consoles have HDMI or something more advanced than RCA connections, and you would only have simulated surround, and not actually be taking advantage of any actual 5.1 surround coming from your device. Be sure to check your sound card, these are for your computer.

People report the tweeter above the speakers are fake. Not sure. Also, be careful when lifting subwolfer, the speaker is exposed and you'll probably put your fingers into it.

title: A couple serious quirks, but otherwise great
text:
I bought this mouse because it's tricked out with heaps of programmable buttons. I love a lot of things about it, and I hate a couple things about it... I think I may never be used to this couple of things. In fact, I'm considering searching for other gaming mice, as a result.

The default modes on this mouse are extremely aggravating. It took me a long time of playing with this thing to understand what the current setting was; the manual wasn't much help, there, but I may just be thick. As usual with Logitech, Linux support is absent, and to my surprise, community support for this mouse is somewhat lacking compared to, say, Razer tech. But that's just software stuff; the solution is to log into a Windows machine and use their tool. I'm just annoyed by the defaults, is all.

The real dealbreaker for this mouse is the horizontal scrolling. It's just hopelessly broken. It's so loose, it's impossible to middle click or even rest your finger on the wheel without scrolling left/right. This hasn't affected my gaming, because none of the games I play utilize horizontal scrolling. But I bought a mouse with HScroll because I wanted to use it for regular browsing, etc, as well, and it's hard to even middle-click close a Firefox tab because doing so scrolls the tabs to the left/right! What the hell, Logitech? I might not be able to name any, but somewhere out there is a game that this mouse will crater, because if your input device can't consistently distinguish axes, you're in for a bad time.

Other than that, the mouse is great. Comfortable, decent weight, good precision. I find that one of the three default settings (the second, I believe) was very accommodating for my day-to-day use, with the sensitivity set to max. It moves the mouse at a decent rate, and I can fine-tune it with the little target button on the side. I like it well enough that I haven't gotten around to reprogramming it, which is unusual for me.

[Edit]
So it's been over a year, now, and I've programmed the mouse to be just the way I like it. If you switch to Windows long enough to run their software, the options you define persist anywhere you use the mouse (including Linux). I do still find the horizontal scroll to be touchy; someone commented that my mouse may just be defective, so I may buy another. I've mostly gotten used to it, though, and am more precise at middle-clicking, now. I'm very happy with this mouse, now, and wouldn't buy another (simply for the large number of buttons).

title: Decent for the $$$ but uncomfortable
text:
One of the most uncomfortable headsets I have ever used. It has decent sound, but its finicky companion software leaves a lot to be desired.

The rough and heavy stitched material on the oddly shaped ear cups will scratch at you with every tiny head movement. The headset itself also tends to wander on your head. The swiveling hinges for the ear cups also tend to twist at just the wrong moment and can send the entire unit crashing off of your head.

For some, this may not be an issue, but the range is fairly poor. Seeing how poor it is, it's quite easy to see how bad the software side of this headset is. Whenever there is a lapse in connection, the equalizer is reset even though the software claims that it is saved to the device. Upon receiving a signal again, it's a crap-shoot on whether the EQ will pop back on with your audio, or not.

Battery life is alright, but only if you don't use the lighting.

The buttons are extremely clicky, and obnoxious as they are right by your ear. Not only are they hard to push, but the loud click that erupts from them is unacceptable for something your are supposed to be wearing on your head. This also plays into how cheap it feels overall. With a mainly plastic body, the whole unit creaks and squeaks as you move your head about.

They get the job done, but really not worth a recommendation.

The one thing I do like is the number of ways you can use these to listen to just about anything. The usb transceiver has an input port that lets you add another audio source to the headsets stream.

text:
This is a great keyboard for HTPC environments- I'm using it with a Raspberry Pi3/Kodi setup. The wireless connection works great even though the receiver is in my closet and the signal has to go through the wall- even when I'm 20 feet away- something that my Apple Bluetooth keyboard has lots of problems with. If you travel with this keyboard once nice feature is that the little USB receiver can be stored in the keyboard so you don't loose it. The trackpad is a decent size, but the keyboard itself is not full-size which keeps the size down- the whole thing is about as wide as a 15" laptop. The whole thing works great while sitting on your lap on the couch. For about $30 it's a really nice deal.

Some reasons why this is not a 5 star item:
- It came with two off-brand AA batteries which I immediately replaced with Duracells because I've had far too many of these off-brand batteries leak and destroy electronics.

- The key feel is pretty bad. No way I'd use this all day for any serious computer work (coding, writing, etc).

- The on/off switch is really cheap and a little difficult to move

- The build quality of the keyboard is pretty cheap. If you've got little kids who tend to break things, we'll they'll probably figure out a way to break this too.

If I had paid more money for this keyboard I probably would of knocked off another star for the build quality, but for about $30 I wasn't expecting quality.

text:
Pros: Comfort, the sculpted shape is fantastic. Requires no arm movement to move cursor. The cursor control is smooth and precise with the trackball. It works perfect with my Belkin KVM switch. Also, the Innovera Softskin Gel, Wrist Rest works perfect for this mouse. Work great with Mac OS and Windows. The back/forward quick navigation buttons can be programmed. Which has been very useful when executing SQL Server scripts. The pointer-finger scroll wheel is very useful also. You can click down which allows you to navigate the page with the trackball alone. The range of the wireless receiver is great. I can set this mouse on my thigh and navigate my screens while sitting back in my chair. I've had the mouse for going on 12 months and the battery life has been successful throughout. The device is plug and play on all of my machines. I haven't run into any problems on any operating system.

Cons: The setting in which the track ball sits has three points of contact. When these settings get dusty your cursor maybe become choppy. You can remove the track ball with a standard pen. This allows you to view the contact points of the track ball setting. If you take a standard eye glass cloth, or a microfiber cloth to the point to remove the dust it does resolve the choppiness of the cursor. It would be nice to design the next generation to resolve that one single issue.

Summary: Do not hesitate on buying this mouse. I am actually a left handed user and love the mouse. The comfort and precision of this mouse cannot be beat. I am completely satisfied with his product. Even if they never fix the dust issue I will continue to buy this mouse without a doubt.

to several keys on my keyboard now, some of which are frequently used (eg letter "C") and others
less frequently used. Give this keyboard a pass - nice industrial design, good feel, but if you

title: Good mouse for CAD software
text:
I am still getting used to this device, having used normal "laser" mice for so many years. I started using a new CAD package recently, and read some positive reviews of the M570 as a preferred alternative to ordinary desktop mice. The idea is that you position the mouse cursor by moving the trackball with your thumb, and clicking with your fingers. The thinking is that for CAD applications where there are unusual combinations of position, then clicking mouse buttons in certain ways, it is easier and more accurate to complete the clicking acrobatics without accidentally moving
the mouse cursor. So far, I find this to be true. I'm not sure it is a good positioning method for normal web browsing or using normal desktop word processors and such. 4 stars rather than 5 since the trackball seems to sit a bit loosely in its frame compared to the (admittedly very high quality and very high cost) trackballs I used at the dawn of computing. Recommended anyways - if you go CAD regularly, give this device a try. For me, this style of input really does work noticeably better than a conventional mouse.
