title: Lasted for only two weeks
text:
Pros: Ergonomic, smooth feet, dual-mode scroll wheel, not much lag
Cons: Small side buttons, scroll wheel very whimsical, horizontal scroll wheel hard to use

I was looking for an ergonomic mouse to use for work - something that would be comfortable to hold all day. I had a Steelseries Sensei, but wanted a wireless mouse to reduce clutter. There's a wireless Sensei, but I didn't want to spend over $100 for a mouse. After some research and reading favorable reviews, I decided to get the MX Master. The last Logitech mouse I used was the G7, and it was a very good mouse. I've generally liked Logitech products in the past, so I was sure the MX Master would be no exception.

My initial impressions were positive. The mouse felt great and was definitely comfortable to hold. The curves, thumb rest, and texture were well thought out, and it is definitely a mouse that has ergonomics in mind. My only complaint was that the side buttons were too small and kind of awkward to press, but not a huge deal. However, things quickly dropped off from there. After about two weeks of use, the scroll-wheel was stuck in free-scroll mode. The dual-shift mode is definitely nice when it works - freely switching between ratchet and free scroll, and the threshold is even adjustable. I've tried reinstalling the drivers, software, reconnecting the mouse, but none of that worked. Upon some googling, it seems like this is a pretty common problem and Logitech hasn't done much to remedy the situation. I don't think it's a hardware issue; it seems like a driver/software one to me. I've contacted support, but as expected, received little help. All I got were canned responses asking me to try things I've already tried. Ultimately, I decided to return the mouse and will continue to look for something else. It's a shame that Logitech has gone down in quality and support. They used to have one of the best customer supports in the industry, but I guess good things can't last forever. I really wanted to like this mouse because on paper it's great. It's hard to beat the features of the MX Master for the price, but poor software support makes the mouse unusable. If you're looking for a wireless mouse, I would suggest waiting for the next version of the MX Master or look elsewhere entirely. This one isn't worth the hassle.

title: Bad Ergonomics, Bad Software, Bad Implementation AND REALLY BAD TOUCHSCREEN
text:
Unfortunately there is no ZERO STARS. Logitech REALLY dropped the ball on this one. This remote was installed as part of a home theater and music system. I would have NEVER bought this if I had to purchase it myself vs part of a package.

PROs - Very Few
1) It changes channels - generally
2) It lights up
3) It has no replaceable batteries

CONS - Way Too Many
1) The ergonomics are horrible. This remote virtually flies out of my hand. It is bottom weighted in a big way. The battery bay forms the major grip area and it doesn't allow you to align your hand/fingers without sliding slightly out of a firm grip
2) WHERE ARE THE BUTTONS!!!! What guy in marketing thought no buttons was a good idea? Most all functions are done via a VERY SENSITIVE touchscreen. Not only are there no number buttons but there are no "hard" Page Up or Page Down buttons so you are forced to used a soft button for those functions which frequently changes the screen to the number pad and begins inputting channel numbers.
3) The touchscreen is the WORST. It is very twitchy and is easy to "miskey" the screen and send you between Activities, Favorites, Functions, and Number Pad.
4) More often than not the software "wears out" and when selecting a channel from the favorites screen ie 428, the remote appends additional random numbers ie, 4281345620485 and will not tune to the channel of the first three digits.
5) The function screen is difficult to key "buttons" unless your fingers are directly above the function and you deliberately (watch) and touch the function to avoid changing the screen or hitting a different function.
6) The response time between the remote and component(s) is slow. Some delays are able to move to fractions of seconds and some are not. With the ones that allow changes, the difference between .2 secs and .3 secs is an abyss. The first setting is so fast the component will not understand the command and the second setting is so slow you yearn for the remote that originally came with the component ie, TV remote, cable box remote.
7) Software and update process is laughable. Instead of allowing the update process to be done entirely on the PC you must login to your "logitech account", contact some server and let the remote talk to the server. The software INSISTS on updating everything before you even know which remote you're using.
8) Who thought it was a good idea to call your remotes, Harmony1, Harmony2 etc. Funny I don't have any rooms in my home named Harmony 1 or Harmony 2 AND THE REMOTES DO NOT ALLOW NAME CHANGES so you have to ensure you're updating the correct remote for the correct room or you run the risk of having one of the remotes overwritten with a different configuration. If this happens you will have to reprogram the remote from scratch.
9) The update software is very kludegy and takes forever - no small wonder since the remote has to transverse the internet to and run through the entire update process if you change ONE KEY!
10) I seem to resync my remotes at least once a month.

Frankly if the cable box remote could understand my TV or my TV remote could understand the cable box, the Logitech would be resting comfortably in the garbage. This is easily the most disappointing technology purchase, I've ever made. If you want a universal remote, SPEND A LOT OF MONEY and avoid this remote.

title: Hours of research - I'm completely satisfied
text:
I'm writing a review because I am a researcher to a fault when choosing a product. This research is valuable to others and can help make the right decision although what is good for one person may not be good for the next. So basically it is all subjective. I am a technologist, very interested in technology and typically are among the first to have new technology.

OK, that being said, I purchased the iPad Pro 9.7 and have owned the iPad, iPad 2, iPad 4 MINI as well. I like to use a physical keyboard with my iPad's and really don't care for a separate keypad. My desire is to be as portable as possible as well as lightweight. That left me looking for an iPad cover with a keyboard.

I've purchased and returned the Apple Cover/Keyboard for the iPad Pro as it was too flimsy, floppy, whatever. When on my lap, it just wasn't stable enough for me although the lightweight and slim profile was very attractive. Also, having the connectors that avoided the need to recharge a keyboard battery as well as deal with frequent bluetooth connectivity issues was a bigger deal to me than I realized.

I've owned 3 or 4 of the Zagg keyboard cases and every single one of them eventually had broken pieces and even the hinge part cracked in the last one. Also the last one I had for the iPad Pro had battery issues as the battery only lasted 2-3 weeks. Two in a row, plus all the broken ones convinced me that I was done with the Zagg products. The idea is great the way you can separate the iPad from the case with just a pull and use it without the keyboard, as well as reverse it to watch movies. But, as I said returning every one I bought to get a replacement just wasn't what I wanted to do anymore.

To be fair, Zagg's customer service was great and never gave me a hassle when exchanging a broken one for a new one. I think they are a good company, but unfortunately their product is flawed. I personally think the plastic used for their cover is too brittle and breaks easily. I am extremely careful with my electronics and don't think misuse is to blame.

My last purchase after returning the Zagg Slimbook was the Logitech Create keyboard case. I didn't think that it had features enough to satisfy me, but after a month of using it, I'm happy. The connectors for quick instant connection are awesome and I never think about having to charge the keyboard. I never lose connection because it isn't a bluetooth connection.

The keyboard lights up instantly when I touch a key and fades to black 8 seconds later if no key is pressed. I do only have two options for the screen angle, which is at approximately 45 degrees and flat on the keyboard. I've gotten used to that and quite frankly don't need any other angle.

When the iPad Pro is laying flat over the keyboard, the keys turn off so that nothing will react if a key is pressed. The 'bend' of the case is thicker than usual, but that actually gives me a good hand hold when it is in the book mode. The function keys across the top are just the right ones: screen brightness, key to display your open apps (like pressing the Home button twice), full play controls for videos or movies, sound control, search key, 😊 Button that quickly brings up emojis and a lock button to shut the iPad down. Basically I don't need to touch the Home button, all functionality is on the keyboard.

The outside of the cover is some sort of fabric material which I think looks a lot classier than the Zagg cover which was black plastic and tended to show all your fingerprints. Closing the iPad also turns off the iPad so no wasting of your battery. The keys themselves are spaced a little further apart than the Zagg and have a nice bounce to them which makes typing very comfortable. I never seem to press the wrong keys, so it works very well from me.

I didn't buy the keyboard from Amazon even though I am a Prime member as I had a rewards coupon from Best Buy which lowered my cost to just over $100. Well that's it and I hope I have helped someone. One real good way to buy without penalty in case you are dissatisfied, is to purchase from a source that has a good return policy. After all, $129 is a lot of money and you should get it right if you are going to spend that much.

title: WORTH IT to do multilingual work during a trip
text:
(I did NOT receive this product for free or at a discount, like many reviewers somehow do. I paid full price, dangit!)

A friend and I have been planning a month-long trip through Europe. My boss agreed to give me the days off IF I could be available to translate documents during the trip (i'm a translator). I accepted the compromise, figuring that I could use my T-Mobile hotspot and WiFi at hostels to connect to the Internet. I thought about bringing my 15" MacBook, but the darn thing is so heavy/expensive that I would hate to lug it around or leave it at a hostel. It was probably a better idea to bring my iPad instead. But, as anybody who's ever used an iPad's onscreen keyboard knows, it would be a pain in the butt to type long documents without a separate, physical keyboard.

So I started doing my homework, researching all sorts of bluetooth keyboard cases and accessories. Some of them had excellent battery life. Others had a great feel to them. Others were really classy. Others were inexpensive. Others were super portable.

But one... one of them had EVERYTHING. The Logitech Keys-To-Go. So I bought it. And it arrived the next day. And I used it. And....OMG.

PROS:
-It's ridiculously light and outrageously good-looking.
-The clicking of the keys is comparable to a regular keyboard. I was afraid that it would feel like typing on a flat surface, with no feedback. But nope. It feels great.
-The spacing of the keys is spot-on. I can type with about 90-95% the precision of a regular keyboard.
-The back is a rubbery eraser-like material that, while not completely slip-proof, provides enough friction so that the keyboard won't move around.
-Battery life claims to be a superb 3 months between charges (I'll update when I know for sure)
-Bluetooth connection was quick to set up and has given me no problems so far (I'll update if anything changes)
-The shortcut keys at the top are AWE-SOME. It has keys for home, multitask app picker, spotlight search, show/hide keyboard, camera, media controls (back, play/pause, skip), and volume. There is a problem with the Language key. See below for more information.

CONS:
-It's ridiculously thin. This makes me a little nervous about sticking it in a bag and traveling with it. (I'll update after my trip)
-The Language key doesn't work. When you click the globe key, it's supposed to change the language of the keyboard. But instead it just takes you to spotlight search. That's not Logitech's fault though. It's Apple's. With iOS 9, Apple changed the code for the language shortcut in bluetooth keyboards. But there is a workaround! Ctrl+Space will give you the language picker onscreen. Hopefully Apple will address this.
-I may be wrong, but it seems like the battery on my iPad drains super quickly with the keyboard connected. (I'll update this if I notice something different)

I am extremely happy with my purchase so far. I'll update this review after my trip, and hopefully it all turns out okay. For anybody who wants to type with tilde (accent marks) in Spanish, press option+E and then the letter you want to have a tilde (same shortcut works with OS X). Also, note that when you first connect the keyboard and select the Spanish language, the layout will be all wonky and you'll get symbols you don't want when you hit some keys. To fix this, go to Settings>General>Keyboard>Hardware Keyboard>Spanish and change it from SpanishISO to just Spanish. Then the keyboard should function just as you expect it to.

TL;DR
After much research, this seems to be the perfect portable keyboard to do work on an iPad during a month-long, lightly-packed trip to Europe. It has all the features and the looks that you want. Buy it.

That workaround key combination is not documented with the product and required an online search. In fact the documentation included in the box is the very definition of minimal. I don't need a lot more than what's there, but a little more about some of the functions specific to this keyboard would be nice. One last criticism is about the camera key. I thought it might function as a remote shutter control when using the phone's camera app, but it only takes screenshots, which makes it slightly more useful than the non-functioning keyboard layout switch key.
But the good points far outweigh the minor irritants, and I would readily recommend this to anyone who is considering getting a portable keyboard for longer typing sessions with their phone or tablet. It fits anywhere you might carry a tablet without adding any noticeable weight, the battery life is very good, and it is comfortable to type on even with large hands.

text:
Very good but just a few little issues compared to my other Logitech K811 keyboard that's better in lots of ways.

Pros:

Long life per charge.
Great responsiveness.
Impressive key feel in spite of the small (slim) form factor.
Easy and accurate pairing.
Great standby performance. — Other Bluetooth keyboards I've used take several seconds to reconnect when they power down to save battery, but this keyboard is always immediately responsive. Logitech does Bluetooth keyboards BEST!

Cons:
No "esc" button.
Can't turn off the iPad screen from the keyboard.
No CapsLock LED.
Strange choice of iOS function keys. — The first function key is like a home button. Fine. The second function key is a double-press version of the Home key. Really? That makes as much sense as having a "77" key for those times you need to type seventy-seven, but just want to press one key. Why no esc function key? You know how to program an esc key because I have one on my other Logitech keyboard.

My favorite Bluetooth keyboard is my Logitech K811. It can pair with my iPad, OR my iPhone OR my Mac by just pressing the appropriate button to switch between Apple devices. AWESOME! And it has an esc key which allows me to turn off my iOS device screens from the keyboard. The reason I bought keys-to-go too, is the super small form factor for travel with my iPad, and so I can take my iPad and keyboard on the road and still have a keyboard with my Mac.

But when all my iOS devices are on my desk/workspace at the same time, I can use the Logitech K811 and easily, quickly switch between devices with a simple button press.

title: Very quiet but a little too small
text:
Received the mouse today so what follows are first impressions the Logitech M330. I have not tried any of the other mice out there advertised as quiet.

Pros:
Buttons are extremely quiet.
Tactile feedback is very pleasant.
Mouse wheel texture and resistance are great.

Cons:
Shape/size - the M330 is only about 1cm shorter than my Logitech G303, but something about its shape makes the latter much more pleasant to use.

Neutral:
Tracking is adequate. I don't know if this is because of the sensor or the wireless implementation, but the M330 doesn't feel as smooth or as responsive as my Razer Deathadder 2013 at the same DPI settings. To be fair, the latter cost a lot more when it was released and is aimed at gamers while the M330 is targeted towards office work.

Untested:
Battery life. Logitech claims up to 2 years with a single AA battery. We'll see...I don't plan on turning this mouse off so hopefully the idle power draw is very low.

I really like the button pressing/scrolling experience. I don't like the shape of the mouse nor how it tracks. I would be very interested if Logitech ever released some of their G Series mice in a silent/quiet form.

title: Can control a ridiculous number of devices
text:
This remote takes some time to set up (it's tedious, but not particularly difficult at least in my case), but once it's set up it will literally change the way you think about your home and entertainment especially if you make use of the home automation devices that Harmony can control.

What impressed me most is the seemingly ridiculous number of devices that this can control. TV, PS4, etc., that's obvious and expected. So then I looked up the 10 year old Frigidaire AC unit in my apartment for giggles... and somehow it was in the Harmony catalog, complete with "deep level" controls like the timer function, etc. Then I tried adding the Lasko heater I bought on Amazon... and again, they had it. Curious how far this could possibly go, I tried adding a Pioneer VSX receiver from the 90's... AND IT FOUND IT. I just about lost my mind when it even had device functions like "Input Tape" and "Input VCR".

The only annoyances in this regard is that for PS4 functionality, at the time I'm writing this, you need to manually turn your PS4 on from rest mode (the Hub will connect right after) as Sony apparently doesn't allow this functionality yet.

The Hub itself can command 8 devices, allowing you to perform individual device functions and also “activities” (combos such as turning on the TV, receiver, and lower the blinds at the same time) via the smartphone app; however the basic remote that’s included in this package only has room for 6 activities -top row of buttons short/long press- that can be configured as you wish by using the app and no individual device control other than basics like volume/channels etc. You don’t have the flexibility of the app in being able to have ‘deep-level’ control over individual devices such as using a touchscreen as a mouse cursor.

If you want a remote that can control more devices or gives you the same amount of control as the app, you would need the substantially more expensive elite remote bundles.

Personally for me, the overlap between the simple remote and the smartphone app is enough that I don’t miss having the blingy remotes and therefore this package offers the best bang for buck. I do have multiple devices connected, but most of the time I use 3 activities (watch TV, play PS4, use HTPC) so the simple remote fits the bill perfectly while being small/discrete, easy to use and comfortable to hold. It’s nice not having to dig around for a phone and being able to press real buttons. For the other devices that I need to fiddle with only once in a while, like HVAC, I just pull out my phone.

The placement of the Hub itself relative to your devices is rather flexible. Despite not being in direct line of sight, it's able to get an IR signal to all the devices that use it in my cabinet, while being able to control my AC unit from across the room. You do have the option of using an IR blaster (one is included) but I have not needed it.

Overall, I would not hesitate to recommend this remote. Being able to use one device to simplify doing several tasks in the home and to do it simply with potential future expandability is amazing, and at this price point it is excellent bang for buck.

text:

Why only the three star rating then? If you noticed I said, when it works more than once.
I do not know what this remotes problem is, but it "forgets" what it is supposed to do a lot. The sequences get all messed up and out of place. When that happens I try to use the "help" feature to get it working properly. It does, about half the time. But the other half I have got to get up and locate all the remotes to the systems that were off kilter and correct things myself. A few times I have even had to use the software to reprogram the remote. I guess with so much to do it can get forgetful.
So, in short I have a Love/Hate relationship with this remote.
Love it when it works.
Hate it when it starts messing up.

There are a few little nitpicks. The base is a bit wobbly, and the legs aren't adjustable. The biggest complaint is that the USB cable can easily fall out. There isn't anything to really hold it in besides tension. This hasn't been a huge issue by any means but it has happened more than once. Combine that with the fact that the cable will usually fall behind your desk into a probable rats nest of cables, this is a decent annoyance.
I eventually built something to keep the cable attached to remedy the issue, but I shouldn't have to.

All in all though, this is a great mic. Its at a very good price point, and fits perfectly as a mid range mic. Anyone wanting an upgrade from a typical headset would be well served here.

title: Old Tech, Bad Design
text:
THE BOTTOM LINE (at the top):
This keyboard costs a lot for the old tech and 1st gen design that it comes with. Its loud, its too heavy, and just doesn't seem well designed for the road. Maybe after some new materials and smarter engineering, it could be a good choice.

ITS MULTI-DEVICE
As advertised.
ITS GOT A SOLID CONNECTION
Always a plus.
ITS HEAVY!
The weight is evenly distributed, which makes no sense. From a counterbalancing perspective, shouldn't all the weight be in front of the keyboard? Its just a lot of unnecessary weight. There is no tablet in the 10 inch market that even weighs half of the weight that this keyboard can handle. It could have been redistributed and maybe cut down but 60% in weight, just by using a better design...
ITS UGLY!
Seriously, this thing should look way better for $35+... It honestly just says old technology all over it.
ITS OLD TECH!
The hardware and plastics used to make this keyboard are obviously from the first generation of flat keyboards. Its super loud by the way. There's no way it would last long in a classroom setting.
IT FEELS CHEAPLY MADE:
For how much it costs, this keyboard sure does creak and pull apart at the seams. Maybe it's just the type of plastic used... Maybe it's the giant flat weight stuffed in the bottom... Either way, it does not feel like $35+ in your hands.
ITS NOT RECHARGEABLE.
I knew it didn't have this feature, but when I received this keyboard and held it for the first time, I thought I had read the description wrong, and maybe it had a rechargeable battery somewhere in there. Nope. Its bulky and heavy just because...

title: Better than I Imagined.
text:
These headphones are even more amazing than I could have imagined.
They may be a bit spending, but well worth it. I had been playing on my PC with my PS4 Gold headset, which goes for around $100, this headset for just $40 more blows them out of the water.
Although I have yet to do an extended gaming session with them, I did watch some 7.1 surround sound videos and listen to some tests of the system. When i first pressed the test button on the Logitech Gaming Software program, I wound up pulling my one ear piece off because i could have sworn that i wasnt even wearing my headphones and the sound had to be coming from the left of me. I could pinpoint exactly where the sound was supposedly coming from.
The ONLY thing I could possibly find to complain about, is that they feel a little tight on my head for my liking, but knowing headsets/earmuffs/headphones i am sure the padding will soften up a bit more and thus alleviate the slight discomfort i feel strait out of the box. This is nowhere near enough of an issue to drop a star off my review though.

Logitech has yet to fail me on any of the devices I have purchased from them, and this headset has impressed me more than any other computer accessory i have ever purchased.

I cant wait until I get a good gaming session in with these, I dont think anyone will be sneaking up behind me on my games any more. I also have already learned that I enjoy watching videos with these on much more than I ever thought i would.

title: Decent for general use, but audio quality has holes throughout the frequency range
text: I needed a decent set of speaker for my computer and did not want to spend much. I just wanted decent sound with decent bass. These were a good compromise, but they lack some mid and high end response. If you sound card or on-board audio has software that has an equalizer built in then you can make up for many of the weaknesses of these speakers. My Realtek 1150 has Sound Manager and picking the "Live" sound effect then tweaking some of the higher end bands gets these reasonable in response across the spectrum. If you do any critical listening these will clearly disappoint you. The default tonal response is very weak and the sub clearly is boomy and will over whelm the rest of the spectrum without some equalization. Again for the money these are decent. for a few $$ more the Z623 would be a better bet, but again if you are a critical listener you need to spend a few hundred dollars to get something that will not have flaws.

title: Best features of any mouse I've ever used!
text:
So a little backstory, my Razer Deathadders' (yes, two of them....... I like the sensor, okay?) right clicks stopped clicking. This officially steered me away from any and all Razer products, as it was the only one that I have ever liked. My Corsair M65 was alright, but I didn't like the grip, and the middle mouse click stopped working (Important in Rainbow 6: Siege). I came across this mouse browsing various topics on Reddit. From what I have seen, on the PC Master Race subreddit, it's the mouse of choice overall.

This mouse has been a joy since I received it. The Logitech software allows SO MANY changes in configuration. The DPI shift button (at the front of the thumb spot) is very cool. It allows you to assign a macro or command to different buttons on the mouse while you're holding the DPI shift button. I have mine set for different macros in Dota 2.

There is a profile switch button (I just have one profile that I use), which will change how every button acts, according to how you set it in the software. I can absolutely see how this could be helpful switching between different game types (shooters, MOBAs, strategy, etc.), but I don't use this feature at all.

I LOVE LOVE LOVE the scroll wheel lock/unlock thingy. It switches between the scroll wheel clicking, and the scroll wheel flying freely. I don't see any point in time where I will need it, but it's fun as hell to open a 50 page document and scroll through it super fast.

Overall, I have to say this is the best mouse I've owned thus far, and I don't see myself switching from it anytime soon.

title: Best $100 I've Spent on Tech in Years!
text:
This is the best $100 I've spent on technology in years! I picked this model because I don't need a touch screen remote and I don't want to use my phone as my TV remote, so the simple remote control with physical buttons served my needs perfectly. I have this set up to control my TV, TiVo, Blu Ray player, Apple TV, Fire TV, sound bar system, HDMI switch, and Wii. I used to have seven different remotes sitting on my end table, but those are all stuffed in a drawer now.

This was also a great solution for me to help my 7-year-old daughter learn how to get to her shows without having to learn the magic pathway through several different remotes. Now if she wants to watch the Apple TV, she just has to walk in and press one button on the remote to turn on the TV, wake the Apple TV, set the TV to the right input, set the HDMI switch to the right input, and turn on the sound bar. Perfect!

Like others have said, however, the initial setup was a beast. The setup wizard needs more tips and clues to walk you through it. I honestly didn't even know I was in a setup wizard at first, so I was confused about how to actually use everything once I had all the devices and activities programmed. I also had a two-day frustration fit because the "Watch TV" activity kept powering my TiVo off, which I did not want to happen. I had to do some digging to figure out how to keep the Harmony from powering off my TiVo and HDMI switch when I was done with those specific activities. Once I found that solution, everything fell into place.

If you expect some frustration from the setup and go into assuming that the THING you want the system to do is actually possible (but will require some time and patience to figure out), you'll probably have a great experience. Now that it's all set up and working correctly, I couldn't be happier!

title: Excellent feature set, great build quality.
text:
I've been using this mouse daily for about a month now, and love it.

It feels comfortable in my hand. The thumb rest is a nice touch, and the weight and balance of the mouse really give it a refined and precise feel.

I didn't think I would enjoy the auto-ratchet-disengage feature of the scrolling wheel... until I got used to it within the first day or so. Now when I sit down at a computer that lacks the free-spin feature on its scroll wheel I immediately miss it. I know many computer mouses allow the ratchet to be switched on and off with a button, and this one also provides that capability. But the automatic disengage when you give the wheel a sufficiently brisk flick is so much nicer -- I never use the manual disengage.

Also worth mentioning is the thumb wheel for horizontal scrolling. Horizontal scrolling is one of those things you often don't need, but when you do need it, it's great to have it at your thumb. This makes it unnecessary to glide the mouse over to a horizontal scroll bar on the screen and manipulate it directly.

The unifying receiver technology is nice. I'm able to use the same receiver that I use for my keyboard. And when I'm travelling, I can pair that same receiver to a smaller mouse such as the Anywhere 2 MX. I haven't used the Bluetooth feature yet because it appears to not be well supported by my Linux distribution, but that should change eventually.

The forward/back navigation buttons, to me, feel like they're not in the most ideal position. I'd prefer to have them forward of the thumb-wheel, not behind it. Or better, put one on either side of the thumb wheel rather than two buttons, one over the other, behind the thumb wheel. The task-switch button at the bottom of the thumb-pad is a good idea too, though once again, a feature not supported by my Linux distribution.

It is nice to be able to pair the mouse with more than one receiver. Sometimes I bring it home from the office, and with the press of a button it switches over to the unifying receiver on my home desktop.

The main buttons are crisp and precise. The center button is achieved by depressing the scroll wheel. Every mouse I've seen with this design (which is almost all of them nowadays) suffers from the flaw that it is almost impossible to make that middle click without moving the scroll wheel a small amount. This mouse has that same issue. I would probably prefer if the button to disengage scroll-ratcheting were re-purposed to be a middle-click button.

Battery life is as good as it needs to be. I use the mouse all day every day at the office, and though I try to remember to recharge it on weekends, I often forget. Nevertheless, I've never run it down completely in a 2-week period. And since it can be used while it is charging, even if I were to run it all the way down I could still plug-in and keep going.

One final note on Linux: If you use this mouse with Linux, install Solaar, which takes the place of Logitech's own management software. Solaar is only necessary if you wish to pair the mouse with a different receiver than the one it came with, or if you wish to add other devices to the receiver pairing. Solaar hasn't caught up with being able to manage other features of the mouse.

In summary, I'm very happy with the mouse, and consider it the best one I've ever owned.

title: This is a pretty cool gaming headset, that works well both for online gaming and for listening to music
text:
This is a pretty cool gaming headset, that works well both for online gaming and for listening to music.

It charges up via micro-USB, and lasts about 12 hours (maybe less if you have the lights on all the time). It works wirelessly, but not via Bluetooth. You need to plug a USB dongle into your computer or game box, and then it automatically connects without any need for a set up. Once it’s hooked up you can control your device via buttons on the headset. One cool feature is that the dongle stores right into the headpiece itself. Just remove the cover plate and it sits inside its own little pocket.

The earpieces are large and easily surround the ears for an immersive sound experience. The sound is quite good with strong bass and an expansive range. Unfortunately they don’t insulate the sound for people who aren’t wearing them as well as most headphones I’ve tried. If I’m listening to music somewhat loud, anyone else in the room will hear it, somewhat muffled but still clear. I had my son listen to them when I was in the same room and heard everything.

You can customize the lighting, which is, I guess, a cool feature though I don’t see why or when I’d ever use it. Maybe it helps some people get into the experience of the game better. You can also customize the three programmable “G-key” buttons - but you do have to install software to make those adjustments.

There’s a built-in microphone that delivers pretty clean audio. I tried recording myself speaking into it and heard some audio artefacts, but my voice was quite clear and this would be just fine for gaming or taking calls, but I wouldn’t try using it to create a podcast. This works fine with both Mac and windows. I’ve tried both. The software, thought, is built for Windows, so to program the buttons and the lighting configuration you’d need to be working on a PC.

title: Great quality and I now have a convenient push-to-talk button.
text:
The Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse is a high quality mouse that does way more than I need. The best features of this mouse are resolution, build quality, and buttons buttons buttons.

On opening the package it is obvious right away that Logitech didn't cheap out on the components. For example, the cord feels like it is made of good quality an long lasting cabling.

As for compatibility, I'm currently using this mouse on a chrome book (only the normal buttons work) and using a cloth covered chair arm as a mouse pad. No problems.

During use, cranking the resolution way up, well, it can make you lazy if you also crank up the sensitivity. Little tiny hand movements can move the cursor all over my three screens. Normal sensitivity and high resolution makes for super smooth operation. The sense of smoothness may be some kind of placebo effect type thing though because my previous mouse has quite good resolution. That other mouse, also a Logitech gaming mouse, is probably a decade old and I've worn the bottom pads through. I suspect this mouse can last as long.

The weights confuse me. I'm fine with the weights in or out. It doesn't effect me. I installed them all 'cause I didn't want to throw them away or store them separately.

The shape is fine. I was worried at first that the strange angles would be annoying. Logitech did its homework, the shape works well.

The scroll wheel is fun. It will spin almost forever in its free run mode. The button right behind the wheel puts the brakes on so wheel clicks through little detents or something.

And those buttons... It's hard to figure out what to do with all those buttons. The best, so far, is setting that lower thumb button to "push-to-talk" for mumble comms during games. It's very natural because it so so similar to a keyed mike. Two other thumb buttons are accelerate and decelerate. That leaves a few buttons waiting for a purpose. This mouse doesn't have a huge number of buttons which is nice. Any more buttons and it would be hard to touch the mouse without accidentally clicking something. There's probably something clever that can be done for switching between desktops or overviews or something. We'll see.

Finally, the RGB aspect. It is weird watching the LEDs change color while randomly poking buttons. The colors do have uses in providing feedback and for finding the mouse in the dark. This is an aspect of this mouse to be played with 'cause it seems like the colors must have some use.

And that's the real key to this mouse. Playing with the controls, programming in profiles, and seeing what works.

title: good for typing, but not general use
text:
I compared this keyboard to the Apple iPad Pro keyboard. Neither is perfect, but the Logitech keyboard is definitely the winner for typing.

Pros:
- The keyboard is better suited to typing. It's bigger and has more functionality. The keys feel like real keys when you push on them (which isn't the case for the flat Apple keys).
- The keyboard also has keys for volume, brightness, and other functions.
- There's no need for bluetooth - the keyboard links up to the iPad automatically.
- The magnet holding the iPad in place is very strong. You don't need to worry about it sliding.

Cons:
- It's surprisingly difficult to slide the iPad into the case. It's only held in place by this plastic rims.
- This case is heavy! Easily a few pounds heavier than the Apple iPad Pro keyboard. I would not recommend the Logitech keyboard if you expect to carry or hold the iPad for extended durations.
- The outer case has buttons for the volume controls, but they're a bit tough to push in.

In short, if you mostly use your iPad to read, go with the Apple keyboard. If you use your iPad to type, go with the Logitech.

title: Really silent and a nice comfortable mouse with virtually no setup required.
text:
[[VIDEOID:9812ea950c2cba1f2e730ef5a9a5598d]] The Logitech M330 is not only truly silent, it's truly easy to set up, too. It is bigger than most Laptop Mice so it is really suitable for Desktop and Laptops. It's comfortable in my palm and there was something very cool about that silent factor. It makes the buttons feel substantial. The base of the unit has everything you need to get up and running, including a two year battery. The tiny usb receiver is in there, too.

To use your mouse, remove the USB receiver and plug it into any available usb port on your computer. Turn your mouse on with the switch on the bottom and there is nothing else you need to do (well have something to put under it if your surface is too reflective). It's an optical mouse so the precision is remarkable but can be adjusted with your own computer mouse software (you know things like, scroll speed or if you wanted to assign different functions for the left and right buttons).

I tried this on both Windows and Mac laptop and on both it worked without a second of hesitation.

The signal between the mouse and receiver is really strong. It will shut off automatically so you don't have to flip the switch when you're done. It's made by Logitech when does tend to make very compatible devices for Windows and Mac based machines.

title: The Remote that Will Spoil You for Other Remotes
text:
Logitech's Harmony 950 is the ultimate universal remote and it will spoil you for other remotes. The Harmony replaces up to 15 other remotes, remembers fifty of your favorite channels and, according to Logitech, plays nice with over 270,000 devices.

The remote easily connects to anything from your Roku device, to cable box, DVD player, DVR, the old VCR, Blu-Ray player, your stereo and a plethora of gaming systems and streaming media players. All we did was connect to to my Mac (PCs are equally easy) and connect to the Logitech site, and enter basic info about our devices. We did this with ease and then the Harmony did the configuring primarily on its own. There's a learning curve, of course, but it's really not bad.

We love the touch screen on this attractive remote. It comes with a sleek round charging station that sits perfectly on an end table. (It makes a great remote holder, too.)

In addition to the charging station, the Harmony comes with a USB cable and an adapter. If you are sick of man-handling multiple remotes, the 950 (or a less expensive model if you don't have too many devices) is just the thing.

title: NIGHT & DAY
text:
I bought a new TV. Didn't expect much for sound as I knew with the thin case the speakers couldn't be very good. I was not disappointed, everyone sounded like they had been sucking on helium balloons.

After a couple of weeks I looked on Amazon and found these speakers. Decided to give them a try. If they didn't work out for the TV I could use them with my laptop. Price was very low and this was almost a concern. You get what you pay for but I didn't want to pay $200-$300 for TV speakers.

The speakers arrived and are exactly as pictured. The two small speakers have cords that plug into the large speaker and the large speaker has a cord that has a switch box and plugs into the TV. On the switch box is a volume control knob, a green light and a female receptacle to attach a headset.

Hooked everything up, no brainer, turned the TV on and no sound. Looked at the switch box and no light. Pushed the switch and the light came on and so did the sound. So much better. The difference is night and day. Tried the volume control on the switch box and on the TV. Both did the same thing. Be aware these speakers can be LOUD so before you turn anything on be sure the volume control on the switch box is turned down. Also tried a headset by plugging it into the jack on the switch box. This turned off the speakers and the sound came through the headset.

There is NO control for Bass or Trebble only Volume. Now I really enjoy my new TV as the sound is so much better. Would buy again instantly. Highly recommend if you are looking for inexpensive speakers that work great.

title: Love this keyboard!  Now we have 2 of them.
text:
Amazing wireless keyboard! After owning several wired and wireless keyboards I have never had luck with finding one that is so comfortable as this one is. The size is just perfect, it is neither too big or, too small.

The keys are so comfortable to use, I love the clicking sound they make-it is really hard to find keyboards like this. The keys themselves have a great spring action that allows you to type really fast without missing a key, this really is my favorite feature. They are extremely comfortable, great for a fast typer and also for someone that needs to look at the keyboard when typing. I love how the keys are not flat to the board but elevated enough to where your fingers fit perfectly on the keys, this is what really helps a moderate to fast typer. Personally I really don’t like keys that are level with the board that is why this keyboard is just so perfect for me. The other feature that I really like is the keys are more round than square, this really fits the finger tips better.

Being able to have 3 devices paired at the same time is just awesome! I am able to use this keyboard on my Iphone, Ipad, and Chromebook and all I had to do was pair each device to the number dial. On the top left there is a dial that has the numbers 1-2-3 and what you do is choose which number you want to use for each device- so, I use #1 for my Ipad, #2 for my Iphone and #3 for my Chromebook. On top of the keyboard there is a Phone/Tablet holder which can hold both at the same time if you wish. When I need to work on both my phone and tablet I put both of them on the keyboard and am able to turn the dial to which device I want to use, then I can send a text message on my phone, write an email on my tablet and then I can also switch it to my Chromebook and work on my budget. It is just genius!

This keyboard is worth every penny! It is priced higher than other keyboards on the market but it is well worth it for the features it has. I would recommend this to anyone who has several devices and wants to multi-task using a keyboard. I own a black keyboard and just ordered a white one to match all of my devices and giving my keyboard to my husband. Hope this review helps anyone interested in purchasing this keyboard.

title: The Gold Standard of Webcams
text:
I guess I’m old, because the Logitech brand still has a strong overtone of “cheap knockoff mice” in my head. But that’s so wrong. I really need to reprogram my head, because I personally own so many premium devices from Logitech, like my premium keyboard, my Logitech Harmony remotes, and these webcams. I work for a large entertainment corporation and we have a funny thing about webcams. Just about everyone is issued a laptop nowadays, and whether you request PC or Mac, there’s an understanding that after about a year into the three year lifecycle of your laptop the integrated camera becomes so disgusting that the other person can’t make out your face anymore. So after a year or so it’s standard practice to request a webcam. We have a lot of latitude in what we can request, within a certain price range, but the de facto gold standard is Logitech. I don’t know anyone who has requested anything other than Logitech. And the interesting thing is that you can tell on your video calls which callers are using integrated cams and who has upgraded to a nice Logitech cam. The video quality is superior and the audio are so far superior to the standard laptop cams. I keep my laptop docked at my desk, so I have one of these Logitech cams clamped onto my monitor for any video calls I take at my desk. I also have another one at home for when I’m working remotely and want to keep my call quality good for those remote video calls.

So what’s special about this one?

First of all, I plugged it in and it just worked. I know that sounds simple, but that isn’t always the case with peripherals. This works right out of the box with all of the video conference apps we use in my office. I wish we were more standard across our organization, but different groups use different tools. I’ve tested this with Jabber, Bluejeans, Skype, Lync (or whatever we’re calling MS Communicator nowadays), and Slack. It worked effortlessly with all of these apps.

I’ve used it on my laptop, my large Dell displays, and our huge conference room displays. I knew it would look fine on my laptop and desktop monitors, but I was pleasantly surprised that the 1080p resolution looked incredible on the large display.

I’m critical and impatient when things don’t work as they should. I know we’re living in the future like the Jetsons, but a simple video call shouldn’t be a tall order. I’ve sure been disappointed with other video devices though. I’m so happy that this Logitech webcam works as well as it does. It is another fine example of why Logitech webcams have become the gold standard in our office.

title: Great sound, lightweight and comfy, but some connection issues
text:
Let me start out by saying I hate Logitech equipment, because there is far too often some problem or problems, Even so, I've handed them a lot of money over the years (Amazon customer since the 90s). They just don't seem to think it all through nor do sufficient testing on their products. But where wireless headsets are concerned there are not many better choices than the H800 that I can find. I intend to keep using it, it's just a little annoying (see Cons) in the connecting department.

Pros - great to really great sound, good bass for an open headset, lightweight, comfortable for long periods on my head. Good gaming headset in my opinion. Much more durable than it looks - I've slept with it on, and plugged in (!), many times. I'm not recommending you do that, just making the point that it doesn't fall apart, even though it's mostly plastic. I actually consider it more durable than many larger, wired headsets that I've owned. Can be folded up when headset band is fully closed.

Cons - battery life is disappointingly shorter than reported, often as little as 3 hours. Takes a long time to charge up too. I tend to use it plugged into a 20,000 mah battery pack that I can cart around with me in my hand or pocket. That keeps it going for a long, long time.
- I can get this to pair with my HTC DNA Droid phone, but ONLY for listening. Mic doesn't seem to function. Same on my friend's Samsung Galaxy S4 with a different H800 ... so there may be problems using this headset as a bluetooth headset for calls with Android phone. Be sure to check that function when you get it if that is your intended use.
- In Windows 7, getting a correct pairing with the dongle can be problematic under some circumstances. If I reboot the computer with the headset on, it doesn't connect properly with the headset - it lights up like it has, but control buttons are inoperative, no sound, no mic. To get a correct pairing, make sure the headset is OFF and UNPLUGGED when you boot up your computer. Sometimes when it fails to pair you can disconnect and reconnect the USB dongle (with the headset off and unplugged) then turn on the headset. But that doesn't always work and I worry about wear and tear on the dongle. So try to remember to unplug and turn off headset before you boot up or restart Windows 7.
- range is so-so, about 20 feet in a straight line with nothing in between. I use a USB extension cable to get it away from electronic interference
- no visual mute indicator, so if you are unsure you have to hit mute/unmute. If you hear a higher tone then a lower one, you just muted. If you hear a lower tone then a higher one, you just unmuted. Bit of a pain but it gets the job done.

All in all, I'd buy this headset again if it stopped working. UNLESS there were a better wireless choice out there, but I'd wish I was buying something that had been better debugged in development.

title: Not good headphones. Lots of flaws that outweigh the small positives
text:
I did a LOT of research culminating in a lot of hours and discussions about the right headset to buy. I found a good deal on the G933's and since I have a logitech orion spectrum keyboard and the spectrum mouse (both FANTASTIC btw, cannot recommend them enough) I thought this would be a good fit to have a nice trifecta of LED syncing glory. That was unfortunately the highlight of this headset. Let's do pros and cons here:

Pro:
+They're comfortable. Not the most comfortable headphones, but they dont hurt after wearing them. I have a normal sized head and they're a little tight when pressing against my head though.
+I'm a sucker for LED lights, even though you can't see the lights, you can sort of see it on the tail end of the mic which has an LED which I thought was a nice touch
+Decent battery life
+Mic quality is good and I like that it folds into the headset and has an auto mute function when doing so

Cons:
-The overall sound quality is OK at best. You have to look at guides online to see how to adjust the equalizer in the software in order to get the correct sound, and even then the sound quality is bad compared to other headsets in this price range, and sadly the 7.1 surround sound sounds like an echo chamber, to the point where people just recommend disabling it entirely.
-They're heavy. You really feel the weight of them on your head. Also, they're TOP heavy, so if you tip your head up to look at the ceiling (I know most people don't do this) the headphones will start to fall off your head. I just didn't like that feeling even though I don't typically look up when I'm gaming.
-While most people won't experience this, I had issues with the headset losing connection, turning off and auto turning back on randomly, and issues with the mic not muting properly. This was all on the most recent firmware and testing in different environments and computers. Likely was a defective headset, but still didn't help my experience with them.

TLDR; I did a lot of research on headphones. If you're looking to spend this much on headphones, go with the Cloud IIs. I am SO glad I bought these headphones. They are wired, but they're hands down the best gaming headset I've ever owned.

title: LIFE SAVER - I love it
text:
It really is a lifesaver -- being able to respond to texts while driving through voice without touching the phone - I love this.

I had a Nokia Lumia 1020 Windows phone which did this automatically, and it was incredible, but then I had to get an Android phone for work, and I was astonished that answering texts (or communicating in general with the phone) by voice is not built into the Android OS.

There are very few products that can save your life, but this is definitely one of them. These days, we have so many demands on our attention and ways to be distracted, a product like this (when the phone doesn't provide the functionality itself) is critical.

This air vent car mount is exactly that - zero touch. Before testing this, I could accomplish a few things on my Android, like asking Google to text someone, call someone, or navigate to a certain destination - however I couldn't answer an incoming text, or communicate through Facebook or Whatsapp messages, share my location, control music on Spottily, etc. hands free.

Simply install the app and put the phone in the magnetic mount to launch the app each time you drive.

Pros:
SAVES LIVES by giving a truly hands-free way to still use the phone
App works flawlessly
Magnetic mount is strong enough to hold my Asus 5" smartphone, even through its rubber case
Magnetic mount REALLY grips the vent and holds securely in place
It's a very bright object - not easy to lose.

Cons:
None really - I just don't know how long the battery will last and if it will be replaceable - doesn't seem to be.

Summary:

Love this product, and the pleasure of feeling safe while I drive, while still being able to respond quickly to incoming messages, is very fulfilling.

title: Great mount, Questionable software, Good potential
text:
The Logi ZeroTouch Dashboard Cell Phone Holder is a very nice magnetic dock with accompanying software that gives your phone more hands-free features for driving. I'll evaluate it as two separate products, here. First, as a holder/dock, and second, as a hands-free device app.

* As a cell phone holder / dock:

Logitech got this part about as right as they could get it. My previous favorite car cell phone holder was the Scosche MAGDMB. It's just a holder, and doesn't have any fancy features like the Logitech offering, but the concept is similar. A metal plate is attached to your phone or your phone's case in some way, and the dock itself has a powerful magnet that holds the phone in place by the metal plate. While the other guys' holder is just a magnet on a small rotating sort of hinge, Logi ZeroTouch is a bit bigger, but that's good. It gives you more surface area, both for mounting the hardware in your car and for mounting the phone on the ZeroTouch.

While the other guys use a semipermanent adhesive tape to secure theirs, Logitech went the smart way and provided a quality suction cup with a sticky substance on it (think wacky wall walker). It sticks fairly well without locking the suction cup into place, but once you press the level on the dock to seal the suction cup, it's not likely to fall off. However, if you need to move it, you can without much fuss. This is great! The Scosche unit's adhesive is VERY hard to remove if you decide you want to move the holder elsewhere (or just want to sell your car). I also found that while the Logitech solution leaves no marks or damage when you remove the holder, the other guys require significant prying and can strip paint or even plastic from your dashboard. Logitech wins in this category, hands down.

My phone is a 6" beast, by the way, and the Logi ZeroTouch holds it without a problem. I do a lot of driving for my career, over all sorts of roads, including lots of country roads, railroad tracks, and even some dirt or gravel roads. The Logi held fast. The only time my phone came off the dock was when I accidentally smacked the side of it with the back of my hand and dislodged it. It took considerable force to free it accidentally.

Of course, when you want to grab your phone off of the Logi intentionally, it comes off easy enough. It works with most cases, though if your case is super-thick, you may need to go with the metal plate on the outside of your case instead of using the plate that goes between the phone and the case.

Positioning is simple. The Logi bends and holds tight at many angles. If you need to rotate, you can rotate the phone on the dock with ease since it's just on there with a magnetic connection. The whole thing just works as a cell phone mount.

* As a hands-free device app:

Now here's where we run into a few problems. Set up is no problem, as the app walks you through it every step of the way, which is good since the Logi doesn't come with any instructions whatsoever. Everything is done via the ZeroTouch app.

The problem comes in with the voice recognition and the Bluetooth connectivity. First, the Bluetooth-- It doesn't see my Ford's SYNC at all. The phone docks with the Logi and the ZeroTouch app works fine, but the ZeroTouch app just doesn't see SYNC, even when I'm paired and music (and phone) play through the car's speakers. What this means is that all the ZeroTouch sounds come from the phone, not the car speakers. It's acceptable, but it leads to the second problem... The voice recognition kind of sucks.

I want to assume this is largely because the Logi is using my phone's microphone instead of the car's system, thanks to the ZeroTouch app not connecting (or even acknowledging) SYNC in my car. Either way, ZeroTouch just stinks at understanding me. I'm a clear speaker. I speak with a northern American, midwestern accent which isn't very strong or unusual. Still, I'll give it a simple request and it will act like an old guy whose hearing aid isn't working...

ME: Play Comedy Radio on Spotify.
ZEROTOUCH: Playing Captain Beefheart on Spotify.
ME: No!!!
ZEROTOUCH: What would you like me to play?
ME: Play. Comedy. Radio. On. Spotify.
ZEROTOUCH: Pardon me?
ME: PLAY COMEDY RADIO ON SPOTIFY!
ZEROTOUCH: I'm sorry, could you repeat that?
ME: PLAY! COMEDY! RADIO! ON! SPOTIFY!
ZEROTOUCH: Pardon me?
and so on.

It's not just "comedy radio on Spotify". It's many things. It seems to understand me about half the time, and that's where the final quirk occurs. On those occasions where it understands me, about 10% of the time it will pop back to the home screen, and then do nothing. It won't dial the phone, play Spotify, shuffle music, send a text, or do anything. It just exits out to Home, leaving ZeroTouch running in the background, and does nothing.

So then I have to "high five" the thing again (to activate it) and ask it to do the thing I asked for again, and maybe that time it will follow through.

My other complaint regarding the ZeroTouch is that right now it doesn't support much. It does, as stated previously, support Spotify. It also supports something called "Deezer" which I've never heard of and I'm not real interested in. It can do text messages on Hangouts, Facebook Messenger, and WhatsApp, but I don't do any of those. It will send and read texts via my choice of Textra, but it won't work with Kik at all at this point. Navigation works alright, but it won't use any of my Google Maps Navigation shortcuts that I already have on my home screen, instead requiring me to enter all my addresses in the ZeroTouch app itself, and that's a pain in the neck since I have a lot of destinations.

Finally, the app doesn't use the Google text-to-speech voices at all, instead opting to use its own rather lame-sounding, three-generations-ago-sounding voice. It does offer some basic controls (you can speed it up or change volume, or pick German language if you prefer) but considering that I have space dedicated on my phone for the really nice Google text-to-speech engine, and it's part of the guts of Android, I think it's a ridiculous thing for Logitech to use their own voice... Or if they're not using their own voice, they're defaulting to the old Android voice despite whatever settings I choose in the Android settings. Either way, it does sound a bit cheap after using Amazon Echo, Cortana, and OK Google.

* The Bottom Line:

I'm honestly not seeing a whole lot that this ZeroTouch app does that OK Google or Cortana can't already do, to be honest. The highlight of the app seems to be that it detects when you're docked and opens up, and then it uses your phone's sensor to tell when you're "high fiving" the screen (holding your hand in front of the phone's light sensor for a half second). At that point, it pops up and offers you the opportunity to speak your command, which it may or may not understand and may or may not carry out.

Sadly, that means that while I'm thrilled with the actual hardware, and give the mounting unit five stars, I have to take away a couple stars until Logitech irons out the software aspect of this package. It works, but sporadically, and it doesn't offer much that I don't already have on my Android phone. Frankly, I think it would be better if the "high five" would just trigger the assistant of my choice (OK Google or Cortana) instead of having me go through the solidly last-gen assistant in this app. However, we'll see if Logitech steps up and makes continued improvements to the Logi ZeroTouch app, or if in the end, the Logi is just a really nice cell phone holder that kinda-sorta works with text messaging, audio commands, and navigation. At this point, all it seems to save me is having to say "OK Google" out loud to activate it, and instead asks me to wave or hold my hand in front of the phone. I'd call this an even trade in terms of waking the device, and one that doesn't come with any major benefits while this app is so loaded with shortcomings.

* My Recommendation:

If you want a really nice dashboard holder that uses magnetic mounting, this is a good (but expensive) choice. The value comes in the app and hands-free features, which are still in the early stages as of this writing (June 2016). I can see potential here, but unfortunately that potential is not being met yet.

However, as an owner of other Logitech devices, I can say that Logitech's trend is to improve their software dramatically over time. As an example, my Logitech Harmony Smart Remote lacked many features and gave many headaches at first, but after a while they nailed down the software side of things and now the app is smart, sleek, and works wonderfully. Give Logitech time, and they may turn the Logi ZeroTouch Dashboard Cell Phone Holder into a must-have device. Right now, it's in its infancy and it shows, but I'm willing to stick it out for now.

Whether that promise of a better experience in the future is worth it to you now is entirely up to you.

As a mount: Five Stars
As a hands-free interface/app: Two Stars
My final score: Three Stars

If the software improves, I will update my review from time to time.

I am really disappointed, because I have a great sound system in my living area, and the one weakness (which feels increasingly major as time goes on) is getting it to play digital musical playlists... I have tried a few permutations, including a WD live. I was really hoping using this to stream into my system would do the trick, but it sounded so bad that I just ended up going back to less convenient methods after all. The deal-breaker, though, was it kept interfering when I tried to link my music device to another bluetooth speaker.

Pros: small, discreet, RCA hook-up and easy set-up.

Cons:

- Sound quality - sounds muddy and weak, absolutely not able to pick up any subtleties in music or deliver presence. This isn't a function of bluetooth or music sampling, because the exact same device's music sounds great on another speaker system with blue-tooth pickup and the receiver this was hooked up to sounds substantially better with every other input source. I can eliminate all other variables in the chain and confidently claim this adapter does not do good things with my music. It really sounds pretty bad.

- Some reviewers claim it isn't so, but this does hi-jack the bluetooth pickup. I figured I could live with that, as I don't really mind manually switching to a different bluetooth device. However, what I didn't quite realize was that even when you disconnect from the Logitech adapter and attempt to link to a different bluetooth device, it will disrupt the attempt to link with something else and keep trying to grab my device. This makes it completely unworkable. Sorry, Logitech, you really don't get to have a monogomous bluetooth relationship with my music device.

title: Unreliable buttons & poor cursor fluidity causes frustration, yearn for discontinued Logitech model.
text:
I'm comparing this mouse to my much better predecessor, the Logitech VX Nano (which sadly is no longer sold by Logitech):

Physical Specs - The Anywhere MX is almost identical in dimensions to the VX Nano, but not as light due to bigger batteries (AA). The MX's Fwd/Back buttons are on the side instead of being next to the left click button. The MX's power is toggled with a physical switch on the base, instead of a small button (Nano).

Cursor Fluidity - Very poor relative to the VX Nano. I noted many cursor lags and "jumping" of the cursor arrow on my monitor, as if the USB receiver was getting signal latency. Very frustrating when attempting to do precision graphic editing.

USB Receiver Reliability - In just two months, my USB receiver has stopped working. I have all the updates, drivers, etc with fresh batteries in the mouse -- yet the cursor no longer moves on the screen. Just embarrassing reliability for Logitech.

Button Responsiveness - Within a month of purchase, I have been experiencing either "ghost clicks" (seems to double-click), failure to click, or a "loss of drag & drop". It is so incredibly difficult to do work when a $40 mouse fails to operate as you would expect.

I have used 3 different Logitech mice over the past years (VX Nano for almost 5 years, M510 for 2 years, and MX Anywhere for 2 months), and I've noticed a steady, significant decline in the quality & reliability of their input devices. Logitech's quality control must be bolstered, or they will lose a patron of their products.

Epilogue: I ended up doing some repair work on my VX Nano, and it now works again. I threw the Anywhere MX in the garbage where it belongs. I'm so glad to have this back, because I bet I can get another few years out of this already 5 year old device!!

title: ❤❤❤  I Kinda Love It - Though I's Not Perfect!!! ❤❤❤
text:
My iPad Pro and Keyboard were Christmas presents that I picked out for myself. I liked the logi keyboard better than the Apple one because of the function keys above the numbers. I got the purple one because I wanted something colorful. I have a Mac Desktop that I love. This is my "laptop" and I can't live without it. I got the pen too, but honestly, don't use it much. I need to find some good apps to take advantage of it.

Pros:
* I think it is a pretty durable case and not flimsy.
* I haven't dropped it, but I hope it would protect it somewhat. Work Around: Don't Drop It!!
* The iPad fits nicely without moving when inserted into the slot - even on a chair arm. It stays put and doesn't wiggle around.
* When sitting on a table and using it like a laptop, the charger works great. The iPad sits at the perfect angle to view and use your finger to navigate.
* I like that you can use your finger to navigate on the screen and not have to use one of those annoying mouse finger pads like on a laptop. I hate those things and that is why I have never had a laptop. So your iPad Pro screen is your mouse finger pad thingy - get it?

Cons:
* When you want to use it just as a tablet on its side, It sits crookedly, not flatly because of the way the case is made. It angles down. Work around - just keep the tablet on the keyboard and use it like a screen for a laptop. It sits at a nice angle, though it is more cumbersome than if it laid perfectly flat. Or just use it at a little slant. Makes it a nice angle for the pen. I can live with it.

* When you want to use it just as a tablet on its end, it is more of a pain to use. In this case, when laid on a table, it slants to the left and isn't perfectly straight. No work around except just use it horizontally when possible. Or prop something under the left side. Again, I can live with it.

* It's true, the buttons for volumn are so hard to find and push that you don't even bother after a while. Work Around: Who needs them, just use the volumn buttons on the keyboard OR drag on the screen from the bottom of the iPad and change the volumn that way. Both those ways would be easier to use even if the case buttons were amazing.

* Typing on the keyboard works pretty much just like an Apple keyboard for a desktop. Maybe even a little better. In both cases, the keys are so flat that sometimes strange things are typed. All in all, this keyboard is better than the desktop Mac one, in my opinion.

* When you are using your son's laptop and try to navigate by using the touch screen because that is how you do it on your iPad Pro, he will get disgusted at you and laugh at you. No matter that you know it isn't a touch screen and how much you try not to use it as one, you will still continue to do it everytime you need to navigate. Get ready to be made fun of. Did I mention I hate those mouse finger pad thingies on laptops. You are going to love this case!!

title: A great if not SOLID 20 dollar wireless mouse for Office/Casual usage BESIDES the somewhat 'odd' shape.
text:
EDIT: Almost three months later. Battery going strong. If it died at this point, I wouldn't have complaints to be honest.

You have a very basic set of buttons, right/left click, middle click, the tilt buttons, and a forward and backward button. The buttons feel solid enough, responsive enough, and the wheel is thankfully silent and hits the correct balance of scroll speed, necessary for just about most you will need in a standard productivity environment.

The censor of the mouse will track on most surfaces (not glass, this isn't dark-laser after all), and it will track well. I am not a firm believer in mouse pads in productivity environments, as I believe they needlessly add to the clutter (unless for gaming, in which case I am adamantly for them). A flat surface is all this mouse seems to need.

The mouse has a 'weighty' feel to it, and the construction of it seems to be sturdy enough (i dropped it a few times already, no noticeable damage), and the rubber grips feel pretty nice, without feeling 'cheap'. I don't want to dwell on 'form-factors' too much because it will always be subjective, and obviously trying to keep both 'ambidexterity' and 'form-factor' meant this mouse might be a BIT off-ball to some.

This mouse is NOT a portability/laptop class sized mouse, which means some might be looking for a fuller grip, but for those who aren't looking for that or those who are left handed, the form factor is certainly sufficient enough, AND it is ambidextrous.

The ambidextrous form-factor has proved to be surprisingly accommodating, EVEN if the side buttons are obviously to the more right-hand favored side of the mouse (the mouse' left side to allow for thumbs to press).

I've actually been inspired by this mouse to try going left handed... just for work at the office. It's been a fascinating and surprisingly productive experience. For someone using this mouse with a left hand, the buttons are perfectly reachable enough with the ring finger, and the fact that the buttons have a big of a groove inward allows you to put pressure on either of the side buttons with your ring finger.

The software, the same also used for much higher end line-ups of mice, is available to this mouse as well. Which means all the aforementioned buttons are configurable, not quite to the extent the gaming mice are with their macro programming and what have you, but most certainly enough for someone looking to use it for daily use.

The dongle, is the unifying dongle from logitech, it receives well, and the mouse seems to transmit well enough through my pointless thick desk, and it's even more worthless layers of panels posing as drawers.

OH RIGHT, the battery life. Apparently the battery will outlast the hardware. The "3 year" claim remains to be seen. It's holding up so far after 2-3 weeks in,

TLDR

It's not for gaming, as my review notes, and it's not really for those with big hands or those looking for a 'full grip'. This mouse doesn't offer that. But remember that form factor preferences of a mouse are SUBJECTIVE, and there's very little the manufacturer can do if at all to make a mouse 'one form fits all'. And if you remember that no one should be looking at this anyway for gaming needs, it's very solid/great product otherwise.

[[ASIN:B003NR57BY Logitech M510 Wireless Mouse, Large Mouse, Computer Wireless Mouse]]

title: The form factor is pretty great, possibly a bit too large. Very cool product in most aspects.
text:
This mouse is quite up to the hype that the reviews build it up to.

1. FORM FACTOR

The form factor is great. Arguably a bit too large, but even for my wife with her relatively small hands she claims it to be comfortable. This is always gonna be subjective. That said the curvatures on the mouse shell should be enough to cater to most.

The placement of the back and forward buttons just behind the horizontal scroll wheel (which I will get to in section 4), which takes up the more traditional positioning of the back and forward buttons takes SOME getting used to. Your thumb will take a little getting used to. I LIKE that the backward button 'feels' bigger and much more prominent than the forward button, as I find the forward button in general quite useless and hardly used. This is somewhat subjective, and some MAY lament the loss of more prominently positioned backward AND forward side buttons in lieu of the horizontal scroll wheel.

2. SENSOR

The 'dark-laser' sensor which allows it track on most surfaces, even glass, is pretty great. The accuracy is more than enough for 'productivity work' and probably decent enough for most 'multimedia work', even graphics, so long as you turn off 'Enhanced Pointer Precision' function OFF in Windows (the thing is such a mess and puts many decent mouse to shame).

3. BATTERY

The battery life seems alright, it's long enough that you don't feel like it really gets in the way, as long as you remember to charge it. The 'micro' cable isn't TOO micro, allowing you to charge just fine while you use it.

4. SCROLL WHEEL*S*

The horizontal scroll wheel on the side will stand out first and foremost. You will probably find most websites are optimized for vertical scrolling anyway, rendering the horizontal wheel largely unused while browsing. However, in productivity/media software, like hulking excelsheets, over the horizontal thumbnails strip inside a video editing software, or zoomed in tight on an image in photoshop, it WILL come in quite handy.

The vertical wheel, positioned more traditionally just about where it is for any mouse, is where this mouse ACTUALLY separates itself. Everyone's seen their share of varieties of 'clicky' wheels, that are physically impeded for control, and some will have seen the 'free scrolling' wheels roll unimpeded for fast scrolls, and a handful will have seen mice that let you switch back and forth between clicky AND free wheel modes. This mouse does that, but it gives you the option to switch 'automatically' without pressing or clicking any switches.

The vertical wheel on this mouse is pressure sensitive. Upon putting pressure on the wheel as you spin the normally 'clicky' wheel, the wheel mechanically switch to a free wheeling mode until you stop the spinning, which will then mechanically switch back with a cool satisfying effect. You can of course adjust the sensitivity of the pressure required to switch on this free-wheeling effect, and you can also simply opt to do it the old school way with a manual press of a button pressed just below the mouse. It's... pretty damn cool

5. LESS-THAN-INTUITIVE / NOT-THE-MOST VERSATILE SOFTWARE

The software is not the most intuitive but it will get the job done for the most part. It would have been nice to have a DPI switch function or a 'DPI Shift" function carried over from the mouse' gaming cousins to bind to some of the keys, but at least you can shift the DPI.

It IS too bad that they don't show what numeric value of DPI you're switching to in the software, instead of giving you the impression that you're simply changing the cursor speed. Also the fact that you can fully customize the gesture keys isn't clear enough. Once again, NOT the most intuitive, but functional enough.

It COULD have done with some support for macro programming, but mleh. It is what it is, this is probably why a lot of tech-savy productivity users are shifting more onto gaming hardware, it would be neat if Logitech decided to spread the wealth a bit.

6. CONNECTIVITY

The included 'Unifier' dongle (which lets you put multiple Logitech devices on one dongle), and continued support of the Unified dongles is a plus. I hope never to see the day when these dongles are phased out.

For those on modern day laptops with little USB ports to spare, bluetooth seems to work quite well enough (provided the rest of your hardware's firmwares are up to date).

7. BUILD

The build of the mouse is good, it's got a weightiness to it that matches it's hefty exterior. Aesthetically, this once again is subjective, it's pleasing. It's not too out-of-worldy like a lot of the gaming mouse, but stands out just enough. The buttons feel solid.....

This is the only place where I MIGHT raise a little complaint, besides the very slightly underwhelming software. The scroll wheel..., at least mine, rattles. It's somewhat annoying. The mouse hasn't been dropped or what not. I am guessing the rattle is inevitable and caused by the 'auto' switching mechanic. The only and a rather minor peeve I have with the hardware.

text:

The big problem were the keys and design. The keys were very hard to press and a lot of effort was required to press the keys.
