title: An excellent piece of consumer tech; exceeded my expectations
text:
For reference, my set-up consists of an LG Smart TV, a DirecTV HR-200 receiver, a Sony soundbar/subwoofer, a Chromecast, Xbox 360, PS3 and a Wii U. I wanted to consolidate the various remotes into one and make it stone-simple for the kids (and me) to press a single button and have all the inputs and devices align themselves for use properly. TL/DR summary: this remote (and hub for the PS3/Wii U) does this easily, and I would recommend highly.

Wanted to write a review to help anyone out there, that like me, wasn't too sure if this was going to be a good purchase or not. There are some significantly negative reviews, and some are probably genuine, based on user's actual experiences. However, there also seems to be more than a few that are based solely on a misunderstanding or misuse of the product. If I can help clear any of that up and provide another perspective, I hope I can do so.

First of all, Logitech's legacy product naming conventions compared to the current Harmony line up (as of early 2016 on their website) can get confusing. The names "One", Ultimate", "Home" and "Touch" can become frustrating when trying to figure out what is best for your remote control needs. Case in point: I purchased this Ultimate One IR remote, knowing full well that I'd eventually need to add a hub to provide Bluetooth control for our Wii U and PS3. I ended up ordering the hub separately, only to find later that I could have ordered this [[ASIN:B00N3RFCBE Logitech 915-000237 Harmony Ultimate Home Touch Screen Remote for 15 Home Entertainment and Automation Devices (Black)]] and saved some money. Again, note that according to Logitech's current website, that package is no longer offered, but if you like this remote and think you'll need or use the hub, I'd recommend this package, as best I can tell, it is the same remote but with the addition of the hub for less then the price of the two were you to buy them individually, like I did. Oh well.

Second, the Harmony compatibility site is pretty excellent. Just tell it the manufacturer and model number of your equipment and it will tell you pretty much everything you need to know. What can be controlled, what can't and which Harmony products you'll need. Comprehensive database of compatible devices, to say the least.

Third, much has been said of the MyHarmony desktop software. Overall, I thought it was fine. Relatively easy to use, but you can tell it's a work in progress, as it's not quite as slick and polished as the interface on the remote itself. However, while you may end up going in a couple of circles, the software does always seem to realize what changes you've made and will ultimately guide you where you need to be. It seems smart enough to realize that some users may do things in a different order based on their specific hardware, and it "catches up" so to speak to ensure your remote and hub if you have one, are kept in sync. I don't think you need to be an expert to use it, but I could see where some on the lower end of the techno-savvy scale might not understand or have difficulty. My overall feeling though, is that if you're considering this line of products in the first place, you'll be fine with the software.

Sidebar for a bit on the Harmony Home Hub. [[ASIN:B00N3RFC4Q Logitech 915-000238 Harmony Home Hub for Smartphone Control of 8 Home Entertainment and Automation Devices]] The Ultimate One remote is infrared only. So, if you have any devices that require control via Bluetooth like my PS3 or Wii U, you'll need this Hub if you want to control them with the remote. (You can apparently also use the smartphone app once you have the Hub, but I haven't tried that, and don't really have any intention either. Still, nice to know it's there.) You add the Hub to your profile in the MyHarmony desktop software, and there are a couple of ways to do this, either by "upgrading" your remote with a hub, or by setting it up as a new Harmony device, but both methods will get you there. Again, the software will realize that installing the Hub as a new device, or upgrading the remote is the same thing, and will route you through the required steps regardless of how you do it. If you buy both, set up the remote first, then add the Hub. Once set up, the remote will have for example your activity named "Play PS3" and will signal the Hub to provide the Bluetooth signal to power on the PS3. Works great.

Fourth, ergonomics and usability. Lot of talk about the ergos and usability of this remote. Have to say, I honestly find the negative reviews quite surprising. In use, this is one of the best pieces of consumer tech I've ever purchased. Works exactly as promised and way, way more of a pleasure to use than a number of the reviews here make it out to be. A big part of this is the operation and behavior of the screen. It's not like your smartphone's screen; prone to accidental brushes and taps. It takes an appropriately deliberate touch to activate anything, and each intentional press is confirmed by a nice little haptic feedback buzz (vibration) to let you know you what you wanted was selected.

Also, and why this is rarely mentioned is beyond me, but the screen defaults to a lock screen. Meaning it lights up, but won't register a touch or press until you swipe to unlock it. In use, let's say you're watching TV and the remote is just sitting there asleep. You get up to do something or want to pause or even record to your DVR using the hardware buttons. You can absolutely use those keys without inadvertently touching something on the screen, and the screen will remain locked out. There is apparently a setting where you can turn the lock screen feature off, but I'm not sure why you would want to, as it completely removes the issue of interference by your hand. And again, it's not like an errant brush of the hand will cause an unwanted key selection anyway.

On top of that, the screen features a slick "gestures" screen that slides up from the bottom and allows you to pause, play, volume up and down, fast forward and rewind simply by sweeping your finger or tapping the screen without ever having to look down. Again, this too works exceptionally well. The gestures screen will persist too, meaning if you slide it up to activate it, then set the remote down and it goes back to sleep. as soon as you pick it up again, the gestures screen is still there. I find myself leaving that screen open most of the time, as it's truly simple and intuitive to use.

A lot has been made of how un-ergonomic this remote is, and I just don't get that, at all. In use it works extremely well, and I really do not think Logitech committed any massive deign errors. Rather it seems very well thought out and super clever.

The Activities, as you set them up via the desktop application just plain work. It is fun to watch everything turn on and set themselves to the correct inputs. And even if for some reason they won't, the remote will guide you through how to fix them, which, when I read about that, I didn't really understand, until I saw it in action myself. First time I went to use my "Play PS3" activity, the PS3 did not power up. The remote asked if everything came on, I told it no, it asked what device didn't, I selected PS3, and it popped up a little tutorial on how to pair the Harmony Hub with the PS3. Took maybe two minutes to pair the two and then worked perfectly. Very helpful and simple.

Navigating the screens is easy, and there are only a handful of them. Dedicated home, favorites, and settings keys around the screen get you back to where you want to be immediately. Spend ten minutes using it and I promise you'll have it down pat. For every Activity or mode if you will, the controls on screen and the physical buttons assume the roles of the equipment you are currently using. For example, my "Watch TV" activity means I'm controlling my DirecTV receiver and the volume through my Sony amp. Therefore, the actions available on the screen and the physical buttons assume those roles. (By the way, I find the hardware keys absolutely perfect for controlling the DirecTV receiver.) Likewise, I can choose my "Watch SmartTV" activity, and it will bring up the apps on my TV and let me select whatever app I want with the physical keys, while the touchscreen displays my SmartTV control selections. Same with PS3, Wii, Xbox, etc. As you cycle through your modes, the remote seamlessly offers you the appropriate control options. Pretty cool indeed.

Fifth, I'm not sure why battery life is such a concern. It comes with a charging cradle, seems like a no-brainer to me that when you're not using the remote, just pop it in the cradle, no? Assuming most of us have to work and kids- if you have them- are in school, there has to be at least some portion of your day where you can let the remote charge up, right? When you're sleeping maybe? Just doesn't seem like this should be much of a concern. Longer term, I hope the non-removable battery lasts a good long while, but I'm not too worried about it.

Finally, I've been more than pleasantly surprised by how well this works. Granted, I'm a smart remote neophyte, and as with any review take this review with a grain or two of salt, but I really and truly found this to be an exceptional product plus a fun grown up "toy" to boot. Unless you have equipment that really cannot be controlled by the Harmony products, I can't think of any major reason why I wouldn't recommend this. It's not inexpensive per se, especially if you need the Hub as well, but for as well as it works and the capability it offers, I think it's a good value.

I bought mine by accident. I was looking for a wireless keyboard on eBay and saw someone in the UK selling one for about $60; it didn't have a working power supply, which was fine because it'd probably have the wrong plug on it. (It needs an 8V DC power supply to charge, and of course the fancy-shmancy keyboard stand.)

It feels solid, with full size keys and a nice feel comparable to some of the best wired keyboards available today. (It's not an IBM clicky keyboard, but what do you expect?)

Battery lifetime is excellent, about three weeks between charges with 8 hours a day of use and it only takes 4 hours to charge from dead. There's a red "low battery" indicator which blinks when it needs a recharge.

I don't use the circular mousepad, I wish they'd put a square one on it. It works but is awkward to use; I just use a separate trackball. For occasional use it's OK, but I can't use it for anything requiring precise mouse movements.

title: Great design, substandard switches.
text:
I own multiple Logitech input devices. Really like this mouse -- feels great in the hand, buttons are well positioned, etc. BUT, this mouse has serious problems with component quality, and it would appear that most if not all newer Logitech mice not infrequently have the same or similar problem. Logitech is probably just simply using cheap, substandard switches for its buttons. In less than a year of ownership the left button started double clicking occasionally and would not hold a click to drag. Now, 14 months after purchasing, the mouse has become unusable. The switch can't be single clicked any longer, no matter how lightly or hard it the button is pressed. Looking around the internet for info, it appears that it is a remarkably common problem with this mouse, and indeed most, if not all, newer Logitech mice. Many accounts I've read are of people needing this mouse replaces multiple times under warranty, until such time as Logitech just starts denying them any further warranty service for it, or until the warranty period runs out. The more adventurous among them have taken the mouse apart and adjusted the failed switch spring or even replaced the failed switch all together.
So, sure, the mouse is under warranty, and that's great. But for a mouse, the component most used to physically input and interact with your machine, and indeed the most used part of that device, the left button, to fail within a year is frustrating. So I've started trying to reach Logitech via their website to begin my warranty claim. Well, that's easy in theory only. My mouse is already registered on the site, and I already have an account, but trying to sort out how to get warranty assistance results in a circular pattern of knowledge base articles or community comments that all lead back to the beginning with a "get help" button that leads only back to the same knowledge base articles and community comments. And it's their prescribed warranty procedure that leads to this circularity pattern. I finally got a claim submitted (I think) by beginning a support claim from within the "my products" list, under "support history," and not by using their warranty claim procedure.
For comparison, I have an 8 year old Microsoft Explorer Mouse that has literally thousands of hours of usage time under it (large areas of the finish are worn off). All the switches still work flawlessly.
So, in sum: Disappointing at best.

title: Best Harmony yet......
text: Logitech has finally got it all together with this product.  I have been using Harmony remotes since they were first introduced and this is my fourth one and the best to date.  Granted it is not plug and play and for the uninitiated the learning curve on how the software wants you to think in order to program it can be steep for the non-technical.  I wouldn't recommend any Harmony remote for an elderly relative but most people can set it up easily enough if you can follow directions.  Although it says you can do this through your smart phone, I would recommend you do it using your desktop for the initial setup.  The newest iteration of MyHarmony software is so much easier to use if you take the time to identify all of your equipment prior to starting out.  You will need manufacturer and model numbers for every device.  The Logitech website has a downloadable worksheet for this but pad and pencil will do.  First you set up all of your devices (TV, DVD, cable box, etc.) and then you set up your activities (Watch TV, Watch a Movie, etc.).  The software walks you through this process but you have to follow the flow.  There are no shortcuts unless you already have a Harmony remote and then the software will allow you to import that existing setup and after syncing the hub with the software you are good to go.  Tweaks and adjustments are easily done later.

title: Surprisingly good sound for the money and size.
text:
Surprisingly good sound for the money and size. I'm quite pleased with the sound quality and volume for this small, single speaker. I used one of these to replace the 2.1 speakers of someone who hates the sight of wires and speakers, and with this I was actually able to hide the entire speaker behind the computer tower, wires and all. It's certainly not a competitor for even a low priced 2.1, but if you're buying this it's probably for space reasons and in that area it's very competitive. I've seen reviews saying that this is insufficiently loud, and I suppose for some purposes it probably is, but in this large living room it was easily capable of much more volume than could be utilized. For any sort of personal purpose, like a PC speaker, I find that it's more than loud enough.

I knocked off a star because there is, in my view, a pretty significant weakness in the design. That is that it needs two separate cables, a power and an audio cable. In my opinion, Logitech should redesign this speaker with a single USB cable. Reducing clutter isn't a priority in 2.0 and 2.1 systems, arguably, but it almost certainly is on the Z50, so that modification would get it 5 stars from me.

title: Useful Features, some Design Flaws
text: Works with up to three separate devices, using bluetooth or Logitech USB dongle. Keys are responsive and installation was instantaneous and flawless. I took away one star because the numeric keypad also serves the home/end, and page up/dn functions. While this arrangement is not unusual, the problem is that there is no status indication for Num Lock, Caps Lock, or anything else, for that matter. This designed in defect means trying to remember the status or using trial and mostly error. Windows 10 lacks any such indicators, as well. The workaround I found was to install a small third party utility (Tray Status) which tracks these keys as well as several others. The keyboard also lacks Sleep and Calculator shortcut keys found on some other Logitech keyboards. It does have a much smaller footprint as a result of these omissions. It is also a good deal heavier than some previous keyboards, but the weight gives it a solid, well-built feel.

title: Awesome Remote
text:
I've owned the Harmony One for several years now. Configuration is pretty easy once you figure out the software interface. It sometimes takes a few tries to get things programmed exactly the way you want.

I've had no problems with the battery swelling with this remote like others have mentioned.

I was a little worried about breaking the screen due to being dropped like others have mentioned but after several years of ownership and dozens of drops from 2-3 feet onto a hardwood floor, I'm no longer concerned. I have a feeling those other reviewers have not been honest about how the screen really broke since the LCD screen is recessed pretty deep in the case and not easily broken.

My setup is pretty complex with remapped buttons, custom buttons, 10 devices and numerous activities to control those devices.

I only have two complaints. One is that even with the delay set as log as possible in the software, the time between commands sent is too long. For instance, If I press volume up 5 times in quick succession, I expect it to be as fast as the actual TV remote, however, there's a delay of about 1/2 second between commands. I still have and use a Logitech 880 that's I've owned since around 2005 and it does not have this delay. It responds to key presses almost as fast as I can press the keys. From my research into this issue, the problem is in the hardware and there's nothing that can be done about it. I've learned to live with it.

The other complaint is the high cost of this remote. Luckily, I was given gift cards for Christmas and my birthday so I used them to purchase this remote.

title: I like many was a really big fan of the Microsoft ...
text:
I like many was a really big fan of the Microsoft Trackball, unfortunately it was discontinued and even used devices were terribly expensive. Previous to that I used the OG Logitech Trackman's and I liked them but the Trackball had more and program-able buttons. I wanted to get away from corded devices so I bought one of the M570 Trackballs and I loved it and eventually paired it with the Logitech K270 keyboard. I've replicated this setup on all of my pc's at home and at work.
I've had very little trouble with my Trackman, you have to pop out the track-ball about every week to clean around the bearings generally dust out the cavity. I've worn a few out over the years and recently during an extended project I started having trouble with it locking up. I'd have to lightly "slam" it on my desk to wake it up. Thinking that the receiver was going bad I replaced it with a duplicate to experience the same problem. What I discovered was the dongle was going bad and after I replaced it problem solved. All it all currently I have 5 of these Trackmans in use and I also have a few new in reserve, thankfully the Trackman works for years. My only problem I have with them and Logitech in general is on their wireless devices is using too many sizes of batteries. Pick one and stick with it, some use AA and others AAA.

title: It's a perfect size to be portable
text:
Over the past 5+ years, I have always come back to this mouse as my go-to laptop mouse. It's a perfect size to be portable, but not too small that your hand starts to cramp. It works well enough to be a primary desktop mouse as well even for a bit of casual gaming. It has a good weight to it to feel sturdy and the four relatively large gliding feet hold up well without ever (hopefully) needing to be replaced.

I've owned 3 or 4 of these and found they all worked well under normal situations (I've never tried to use this underwater or anything like that). I've been throwing these in my bags for travel and work and they continue to work. One of the details I really like about this mouse is the sliding "door" at the bottom that covers the sensor and acts as an on/off switch while protecting the lens. It closes tight enough to not accidentally open while it's in your bag and is probably one of the reasons for low failures over the years.

The mouse comes with several more buttons than your standard mouse, which can all be customized using Logitech's software, and actually have a pretty ergonomic design. The options for each button are pretty wide, but if you don't find what you're looking for, you can even set a custom action. I'm currently using 3 across different systems and the oldest one probably has been in use for 3+ years without any failures.

The name Anywhere claims to function on any surface, and this turns out to be mostly true. Glass, wood, carpet, iPads, dogs, it can pretty much track on any surface you throw at it, although the one weak spot I've seen is on glossy magazine covers with lots of color changes, but if you find a section that's a constant color, it works fine.

If you're using this on a desktop that's placed on the floor, I'd recommend keeping a line of sight with the receiver by attaching it somewhere on your desk, otherwise you might see some connection issues.

I've come across a couple issues, a button that always double clicks, and an issue with the mouse wheel, but each time, Logitech has been very helpful and willing to provide a warranty replacement. Be prepared to answer a couple questions, but they are generally trying to help you so I've always had a good experience.

title: Good keys, Ok case, TOO HEAVY.
text:
In choosing between the two keyboard offerings available for iPad Pro (12.9), I initially went with the Logitech Create (in black on black) primarily due to the backlit keyboard, overall protective capabilities, and mostly full-travel keys. Bottom line - it's just too heavy (3.2 lbs combined with the iPad Pro, it weighs a hair more than the actual iPad). So I returned it, and got the Apple Smart Keyboard instead. It is almost a pound lighter combined with the iPad than the Logitech Create.

My logic was such that If I really need a great keyboard to dig in and do some serious typing I could always connect any Bluetooth keyboard. And as it turns out the interesting canvas feel of the Smart Keyboard is growing on me.

Keyboard:
The actual keyboard mechanism is great. Feels high quality just like a MacBook. It's awesome that there is a backlight - but it's limited. First off, unlocking the device via the unlock button on the keyboard doesn't turn the backlight on, so you have to find the key to do it in the dark, or risk typing unnecessary characters. Also, it turns off after an incredibly short time and there's no way to change that setting.

Putting the iPad in and taking it out is a nightmare - you're never quite sure if it's seated 100% properly, and some of the reports of people having their iPad screen scratched spooked me. Once it's in, it feels inelegant to take it out and put it in, and it's still just as awkward to unfold it and prop and unfold it as the Smart Keyboard - so it's neither here nor there. Not robust enough to make it feel like part of the device like a laptop feels, and not portable enough to accentuate the advantages of the iPad. It's heavier than some MacBooks and MacBook airs, and that defeats part of the purpose of an iPad.

title: Logitech G933 vs Razer MANO'WAR Review
text:
Wanting a good wireless headset, ultimately came down to two options, Logitech G933 and the Razer ManO'War. I purchased both products from a local store to try them out on a 30 day return policy. You wont find any pictures here, as both products have tons of pictures of them already, but this is my side-by-side with pros and cons for both.

Logitech G933:

OBSERVATIONS:
*Snug Grip. It does not feel crushing like some headsets as it has a thick padding, it does grip firmly and there is no fear that it will fall off when I tilt my head forward.
*Some Macro Buttons (called G Keys) are awkward to press based upon grip around headset
*Macro Buttons have different shapes to allow you to identify which button you are pressing without looking

PROS
*Room for Glasses. While it has a snug grip, I do not feel any discomfort wearing my glasses, though I have thin frames.
*Programmable Macro Buttons. This is huge if you use Ventrillo to play games as you most likely have Vent set to a keyboard key to talk while playing. This is the first and only headset I can find that allows you to program a keyboard key into the macro, thus allowing you to both PushToTalk on the headset as well as use the keyboard key.
*Thin band over your head with thick padding. This counters a huge negative for me you will see on ManO'War, but the G933 feels comfortable no matter how you have it positioned on your head, especially if you have a shaved head like I do.
*7.1 Surround Sound Effect works really well, and I had a much better sense of that with the G933 than the ManO'War

CONS
*Padding is scratchy. Really. I have no idea why this material was chosen, it may have been about anti-microbe properties, but it is not a simulated leather and it took some getting used to. I am hoping in time the material will break in and become more soft.
*Significant 1 Star reviews about hardware failure. All products have a certain percentage of failures, this one seems high, with a glowing 20% negative 1 star reviews on several sites. While I hate AddOn warranties with a passion, this one might warrant the added purchase for long term peace of mind.

Razer ManO'War

OBSERVATIONS:
*Very soft grip. Feels too loose at times, will fall forward if you tilt your head forward swiftly.
*Not much bigger than the G933. Initially I was worried about the size, but both headsets are definitively in the 'Large' section of the catalog and I didn't find any additional clunkiness of storing it or holding it over the G933.

PROS
*Very Soft padding materials. This one wins hands down in terms of comfort to wear. Even given the scratchiness of the G933 material, I doubt you will find a softer material on another headset.
*Diverse and dynamic sounds. Both headsets have an excellent sound, to the point where I think this will come down to preference in how you like your music to sound, but I slightly prefer this headset in this category.

CONS
*Padding does not cover the entire over the head band. This one really bothers me as there seems to be no reason for it. ManO'War has a HUGE width to the overhead band, and the padding is a very small strip in the middle. If you like to put your headset in different positions, such as 'One Ear Off' to hear people around you, the jointing of the headset is more than capable, but the head band scratches really bad as it has a sharper edge than most. Very uncomfortable around exposed skin.
*Falls off easily. You wont be rocking out with this headset unless you plan to hold onto the headset.

My Choice:
I chose to keep the Logitech G933, but it was really close. Ultimately, having a shaved head I found the ManO'War too scratchy, despite the G933 material being much more abrasive, and the Macro Buttons (G Keys) were too good to pass up. The ability to be able to PushToTalk on the headset while away from my desk on Vent while keeping Vent set to a keyboard key is a very overlooked concept, in my mind.

Well there you have it. Both headset companies are known for good customer support (unless you get THAT employee) with great replacement policies while in warranty. Hope this review helped if you are like I was, stuck between choosing one of these two.

title: This controller is perfect for this price-point
text:
I have a Macbook Pro and a Raspberry Pi running RetroPie and needed a game controller. I originally bought the [[ASIN:B004QRKWLA Microsoft Xbox 360 Wired Controller for Windows & Xbox 360 Console]]. There is a driver for MacOS/OSX out there that works, but RetroPie would not recognise it. So I needed another USB controller, and because I'm not a really serious gamer, just needed something reasonably priced.

This controller is perfect for this price-point. It is well constructed, though a little light, could do with some more heft. I personally like the placement of the two sticks on the bottom and the D pad in line with the buttons, while the Xbox controller has the left stick and D pad reversed. No driver required for Linux or Windows. It worked with the unofficial Xbox controller driver I already had installed on MacOS, so am not sure about Mac compatibility (I'm guessing there shouldn't be a problem).

If you're a Windows user, spend the extra $10 or so on the Xbox controller. But even if you opt for this one, unless you're an e-sports aficionado, you won't be disappointed.

title: GREAT Experience!!!!!
text:
First, this review is by Ken not Cynthia.

Christmas day, my wife (Cynthia) fried the remote that came with our B&K Ref 50 as she attempted to clean it. As a result, off to buy a new remote. We reviewed a number of replacements. Specifically, there were many references on the web to Harmony 650 remote as a current (modern) replacement for the B&K sr10.1. After digging into the reviews, my concern was being able to easily setup a remote that would allow us to integrate the 8 devices hanging on the Ref 50. Most importantly, allow remote integration with the digital TV converter (yes we cut the cord.. 4 years ago) with the other devices.

After reading the reviews for the Harmony 950 I was concerned, but having setup the sr10.1 myself, I had a really hard time believing many of the reviews stating the difficult time they had programming the Harmony 950. Well it arrived yesterday and I was ready for the process to take multiple hours, including taking some anger suppressants as I called tech support (woo-sa). I'm happy to report that the process was a snap. I am very sorry those other reviewers found this device so difficult to use, but using the download software made the process way too easy.

Now with one button I turn the projector, Ref 50, and TV tuner, the Ref-50 and Projector sync to the proper video input and the Ref-50 and tuner are set for the proper inputs. SWEET

And most important, the wife is even happier.... she blew up the other remote on purpose ..... just kidding :D... Glad she did

Surprises:
* Found a few Roku apps already programed on the device once I got it started. Now, no need to search my listing of Roku apps just hit the button.
* The "activity" setup was way too easy... Come on Logitech at least make that part hard.. joking :)

I wish they had:
* I was a bit concerned when I opened the box and there was only a very small setup guide manual. Hey where's the software? I guess that's a way to save money. As long as the savings is passed on, I'm ok with it. Bottom line if you don't have internet that could be a problem.... Oh, but you're reading this review so let's assume you have internet access. No big deal.
* I wish the setup would/could have ability to read the Roku apps I've already setup, that way when I use my remote all my apps are already there..... Hey Harmony 950 product manager ... go work on that partnership ;)

All in All.. Good job Logitech.
I guess I can start looking to you all for more than my mouse point device.

title: Great Console headset... Few drawbacks.
text:
The G933s are a good overall headset for someone (like me) who wanted one headset to rule them all. Owning all consoles and pc... I wanted one to use on all. It does this and more. Mobile sounds good. Even sounds good going out of my roku 3s remote. I went wireless because I was hoping it would amplify the sound from the ps4 a bit more, and it does.

Pros:
1. Great audio quality but not perfect. Mess with the EQ settings to your liking. Powerful bass can become too much if not careful. For a wireless headset though, it sounds pretty freaking good.

2. Wireless range. I walked to the opposite corner of my house through several walls from my pc chatting with a friend of mine on Skype. No drops. Mind you I run my wifi at 5 ghz only so that might help.

3. Mic quality. Good enough to chat online. Friend of mine said it sounded better than my aging plantronics d500 headset which is about 7 years old. Still works, just wanted a headset for console as well. Once again not perfect but not a con.

4. Wired mode works great too. Sounds good on Xbox one and ps4 if used that way, although wireless adds EQ effects.

Cons:
1. Battery life indicator. If you're not on your computer, you have absolutely no way to know what percentage the battery is at. Luckily it uses micro usb to charge, so charging it isn't that big of a deal. Just would be nice to know what percentage it's at.

2. Wireless mix mode volume drop. If you use it say wireless to ps4 and wire it into your phone for music, it works, but at the sacrifice of volume. Not sure why it does this but it does.

3. No "wired mode". The USB port on the headset is for charging only. No data is sent through like 633s. This doesn't make sense to me... Why can't it do both Logitech?

4. RGB gimmick. Yea... Just no. Turn it off for more battery life.

Conclusion: I told myself if this headset wasn't louder on ps4 wireless mode then it was going back for say the hyper x cloud 2s... But since it is I am keeping it. So far no issues like the others have had. It is a large headset but mine will primary never leave the house.

title: Terrible software, Poor quality video at medium distance, but Good as an upclose webcam - buyer beware
text:
[[VIDEOID:b3687a545448bbab0256bd871e6f13e9]] So I've got VERY mixed feeling about this webcam. My use is for conference room video coverage, and I purchased this webcam based on several good reviews on conference room usage; I am not using it for single-person in front of the cam use, e.g. vlogging.
Photos and video sample attached.

TLDR;
I DO NOT recommend this product for any conference room usage. I am looking into return & refund options.
(update: after calling Logitech support and following their steps = no improvement. They confirmed the software window is fixed and unable/unwilling to make changes. Asked about refund options, but because it was purchased on Amazon and after 30-days, they would not honor a refund--only used webcam 2 twice plus testing.)

PRO:
Very portable
Tripod mountable
Quickly recognized by Windows
Easily used a secondary microphone (USB)

CON:
Inability to resize webcam software window--MAJOR problem for me.
Tinny sound at medium distance
Poor video resolution at medium distance, although software said was at 1080p

Posting this review after using this webcam for two different types of presentations.
First presentation recording was a single speaker in a classroom setup. Webcam was about 10-15 feet from the speaker, depending where he moved about. The recorded video consistently went in and out of focus and was never very sharp--despite plenty of classroom lighting, being set to 1080p, and mounted to a tripod. Audio quality was very poor; it was often distant, hollow, and tinny sounding, despite the presenter being somewhat naturally loud.
See screenshot of single presenter--most of video is like the clip, not much is well focused.
See first part of video sample (~15 sec.) for video and audio quality; webcam is stationary and speaker about 10 feet away.

Second presentation is a 4 person panel in a large conference room. Like before, the webcam was mounted on a stationary tripod with lots of good overhead lighting. The speaker panel were also fixed, sitting in chairs. I used a separate conference microphone for the audio, which was on the black chair in the video sample (MXL AC404 USB Conference Microphone). The webcam software preview window looked good, but because it was so small I could not tell how good/bad it was--more on the software below. The recorded video quality was absolutely terrible, nowhere near 1080p and entirely out of focus despite the auto-focus feature turned on. When I uploaded a 'best quality' version to YouTube it was classed as 360p.
See screenshot and second half of video sample (~10 seconds).

Most frustrating about this device is the Logitech webcam software. I use it on a Surface Pro 4 running Windows 10. The installed software is up-to-date as of this review, running version 2.51. The software window occupies perhaps 20% (generous estimate) of my tablet screen size and does not have any options to maximize or resize the window--it is completely fixed. The software setting and video capture windows are even smaller. Those with less than perfect eyesight would strain to read the text or click on the right spot for menu options. Naively, I didn't think to check the Logitech community support forums about the webcam software before the purchase; however, there are MANY posts on that site complaining about inability to resize the software windows for the c920 and other Logitech webcams. Logitech reps comment on those forums about it being a known issue, which has gone unresolved for years. I might have avoided poor video quality recordings if I could have seen a decently sized preview window; instead I had about a 2 inch preview box--hard to tell the difference between 1080 and and 480 in a 2 inch box. I could probably workaround the tiny window problem by lowering the resolution on my tablet, but I shouldn't have to do that.
See the screenshot for the software window static size.
The one saving grace about the software, was that it had no trouble detecting the USB microphone and selecting it as the audio source.

title: This mouse is a MUST for text editing!!!
text:
I write and edit documents for a living, and this mouse is the best one I've ever seen/used for text editing. (Coders take note too!) Why? It doesn't even mention it in the description, but this mouse has FIVE programmable buttons in addition to the left and right click main buttons. FIVE!

So why is this so great? I have the 2 thin left-side buttons assigned to Copy and Paste, and the large left-side button is Cut. So, it's easy to cut/copy/paste with just your thumb, and your hand never leaves the mouse! The scroll wheel also has 2 more button functions when pushed left or right, which I assigned to Backspace and Delete respectively. This lets you perform all FIVE basic text editing functions easily with your hand remaining on the mouse. I don't even think about it anymore, as all button functions have become second nature.

Besides this GREAT programmability, the mouse itself is a convenient size. All buttons feel great, clicks are not loud or stiff, scroll wheel is either smooth or "notched" by pressing the small button just behind the scroll wheel. Batteries last FOREVER (over a year of daily use with just 2 AAs). And, as someone noted, the mouse works fine with just one battery, so you can make it lighter and shift its center of gravity. It's a full-sized mouse but the convenience of the buttons means I always travel with it. Editing text with a regular mouse seems like a huge hassle to me now that I've been spoiled by the M705.

text:
There was a time that Logitech meant good quality and reasonable price. Sadly that time has passed. Having paid $50 for a combo if this keyboard and M510 wireless mouse I had high hopes. Unfortunately those hopes have been crushed.

First issue is wireless connectivity. I kb has a range of about 2 feet, compared to about 15 feet for the mouse. Since I'm 10 feet from my computer, which is the reason for buying a wireless kb and mouse in the first place, I have to attach two usb extensions to keep the kb in range of it's receiver. Still, periodically it starts gaining a delay between typing and the keystrokes being recognized by the computer. When the delay becomes intolerable I switch the kb off and back on and it clears it. This happens 2 or 3 times a day.

The second issue is the keys. They sometimes stick down. I usually can free them by tapping the stuck key repeatedly but sometimes I have to jar the whole kb to release them. This brings up the other key problem. When the kb is bumped it presses space or a random key on the bottom row. This wouldn't be a problem for a corded kb that sits on a desk but cordless does indicate portability which means it will move around a bit.

I bought this product to replace a corded logitech kb that came out of the box with sticky keys so I've decided it's time for me to divorce logitech.

title: Some good points, but side scrolling impossible to configure.
text:
Didn't work for me. I like the idea of relieving my wrist and arm from wandering all over the desk, and the ball under my thumb seemed like something I could get used to that would ultimately work better than a mouse. I didn't really need wireless; a cable is a hassle with a mouse because it's always pushing the wrong way or tangling with something as you push the mouse hither and yon around your desk, but a trackball stays stationary, so where's the need for wireless?? For my setup, the little USB receiver was barely 18 inches from the trackball, and it seemed to work fine, And I really liked the light touch of the left and right buttons--such a relief compared to the Mac BB mouse where you have to push the whole right side of the mouse down to right click, which far too often gets interpreted as a left click.

Definitely some positives, but I just could not get side scrolling to work on my M570. I reloaded the driver twice--Mac OS 10.11.4--but no dice. After configuring side scrolling, I could get side scrolling in one direction only. After re-configuring, either left or right side scrolling would work, but never both. Regardless of whether I pushed the scroll wheel left or right, it would only scroll one way. After re-configuring, the same situation, though the one way it scrolled might or might not have changed. In other words, I could use the track ball to scroll laterally one way, but to scroll the opposite way, I'd have to drop the cursor to the bottom of the screen and drag the slider bar. Impossible to get anything done. I rechecked configuration, thinking maybe I could configure one of the little secondary buttons to reverse the side scrolling, but that didn't seem to be an option.

I checked a couple of forums, and side scrolling seems to be an ongoing problem with Logitech track balls. The most-often suggested solution was to try various different drivers. Hmmm. Sorry, I can't spend hours at work doing Logitech's development; Logitech gets paid for that, my company does not. So I took it back. (Best Buy, not Amazon for this one.)

Unfortunately, this jives with my previous experience with Logitech; years ago, I had a Logitech mouse that I was never able to use because, unlike every other mouse I've ever had, it wouldn't work with the generic PC drivers, and Logitech didn't support it anymore. I took a chance on the M570, and it was a waste of time. I will think long and hard before ever buying another Logitech product.

title: Good, but certainly not perfect...
text:
* Please note that this review is about the CASE, NOT the seller, please see my review regarding the seller on the seller's account!

Being the only alternative to the Apple case that still utilizes a smart keyboard, this case is pretty good. The following is my opinion, so it may not be fully applicable to you.

What I like:
- The quality of build - This product is really well built. The keys are sturdy, and are "island"-style, mimicking apple laptops. The exterior is a water resistant tough fabric. Magnets are strong and sturdy and the plastic is hard, but smooth/comfortable.
- The backlit keyboard - This may not be a big deal for most, but having a backlit key board is nice when you are taking notes on a presentation in a dimly, lit room. Being able to control the brightness is also great (so that you do not bother your neighbor). There is no color changing capabilities, but IMO, that's a silly gimmick. Its an ipad keyboard case, not a gaming mechanical keyboard...
- The quality typing experience - Prior to this keyboard, my main typing tool for work was a macbook pro 2014, and I loved it. This case is the closest to mimicking that typing experience. Also, since it is powered by the smart connector, there is NO LAG, and there is no need to charge a battery, so no surprise dead batteries.
- The method by which the ipad is held in place - Many keyboard cases that have similar styling do one of two things to hold ur ipad: (1) have a thing piece on either side to generate minimal blockage to your ipad, but breaks VERY quickly because their are not engineered from the proper material and endure a lot of stress or (2) cover up large parts of the ipad to keep it in place, which is effective, but unsightly - This case solves that issue. The hold is all around the top and 1/2 of the sides, and made of a tough rubberized material that allows flexibility, without sacrificing hold or being unsightly.
- The function keys at the top are extremely useful. Here they are in order from left to right: Home, brightness down, brightness up, search, keyboard language change, keyboard backlight down, keyboard backlight up, rewind, play/pause, forward, mute, sound down, sound up, lock
- The outer looks - Protective, yet minimalistic (this is super subjective to me tho)
- The smart-connector capabilities
- The ability to use this on your lap (since it is study and not flexible like other leather cases)

What I do NOT like - I am going to try to limit these to objective issues with the product, leaving my opinions out
- Single viewing angle when in the upright position - There is no way to adjust this, although it seems to be a decent set-up for viewing/typing on a desk/table
- Unlike the 9.7'' version of this case, the 12.9'' version LACKS A LOCATION TO HOLD YOUR APPLE PENCIL - This is a huge annoyance..why put it on the 9.7 and not the 12.9?? After all more people who own the 12.9 use the apple pen regularly for art than 9.7 users
- No soft touch contacts for when you are using the ipad in "non-keyboard" mode - When you fold your ipad down to, say, use your apple pencil without the keyboard in the way, the bare back of your ipad makes contact with the hard plastic of the keyboard - This is just asking for scratches - They could have very easily/economically included either (1) a piece of clear silicone to cover the back of the ipad or (2), put small rubber risers along the rim to make sure contacts points were not rough

I will continue to update this review as I use the product more

Using a traditional point-and-click laser mouse for long periods of time was starting to cause pain in my hand, so that's why this Logitech touchpad is so awesome: I can place this touchpad either to the left or to the right of my keyboard for omnidextrous usage. title: Good Value for Your Money
text:
I’ve recently started to use headphones when gaming so my old surround sound system wasn’t being used very much and was just cluttering up my desk and putting a ton of cords behind it. These speakers are a bit of a downgrade from my old system in the sound department, but accomplish the goal of cleaning up my desk.

They’re not that big of a downgrade though. While only being a 2.1 system compared to my old 5.1 they still manage a good range of sound with no distortion at reasonable volume levels. The bass starts to distort at high volume levels but that’s not a huge issue for regular video watching and music listening unless your goal is to wake your neighbors.

I was a bit surprised to find that the control puck wasn’t on it’s own dedicated line but sat in between the computer and the woofer. This can limit your options as the lines between each aren’t very long, so expect to place your woofer close to your PC. It is very convenient however to have the volume and power controls separate from the speakers so you aren’t bumping them around and have a bit more flexibility in where you place them.

Overall these are a good value set of speakers that are doing exactly what I wanted.

title: Garbage! Beware!
text:
This was THE worst purchase I have ever made. I hooked these speakers up to my computer, and immediately was greeted with loud 60 cycle hum along with loud buzzing. While sounds from the computer did also play through the speakers, the hum and buzz were loud enough to compete with the audio unless something was at maximum volume. Completely unusable. I tried many different power configurations in case there was some sort of ground loop, and even bought a 2nd sound card for my computer to see if that would make a difference, but the speakers continued to make the same unpleasant noises in all cases. I then bought a Klipsch 2.1 speaker system locally and hooked it up to the same PC, sound card and power ... and the Klipsch system worked perfectly, with no buzz or hum at all. So fine, I said, maybe I just got a bad Logitech system and I can at least return it, since I bought it new and directly from Amazon (not a Marketplace seller) only a few days before. But NO! ... I go to try to request a return, and the website says the item is non-returnable! WHAT????

Edit: fortunately, Amazon Customer Service came through in a big way and refunded my money after all. While I won't buy anything from Logitech again, at least I feel that I can continue to trust Amazon with my future online shopping. Thumbs up to Amazon, but a big thumbs down to Logitech for manufacturing junk like this.

title: Useless as a universal remote. Satisfying to snap in half out of frustration
text:
This is a truly terrible product. When a company adds a little bit of smarts to a product, but not enough to really know what's going on, it has the effect of fighting the user in every action rather than helping.

For example, many components don't have discrete on and off functions, just a toggle. Harmony wants to perform linked actions, eg turn on TV, set receiver to cable box. The linked functions try to be smart, but in effect it gets out of sync with the one component that has toggle on/off and turns it off rather than on. So that entire feature set is useless.

So you lower your expectations and perform actions one at a time. Unfortunately, Harmony still wants to couple actions. Want to set your receiver to aux? It "helpfully" performs action twice and receiver goes to a different input.

I ended up breaking this product in half and going back to my collection of six remotes. I was pleased with how well it snapped in two: boo jagged edges, little flying debris.

title: Logitech's wireless receivers usually work pretty well, but I've been having more and more ...
text:
Where is the bluetooth or cable? Logitech's wireless receivers usually work pretty well, but I've been having more and more trouble with them the last couple of years. Long a user of multiple pointing devices to reduce RSI, I have spent many hours using bluetooth and Logitech's wireless side-by-side. Bluetooth wins every time. Unless the battery on the bluetooth mouse is low, it always works. The Logitech performance is dictated more by interference and distance where one day it works perfectly, and the next day not at all.

That said, I would have long ago started camping out at the orthopedist if I hadn't started using thumb trackballs. I started on wired Logitechs and moved to wireless when the wired models were discontinued. Even though there are very few on the market, the Logitech has always been the best fit for me. I recently thought I found a new competitor, but it had a major design flaw that prevented me from making the change. Just keep the wireless receiver close, the trackball area clean, and it should work well.

title: The best universal remote -- especially for technology-challenged family members.  Press help!
text:
Fantastic remote! Remote controls need tactile buttons -- something you can feel with your fingers when the room is dark. This remote has a great feel to the buttons, not too squishy, and very responsive. It has good balance, fits in small hands, and has most of the buttons in easy reach.

The software takes some time to get used to, but after re-programming it for different devices and rooms, the software becomes very intuitive.

The best feature of the remote is the "help" button. If something gets off -- an input doesn't get switched, a device doesn't get turned on, etc., then family members who aren't good with A/V equipment can sometimes get frustrated. With this remote, you just need to show them to press"help" when they get lost. The remote will take a series of steps to fix the problem.

I own 4 of these remotes for our 4 rooms with TVs, and have gifted 3 more to family members. Everyone says it's very easy to use, even for our older family members who aren't tech-savvy.

Highly recommend the 650. I prefer the 650 without rechargable batteries, simply because I don't like having to plug in the remote every week.

title: A breeze to set up compared to other programmable remotes.
text:
I've had this remote control system for 9 months now, controlling a TV, audio/video amplifier, Blu-Ray player, LaserDisc player, Tivo, Roku3, and an Amazon Fire stick. Previously, I had been using a Universal-brand programmable remote control that was a headache to set up because I had to write macros for it and painstakingly input text screens using a numeric keypad for input. This Harmony product was a breeze to set up by comparison - no macros to write, no screens to lay out, just pick stuff off of drop-down menus. It found all of my devices in Harmony's huge database of products. To be fair, I'm a technical person and it did take a bit of time to get this all going with 7 devices, but I was able to start simply with just the TV, Tivo and video amp, and then gradually add more devices and activities once the basics were working. I use an old 7" Android tablet propped on a stand as a remote, and it is wonderful, especially at the dining room table when my hands are too greasy to pick up and operate a normal remote control with buttons. Even though the tablet stays powered up the whole time I'm watching TV or a movie (Harmony prevents it from auto-sleeping), the tablet's battery usage is low because the menus are mostly thin white outlines on a black background. My tablet is good for a whole day or more of use as a remote on a single charge, even though it's on all the time. And the included handheld remote control works well too, although the buttons are a bit small if you have large fingers. The only problem I had was losing my wi-fi connection, but that was not Harmony's fault, it turned out to be a router problem. I will say you must have a solidly working wi-fi network for this system to function properly. Other than that, it's been a great and reliable system.
Update: Two months ago I replaced my router with a newer, more powerful one, and that has solved all the problems I had with the Harmony Hub occasionally losing connection. It has been 100% solid since I replaced my wi-fi router. So that confirms my suspicions that it was the router, not the Harmony Hub, that was the problem. I also linked the Hub to my Amazon Echo, and now I can verbally tell Alexa to turn on my TV and do some limited things by voice command without even touching a remote! It just gets better!

title: Good Upgrade from Harmony 650
text: I bought this to replace a Harmony 650 that served for several years but was starting to have problems with buttons not working and needing to be reset about 2x a week. Am very pleased with the 700 so far! It works exactly like 650, except for two things: first, instead of replacing batteries, you plug it into a charger (no, it's not a cradle)--haven't had it long enough to see how long the rechargeable batts last between chargings, but expect it to be a week or so--certainly, you don't have to charge it  every night. The second difference was a pleasant surprise: when you pick up the 700, its backlit buttons light up. My 650 didn't do that, and this feature is a welcome change, the small channel number buttons are now always easy to see anytime. I was able to use the 650's settings in the My Harmony PC software, it was relatively easy because it gives you the ability to add another remote, and then recognized that the 700 was there to be programmed through its USB cable. There were a couple of goofy moments with the transfer (such as the transfer screen on the PC showed 99% for a very long time, then showed Transfer Complete and still said 99%....so I just either pulled the plug or canceled the transfer, and bingo, everything was fine and the unit was completely programmed with my old settings. Just the usual "stuff," an Oh Well rather than a Don't Buy! If it lasts as long as the 650, several years (I'm guessing 7 or more?), I'll be very satisfied with this item!

title: Great for entertainment devices, terrible for 'smart' homes.
text:
I'd give it a 2.5 if I could. Its the best smart remote for IR devices. I have my equipment in a separate closet from my theater room so the hub and IR blasters are a must. The 'smart home' features are really half baked. So much potential with arbitrary limitations. I had the prior non-smarthome version and moved that to another room and bought this for my dedicated theater room. I envisioned being able to control my IR dimmer with the dedicated light dimming buttons instead of trying to remember which keys were programmed for long press lighting control. Only to find out:

Limitation #1) While every single button on the remote is very customizable, the smart home buttons are not. You can only use them for a short list of specific smart home hubs and accessories or you buy the $99 extension just to connect to other non-friendly hubs like wink. I wish those buttons were fully available like the rest of the remote. Especially for a lighting device that can be controlled by the hub.

Limitation #2) Even more, you really can't customize those buttons. Since my IR dimmer wouldn't play nice, and I've thought about putting hue lights in anyways, I bought a Hue hub and a couple of lights to try that route. Basically you can select a group of lights to dim or brighten. You can't pick a scene (even though the outdated online documentation says you can, they seemingly removed this feature). You can't even say one button is on and one button is off. Your only option is short press=on, long press=off. The dimmer buttons are totally locked- you can't customize or change. I'd love to program the plug buttons to specific scenes based on whether I'm watching a movie or sports or if I need to temporarily bring the lights up for a bathroom break, etc.

Limitation #3) You can't combine smart devices and activities, which would seem like the main reason to combine a home entertainment remote with a smart home remote. Sure, you can setup some very basic controls for the launch of an activity, but you can't change anything during an activity. I have a sequence with my IR dimmer where the lights come up when I hit pause and darken when I hit play. can't do that with any 'smart lights'. It's a minor quibble I guess. I can pause and then bring up the lights but with the software and custom sequences, connected devices like this should easily be made automatic. I can use my Nest app to turn the AC fan on to circulate air in the theater for a predetermined amount of time (3 hours) to keep it from heating up. I was hoping to be able to tie that sequence into an activity, nope. The smart home features are very very very basic. Almost dumb. I can do everything I want by using the Hue app, and the nest app, and the logitech app. I was hoping to be able to consolidate those just like this lets me consolidate my TV remote/receiver remote/satellite remote, etc.

Limitation #4) 8 devices. The exact same hub does 15 with the Elite. Just an arbitrary way to get you to upgrade. Their prerogative I guess. Display+Satellite+BluRay+Streaming device+receiver+game console+IR dimmer+Zone 2 eats up all my options. I can't control Zone 3 of my AVR without jumping through major hoops. Different zones of the same device shouldn't count against your total. I digress...

Limitation #5) the biggest limitation is the app. The software is slow, buggy and terrible. The desktop software is not bad, but they are removing capabilities one by one from the desktop to push you to the app. You can no longer program the home automation buttons with the desktop, that used to be available but now it's gone. Only on the app. You can no longer assign scenes to those buttons. It used to be there, it's still in their online documentation but the feature has been removed.

If you don't want/need home automation stuff, save money and get the older version which is otherwise identical.

title: Really nice, but also lacking.
text:
We bought this remote to replace our Harmony 650. All in all, this is a good remote. If I could, I'd rate 3.5 stars, but I rounded up.

The good: Can handle more devices/activities than the 650. The touch screen is clean and responsive, but not overly sensitive so you don't have to worry about accidently launching a command while swiping. Scrolling up/down or side/side is a breeze. It has the most commonly used hard buttons available, so you can perform many functions without needing to look at the remote. Has an internal battery and comes with a charging stand.

The bad: It doesn't have a very fluid design at all, nor is it easy to grip if you're trying to use the dvr/dvd controls at the top of the remote. Not sure why they went away from a more traditional remote design, but this was really bad decision making by Logitech.

The remote is also kind of slow during the power on phase of various activities. Ex: I use the Watch TV activity to power on my tv/satellite receiver/theater and the remote stays in the starting mode for a good 15-20 seconds, so you can't immediately change to the channel you want or adjust volume until the remote finishes it's cycle. And you need to keep the remote pointed at your devices until they all power on. First world problems for sure, but the 650 didn't do that.

Activities don't work once they've been activated. Ex: Using the Watch TV activity to power on my devices, let's say the theater doesn't power up. With the 650, I could just hit the Watch TV button a 2nd time and it would power the theater on without powering off the tv and satellite receiver. Not the case here. You have to go to the Help screen and once it turns your receiver on, it turns everything else off. Very frustrating when this happens.

Battery life isn't that great. I get about 3 days between charges. Maybe I'm expecting too much, but I expected to be able to go at least a week. Good news is it only takes about 30 to fully charge.

The touch screen has a swipe to unlock feature. I guess this is great if I'm worried about a stranger seeing what my favorite channels are, but it just seems kind of pointless.

Most of the shortcomings for this remote are pretty minor, buy there's a lot of minor shortcomings which is what keeps me from giving a better rating. I don't hate the remote at all. Overall I'm happy with it, but it seems like Logitech tried to literally break the mold with this remote and came up short. If they made a remote that was basically the 650 but with a touch screen, they'd have the perfect remote imo.

title: Up in the air about the Ultimate one...
text:
This one is up in the air, it seems like a good but it doesn't seem well executed. I've basically used all Harmony remotes each with very minimal issues (tweaking settings) but nothing a little programming and a sync couldn't fix. All with the exception of the Elite model, it's very tempting but the price is not premium I want to fork over if it ends up like the Ultimate One model. this is a nice remote and a bit of a conundrum in itself with other issues. The layout and ergonomics are not pleasing to hold and use, although I can use the top video controls (play, pause, rewind, FF, etc.) I rest my middle finger and index finger between the little fin on the bottom, still a klutzy feel. I've been using this for about two week, I'm working with it. I had to setup the swipe lock for the screen because my palm wrecks my entire viewing experience with just a light brush of skin to screen contact. The ability to fully customize the pages would be nice, other than changing a background picture adding and deleting favorite channel icons.

The make it or break it part, when I return it will be because of the activities I set up. It's getting old when you switch between activities and one or more component either responds when it shouldn't or doesn't respond at all. My programming is right, I have or currently use at least three of the lower tier remotes. It's frustrating for over $200 dollars, a $40-$50 dollar pricetag wouldn't burn me so much. This Ultimate One remote has problems pretty much all the time. Once, a message popped up and told me a sync error, it was hung up for thirty minutes. The message told me to unplug/plug the remote and restart sync, it took maybe two minutes after that. I do it now each time it gets hung up for more than ten minutes I unplug it and restart the sync, two minutes and I'm fixed for that moment. I'll use my 350's, 650 and 700 remotes because it's beginning to look like those are my only reliable options.

This is a nice remote, but everything I mentioned above will cut its lifespan short in my home. I desperately would love to try the Elite model but don't want to deal with another letdown. I've heard that customer service is mostly overseas, that's lovely when you need help on a complicated, technical device. Always a pleasure. The 12 month warranty is a little scary as well, 2 days out of warranty, we can't help you. These (all) companies are consistently cheapening materials and other components, making customer service lousy so everybody will give up and go fork out more money for replacements. I'll go back to using the individual component remotes. I'm still up in the air about this remote. Again I would love the Elite model but 367 days later and it bites the dust, I would not be very happy.

title: Excellent remote that could use a couple of design tweaks...
text:
BLUF: Great remote and would buy again

This is a replacement for a Harmony 700 (discontinued) that was beginning to fail and this was a great upgrade.

For background, I have been using and programming various remotes for years going back to older Philips Pronto remotes- This is a very intuitive and powerful platform in a reasonably priced package! Coming from another Harmony remote, the initial setup was very simple with a few tweaks for preference and new capability. I say that acknowledging I am something of a geek and understand the basics of how remotes work and their limitations. Even for the technologically challenged, Logitech has done a good job of making the programming interface intuitive and easy to use but still powerful enough for advanced users to customize. If anything, it errors on the side of simplicity vice functionality.

Some of the biggest concerns I had was the fast-forward/skip button since the two functions have been combined into a single button with this remote. I was quite leery of this as a DirecTV customer but happy to report that with a bit of tweaking and use of the gestures this is completely a non-issue. Only shortfall I can complain about is the lack of immediate access to the number pad- you can swipe left/right to it but I would prefer to map a soft key to bring it up. Niggling issue that may be possible but I haven't found an easy way to do it just yet.

The biggest complaint and the area where Logitech misses the mark is (as others have pointed out) with the basic ergonomics. The hard buttons are great, the touch screen is great and the overall size of the remote is great, they just need to re-organize! Put the touchscreen at the very top and move the transport controls (FF, pause, record, play etc.) under the screen! It would even benefit from being slightly longer to allow the main controls to sit just above center (where your thumb naturally sits) and fit better in the hand. I complain about this, pointing out this is a great unit that could benefit from a refresh- same functionality in a slightly different package.

To wrap this up, I am VERY pleased with this remote overall. It is not perfect and could use a change to the basic layout BUT it is a SOLID unit that is very flexible and a pleasure to use. If you are considering this a a first universal remote or an upgrade to an existing one, it is well worth it.

I have found the ability to pair to multiple devices handy.  If there is one design flaw it's that the forward and back buttons on the left side are too far toward the rear of the mouse. I have never used horizontal scroll wheel. A better design would have the scroll wheel and forward/back buttons position swapped. It would make it easier to use the tip of the thumb to press the buttons and still be able to scroll with the middle of the thumb. I have reprogrammed the "gesture" button in the left base of the mouse as my browser back button to compensate. I would give it 4.5 stars if that were an option.

I just bought this thing recently only a month ago. It was fine for a month, but it just abruptly became useless. The scrolling wheel has suddenly gone defective. Sometimes when it's not trying to scroll down automatically, if I as much as touch the scrolling wheel, then it will rapidly scroll down to the bottom of the page.

title: but I had plenty of painful memories. This remote didn't trigger any of them
text:
It's been awhile since I tried a universal remote, but I had plenty of painful memories. This remote didn't trigger any of them.

It's a great setup process with an online database (presumably it's updated regularly). This allows the less-standard buttons (stuff like menu, setup, exit, etc) to be mapped correctly for each device.

You get to define actions that allow you to do things like turn on 4 devices, select particular inputs on 2 of them, and have the volume buttons control one of them with the push of a single button. These actions (plus the "power off all" button) address most use cases. You hit the button for what you want to do, and then have the arrow keys to navigate on a DVR/streaming box and the volume keys to control volume on the amp. But if you want to configure your amp, you can just select it as the device on the remote's screen and all buttons are mapped to the amp.

I'd highly recommend this to anyone with multiple components. Easy setup, smart actions, and great button mappings. Bonus: Instead of an "illuminate" button, the remote has a motion sensor so picking it up will cause all the buttons to glow.

And if you think this wont hinder your gaming trust me it does. I've had multiple deaths and errors during MOBA raiding and PvP because of my left and right click not being able to be held down for movement. And with FPS games i'm not able to use automatic weapons because my left click simply will not hold down.

title: Great Travel Mouse with Excellent Features
text:
As a traveler or a person who constantly needs to use laptop anytime anywhere, you might long for a compact mouse that works flawlessly on any flat surface. While touchscreen and mousepad are enough for simple task on the go, there are many occasions where you just have to use a mouse for better navigation. With Dark-Laser tracking system, a dual mode scroll wheel, a back and forward buttons, ambidextrous design, storage for the Wi-Fi Unifying receiver, and a 3-weeks charge from a single AA battery, Logitech Anywhere MX might be the best travel mouse you can find.

Features and Design

Anywhere MX has “Travel mouse” label all over its design. It is small; it is light; yet it is still comfortable to use. The mouse has an ambidextrous design, so left-handed users will never find a trouble using it. The side has rubbery surface that helps your hand hold the mouse. The mouse also features a back-forward button on its top side for easy web navigation. Additionally, the scroll allows you to switch between click-to-click scrolling and hyper-fast scrolling as easy as pressing down the scroll wheel. Both back-forward buttons and the scroll wheel function can be customized by using the SetPoint program from Anywhere MX support website. [[...]]

Performance and Battery Life

Using a mouse on a glass tabletop has always been a nightmare for many of us; but thanks to Logitech new tracking system “Dark-Laser”, it is not a problem anymore. Utilizing this new technology, Logitech Anywhere MX works virtually almost on any surface, including glass or even mirrors. Two AA batteries are needed for the mouse to be functional, and they can last for around 140 hours of intensive use. This mouse also uses Logitech Unifying Wi-Fi system, which means you can now connect several Logitech Unifying compatible products under one single Wi-Fi receiver. Since the Unifying receiver itself is very small, you do not need to remove it from your laptop USB port when you store the laptop in your bag. There is also a small compartment under the mouse where you can store the receiver; in case you do not need it. To register your compatible products to a Unifying receiver, you need Logitech Unifying program which can be downloaded from Logitech website. [[...]]

Logitech Anywhere MX is like a blessing to anyone who use a notebook as their main machine. Judging from the mouse’s ergonomic design, customizable buttons, and flawless tracking system, you can safely argue the benefits outweigh its premium price. In the last two years, Logitech Anywhere MX has performed flawlessly for me and, I believe, many other users as well.
