title: An only slightly flawed work of art
text:
This will be my impression after a little over a week of use. I'll try to update this at a later time, if anything changes.

The first thing most people will notice about this mouse is its size. It's designed to really fill your hand. The back arch can easily fill my palm without my fingers falling off the front of the mouse or dragging on either side. I'm not sure what the experience would be like for someone with especially small hands but it feels great for someone with larger and bulkier hands. If you're bothered by other mice with really low profiles, this mouse should make you quite happy. The same for people who like heavier mice. The weight is on the heavier side and isn't adjustable (like some gaming mice allow) but I prefer heavy mice for better accuracy.

If you're still a hardcore claw-grip user, like I am, the size and weight are still quite comfortable, though. I tend to plant my wrist on my desk and move the mouse with just my fingers (so my palm is well above the mouse) and it's definitely not an issue for accuracy or comfort.

The second feature most people will likely notice is the scroll wheel. This is quite a unique feature for this mouse. It has three modes of operation. A traditional ratchet action where it clicks to a stop as you roll it. A free spin mode where the ratchet physically disengages and the weighty wheel spins with as much momentum as you give it (a very long spin time). And a "SmartShift" mode where it operates as a ratchet at low speeds and free spins at high speeds.

The ratchet engagement is software driven so the modes can be entirely customized. There is a button behind the wheel to switch between your default mode and the freespin mode. And the software allows you to turn SmartShift on or off, set a default mode (ratchet or freespin) when SmartShift is disabled, and set the SmartShift sensitivity. That sensitivity determines how fast the wheel has to move to switch from ratchet to freespin and goes from all but the slowest spin triggering it to you having to really throw the wheel to trigger it. So there shouldn't be any problems with you accidentally entering freespin when you don't mean to.

With all of that in mind, the free scroll is an amazing feature. If you open long document or browse tall web pages, you'll wonder how you ever got by without the ability to just flick the wheel and glide to your destination in an instant.

As for the wheel itself, it has quite a nice feel to it. The middle click has a lengthy actuation with a satisfying click at the bottom. The grooves on the wheel are quite a bit deeper than most mice', likely to help the ratchet catch the wheel when it's freespinning. The wheel is a bit looser than many mice I've used, though. If you really enjoy a stiff roll with solid resistance between clicks, you might find this a bit uncomfortable, at first. I was worried about that myself and tested it in ARMA (where a precise scroll wheel can be very important) and didn't have any issues with overshooting my target menu item. If it's really an issue for you, though, you can change the scroll wheel behavior per application so you could set something like ARMA or Photoshop to pure ratchet mode.

Along those lines, the software is quite flexible. Every button except left click, right click, and vertical scroll can be reassigned (the left and right buttons can at least be swapped). Even the scroll mode button can be reassigned. Which brings up a more hidden feature. The thumb rest is actually a 5-action tilt pad. You can press down or press down and tilt in a cardinal direction to issue any command you want.

By default, the software comes with a library of pre-made commands such as opening the calculator, maximizing the selected window, controlling media, and the like. It also allows you to create custom key combinations (eg. Ctrl + Alt + Shift + 0). While it's not quite as flexible as some higher-end gaming mice might allow with fully-timed macro playback or even lua scripting, it should handle most user's needs well and can issue commands to open a file or application, which you could probably dump your lua script into. I haven't tested it yet but I'd likely use the thumb click to control Push-To-Talk in VOIP applications.

And, as mentioned above, almost all of the settings (keybinds, scroll mode, sensitivity, etc) can be set both globally and per application).

Other settings you can customize include:
Smooth scrolling: Software emulation for phone scrolling that seems to apply a smoother velocity curve to the scroll wheel (in software, not the physical wheel's motion) so your scrolls come to a feathered stop. I found this to be a bit choppy but it could be my browser as much as the mouse.
Scroll wheel direction: Inverted or not.
Thumb wheel direction: Inverted or not.
Thumb wheel sensitivity
And Pointer speed.

That last one is probably one of only two weak points for the mouse. The sensitivity can only be controlled two ways. 1. Open the settings and change the sensitivity slider. 2. Assign the "Change Sensitivity" command to a button. The latter would be great if it allowed for three or four settings, as with my old rat7. Instead, it only allows for a toggle between the global sensitivity and your custom one for that command. That could well be enough for most people but it would be nice to see Logitech expand their software to allow more options. If you're really desperate for more, I guess you could assign the tilt pad directions to different sensitivity levels but that starts getting a bit silly quickly.

The other weakness would be that the mouse is wireless. This is very subjective, though. Since I don't travel or use the mouse with a laptop, I'd prefer it to be wired for better reliability and lower input latency (as well as avoiding the need for charging). That said, I've yet to have any problems with it being wireless. I charged the mouse when it first arrived and the indicator still says it has a full charge after a week of use (A total of probably 48-60 hrs of continuous use). The mouse has a sleep timer (~30 min, I think) so it will automatically turn off when not in use. It was already mostly charged from the factory so I don't yet know how long a full charge takes but it doesn't really seem to matter much since you can use and charge the mouse simultaneously and, at presumably a month or more on a single charge, I'd be happy to let it charge over night, once it gets low.

And, if I had to nitpick, I'd wish Logitech had put the forward and backward buttons (mouse 4 and 5) in front of the horizontal wheel and made them taller, rather than intertwining them. I use those two buttons way more than I'd ever use the horizontal scroll so it's a bit of a bother having to reach my thumb so far back to find the buttons.

--

Overall, the mouse appears to be a great buy, even for the somewhat higher price (though, still less than some). The build quality is solid, the slightly tactile material feels great, and the mouse looks sleek and classy. The software is very well presented and should be easy for both novice and advanced users to customize (though, it would be nice to see Logitech continue to expand on it for power users). And the battery life, so far, appears to be excellent.

This is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for a high-quality mouse.

title: READ THE MANUAL! YOU WILL BE SHOCKED WHEN YOU FIND OUT WHAT THINGS CAN AND CAN'T DO!
text:
This is for all those people who were not smart enough to realize that if your remote cradle does start to act up, it's not the end of the life for our remote, in case you haven't noticed there's a USB port in the front of the unit that you have been using to update the remote. well guess what
that same port will charge your battery! HUH? YUP! I cannot believe that so many users have not figured this out yet? This is how you are supposed to charge many of the other models logitech has out. that USB port is the only way to charge up the 676 models so what's the big deal if you charge it once each 3 weeks using the USB cable? You can still use the remote while it's charging too. So just ditch that stupid cradle and quit crying your an adult now so start thinking like one. Plus my batteries last me 3 weeks between charges, it takes about 15 minutes on the USB port to fully charge then and I won't need to even worry about it again for 3 more weeks so I'm not sure what the big deal is. sure it's not as you may have wanted it to be , but is it better to constantly whine about it or just plug a cable into it every so often to not have to even deal with the cradle?

And for those who claim that the battery is unable to be charged in any other way they too are wrong there are a huge amount of generic battery chargers out there made to charge every single type , size, and design of LiIon battery made. they sell for $1 and up, I know of at least 10 models for sale right now on an auction site that are less than a buck. all LiIon batteries are the same design. they all will charge using a cheap off brand charger it may take them 8 hours to do it but it will work.

So now that the 2 main problems are solved the button size is something that i believe you are going to find no matter what you do since these remotes are trying to offer you as many possible functions as they can so you won't be complaining about how there is no button to preform that function as your old remote does. they have to put them someplace. imagine if you took every remote you own and took all the buttons off of them and placed them on your table , then arranged them all in a way that you want. A way you remember them to be, so they are always where you are used to them being. now look at how large your imaginary remote will be. is it any easier than the harmony model? No it's probably even more confusing.

But here's the thing that will probably blow your mind if you would have taken the time to read the manual you would have already known that you can remap the keys!! Oh Yes I said it! You can move them to be where you will remember them easier, that way you won't need to be grabbing a magnifying glass each time you want to turn up the sound because you're going deaf as well as blind. these little features that are available to those who are willing to take the time and read about will end all the moaning and groaning, it's almost as if they expect someone to be there and change the channel for them since they bought an expensive remote that be be configured to do about anything you could ever imagine, if you could actually imagine and took the time to read about how to make it happen.

So for the Computer programmer who obviously didn't read his manual since he knew everything already, this is how you remove the foot from your mouth, read the manual! for all of those who connected the USB port and couldn't figure out that it was charging their remote at the same time, read your manual, for all those who have bad charging cradles, unplug the thing and put it in a drawer, buy an new battery for $ and plug in the USB cable every 3 weeks for 15 minutes and read your manual.

For the poor guys mother who had a battery blow up on her I totally agree, they have our email addresses why not alert us of the situation? That's just poor customer relations, they were probably too busy selling your info to take the time to save someone's life or keep their homes from burning to the ground. Shame on you logitech! See I'm realistic and I have read my manual that's why I can say these things and hope that others will do the same to avoid being pointed out in the future by another sarcastic jerk like me! people not reading the manual has cost me thousands of dollars in sales I made on good products, just to end with me up paying return shipping because someone refused to read and understand the manual that I made sure to include with that item.

title: Your Buying Guide to the Harmony Hub:
text:
Update 2/15/16
This will likely be my last update. After initial success with voice commands, Alexa has seemingly gotten worse, not better at working with the harmony. Alexa will report back 50% of the time that the harmony is not responding. After many reboots and harmony skill re-ininstalls, I'm sad to say that no improvement has been made over the last 1-2 months. With that being said, commands run through the 3rd party service, IFTTT, have run flawlessly. If you are buying this product strictly for voice integration, you may want to wait until all of the bugs are sorted out. I'm sad to say I'll be taking away a star. For such hype and initial promise, it's disappointing to see that the product still has many shortfalls.

*Update 01/12/16*
Additional Amazon Alexa support is here! You are finally able to control volume/channel using just your voice if you own an amazon Alexa product (echo, echo dot, etc.). And while not as intuitive as controlling the volume on the echo itself, you can use the following voice commands to control your TV, sound system, etc.
-"Alexa, ask Harmony to turn up the volume"
-"Alexa, ask harmony to mute the volume"
-"Alexa, ask harmony to turn on the ___channel" (using channel favorites)

This is just a short list of the commands added, but functionality is improving almost every month. Aside from the voice updates, stability and reliability is drastically better through the native Alexa skill, so take older reviews complaining that voice commands don't work very well with a grain of salt. To enable these new commands, you have to download ANOTHER Alexa skill called "Harmony" in addition to the previous one called "Harmony—Optimized for Smart Home." If you have any further questions about the hub, leave a comment on this review, and I'll try to answer it as fast as I can.

***The Review***
I decided to brave the "horrific set-up" reviews and buy this in hopes of ditching my numerous remotes once and for all. The verdict? So close! While I initially planned on only buying the hub without the remote for use with my Amazon Echo, the lack of native support for the Echo and being forced to go through IFTTT recipes makes this task extremely unreliable. Overall, I was pretty surprised with how easy the setup process was and would recommend for anyone with a relatively simple setup that's looking to clean things up. *One thing to note, this product is definitely for someone who has some previous knowledge or experience with setting up electronics. For everything to work properly, you'll have to perfect the setup sequence and potentially add some action delays. But have no fear, I have a step-by-step guide for how to do just that below.

Here's the breakdown:

THE SETUP: (Samsung TV, Vizio Soundbar, Xbox)
###
•BEFORE you buy this product, go on the harmony website and check to see if your devices are compatible. This is the #1 cause of half of the frustration seen in the comments. If your devices are supported, the setup process should be fairly simple.
•I used the mobile app to complete the setup because I did not get the accompanying remote. Simply search the model number (often found on the back or bottom of your device) and that's it...No tapping the channel up and down buttons repeatedly for what seems like hours till your device turns off. Just find and press enter.
•Last thing to note, and maybe MOST importantly is the use of delays to make sure everything works fluidly and correctly. If you have a device that takes a while to boot up (Like my Vizio soundbar), if you do not add a delay, when the device turns on, the Harmony will have already issued the command to switch to the correct input before your device was fully functional..thus, you'll get angry because now you need to go find the remote to turn on the thing you bought the harmony to replace. No one's happy.

Here's how to add a delay to one of your devices through the mobile app:
1. After you've gone through the Harmony setup and created an activity (ex. Watch TV), select the activity you wish to add a delay to.
2. Select "Edit Start Sequence" and scroll to the bottom and select "Edit Entertainment Devices".
3. Scroll to the bottom again and select "add delay".
4. Choose the amount of time you want an action delayed (in my case I want my Vizio soundbar to wait 3 seconds after powering on before trying to change inputs).
5. Order the delay to the right position in the sequence using the drag and drop tabs on the left of the screen... and you're done!

The Harmony Itself:
###
•First thing to note is its size. It's about the size of a drink coaster, which was much smaller than what I was expecting.
•The device is made out of plastic but feels reasonably substantial and well made.
•Because of its small profile, you could easily leave the hub out on your entertainment center or what have you without much notice.

The Gripes:
###
•OKAY, yes... the setup could more intuitive, and the use of delays and re-ordering your activity sequences shouldn't be buried in endless mobile app menus. But if you take the 30 min to set everything up right, you shouldn't have many issues in the future
•I bought this to use with the Amazon Echo, but I would say the IFTTT recipes needed to make this work only work 50% of the time. They have apparently begun beta testing native support with the echo, so hopefully this problem will be resolved in the coming months, but as of right now...not worth it.
•My last gripe is that it takes a while for the harmony app to connect to the hub. So for people without the remote, you could honestly manually turn everything on in the time it takes to open the mobile app, connect, and choose the activity you want to perform. Hints: WE NEED NATIVE ECHO SUPPORT (If anyone at Logitech is reading this)

Overall, the hub shows immense promise, and with the remote, could make this a well-worth product. HOWEVER, If you are like me and planned to use this with the Amazon Echo, I would wait till native support arrives. In the meantime, look at the Samsung Smart Things workaround for more reliable performance than IFTTT recipes.

Nothing works, not even the buttons, it is an amazing crash and burn. You have a brick on your hands. Even at Amazon prices, this is ridiculous. I am not the sort of person prone to write negative reviews, though of course finding a product inadequate is a good reason to alert fellow buyers. I am doing so with this review. text:
I'm on my second M705 after using the first one for about 4-5 years. On the original, I experienced the double click issue that many users have posted about but easily fixed that by opening the mouse up and bending the leaf springs back into place. (Google how to fix Logitech mouse switch, it's a bit tricky to do). After performing this fix the mouse was as good as new in terms of clicking and use. I eventually had to replace the mouse because both sides of the mouse, where the cushy gel-like area was, was tearing and falling apart.

Range is far, tracking is decent (not the best by any means), but battery life is king. The mouse is also very ergonomically shaped, comfortable for a finger-tip gripper like myself. For portable use, I can't go to any other mouse (maybe the MX Performance but that's much larger and takes longer to get used to).

title: Fantastic mouse with one flaw :UPDATE:
text:

However, there is one flaw; the mousewheel. The mousewheel feels very flimsy, and has a tendency to either not scroll at all when moved, scroll too much when moved just a bit, and sometimes scroll when barely touched by accident. You know that clicking sound that is typically made whenever you scroll with the mousewheel? The wheel is almost completely silent on this one, leading me to believe that whatever divides each section of the of the wheel internally is insufficient. Maybe the added functionality of being able to scroll sideways with the wheel is what lead to this compromised efficiency when scrolling vertically, but I hope that isn't the case, as horizontal scrolling isn't nearly as important. This frailty brings up concerns regarding the mouse's longevity, but we'll see.

UPDATE:
Well, after less than 4 months of use, the mouse is now double-clicking by itself when single-clicked. Very disappointed in this shoddy product from the usually reliable company of Logitech.

title: The best and only home theater accessory you'll ever need.
text:
Harmony remotes have come a long long way. This one is awesome. The activity buttons work great. Programming the remote is easy. It works with every device that I've thrown at it. The phone app doubles as a second remote or a way to program the remote. The hub sends IR over a wide area and comes with an IR blaster for devices that don't have line of sight. It also works great with bluetooth devices and network controlled devices. It updates itself automatically and regularly.

My devices (all work great): Vizio TV, Denon Receiver, PS3, PS4, Roku 3, Apple TV 4(no siri), LG Blu Ray player.

I actually bought the touchscreen version first that was $200 more and returned it for this one. With your phone as a remote, why do you need another vibrating touchscreen that you have to recharge all the time? The battery with this one lasts for months and never has to be recharged. That's one less wire to manage. One less charging station. One less thing to worry about whether you put it on the charger when you go to bed. I'm still using the battery that came with it after 10 months. On a technical note; the remote only connects to the hub, not directly to your devices. So the hub actually does all of the communicating with your home theater devices, and you command the hub by the included remote or the harmony app on your phone.

The desktop/mobile app really lets you take serious control of your home theater. When on an activity, the buttons of the remote default to the A/V source (except volume). So as an example; when watching my roku, the menu button sends the menu command to the roku. But what if I want to enter the menu of my TV to change the picture mode? Well, you can reprogram remote buttons to send signals to OTHER deices without switching activities. With this, I've programmed all of my activities to use the DVR button to open the TV menu and the number pad on the remote as a directional pad (think keyboard number pad here) with "5" being the "ok" button. This allows me to change TV settings on the fly while leaving my TV remote in my junk drawer.

If you absolutely have to talk to siri to be content in life, then this will not replace your Apple TV remote. Siri never does what I tell her anyways, so this is a non issue for me. Others may dock a star for it, but I'd give it an extra star for the same reason.

title: Not only are those horrible remotes IR-only
text:
Certain cable providers in the Los Angeles area with a name that rhymes with "Shmime Shwarner" still provide IR-only remotes with their godawful DVRs. Not only are those horrible remotes IR-only, but they also have completely separate page up/down buttons, the world's most obtuse button layout, and size that requires moving your hand to get to different buttons. I know, I know, #firstworldproblems, but for all the trouble I had with an east coast cable provider that rhymes with "Shomcast," at least their DVR/remote setup was logical.

I figured the Harmony would be a solution to the remote problem, at least. The verdict? Sorta.

The remote itself is really pleasant to hold. It's very thin and backed with a vaguely rubbery coating that makes it easy to grip. The buttons themselves have a very satisfying click, tactile feedback that's much better to use than a typical marshmallow-buttoned remote. I also really like the layout, and having a remote that's RF-based means I don't need to worry about aiming it at the device I'm controlling.

Setting everything up was about a 6/10, where 1 is pleasant and 10 is "should've hired someone." My TV has a model name that is 16 characters long and it has to be entered, not looked up. Worse, the initial configuration never worked, so I had to run it at least twice per activity. It's cool that it works through an iPhone app, but it would be cooler to do this on a real website with a real keyboard attached to a real computer.

Now that it's all set up, I have a different set of problems. If one device turns on but another doesn't, this remote doesn't offer an way to power on a single device, unlike the older Harmony remotes that had device-specific controls regardless of what activity you're in. This means I can't stash my remotes in a drawer and forget about them, because I'll need them if one device doesn't fire correctly.

The worst thing, though, is the short press/long press split. I was excited to reuse the channel buttons as page up/down buttons in the channel guide, but the Harmony isn't smart enough to know when the guide is in use, so my page up/down buttons had to be mapped to the long press, which means it takes a long time to make it through the guide. Additionally, the long press takes long enough that I accidentally short press the channel button in the guide, which changes the channel and exits the guide. I was really hoping the Harmony would help override the miserable UI, but no such luck. With a smarter understanding of how the devices attached to the Harmony work, Logitech could push hardware manufacturers to build better software.

Despite only solving half my problems, I do like the remote, and I do like that it can be integrated with an Echo using IFTT to do things like turn the TV on and off.

text:
While this mouse is functional its' ergonomics leave much to be desired. For starters, the on/off switch is placed in a small cut out on the bottom of the mouse, if you keep your nails trimmed this switch is difficult to activate both because of the depth pf the switch and the small size of the opening. The sides of the mouse are made of hard, slick, plastic and offer nothing to really get a grip on. The sides are not even slightly undercut to provide a detent to allow any positive means of picking up the mouse or handling it without risk of it slipping out of your grasp.

Additionally, there appears to be a lag time in between the time you operate the switch and the time the mouse begins to function with the computer. This mouse, also, emits no light so the only way you can know it's "on" is if it is functioning. The slider for the switch is color coded, green for "on" red for "off" but these indicators are at the bottom of the switch, in a very small hole so you'll, more than likely not even be aware they are present if you don't actuate the switch in bright light.

Will replace this mouse with another and save this for a backup as that's probably a more fitting role for it.

title: Best Overall Value for the Price.
text:
The camera doesn't require a lot from a computer memory-wise, so if you have a low-end or older model computer or laptop it will likely run without too much strain on your system.

The image quality is good; I wouldn't say it's as perfect as some tout on the reviews, but it is good quality, especially for keeping contact between friends and family on Skype or other messaging services. You can use lighting to your advantage and it can improve the quality of the video/image immensely.

In terms of the audio, it records voice very well. The mic is excellent at picking up your location and blocking out other sounds even from other areas of the room it's recording in, so you get a decent-quality sound without having to purchase a separate mic.

Overall, I'd say the value of the product is great for the price margin (more so than some other models in this range), and if you want more in terms of audio and video output, you'll have to go professional or upgrade your computer.

title: Superior to Apple Keyboard Case
text:
I bought the ipad Pro right after Thanksgilving and tried the Apple keyboard cover and found the keys a little small for my fingers and the feel of the keys a little shallow so sometimes it didnt feel as if I had pressed the key all the way down. For comparison I tried the Mac Book Air. The keys were bigger and had the feel I wanted for about the same price. But I hate the keypad on laptops, my fingers are always hitting the pad inadvertantly while I type - screwing everything up. I also prefer the touch screen, so the ipad pro offered me everything I wanted except the ability to add memory and an unsatisfactory keyboard. Logi Create backlit keyboard solved my problem. It has a keyboard feel as good as the MacBook Air-- the keys are as wide as the air and have good action feel. Its true the case is heavier but I did not buy the Pro for potability. I have an Ipad Air and Mini for those purposes.

Some have reported problems fitting the case and complain about loss of response on the volume key through the case, but the volume keys and brightness keys are on the key board just above the number keys and work flawlessly so you dont neet to control through the case. The on and off button you do need to use through the case and works just fine. The Logi keyboard case is perfect for typing emails, imessages, etc or more abitious reports, etc. I do all this with the Pro on my lap while watching TV and the screen angle is perfect. I had no trouble getting the Ipad Pro into the case but it is a little difficult to get out, but I seldom need to do that. For my needs the keyboard is perfect and I recomment it enthusiastically. With this case on the Ipad Pro, who needs a traditional computer.

Djf

2- The sub woofer gets insanely hot in just a few minutes since it has no fan. (you gotta fix that yourself)

7- lastly the audio is great for a not so big room. If you have an EQ use it, it'll help it.

title: Wonderful remote if you have a very basic setup
text:
First impressions: Wonderful remote if you have a very basic setup. Remote has a good feeling in your hand, good button placement and offers a certain amount of customization. It shares similarities to other more expensive Logitech remotes but it is not for everyone.

The 350 is program via your PC and the web. It is best if you can use a laptop in the same room as the TV and other electronics to be used with this remote as there could be a bit of trial and error with setup. The 350 is a decent replacement remote if you only have a TV and one other component but If you need remote for multiple component you really should consider going with a 600/700 series remote.
It has a single action button built into it “Watch TV”. If you have a simple setup this may be fine but if you have a TV, stereo, Blu-ray, DVR…. you are wanting to control then the 350 is probably not going to be the right choice for you and you would be much happier spending the extra money for the 600/700 series remotes.

Conclusion:
For a simple home setup the 350 is a decent remote for the money. It is not terribly difficult to program and you have the ability to customize the remote in ways you cannot do with other basic universal remotes. If you have a more complex setup then spend just a bit more money and go with a higher series Logitech model. Logitech makes great TV remotes you just have to make sure you choose the one that meets your needs.

title: Headphones Broke Logitech Customer Service isn't Helpful
text:
I bought these headphones back in 2014 after doing a ton of research. Once I bought them, I was very satisfied with the sound performance and the comfort. I love the black blue and silver aesthetics of the headphones. I was a happy camper for about a year or so until...

The headband cracked.

I was putting these on one day and the plastic on the inside of the headband cracked. This exposed the wiring for the headphones and I had to reattach it every time I put them on. "No worries though" , I thought. "l'll just contact customer service and they'll replace them since it's still under the 2-year warranty." So I did that. Logitech said this would be a warranty issue, but there's a small problem.....

They don't make the headphones anymore.

This means they can't be replaced with another pair of headphones. I asked them if I could just have my money back and they said they couldn't do that either. The only option I had was to pick from their current selection of products. I didn't want to do this because I bought headphones because I need - headphones. But I looked anyway.

When I looked, I couldn't find anything I needed: I already have a wireless mouse and keyboard, I don't need speakers, and I don't need a webcam. I did find their Harmony Remotes appealing, so I asked about them. They then told me that Harmony Remotes can't be used for warranty trade ins.

So you can imagine by this point, I'm pretty frustrated. My headphones broke, they can't be replaced and the one thing I would take as product exchange isn't eligible. These headphones aren't cheap and the experience I've had with their customer service leads me to believe they don't really care about their customers.

So I don't recommend buying these headphones or any other pricey product from Logitech. If the product becomes discontinued, you'll be out of luck - even if it's under warranty.

title: A good, basic remote (That is...basic in the Harmony universe)
text:
After years of use, and being dropped and sat on, our Harmony 300 was dying. I found the Harmony 600 on sale, and was excited to "upgrade" our remote. After several months, the 600 had just proved to be a little to complex to use. I got the "activities" functionality of the 600 right away, but it still proved to be a bit of a pain. If you want to do something other than an activity, you have to go 3 levels in to get it done. And then my wife said she hated it and just wanted to go back to what we had.

Enter the Harmony 350. Almost the same as the 300 we had for years. Nice to have the "DVR" button instead of me having to program a different button for that and tell people which one it was. The 350 is simple, I was able to transfer my devices to it easily, via their web setup, and it just works.

Pros:
-Easy to use
-Seems to have the same build quality as the previous 300
-Adding my devices to it was easy, since I already had them from my previous setup

Cons:
-The only thing I would like to see on a basic model like this would be some lighted buttons. Then again...it wouldn't be a basic model. Hmmmm...conflicted.
-Still a little too difficult for my 70+ years old in-laws. They can work the Directv remote, but just don't get this one, conceptually. I don't necessarily blame the remote for this, though, as the concept of changing the TV input from Directv to DVD1 to DVD2, etc., is what causes more of a stumbling block for the older generation than the actual remote. Having to push a combination of buttons to change the input and get the DVD player on and playing is too foreign for people that haven't grown up with this.

For those that understand this kind of functionality and are looking for a fairly simple remote to control multiple devices, this one will do nicely.

text:
I purchased one of these cases in the Apple store. I noticed the thin clearance and the possibility for scratching, but decided to give it a try. After about a month of usage, a different problem cropped up: a part of the clip on the right-hand side of the case (which holds the iPad in place) broke off into my hand as I was opening the case. I decided to call Logitech and ask for a warranty replacement.

The warranty process was a bit time consuming, but worked out in the end. You call their number, explain to the representative what the situation is, and then they email you a prepaid UPS label to send the defective unit back to them. Once they receive it, they ship you a replacement. In the mean time, you are bombarded with emails from customer service asking if they have resolved your issue. Just keep telling them that your issue is not resolved until you receive a replacement.

When I received my replacement (about 1 1/2 to 2 weeks later), it appeared to be a new and improved model of the same case. Although there was no indication of a model change on the packaging (apart from the fact that the serial number on the new unit was higher than the serial number on the old unit), the plastic clips had been significantly thickened, and a much larger buffer had been added all around the screen remove the potential for scratching the screen when the unit is closed. There also appears to have been some slight redesigning of the keyboard. The case is ever-so-slightly bulkier now, but it has none of the flaws that it did before. It also has a new color scheme (black case/ black keyboard, rather than the original black case / grey keyboard), which looks a lot sleeker.

Although I was disappointed that the first case didn't work out, the new model is very promising, and I rate it 5 stars.

title: Very disappointing for a Harmony product.
text:
I have loved my [[ASIN:B000IMSK8Y Logitech Harmony 670 Universal Remote]] almost to death, so when I setup a new smaller system with just a TV and a Roku, I looked to Harmony for a single remote solution. Sadly this isn't it.

You would think that the single activity button would have similar functionality to activity buttons on other Harmony's, but it does not. It does not allow you specify which TV input to select. It does not allow you customize the buttons within the activity. In fact other then selecting which devices it turns on, I can't seam to find any activity customization at all.

What I had hoped for, and what I had expected based on using other Harmony remotes, was a press of the Watch TV activity button would turn on the TV, set the correct input, and allow me to run the Roku, while controlling the TV volume. One button. Magic. What I have is no better then any other universal remote. I have to Press "Watch TV." If the input was changed, I have to manual change it back. Finally I have to press the DVD button to start controlling the Roku. Not even close to magic.

title: The lost coin
text:
I bought these UE 900 earbuds directly from Logitech in Aug 2013 and paid nearly $400 for them. At the time I was looking for noise canceling ear buds, but they really don't exist (or didn't then) and so I went for the next best thing, noise-isolating.

These ear buds have held up to my busy travel schedule and never once gave me a problem. The sound is clear for watching movies in my iPad (in flight) and also works great for iPhone calls (both cell and Skype). About a year ago I left them in a shirt pocket and my wife accidentally washed them. I thought for sure they were done, but after shaking the water out of the ear cups they still work great. I could not believe it, and I still use them almost daily with no problems.

Why am I posting this? After my last trip I thought I had lost them - couldn't find them anywhere. So, today while I was booting up my PC to buy a replacement pair (I see the price is dropped considerably), I happened to look down along side my desk and there they are. My lost ear buds. I am so happy that I don't have to buy them again that I thought y'all might want to hear the story.

text: Using it on Linux... works great... mostly. Nice convenient design with decent key travel, volume and mute keys as well as a few media keys (function keys require using the Fn key). I do wish it also had built in brightness control keys so I didn't have to use the shortcut key combinations I configured. The keyboard connection has yet to drop, though very occasionally the trackpad quits out. A quick off and on of its power switch immediately sorts it out. (My previous wireless keyboard, a bluetooth one, dropped often and was sluggish, especially if also using bluetooth audio. I was trying to avoid using up my USB ports, but gave up on that idea.) Unfortunately the speed of the trackpad is a tad bit slow (also sometimes sluggish) and isn't configurable on Linux as there's no Logitech driver blob available. I dual booted into Windows to max out the trackpad speed with the Logitech software (as a claim was made that the settings are saved in the keyboard itself) and upon rebooting Linux I think it did help some. Overall, and for the price, I'm happy with it (also because its wireless is encrypted), and I expect to stay satisfied until something better in this price range becomes available.

text:
I ordered mine at the prerelease price. I have live streamed four contemporary church services on Facebook using public wifi and my iPhone 5s. I have it 5ft from the (elevated) stage on a mic stand. I use an external battery designed for a GoPro since I record 2-2 1/2 hrs continuously. I use the built in mic with fairly good results. Auto color balance and exposure are good inspite of frequent harsh lighting. I am generally pleased. I am very pleased with the responsiveness of the manufacturer. They have already released 2 updates. They also respond on the customer Facebook page.
Please consider your intended use and MEVO's limitations. Then lower your expectations a few notches. It does much better in good light—grainy otherwise. It's mic can't work miracles—external micing is possible at an added expense. Internet speed (upload>6) is needed for highest quality streaming. It can stream in 2 lower qualities. It is designed to be a one camera solution to streaming a multi cam event. In August 2016, it is in it's first iteration with evolving software. It hasn't met my all of expectations; but, I really like it and look forward to seeing it mature.

title: The most comfortable mouse I have tried
text: The most comfortable mouse I have tried, but was extremely quirky. Could not use until I followed these instructions on Logitech's site to remove the "static energy trapped inside the capacitors in the mouse. To drain this static energy, please plug the USB receiver into a different USB port and follow this procedure: 1. Shut off the mouse and remove the battery. 2. Press all the buttons repeatedly for 30 seconds. This will drain all the static energy that may be trapped in the mouse. 3. Put the battery back in the mouse and turn it on. 4. Wait a few seconds for it to re-connect and test the button." This is so quirky that the instructions must be exactly followed. Another user reported the procedure did not work unless they followed the instruction to move the receiver to a different USB port. This documentation was not included with the mouse and the eighty dollar mouse sat in a drawer for over 3 years when things like the left button would not click and the unit continually disconnected from the receiver. Now that its value has depreciated, I found the answer on their site in 2016 and can use the now-fifty dollar mouse for the first time, until the hyper scroll wheel stops working like all of my other Logitech mice with the rubber in the center that stretches over the years to prevent the scroll wheel from turning. Logitech still offers the most variety that I have found for business applications, so I will keep replacing them and sending their children to college.

title: Generally Lag Free
text: I've been using this mouse with my iMac for a couple weeks now. It paired easily, though after pairing the mouse my iMac asked me to pair my Apple bluetooth keyboard again. However, both the mouse and the keyboard have worked without issue since that initial pairing. The action of the buttons is fine for me. The scroll wheel turns with relatively little resistance. It is easy to scroll farther than I want to. I have not loaded any Logitech software onto my Mac OS X 10.10.5 (Yosemite) machine but the two buttons and scroll wheel work just fine. I'm sure with the Logitech software I could get additional functionality, but the mouse works well enough for me as it is. The single most valuable characteristic, in my opinion, is that this mouse is generally lag free. With the exception of Apple's Magic Mouse, most other bluetooth mice I've used go to sleep and take a few seconds to wake up. This wake-up lag is very frustrating. With this mouse, the first time I click it in the morning, I have a second or two of lag as it wakes up, but then I never notice it again for the rest of the day.

title: Slim, lightweight, long battery life. Highly recommended!
text:
I had an older version of this Logitech keyboard for my iPad 2, so when I upgraded to an iPad Air, I immediately searched for the newer version of this keyboard because it's secure and easy to take to conferences. I am so happy that it's still available! This version has been redesigned and actually feels easier to type on than the older version; perhaps a better use of the surface space when it comes to key placement. Easy setup, and the Bluetooth connects almost instantly when you are ready to turn it on.
I LOVE the battery life of this product--I don't use it too often, which means that I only charge it maybe once or twice a year (and often, I charge it before traveling just to be sure it's ready to go). My only complaint (which prevents me from giving a 5-star rating) would be that the connection clip on the back edge is a bit flimsy; on the older version, the magnetic strip would attach itself to the iPad easily and securely as soon as I even put my iPad near it. With this version, that doesn't happen--you just have to lay the iPad on top of the keyboard and be sure the clip is in the right spot, and then it's totally secure. Overall, though, I would definitely recommend this product!

title: Awesome now that I fixed the dropouts
text:
Let's get this out of the way right away- you will need a 30 pin to lightning adapter if you have a newer iDevice. Logitech decided to stop making this instead of changing to a lightning connector. Too bad because the sound is amazing. This is a great AirPlay speaker. While you don't NEED to dock your device to set this up, it does make things much easier. So add an adapter to your shopping cart and place your order. Also, if you assign a fixed IP to this device in your router, it helps.

There are other reviews with specific instructions on how to pair this speaker to your wifi network so I won't get into that, it's relatively painless using the app. I did find a solution to the intermittent dropouts that I was experiencing and other reviewers have noted as well so let me get into details about that:

A disclaimer: I am not a wifi engineer. If you are a wifi engineer, that's awesome you probably don't need this advice and/or will find errors in my analysis. But I'm a technically competent guy who had a problem and solved it and wanted to share that solution with others.

Initially I set this speaker up to connect to my primary wifi network which is 802.11ac from my Airport Extreme in the basement and 802.11n from one of my Airport Expresses setup as a network extender upstairs. I have 6 Airport Expresses upstairs hardwired to the network with audio out from each one connected to a separate audio zone on my whole-home audio amplifier. This gives me AirPlay to each room of the house. Wifi was turned off on 5 of those Airport Expresses. The UE Air Speaker is placed in our master bath (where we don't have in-ceiling speakers) and worked well, but when I would play from my iPhone I would experience audio dropouts every 5 minutes or so. This speaker is an 802.11g device which is a pretty old wifi standard with limited bandwidth. It is my understanding that when there is one 802.11g device on a wifi network, all devices will operate as 802.11g. So I was sending audio from my phone over 802.11g to the Airport Express then the Airport Express was sending the audio to the speaker on the same 802.11g network to the speaker. I speculated that perhaps the wifi was bogging down under the load. As an experiment I setup a hidden 802.11g network on one of my spare Airport Expresses (on a separate channel from the main network) and connected the speaker to that. Now the phone connects to the primary network and the speaker connects to the hidden network. Since the Airport Expresses are all hardwired on the same network through a switch the speaker shows up in the Airplay listing of devices.

I have not had a dropout since switching to this setup. Everything works exactly as you would expect and the sound IS AMAZING. We are rocking out in our shower every morning.

I know that not everyone has an extra wifi device laying around to setup a dedicated network for a speaker. But I did and I actually know a few people who have similar setups so if you are in the same situation this may work for you as well.

In addition, if you connect this mic to the USB port of your computer, it will likely pick up the hum or hiss of your laptop's fan and other sounds (from desk surface). You can Google strategies for minimizing the surrounding hiss / hum interference... once you get all the outside sounds minimized, this mic is amazing!! Hence the 5-star... I initially purchased this to help me create educational videos for a publisher, but have used it for many other things including web meetings, skype sessions, etc... rich sound with a balanced range of pitch and sound. Easy to set up and easy to use... the challenge will be to minimize the hum.

title: Analog inputs are unacceptable for fighting games
text:
I've been using a Logitech Rumblepad 2 for almost a decade and have never had any issues with it. However, the cable is starting to fray, and I bought this controller as an insurance policy for when the day comes that it finally dies.

Since I've been very happy with my existing controller, I neglected to actually read the negative reviews, which would have let me know to stay away. When I got it out to test, I was horrified to see how sluggish it seemed to behave. After some experimentation, I realized the joysticks have a massive deadzone (about 15 degrees off center) and a very sluggish response time (around 1/10th of a second, tested with a camera).

I don't consider myself a hardcore fighting game player, and most others wouldn't either. I play Super Smash Brothers through Dolphin, and have never had a problem with my Rumblepad, so I assumed I wouldn't have an issue with the F310. Doing any basic maneuvers like smash attacks and wavedashing become near impossible on this controller due to the significantly distorted timing. I could re-adjust my muscle memory to the new timing, but then I would be unable to play on an actual console. Now I know why people think playing Smash on a Logitech controller is a terrible idea.

The controller is otherwise functional though, and works well enough for games that don't require twitch movements, such as Dark Souls. The buttons have instant response times, but all the analog inputs (sticks and triggers) have massive deadzones and response times which make it downright unusable for games like Super Smash Brothers.

title: Beware of Buying This Webcam If You're Operating On Windows 8.1!
text: While Logitech says that this camera is compatible with Windows 8.1, this has not been my experience with it. I simply could not get the audio to work, even though it appears that the video features within the camera are solid. I spent about an hour on the phone with Logitech support, and they confirmed that the only software they have for both Windows 8 and 8.1 was last updated in 2012, and Windows 8.1 wasn't even released until 2013. In addition, Windows 8.1 had some major changes in it, making it different than the original Windows 8. I'm really quite stunned that no updated software was created to have the camera work better within Windows 8.1, and it seems that the company is somehow OK with this. When you search online you will see many threads and postings from 2013 through today, with people stating that they're having problems getting this Webcam to work within Windows 8.1, and asking people for their help. I'm shipping this Webcam back, and this has really been a disappointment, as I've had many good experiences with Logitech products. I'm not ready to upgrade to Windows 10 yet, as people have been telling me about the problems they've had after the conversion, including losing some of their data, and I know that I'm going to have to buy newer versions of some of my software products so that they can work well within Windows 10.

title: Mount the dongle anywhere but behind the machine
text:
I replace a Logitech G930 with this. I'm very happy I did. The sound is noticeably better, even to a non-audio-phile like me.

I don't really have any cons, but I do have a tip. Other reviews have stated that the range is greater than the G930, and that's true. However, you must position the dongle correctly in order to get that greater range. Initially, I tried to use the G930 extension to get the dongle out from behind the computer, and that failed--the machine didn't register that it had been plugged in. So for three days, I used the headset with the dongle in the back of the machine--facing an exterior concrete basement wall. With the G930, I could go in the next room and hear sound in most places. But with the 933 in the behind-the-machine location, I couldn't move more than five feet away.

Finally, I remembered that I had a couple of Logitech extenders for mounting dongles for mice lying around. These things: https://www.amazon.com/GenuineLogitech-Part-Logitech-Extension-Replacement/dp/B00S38H5XG

I decided to try it, and mounted the headphone dongle about six feet off the floor on top of a bookcase. That did the trick. Now, not only can I go in the next room, I can go anywhere in the house. I have a older two-story house, with a couple of interior concrete walls getting in the way of RF transmission. I have to have two wifi access points for full coverage. With the G933 dongle in the improved location, I can answer the front door wearing the headset and not lose connectivity. The front door is about 40 feet away from my computer, through two concrete walls.

Build quality is also substantially better than the 930, with the most noticeable difference being the flip-down mike. On the 930, it was difficult NOT to catch the mike on a cord, or your clothes, or an innocent passer-by. With the 933, you have to work a bit to catch the tip on your finger to flip it down. That little detail makes all the difference.

My keyboarding skills took years to acquire, and are not something I want jerked around every few years when I am forced to upgrade my office computer. title: Small But Ergonomic, Would not Recommend for Really Large Hands.
text:
Pros:
Very Ergonomic
Small (better for people with small/normal sized hands)
Reliable/comfortable during extended use (at least for the first few years)
Infra-Red Lazer
Runs off of two aa batteries, which can be found almost anywhere
Lots of buttons!

Cons:
Small (worse for people with large hands)
Starts to act up after a few years- rendering it useless for gaming after that time.
Runs off of two aa batteries, making it pretty heavy
Lots of buttons! Some people may find this as a con, thinking that more buttons are unnecessary and confusing.
Infra red lazer - you cannot blind your friends with this mouse. Works on snakes, boids and pythons though.

The best part about this mouse is the ergonomics. Even after hours of use in one sitting with only bathroom breaks to give your hands a break, this mouse will not give your hands any cramps, unless you're Robert Waldow. This makes it a great choice as a work/gaming mouse.

title: An affordable trackball mouse which makes your life easier
text:
People who use the computer for extended periods of time need to sit in a comfortable position. Programmers in particular who often switch from the keyboard to the mouse need to keep the mouse close-by to the keyboard to reduce the wrist travel.

A trackball mouse helps in reducing this wrist travel significantly. I don't need to move my hand at all. Using a trackball with the thumb definitely takes time to get used to. Try this mouse for a week or two and if you are still not comfortable you should go for a index finger trackball like the Kensington expert.

It took me a week to getting used to the trackball with my thumb and now I don't want to use the regular mouse anymore. It is that easy and comfortable. I also played AOE-II with this mouse and it fared reasonably well. I will be getting more of them for my home computers too.

title: The M705 used to be fantastic, but quality has slipped over the years
text:
UPDATE: I returned my flaky mouse to Logitech and received a replacement. The plastic top fist better on the new one, so it doesn't creak like the previous model. However, slider pad on the bottom is still too small to actually slide on the desk. The interface to the computer is still flaky; occasionally the mouse just loses the ability to move the cursor (MacBook Pro). Clicking and scrolling still work, but the cursor is frozen until I either re-pair the mouse, or re-plug the USB dongle. I never had this problem with my 10 year old mouse on this computer! Come on, get it together...

I had an old M705 that was rock-solid! I used it daily at my work computer for about 5 years, and then I took it home and used it occasionally for about 5 years. Finally, after about a decade of use, the left button started to become unreliable. I would give this old model 5 stars.

About a month ago, I bought a new M705 to replace it. Unfortunately, the quality of this mouse has slipped over the years. I immediately noticed that the new mouse didn't move across my desk as smoothly as the old one. One of the little plastic "sliders" on the bottom isn't thick enough, and the plastic bottom of the mouse drags on the desk. After about a month of use, the plastic cover started making a creaking noise when I lay my hand on it. Pressing one of two main buttons also makes a creaking noise in addition to the click.

The ergonomics of this mouse are great. It's big enough that most of my hand can rest on the mouse, with my fingers perfectly positioned on the buttons, while the heel of my hand rests on the desk. The scroll wheel can be used in click or smooth-scrolling mode, and it can be clicked as a third button. It's the best-feeling scroll wheel I've ever used. It moves easily enough, yet doesn't move so easily that you will accidentally scroll when you didn't mean to. There are three auxiliary buttons for your thumb, but I don't find them to be useful. Only one is easy to reach with my thumb, and the "hidden" one requires so much force to press that it isn't really practical.

title: Stupidly useful, with a little flaw
text:
This is for all the editors and animators out there: this thing is awesome.

I bought this to make working in Avid, Premiere, After Effects, Blender, and others faster. You may notice throughout your work flow that you'll need two hands to put a lot of good keymaps to use. Copy/Paste takes two hands. Activating certain tools takes two hands. Using all of the available shortcuts across all these programs requires a mind like a steel trap and lots of time to add shortcuts that aren't there by default.

The G13 here, solves a lot of those problems. I have every major shortcut I could possibly need linked to the pad. It has custom layouts for every app. It has multiple layouts for those apps. If you're clever, you can even use the ctrl, alt, and shift keys to cram in even more layouts. It does take a little time to configure, but once you're done, you're all set. When I used to edit, I would take my hand off the mouse to do some shortcut every few seconds. Now, I don't. Everything rests at my right hand, in easy reach.

My only complain is the stupid joystick. I had wanted to use the stick as a jog control, but it didn't work out that way. The API doesn't let you fully poll and use the joystick's position. It's either a button, or a joystick input in a game. It can be nothing else.

text:
UPDATE:
I really liked this keyboard, however, I feel that the particular keyboard I received was either refurbished or used, and repackaged as new. Why? Shortly after writing my initial review, the left arrow key fell off. No biggie - until I looked where the key sits and saw what looks like glue residue.

I called Logitech to start a warranty claim. They asked for the particulars, such as the serial number, and behold THE SERIAL NUMBER IS BLACKED OUT BY FELT MARKER. So for sure I feel duped by whomever sold this through Amazon.

To make matters worse, Logitech does not make this folio any longer, and cannot replace, although they're sending me something else, but it's a separate KB, not integrated into a folio.

So I'm going to contact Amazon regarding this but I thought I'd give you all a heads up - check the serial number immediately upon receipt to ensure your KB is new.

Initial Review:
I've only had this keyboard for a couple of weeks, but it absolutely transforms the Galaxy Tab A 9.7. The keyboard comes equipped with hot keys for home, open apps, search and context, among others. No home or end keys but there are ways around them. The keys have decent feedback and the tablet fits snugly in the unit, but is easy to remove for tablet-only use.

Bluetooth is required for operation and this sucks down the power reserve, but I find I can still go a couple of days without charging. The Tab is smart enough to go into power-save when left idle for a time. The stylus needs to move to an external sleeve for access, which isn't the greatest, but it's really a minor point.

Overall, a solid keyboard, particularly at the price, and I'm really pleased with it. What I wasn't crazy about, was the carrier that was tasked with delivery. OMG, a snail would have been faster (but at least I got it). But that's no reason to fault the product so hence the five stars. However, Amazon should take note and stop using that particular carrier.

title: A very good, near perfect mouse.
text:
About a month ago I was offered a free Logitech G502 mouse for review and I accepted.

Working in information technology and graphics, I have used A LOT of mice over the years, from the classic mechanicals to modern opticals. In addition, I am a lifelong gamer nerd. From very early, single game consoles to modern, home built, overclocked Windows PC monsters with expensive graphics cards. My favorite mice have been Logitech mice, specifically a couple of over ten-year-old [[ASIN:B0001YGIB0 Logitech MX510's]] that I still use to this day. The MX510 was ergonomically designed, so it was comfortable to use on a daily basis. It had good switches and a good optical sensor. It had programmable buttons in logical locations and a relatively light software driver that worked well. I have played many, many games with the MX510's I own. It was only last year (2015) that I replaced [[ASIN:B0062WNDLI the main switches]] in one of them and now it works like new again.

The Logitech G502 is only the second new mouse I've owned since 2005. The ergonomics are improved and there are the customizable profiles, adjustable optical resolutions, and adjustable weights. It has a neat, full color lighting engine, if that's important to you. Braided nylon wraps the cord. As both a gamer and a professional Photoshop user, I've been using the G502 exclusively since I received it last month and I have the following observations...

For the most part, it works really well. It is very accurate and works better on multiple surfaces than other mice I've used. It has good switches (though, I'm not 100% sure about the one under the wheel). It feels good. It's comfortable. It looks nice. The G502 software allows you to tune and change just about every operational aspect of the mouse from every button definition to DPI resolutions to profiles to lighting to surface tuning and more (Note that the G502 software does not work in Windows XP). It also updates the G502 firmware. However, I found the additional weights to be unnecessary. On the first day, I inserted them all. A day later I removed a few and within a week I removed them all. I think it's too heavy with any of the weights in place and they fatigue my wrist very easily. Since they are completely optional, you can do what you want with them. For the most part, all is good in the G502, except for four things - two are fixable via the G502 software and two are not.

One, I find it far too easy to switch DPI resolution accidentally with the default button configuration. The default buttons to change DPI resolution are located just to the left of the left mouse button. In that location, it's very easy to hit one while gaming or doing whatever. Luckily you can change the function of these buttons via the G502 software or redefine a profile that uses only a single DPI resolution so you can't accidentally switch it up or down. But if you leave those buttons in the default config, you'll likely be switching DPI resolution often without intending to.

Then there is the profile button, which cycles between three pre-set or custom profiles. That switch is located just below the mechanical switch to lock and unlock the mouse wheel. It is very easy to accidentally hit it when locking or unlocking the wheel. Changing profiles can also change DPI resolutions. Before I edited the profiles via the software, I often found myself in a profile I didn't want to be in. Luckily, you can also redefine this button and/or you can deactivate unwanted profiles via the G502 software.

Third is the all metal mouse wheel. Sounds like a good thing at first, right? All metal. Oooh. But there is no rubber or grippy surface on the edge of the wheel. When you use the wheel in "locked mode," it becomes less than ideal to turn as even clean fingers don't grip the all-metal wheel surface perfectly and it will slip *just a little* under every slide and flick of your finger - this can be especially noticeable on slow movements in the "up" direction. Also, in locked mode, the amount of physical wheel turn per notch is too high. I think it needs to be about half of what it is now.

Finally, two more things really, when you use the mouse wheel in "free mode," the wheel becomes very twitchy and it sometimes moves by itself when moving the mouse around unless your finger is resting on the wheel. This may be due to the mass of the wheel. You'll be forced to switch it back into "locked mode" to prevent that from happening. The mechanical toggle switch to lock and unlock the wheel is located just below the wheel. Sometimes the action of that switch feels a little "off," and I wonder how long that switch will last.

Overall, I like the Logitech G502 a lot. For the most part, the hardware works really well. The Logitech G502 software, which allows such fine custom control over the mouse, is excellent. If I could change only a few things, I would add a grippy surface to the edge of the mouse wheel and make the wheel less twitchy when unlocked. Make no mistake, this is a relatively expensive mouse, but if you're looking for what is probably one of the best mice on the market, look no further.

title: Works as advertised
text:
This seems to be a pretty good keyboard. It is targeted to those who want to use their TV screen as a computer monitor and the features that make it good for that use make it not quite as useful for fast typing such as word processing.

It is not a Bluetooth Keyboard. It has a small USB wireless receiver as its interface. They probably used this in order to get more range which is advertised as 30 feet. I was able to get a line of sight range of 40 feet, so their stated range seems to be pretty accurate.

It's handy to have the touchpad built into the keyboard so that using a mouse is not necessary. The touchpad works nicely and can accept gestures such as a two finger tap or swipe. You can also do a pinch motion to zoom in or out.

It connected without any hassle to my Windows 10 netbook. The description talked about its features for Windows 8, but it works perfectly with 10 as well. Several of the buttons are mapped to work with 8 or 10, but these can be remapped for other uses, although I haven't tried that.

The main negative I have with it is that the keys seem to be a bit closely spaced. That's why It is hard to use for fast typing. I compared the key spacing to my Toshiba Netbook and they are about the same. The keys are also a bit soft with only a little discernible tactile feedback.

For its intended purpose of using your TV as a computer monitor for viewing slide shows or watching videos, it will work well. Amazon Prime members will find this keyboard to be handy. I don't think it would be so useful for any fast or extensive typing.

title: Highly usable and convenient but not at all durable
text:
Over the past few years I've bought about half a dozen of these. Yet I've felt the need to downgrade the evaluation to 3 stars. What's up with that?

The trackball is excellent and easy to use, and it "just works" on my Linux systems. The motion is generally quite smooth and the big thing is that the unit is symmetrical: it makes no assumptions about left or right hand use, as so many others do. (I prefer to switch hands from time to time in order to reduce repetitive strain; for that you need a unit that is "omnimouseterous" if you will.)

The size and weight of the unit is just right; it's easy to grasp and it stays put on most surfaces.

So what are the problems?

1. No center button, though it's easy enough to remap one of the "extra" buttons.
2. You have to jump through a few hoops to get it to do scrolling, and even then it's not convenient.
3. It's mechanical and gathers dust; the sensors need frequent cleaning.
4. The sensors eventually wear down (from friction) and then the unit is permanently unusable (see below)

I've found the unit highly usable, and now that the price is reasonable, I keep buying them. Note though that under frequent use they have a very short lifespan; for instance, I just had one die after a mere 13 months. So, three stars overall. (review revised 5/2018 to reflect experience with lamentable lack of lifespan).

title: Fantastic Gaming Gear!
text:
Not long ago I got my son a pair of gaming headphones and it put him into the stratosphere. He loved them, even if they weren't very good one's. He liked the sound, and they were very comfortable but the prevailing opinion was that hardly anyone could actually hear him talk on the mic. When the opportunity to grab these came my way I jumped on it.

A little backstory: I'm in broadcasting and I wear headphones for hours on end almost every single day. Without trying to sound arrogant, I fully understand what good sound is. Trust me I know. However, I am NOT a gamer, so I rely on some advice from my oldest son who not only is a gamer but works with computers for a living. He told me that Logitech is just about the most respected brand in the gaming world and should I ever have the opportunity to get a pair, I should (not for work, mind you...but for my younger boy who also is a gamer).

My son was able to do the set up quickly and after about 30 minutes with them on, he came and gave me a big hug and told me that they were awesome. I asked if everyone could hear him better and he said it was like night and day. He also said the sound was much better but he was spoiled because his other headphones were actually more comfortable, but he said it was a tradeoff worth making. Time will tell if he is happy with the comfort level after a few weeks. It is entirely possible that they simple don't fit his head all that well and is not a reflection of the headphones at all. I have worn many headphones over the years that sounded exceptional but never truly fit my particular noggin all that well, so I won't hold it against them for that.

If you want a great set of gaming headphones, I honestly believe you would be hard pressed to do better--especially for the money.

title: Functional, But Not Perfect. Biggest Problem is That It is Identical in (Almost) Every Respect to the K-400r But Costs More
text:
This is a reasonably-priced all-in-one keyboard/trackpad that isn't limited to its advertised use as a "living room keyboard." One of the ways I've used this keyboard is as a replacement keyboard for my all-in-one desktop. And it isn't strictly a Windows-only keyboard; it can be used with a Mac (though not as seamlessly as with Windows; before you ask, I have no idea how well it works with Linux...).

Is it perfect? No. The feedback of the keys reminds one of the old IBM Selectric typewriters. Until you get used to it it's really disconcerting. But it is functional. Lightweight, so no lugging around; if used in the living room you get to using it and throwing it around like a TV remote. Battery life is good. Setup is simple: just plug in the unifying receiver (Logitech's solution to "dongle over-population") to a available USB port (haven't tried it on a hub and don't plan to), wait for the device drivers to download, and use. The five buttons ("hot keys") across the upper left portion of the keyboard are pretty self-explanatory: the first is the "left mouse button" and it functions just like the left mouse button (i.e., command execution). The second hot key (first in the "group of three") opens the default media player. The third loads the home page(s) of your default web browser. The fourth locks the computer (same as the "Windows key" + "L"). The fifth button puts the computer to sleep. The function keys (the F1-F12 keys) are mapped to commands; to use them as function keys mirrors what most computers do today: require you to press the "FN" key down by the "Windows" key to get the function keys to function as F1-F12. Not all of the functions keys worked. The volume keys (F10, F11, F12) did. F1, F2, and F3 did as well. The F1 key was mapped to "Show the Desktop" and did. The F2 key apparently backspaces word by word. F3 did bring up the Firefox "Search" function. F4 ("Share") does nothing at this point; nor do the F5 ("Devices") or F6 ("Settings"). I expect the media keys (F7, F8, and F9) to work without issue. So no real complaints regarding immediate use without worrying about remapping the keys.

So if it's reasonably-priced and functional, why only 3 stars? The big reason is that it's no different than another keyboard I have: the [[ASIN:B005DKZTMG Logitech Wireless Touch Keyboard K400 with Built-In Multi-Touch Touchpad, Black]]. With the exception of the color of some of the keyboard decals and the "art" on the trackpad, the two keyboards are identical. Well, identical except for price; the K400r is $10 cheaper ($20 cheaper if you can handle a white, rather than black, keyboard). Really? Identical? Yup. Having both in hand and having used both I can say that I have found absolutely NO difference between the two. I also did a bit of research on-line and I couldn't find anyone who could say what the differences might be: even Logitech failed to respond to this question on the support page for these keyboards.

In the end, the keyboard is nice enough to merit 4 stars, but not so nice as to earn 5 stars. But since the K-400r is exactly the same and costs less, a 4-star review can't stand. Hence, 3 stars.

text:
Best mouse ever? maybe. I put off buying this mouse for a long time, because I thought it looked weird. It's super comfortable, basically the same shape as the mx518/g5/g400 etc. with an extra thumb button, 2 buttons to the left of left click, a tilt wheel, and some styling decisions. Weights are tough to get in and out, one of the weights causes the cover to not really sit flush, I don't use the weights so this didn't bother me, and it could just be my mouse not necessarily all of the g502s.

Optical sensor.

Comfort

Cons:

title: the Logitech hasn't disappointed me. It was easy to setup (assuming you ...
text:
I'm creating an inexpensive multi-point business video conferencing system using low-cost, off the shelf commodity components, and I'm using the Logitech C920 as part of this effort.

Considering that a top quality PTZ (Pan/Tilt/Zoom) camera can be several thousand dollars, I needed an alternative that could put out a reasonable 1080p image at an affordable price. Since I can control the lighting and so forth, I don't really require anything special in terms of low-light performance...all I really need is a camera that puts out a credible image when displayed on a 10 foot projection screen, and is simple enough to work with a variety of online video conferencing systems, including Skype, WebEx and so forth.

So far, the Logitech hasn't disappointed me. It was easy to setup (assuming you have a Windows PC in the mix) and it performs well. Construction quality is good for the price, and it's so small as to be easily mounted in a variety of settings (mine is attached to the top of a 65" plasma monitor using a custom bracket). With good lighting, I get very good video quality out of this small camera, even when compared to my firm's $100K Telepresence system.

I can't really speak to the audio quality - we're using an in-ceiling microphone and speaker system, so we have little need for the built-in audio on this camera.

On the software front, so far we haven't had any issues whatsoever, and the camera works with just about everything we throw at it. The one exception is Macs - although we have good results viewing video on Macs, it doesn't seem possible to connect the C920 to a Mac directly - you need a Windows PC somewhere in between (it *does* work with Windows under VMware Fusion on a Mac, so long as you have a really fast Mac).

Definitely recommended at the price.

title: So comfy! Great sound :)
text:
I bought this for work. The headphones are *really* comfortable. I do wear glasses, so around the 2 hour mark, i have to take the headphones off and readjust. I start to feel a dull ache where my glasses meet the headphones on the side of my head.

The volume adjust and the mute on the right side are great features. My favorite feature, though, is the boom mic. It tucks between the earphone and "headband" part perfectly. It looks well protected in its place, and I can lay the headphones perfectly flat. It's also great that the mic is not obnoxiously or noticeably in front of my mouth when using it.

One review I read said that you can hear yourself in the headphones. That happened to me the first time (30 minutes) I used it. Since then, I've worked 17 hours and with fast and slow internet connects (other person, not me). I haven't heard myself in a delayed loop back since that first time. Now, it's crystal clear. I have no idea what made it loop back at first.

The cord is a little stiff- the bends from storing it during shipping have not straightened out yet. It hasn't gotten in my way, though.

I hate Windows 10. But it's on my desktop...and the headohones work with all the applications.

(Off - topic - don't be fooled by Skype Preview or whatever it is on Windows 10. It's completely worthless. Stick with traditional Skype so that you can use all the features. Chances are good that tbe person in the other side of the camera has access to traditional Skype anyway.)
